title: DJ Asia Stock Markets End Lower; Southeast Asia Slump Continues
text:
By Abhrajit Gangopadhyay, Mia Lamar and Nopparat Chaichalearmmongkol 
 

Markets across Asia slumped Tuesday, sending Indonesian stocks tumbling for a second day and the Indian rupee to a fresh record low, as the end of U.S. monetary easing draws attention to slowing growth in the region and rising debt.

The most dramatic moves were in Southeast Asia, with Indonesian stocks falling 9% over the past two days and 20% from a high in May. Thailand shed 2% Tuesday and touched its weakest this year, while the turmoil caught up Malaysia's ringgit, which hit a three-year low.

The broad selloff comes just before the release Wednesday of the Federal Reserve's June policy-meeting minutes, which may give more clues to how close the U.S. central bank is to winding down its stimulus program that has pumped the global economy full of cheap money.

Investors are fleeing emerging markets as rising Treasury yields lessen the appeal of riskier assets such as Indonesia, India and Thailand. That's left the MSCI Asia ex-Japan index down about 6% this year.

Meanwhile, signs are growing that Asia's economy is losing its shine. Thailand said this week it has entered a recession, while Indonesia reported its trade imbalance worsened with its current-account balance widening in the second quarter as the economy sputters along at its slowest pace in three years.

"There is massive outflow of funds from the emerging markets" around the world, said Choo Swee Kee, chief investment officer at TA Investment Management, who manages an equivalent of 700 million ringgit ($213 million) in Malaysian assets.

The Thai currency fell 1% to 31.74 baht per dollar, its weakest level in more than a year. Malaysia's shares fell as much as 2%, with the benchmark up just 3.5% this year compared to a 10% rally over the course of 2012.

Credit Suisse said Tuesday that pressure on Malaysia's currency is likely to remain high because of its trade imbalance and heavy ownership of the country's bonds by foreigners.

Funds have been drifting out of emerging markets and into developed markets as they are showing signs of recovery, said Komsorn Prakopphol, an analyst at Tisco Financial Group.

U.S. jobless claims are at their lowest level in nearly six years, helping push up the 10-year benchmark Treasury yield to within striking distance of 3%--a two-year high. Meanwhile Europe's economy, which has been battered over the past few years because of a debt crisis, is starting to turn up.

The selloff in Asia's emerging markets comes after a heady stretch for the region that began building in force late last year. Thailand's benchmark index, for example, gained nearly 30% between mid-November and its May high, while Indonesian shares rallied 20%.

"If there's a redeeming feature to the current selloff, it's that investors are the most concerned about the emerging markets" which are showing signs of weakness, said Nicholas Spiro, managing director of Spiro Sovereign Strategy in London. "Unfortunately, it took a sudden rise in U.S. interest rates to force investors to pay more attention to country-specific risk."

Some signs are emerging, too, that Asian governments are starting to fight back.

Traders said Malaysia's central bank was intervening in the currency markets to slow the ringgit's slide. Bank Negara Malaysia doesn't comment on market intervention but has said that when it takes actions, they are aimed only at reducing volatility in the market. The central bank will release second-quarter economic growth and balance of payment data Wednesday, with some investors worried a shrinking trade surplus will squeeze Malaysia's current-account surplus and push it into deficit territory for the first time since 1997.

India banned duty-free imports of television sets by individuals late Monday in its latest effort to narrow the country's current-account deficit, which traders blame for the rupee's slide. Still, that didn't stop the rupee's woes Tuesday, with the currency hitting a record low and stocks falling again.

Wall Street bank J.P. Morgan on Tuesday downgraded the outlook for Indian stocks to neutral--or hold--from buy, saying the falling currency had changed the calculations for India's potential growth.

Elsewhere, the Nikkei Stock Average slid 2.6%, and the yen strengthened to Y97.11 to the U.S. dollar versus Y97.57 late Monday in New York. Chinese stocks were also stuck in weak trade, with Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index down 2.2% and the mainland's Shanghai Composite Index off 0.6%.

title: Southeast Asian Stocks,  Currencies  Extend Slide
text:
Stocks and currencies fell in Southeast Asia's major markets Tuesday, reflecting concern that foreign investors and firms will be investing less in the region as they shift their focus to opportunities for better growth and returns in developed economies.

The Stock Exchange of Thailand's composite index tracked steep declines in Indonesian stock prices, slipping 2.8% to reach its lowest level in eight weeks by midday.

The selloff started Monday after the Thai government's economic planning agency reported second-quarter gross domestic product growth of only 2.8% compared with a year earlier. GDP declined 0.3% on quarter.

Funds have been perceptibly drifting out of emerging markets and into developed markets, which are showing signs of recovery, said Komsorn Prakopphol, an analyst at Tisco Financial Group.

Mr. Komsorn said that although growth potential in Asia will continue to make it "an interesting investment destination over the long term," the short-term prognosis is for the outflow of funds to continue.

Meanwhile, the Thai currency lost ground against the dollar, weakening by more than 1% Tuesday. It hit a low of 31.74 baht per dollar around 0310 GMT, its weakest level in more than a year.

Malaysia's shares fell as much as 2%, while the ringgit swooned to a fresh three-year low against the U.S. dollar. The benchmark FBM KLCI has shed 2.8% over the past five sessions to end Tuesday at 1745.42. So far this year, it has eked out a 3.5% rise compared with a 10% gain over the course of 2012.

"The weakness isn't specific to Malaysia, as there is a massive outflow of funds from emerging markets" around the world, said the chief investment officer at TA Investment Management, Choo Swee Kee, who manages the equivalent of 700 million ringgit ($213 million) in Malaysian assets.

The ringgit declined against the greenback for a seventh straight session. Investors say they are worried that a shrinking trade surplus will squeeze Malaysia's current-account surplus and possibly push it into deficit territory for the first time since 1997. Bank Negara Malaysia will release data on second-quarter economic growth and balance of payments on Wednesday.

Earlier Tuesday, Bank Negara Malaysiaintervened to rescue the currency from a sharp decline, foreign-exchange dealers said. The central bank is suspected to have sold more than a billion dollars in the spot market after the ringgit touched 3.30 to a dollar, dealers familiar with its actions said. Bank Negara Malaysia doesn't comment on interventions. It has said that when it takes actions, they are only aimed at reducing market volatility.

"At the moment, there is a lot of momentum behind the [dollar] rally, and it is hard to identify any significant changes that could reverse its direction," said Goh Khoon, a senior foreign-exchange strategist at ANZ Bank.

text:

(Ranges are calculated using recent highs and lows, information on the placement of option strikes, and technical analysis - Bollinger Bands, Fibonacci levels, trendlines and moving averages.)

USD/CNY - consolidation with downside bias. Spot USD/CNY is likely to drift back down after Monday's late spike resolved lower eventually, keeping the pair firmly within the Bollinger downtrend channel. A stable USD index likely means the PBOC USD/CNY parity rate will stay close to 6.1690. Investors are still positive on the yuan, though their expectations of the pace of appreciation have been trimmed greatly due to fear of the U.S. Federal Reserve tightening monetary stimulus. PBOC governor Zhou said Monday that there is unlikely the need for major shift in monetary policy, but that more reforms might be coming to the financial sector. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support for USD/CNY is at 6.1200 (psychological support), then at 6.1159 (base of Bollinger downtrend channel), before 6.1090 (Friday's record low). Immediate resistance is likely at 6.1237 (top of daily Bollinger downtrend channel), then at 6.1315 (20-day Bollinger mid), before 6.1393 (daily Bollinger uptrend channel).

USD/TWD - consolidation. USD/TWD is likely to remain trapped by the daily Ichimoku Cloud zone that spans 29.850-30.040. The 20-day Bollinger mid resistance line meets the Cloud top at 30.040, adding to the strength of the technical trading barrier, and will likely keep a lid on the dollar. A close proxy to the yuan - which continues to appreciate gradually - the Taiwan dollar's value is hence unlikely to erode much despite the broad rally of the greenback. Taiwan releases its July exports data as well as Balance of Payments numbers later. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support is at 29.930 (daily Bollinger downtrend channel), then at 29.850 (base of daily Ichimoku Cloud), before 29.800 (base of daily Bollinger downtrend channel). Immediate resistance is likely at 30.000 (psychological resistance), then at 30.040 (top of daily Ichimoku Cloud and 20-day Bollinger mid), before 30.180 (daily Bollinger uptrend channel).

USD/KRW - likely upside bias. The dollar gaps up significantly to 1,119.5 from a Monday closing of 1,115.6, in reaction to another rally in the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield. The USD/KRW could take on a more bullish bias if it ends Tuesday above 1,120 - where the Bollinger uptrend channel begins. From there, the greenback could go on to challenge the Ichimoku Cloud hovering nearby at 1,123. Expectations are high for the Fed to begin tapering monetary stimulus next month, and the release of the FOMC minutes tomorrow could confirm this belief. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support is at 1,116 (20-day Bollinger mid support), then at 1,112 (daily Bollinger downtrend channel), before 1,110 (psychological support). Immediate resistance is at 1,120 (psychological resistance and daily Bollinger uptrend channel), before 1,123 (daily Ichimoku Cloud resistance), before 1,124 (top of daily Bollinger uptrend channel).

USD/SGD - upside bias. USD/SGD is now well within the Bollinger uptrend channel and also above the daily Ichimoku Cloud - together creating a fairly bullish signal that could propel the pair toward its year-high of 1.2859. The greenback rallied overnight as U.S. government bonds were sold off again, sending the benchmark U.S. 10-year Treasury yield up and the dollar along with it. The rally of the U.S. dollar could intensify after Wednesday's release of the U.S. Federal Reserve's July meeting minutes - which could show the Fed leaning towards tapering in September. Dow Jones technical analysis shows immediate support is at 1.2732 (base of daily Bollinger uptrend channel), then at 1.2700 (psychological support), before 1.2691 (daily Ichimoku Cloud support). Immediate resistance is at 1.2785 (top of daily Bollinger uptrend channel), then at 1.2800 (psychological resistance), before 1.2859 (2013 high).

USD/MYR - upside bias. The daily Bollinger uptrend channel continues to pull USD/MYR upwards, potentially to the major psychological trading barrier at 3.3000. The Malaysia central bank is expected to intervene to slow the pace of ringgit depreciation, and may even attempt to draw a line in the sand near 3.3000 as the ringgit is already at a 3-year low. Confidence in the Malaysia ringgit is shaky as the market awaits the release of Balance of Payments data Wednesday, which might show the country falling into a current account deficit for the first time since 1997. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support is at 3.2730 (base of daily Bollinger uptrend channel), then at 3.2500 (psychological support), before 3.2460 (20-day Bollinger mid support). Immediate resistance is at 3.3000 (major psychological barrier), then at 3.3010 (top of daily Bollinger uptrend channel), before 3.3240 (top of weekly Bollinger uptrend channel).

USD/THB - upside bias. USD/THB has entered the Bollinger uptrend channel at 31.30 and is now on track toward the channel ceiling at 31.49, implying more baht weakness to come. The baht is under pressure not just because of broad greenback strength, but also because Thailand's GDP fell for the second quarter in a row, data released Tuesday showed, signalling a mild technical recession. The government has trimmed its forecast for full-year growth to 3.8%-4.3% from its previous estimate of 4.2%-5.2%. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support is at 31.30 (base of daily Bollinger uptrend channel), then at 31.20 (psychological support), before 31.11 (20-day Bollinger mid and Ichimoku Cloud support). Immediate resistance is at 31.49 (top of daily Bollinger uptrend channel), then at 31.50 (psychological resistance), before 31.69 (top of weekly Bollinger uptrend channel).

USD/PHP - closed.

USD/IDR - upside bias. USD/IDR may notch another 4-year high as Indonesia assets collapse under pressure from the country's slowing growth, high inflation and widening current account deficit. Stocks in Jakarta fell 5.6% Monday, and could continue Tuesday as panicked investors rush for the exit. Bank Indonesia last Thursday said the risk of slowing growth "remains significant". Southeast Asia's biggest economy expanded 5.8% in the second quarter, its slowest pace since 2010. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support for spot USD/IDR is at 10,400 (psychological support), then at 10,260 (base of daily Bollinger uptrend channel), before 10,200 (psychological support). Immediate resistance is at 10,500 (psychological resistance), before 10,540 (top of monthly Ichimoku Cloud resistance zone).

USD/INR - upside bias. The rupee could continue falling as no clear support levels are in sight because the USD/INR is in uncharted territory again. Yet another historical high of 63.22 was set Monday, a sign that the market is not convinced by the government's recent moves to buffer the currency. The rupee has been a on streak of record-setting losses this month, and the government can't seem to rein it in despite various measures to lower the current account deficit and simultaneously making it more expensive for banks to short the rupee. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support is at 63.00 (psychological support), then at 62.50 (psychological support), before 62.00 (psychological support). Immediate resistance is at 63.22 (record high), before 63.50 (psychological resistance).

title: FX  CHAT: USD/MYR Higher; May Rise Toward 3.3000
text:
Contact us in Singapore. 65 64154 140; MarketTalk@dowjones.com 
 

USD/MYR is at 3.2840 versus 3.2770, the highest since June 2010, reflecting strong investor buying interest and the greenback's strength against other regional currencies. Concern over Malaysia's slowing economic growth and firm USD bids may lift the pair toward 3.3000 in the near term, a local trader says, although he also warns that gains may be capped on possible intervention by Malaysia's central bank to prevent sharp declines in the local currency. (shie-lynn.lim@dowjones.com)

USD/TWD is higher, boosted by foreign investor buying while also reflecting the greenback's strength against regional currencies, say two local traders. The pair is at 30.032 versus 30.002 late Friday in Asia. Taiwan's central bank is suspected of buying around 29.960 to keep the pair in its target range, the traders say. They add that importers buying below 29.930 and the USD/KRW's rise to 1,115 lift the pair. The Taiwan dollar often tracks the won as South Korea is Taiwan's major export competitor. "With rising yields of U.S. Treasurys pushing down emerging market bonds and currencies, the greenback is still likely to rise further in the near term," a trader says. But the pair is unlikely to rise sharply as exporters' selling will likely intensify near 30.000, she says. The two traders tip the pair to trade in a 29.930-29.990 band Tuesday. Taiwan government bonds fall in thin volume, with the most-traded five-year bond yield at 1.1720% vs 1.1650% late Friday; a trader tips the yield to test resistance 1.2000% Tuesday. (fanny.liu@wsj.com)

as the daily Ichimoku Cloud caps 0.9241. The AUD/USD pair has turned away from an earlier probe of the Cloud resistance zone and is now lower. Failure to close above 0.9222 would also deny the upside potential that the Bollinger uptrend channel could impart to the Aussie. The presence of these two strong technical resistance levels suggests that AUD/USD could drift lower toward 0.9106, where the 20-day Bollinger mid lies. AUD/USD is now 0.9196.(ewen.chew@wsj.com)

The U.S. dollar rises to a three-year high of 3.2835 against the Malaysia ringgit as the market braces for a withdrawal of U.S. quantitative easing. The ringgit is under pressure as analysts forecast a possible 2Q current account deficit Wednesday. It may continue weakening, the daily chart suggests. The greenback is rallying in anticipation of a possibly hawkish tone in the U.S. Federal Reserve's FOMC minutes. The minutes, to be released Wednesday, could affirm conviction that the Fed will begin tapering monetary stimulus next month. USD/MYR rises toward 3.3000, along the daily Bollinger uptrend channel that now supports at 3.2700. USD/MYR is now at 3.2830. (ewen.chew@wsj.com)

0559 GMT [Nikkei/Dow Jones] Kawasaki Heavy Industries (7012.TO) is up 1.9% at Y375 following a Nikkei report that the firm will team up with Rolls-Royce (RR.LN) to develop a new type of aircraft engine that is 30% more fuel efficient than conventional jet engines. The British engine manufacturer is leading the project and is discussing the engine's commercialization with aircraft manufacturer Airbus SAS, with Kawasaki Heavy expected to develop and supply a key control component, the paper says. "The arrangement likely won't help with short-term profits for Kawasaki Heavy, but the gradual penetration of such engines in the global market should eventually help to support its share price," says an analyst at a domestic brokerage. (bradford.frischkorn@wsj.com)

0512 GMT [Dow Jones] Results from the Australian earnings period so far are supportive of the view that earnings for the market ex-resources have troughed, despite tough operating conditions in fiscal 2013, say Macquarie equities strategists. With about 1/3 of companies by market capitalization having reported, Macquarie analysts forecast aggregate EPS growth of 14.7% for all listed Australian companies, up from 13.4% last month. "While earnings growth remains weak, and the upswing in growth is uneven across the market, the tone of the results reflects the resolve to lift earnings through the increasingly intense focus on cost reductions," the strategists say in a report. They add that reports also suggest that negative momentum for resources earnings is also slowing, albeit mainly due to cost control. Mining services is now the only broad group of companies where reports suggest the balance of risks for the fiscal 2014 earnings outlook remains skewed to the downside, according to Macquarie. (david.rogers1@wsj.com)

The USD/INR hit a new all-time high of 62.45 amid ongoing expectation that the U.S. Federal Reserve will, as soon as September, reduce its monthly purchase of government bonds. The rupee has depreciated close to 12.0% this year, and with this new record low, there is little basis for suggesting where the collapse might bottom. Psychological trading barriers such as the round-number of 63.00 to the dollar might be the next most obvious support level for the rupee. There has been little respite for the Indian rupee despite a recent slew of measures to correct the chronic current account deficit while simultaneously making it more expensive for onshore banks to short the currency. The U.S. Federal Reserve looks set to withdraw monetary stimulus in a gradual manner as soon as next month, adding to dollar-bullish pressures on the USD/INR. The pair is now at 62.26.(ewen.chew@wsj.com)

0351 GMT [Dow Jones] Malaysia's economic growth likely slowed sharply in April-June period, rising 4.7% from a year earlier, according to the median forecast of 15 economists in a Dow Jones poll. This compares to the 4.1% on-year expansion in 1Q. For the full-year, economists expect 4.7% growth, slowing from 5.6% in 2012, the same survey shows. Economists say a slew of weak exports data likely hurt GDP growth in 2Q despite resilient domestic demand. "Malaysia still needs a stronger rebound in the global economy, particularly with the anticipated positive impact on commodity prices, for the economy to maintain its growth momentum," says OCBC economist Gundy Cahyadi. Separately, DBS Group says exports may improve but still remain subdued due to "overhanging uncertainties" in the global economy in 2Q. The official data is due Wednesday at 1001 GMT. (jason.ng@wsj.com)

0340 GMT [Dow Jones] The NZD/USD has drifted higher on the absence of any news and little to focus on before the release of FOMC meeting minutes late in the week, says Western Union Business Solutions Corporate Dealing Manager Chris Hunter; "It's fairly light this week. There are a lot of second-tier and third-tier releases, so the Kiwi is likely to move sideways until we see some sentiment swings." The pair is at 0.8123 versus 0.8102 early this morning. Hunter puts support for the pair at 0.8085 with resistance at 0.8166. (lucy.craymer@wsj.com)

0337 GMT [Dow Jones] Crude prices appear to be on the high side and once supply concerns ease, a correction could occur, says Lee Chen Hoay, an investment analyst at Phillip Futures. Traders remain focused on the upheaval in Egypt and the prospect of oil-supply disruptions due to its status as a major oil-transit point. title: EM ASIA  FX -Greece hopes lift Asia  FX , but  intervention  caps
text:
* Taiwan, Malaysia and Philippine c.banks spotted -dealers

 * Stock inflows lift Taiwan dlr, won

 * Rating upgrade bets support Philippine peso 

(Adds details, updates prices)

 By Jongwoo Cheon

 SINGAPORE, Feb 8 (Reuters) - Most emerging Asian currencies rose on Wednesday, driven by capital inflows and demand from offshore funds as investors remained hopeful that Greece will strike a debt restructuring deal, but local investors remained wary of further intervention by regional authorities.

 Taiwan's central bank was buying dollars to cap its currency's gains, while Malaysia's central bank may also be in the market, dealers said. This comes at a time when many emerging Asian currencies are approaching major resistance levels.

 The outlook for regional units remains firm, given improved risk appetite, and they are expected to break through resistance levels if Greece succeeds in securing a 130 billion euro ($170 billion) rescue fund, analysts and dealers said.

 Even though Greece is seen close to an agreement, its politicians have yet to accept to painful austerity measures to receive the second bailout package. They have delayed, once more, the deal deadline to Wednesday. 

 Meanwhile, Asian central banks are also likely to continue to intervene and slow the rise in their currencies to help support weakening exports, they added.

 "The strength in Asia ex-Japan (currencies) is impressive considering the state of the global economy, though momentum seems to be improving. Thus intervention is to be expected," said Sacha Tihanyi, senior currency strategist for Scotia Capital in Hong Kong.

 "I just can't get the euro zone out of my head. I think one should trade with the trend, but remain vigilant as it could turn should Greece give us negative headlines," he added.

 Most emerging Asian currencies have risen this year, thanks to resumed foreign inflows amid high liquidity and growing hopes that the euro zone's debt crisis is easing.

 TAIWAN DOLLAR

 U.S. dollar/Taiwan dollar slid on stock inflows, while Taiwan central bank and importers supported the pair, dealers said.

 The central bank's demand for the greenback was relatively small around the current levels, but many local banks were lined up to buy the pair between 29.40 and 29.45, they add.

 Foreign investors were net buyers in Taiwan stock market in the previous two sessions and market has had net inflows of T$15.7 billion ($531.24 million) so far this month until Tuesday.

 WON

 Dollar/won fell on selling by offshore funds and custodian, but its slide is limited as investors stay wary of possible intervention by South Korean FX authorities.

 The pair has a support line at 1,110, around a 200-day moving average.

 Investors are keeping an eye on demand linked to Lone Star's sale of a stake in Korea Exchange Bank (KEB) to Hana Financial Group.

 A market source said the U.S. private equity fund appears to still need to buy some $900 million.

 "Everybody is reluctant to sell dollars here. So, even though dollar/won is seen sliding more, but it would be very slow," said a foreign bank dealer in Seoul.

 Still, some dealers see low possibility of intervention as the country remains wary of inflation.

 BAHT

 Dollar/baht breached a support line at 30.80, near the 50 percent Fibonacci retracement of its July-January rise.

 The pair is expected to fall further, given improved risk appetite, dealers said.

 "A trend is very clear for Asian currencies, so market is waiting to sell (USD/THB) on rally," said a Bangkok-based dealer. 

 Dollar/baht may head to 30.67, the low of December. The next level would be 30.50, around the 61.8 percent retracement.

 PHILIPPINE PESO

 Dollar/Philippine peso fell on inflows, although the central bank was spotted buying the pair, dealer said.

 "Especially after IDR got upgraded, punters are looking to PHP to be the next," said a Singapore-based dealer, referring to Indonesia's sovereign rating upgrade last month.

 Remittance inflows are expected to put more pressure on the pair, the dealer added.

 The central bank was spotted buying the pair around 42.30 initially, but lowered the bid level to around 42.20, dealers said.

 RINGGIT

 Dollar/ringgit hit a five-month low on catch-up plays after holidays, falling to as low as 2.9950, the first time to breach the 3.0000 level since Sept 9.

 Some dealers suspected the central bank of buying dollars to defend the 3.0000 support line, around the 76.4 percent retracement level at 2.9983 of its July-October rise.

KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Malaysia's economy expanded 5.8% year-on-year in the third quarter, much faster than market expectations and accelerating from the revised second-quarter growth rate, data released Friday show.

The 14 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires had expected growth of 4.7% for the July-September period from a year earlier. During the second quarter, Malaysia's gross domestic product grew at a revised 4.3% on year.

The agriculture sector was the main contributor to on-year growth in the third quarter, the Department of Statistics said in a statement, while the mining sector was a drag.

Bank Negara Malaysia Gov. Zeti Akhtar Aziz, speaking at a press conference announcing the release of the data, said, "The risks to global economic growth increased following developments in the third quarter and it is likely that some of the impact of this will be experienced in the fourth quarter."

She also said, "Indicators show that consumption demand is likely to continue, private and public investments have gathered momentum in the third quarter and we expect it to continue in the fourth quarter."

She also said the impact of slowing external demand on Malaysia's economic growth remains to be seen. "Malaysia is a highly open economy and it will affect our external sector," she said.

In 2010, Malaysia's economy, the third-largest in Southeast Asia, grew 7.2%, reversing from the previous year's 1.7% contraction.

title: HIGHLIGHTS-Malaysia c.bank governor Q3 GDP press conference
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Following are the highlights from a press conference by Malaysia's central bank chief Zeti Akthar Aziz:

* On the Q 3 performance:

"Despite the (external) challenges, Malaysia registered third quarter growth of 5.8 percent supported by mainly stronger domestic demand, higher private sector expenditure and higher public spending."

* On prosepects for fourth quarter:

"The risk to global economic growth have increased and following developments that have taken place in the third quarter it is very likely that some of the impact of this will be experienced in the fourth quarter and this will indeed happen as Malaysia is a highly open economy."

"However we expect that our domestic economy and domestic demand will continue to sustain its growth. Indicators show that consumption demand is likely to continue and private sector investment and also public investment has gathered momentum. We saw in the first half of the year this was slow. This has gathered momentum in the third quarter and we will continue to see it in the fourth quarter."

* On whether Malaysia will see 6 pct GDP growth this year which it needs to in order to achieve developed nation status in 2020 and the country's economic transformation programme goal:

"This has already been revised in the budget to 5.0-5.5 percent and given the very recent developments in Europe, even if we have a rate of growth of 5 percent or even the high 4, 4.8 or 4.9, this will be considered very good growth in such a challenging environment."

* Is Bank Negara Malaysia considering re-establishing US dollar currency swap lines with the U.S. Federal reserve in light of the current situation:

"At this stage we don't have any plans, there's adequate dollar liquidity, and we have other arrangements within the region, other swap arrangements and we believe that for us that is sufficient."

* On outlook for growth in 2012:

"The external environment is challenging and uncertain and therefore this is why we need to make a careful assessment and monitor very closely to what extent the global developments will affect our overall economic growth and to what extent the strength of the domestic economy can offset the impact of these developments on our trade sector."

* On whether BNM will intervene in the event of sharp volatility in the ringgit currency:

"Most central banks in our region have intervened and Bank Negara Malaysia will do so in the event of excessive movements in any one day that will be destabilising to our foreign exchange market. But our intervention is entirely to smooth out these excessive volatitlity or movement in any one particular day and we do not influence the underlying trend of the excange rate."

* Elaborating on the external risk and how exactly it will affect the economy:

"The disruptions and destabilising effects are through many channels. Of course, it's through the trade channel but Europe mainly trades with itself among countries in the Eurozone rather than with other parts of the world, and therefore that is not going to be having such a significant impact. But because of the uncertainties generated by the volatility in the financial markets this is destabilising."

* On key interest rate outlook:

"At this point, out interest rate at 3.00 percent remains supportive of growth and unless there are any other significant developments that pose a major risk to our domestic growth and if there are any developments in inflation this will determine interest rate policy, but for now the current interest rate remains supportive of growth and that is important for our economy."

title: EM ASIA  FX -Ringgit, baht breach L-T support; Asia outlook weak
text:
* Ringgit, baht break through 100-week moving averages

* Intervention from Malaysia, Taiwan, Philippine spotted

* Hedge funds, real money, leveraged hit Sing dlr

(Updates prices, adds snippets)

By Jongwoo Cheon

SINGAPORE, Oct 3 (Reuters) - The Malaysian ringgit and the Thai baht breached long-term support lines on Monday, while the Taiwan dollar and the Singapore dollar hit 10-month lows, as offshore funds cut risk exposures further in Asian currencies amid increased worries about the European crisis.

Asian foreign exchange authorities including central banks of Malaysia and Taiwan were spotted selling dollars to limit falls in their currencies, dealers said.

Still, players are abandoning riskier assets and looking for opportunities to sell emerging Asian currencies as concerns over the festering debt crisis in Europe and the slackening global economy roils markets.

Unnerved investors are opting for safe haven USD-denominated assets by dumping stocks, commodities and other growth-linked currencies such as the Australian dollar .

"I will buy USD on dips unless we see really concrete measures coming out from Europe," said Kenneth Kan, head of emerging markets forex trading at Credit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank in Singapore, adding real money funds still hold short dollar/Asia exposure against their local currency fixed income and equity holdings.

On regional intervention, Kan said, "They won't be too keen to deplete their USD reserves too quickly, so USD selling intervention in general is not as easy compared to USD buying intervention for Asian central banks."

Emerging Asian currencies have been hit by strong dollar-demand in non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) from offshore institutional investors, which in the past weeks have rushed to hedge against further falls in the regional units. Some funds built up dollar-long positions against them.

In the third quarter, the Taiwan dollar suffered its largest quarterly fall against the U.S. dollar since the Asian financial crisis in 1997, according to Thomson Reuters data.

The South Korean won, too, suffered its worst quarterly loss since the third quarter of the 2008 financial crisis.

Asian components were not the only victims. Latin American currencies also suffered as Brazil's real raked up the world's worst performance in September.

The weakness in the emerging Asian currencies continued even after traders spotted dollar-selling intervention by the regional central banks.

Dealers and analysts say intervention may not be as strong as before as growth slows both inside and outside. Earlier this year, Asian central banks and governments had been seen selling dollars to contain inflation.

"I believe Asian central banks are all very happy (with their currency falls) as they will worry if their export numbers drop at some point with the euro zone's slowdown," said a senior dealer at an Asian bank in Kuala Lumpur.

Adding to worries about a slackening growth, September's factory activity in some of Asia's biggest economies slumped to levels last seen during the depths of the financial crisis.

Indonesia's inflation slowed in September but the authorities are under pressure to stabilise financial markets as outflows have increased in recent weeks.

After continuous falls in emerging Asian currencies, some dealers see possibilities of rebounds with many of them staying in technically oversold territory, albiet only for a very short term.

"The rise (in Dollar/Asian currencies) is getting a bit tired. In the short term, I will probably play from the short side with tight stops," said a European bank dealer in Singapore, adding he plans to take profit "very quickly".

"But this strategy is purely short term. Should conditions in Europe continue to deteriorate, Asia will continue to see outflows from real money."

Financial markets in China and South Korea are closed for holidays.

RINGGIT, BAHT

The ringgit and the baht broke through 100-week moving averages, indicating further falls.

The Malaysian currency weakened past 3.1560 per dollar and has room to soften more, probably to 3.2400, around the 38.2 percent Fibonacci retracement of its appreciation between March 2009 and August this year.

Malaysia's central bank was spotted selling dollars at 3.2070, dealers said.

Dollar-long positions against the ringgit were second-largest after dollar/rupee, a Reuters' poll showed last week.

The baht also weakened the average of 31.26 versus the greenback on selling by foreign banks and real money funds. It has crossed this technical level for the first time since September 2009.

The Thai currency could weaken to 32.10, the 38.2 percent retracement of its strengthening between March 2009 and November last year. It has minor support around 31.45 and 31.90.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

The Singapore dollar slid as hedge funds, real money accounts, leveraged names and interbank speculators offloaded.

KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Malaysia's economy expanded 4.6% from a year earlier in the first quarter, a slower-than-expected pace that was mainly due to a mild slowdown in the manufacturing sector, data released Wednesday show.

The 12 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires had given a median forecast of 4.8% expansion in the first quarter, matching the previous quarter's growth.

In 2010, Malaysia's economy grew 7.2%, beating an official forecast of 7.0% in a reversal from the previous year's 1.7% contraction. The government forecasts the trade-driven economy to grow between 5.0% and 6.0% this year.

Bank Negara Malaysia Gov. Zeti Akhtar Aziz, speaking at a press conference announcing the release of the data, said "In the first quarter global economic growth has continued but at a slower pace. While growth in the advanced economies has been modest, in the emerging economies economic activity has continued to be robust supported by domestic demand and augmented by stronger than expected export performance."

Malaysia's first-quarter GDP growth was "driven by strong domestic demand and improved external sector performance. Domestic demand was supported by sustained private sector spending. The external demand during the quarter was supported by sustained strong regional demand for commodities and non E&E products," Zeti added, referring to electricals and electronic goods.

"There were however some emerging risks to the global recovery which resulted in increased volatility in the global financial market during the quarter. These include the alleviated commodity prices that has resulted in higher inflation, sovereign debt conditions in several advanced economies, the disaster in Japan and its impact on the production chain across the world and the surges in capital flows to emerging economies," she said.

She, however, voiced confidence that Malaysia's "strong economic fundamentals and policy flexibility" will enable the domestic economy to perform steadily this year.

For the first quarter, she said the consumer price index rose 2.8% on an annualized basis.

title: UPDATE: Asian Shares Mostly Higher; Fed Stance Buoys Risk Appetite
text:
(Adds information, quotes, updates/adds market levels)

By Shri Navaratnam and Puja Rajeev

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian stock markets were mostly higher Thursday, while the U.S. dollar fell across the board, as the U.S. Federal Reserve's commitment to retain its ultra-easy monetary policy buoyed sentiment and drove riskier currencies up.

The ongoing earnings season also played a big hand in Tokyo, Seoul and Sydney markets.

Japan's Nikkei Stock Average was up 1.3%, Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was 0.4% higher, South Korea's Kospi Composite was off 0.1%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index tacked on 0.5% and China's Shanghai Composite was off 0.1%.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up 34 points in screen trade.

Wall Street's surge Wednesday bolstered regional sentiment, after the Federal Open Market Committee signaled the end of its controversial $600 billion bond buying program as planned, and Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke said the central bank would keep interest rates accommodative. He said there was no specific time frame to hike interest rates.

"The comments from Bernanke are very bullish for equity markets, via a weak U.S. dollar, U.S. earnings and commodity prices," said RBS Morgans investment adviser Chris MacDonald in Sydney.

The news spurred risk appetite, pushing stocks, gold and oil prices higher. Risk-sensitive currencies surged, with the euro and Asian currencies tapping multi-year highs against the U.S. dollar. Central banks in Korea, Thailand and Malaysia intervened to weaken their currencies in an effort to protect their export-led economies.

Gold bulls took a breather after earlier driving spot gold to a record high $1,530.30 a troy ounce; the yellow metal was recently fetching $1,526.90, down 40 cents from its New York settlement Wednesday. Oil prices remained bid, with June Nymex crude oil futures up 48 cents at $113.24 per barrel on Globex, off its 31-month high of $113.70 tapped in early trade.

In Tokyo, strong earnings offset concerns over grim March industrial production data.

Industrial production dropped a record 15.3% in March, but Japanese manufacturers expect their output to rise 3.9% on-month in April and increase 2.7% in May.

"The market seems to be reacting more favorably to earnings than we had anticipated (and) expectations are growing that Japan will display its underlying strength through speedy recovery efforts," said Cosmo Securities equity strategist Toshikazu Horiuchi.

Kyocera rose 2.6% after reporting strong fiscal fourth-quarter earnings and Advantest jumped 5.2% after posting a sharply narrower loss in its fiscal fourth quarter.

Sony extended its losses on news Wednesday that its online video game network had been hacked; the stock fell 3.1%.

A handful of profit warnings and a strong Australian dollar tempered gains in Sydney. The Australian dollar hit a new 29-year high of US$1.0903 in early trade, pressuring currency sensitive stocks such as Westfield Group and Bluescope Steel, which fell 0.7%, and 2.6%, respectively.

Goodman Fielder and Whitehaven were hit by profit warnings, falling 8.6% and 3.1% respectively.

In China, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index gave up morning gains. The reversal was triggered by sharp losses for the country's foreign currency denominated B shares, which were hurt by a weaker U.S. dollar and lingering concerns over China's launch of an international board.

"The B share market was designed to attract foreign investors and the international board will definitely attract many of the B share's target investors," said Duan Junfang at Dongfang Securities.

The Shanghai B Share Subindex was down 4.1%. Wuhan Iron & Steel was down 0.6% and Poly Real Estate Group fell 0.5%.

The Seoul market turned lower as investors booked profits in heavyweight technology and construction stocks. Still, a few other stocks rose on earnings-linked news.

LG Electronics tacked on 3.8%, buoyed by expectations of a firm turnaround in second-quarter earnings after the tech giant Wednesday reported an unexpected first-quarter loss. Hynix Semiconductor rose 2.5% after the world's second-largest producer of computer memory chips gave an upbeat outlook, and topped market expectations for its first quarter net profit, which fell 66% from a year earlier.

Among other markets, New Zealand's NZX-50 was 0.4% higher, Singapore's Straits Times Index gained 0.5%, Malaysia's KLCI rose 0.3%, Taiwan's Taiex fell 0.2%, Indonesian shares edged up 0.3% and Philippine shares slipped 0.5%. India's Sensex fell 0.1% and Thailand's SET was flat.

The U.S. dollar continued to suffer against its major rivals after slipping sharply on Wednesday. Emmanuel Ng, currency economist at OCBC Bank, said: "Dollar weakness is looking pervasive, while risk appetite remains strong."

The single currency is at $1.4862 against the dollar, its highest level since December 2009, from $1.4788 late in New York on Wednesday. It was at Y121.59 against the yen, from Y121.44. The dollar was buying Y81.81, compared with Y82.17.

Taking advantage of the greenback's woes, Asian currencies soared. In addition to the Australian dollar's fresh 29-year highs, the Singapore dollar hit a record S$1.2276 high against the US dollar and the Korean won rocketed to a fresh 32-month high at KRW1,071.90.

Japanese government bond futures were up 0.05 at 139.99 points, after the Bank of Japan left its unsecured overnight call loan rate target unchanged in a range of 0.0%-0.1%, as expected, and finalized a lending facility to help sustain money flow following the March 11 earthquake.

title: DJ Asia Central Banks  Intervene  Again As Asian  Currencies  Climb
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Central banks in South Korea, Thailand and Malaysia intervened Wednesday to slow a surge in their currencies in a broad Asian rally that carried the Singapore and Australian dollars to fresh highs against the U.S. currency.

The People's Bank of China's decision to fix the yuan at a fresh high record against the U.S. dollar added to bullish views on Asian currencies, which have been trending upward as central banks around the region tighten monetary policies to fight rising inflation.

The Asian currency rally Wednesday appeared to be driven by a rebound in risk-taking sentiment. Recovering from temporary misgivings about U.S. fiscal health following Standard & Poor's rating warning, investors warmed to risk again, pumping more money into Asia's fast-growing economies.

Wai Ho Leong, senior regional economist at Barclay's Capital, said improved risk appetite and also continued high oil prices are some of the factors influencing Asian currencies' move higher. High commodity prices "give policymakers the willingness to tolerate a stronger currency" as a check on inflation, he said.

Many Asian countries have intervened in recent months to stem a decline in the U.S. dollar, which could hurt their export industries. The foreign exchange interventions by the Korean, Thai and Malaysian authorities Wednesday appeared to be aimed at tempering gains in the won, baht and ringgit rather than an effort to stop the upward trend in those currencies.

The Australian dollar reached a new post-float high against the U.S. dollar, fetching US$1.0611 before easing back to $1.0602. Its climb was in part driven by a Dow Jones Newswires report that Australia is weighing a tax break on passive investments by sovereign funds.

The Singapore dollar also notched record highs, as the greenback fell to S$1.2400. The Singapore currency's nearly year-long rally gained momentum last week when the island's central bank revalued the currency and pledged to continue to guide it higher to curb rising inflation.

The PBOC, which tightly controls the yuan, fixed the dollar's exchange rate at CNY6.5294, down from Tuesday's fixing of CNY6.5346 and close of CNY6.5305 in the over-the-counter market. Traders said they expect the PBOC to let the yuan rise further ahead of a May 24-25 U.S.-China strategic economic dialogue in Beijing, since China has a record of yuan strengthening ahead of such international events.

The Bank of Korea likely bought about $500 million Wednesday in an effort to curb the won's ascent, traders said. The dollar dipped to KRW1,082.00 before ticking up to KRW1,082.20 late in Asian trade.

Against the Malaysian ringgit, the U.S. dollar fell to MYR3.0160, its lowest level since September 1997. That was down from MYR3.0230 at Tuesday's close. The ringgit rebounded somewhat on buying by Bank Negara Malaysia, traders in Kuala Lumpur said. The dollar was last at MYR3.0155, with the central bank suspected of more buying at that level.

Further gains could be in store for the ringgit, as it has lagged recently against regional peers like the Singapore dollar, which it tends to track closely. Continued high oil prices will support the ringgit, as will expectations of a rate hike at Bank Negara's next policy meeting, set for May 5.

The Bank of Thailand was suspected of buying dollars as the baht gained ahead of a monetary policy meeting at which the central bank raised interest rates by 25 basis points--as expected--and said interest rates remain on an upward trend. The action helped keep the dollar supported at THB30.02, traders said.

title: DJ US Dollar To Remain Pressured Despite Singapore  Currency  Move
text:
-- Asian central banks unlikely to end dollar recycling

-- Singapore's currency move not likely to herald regional shift in policy

-- U.S. dollar set to remain under pressure By Siva Sithraputhran Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

LONDON (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar is set to remain under pressure over the long term because most Asian central banks are seen as being unlikely to slow the pace of greenback sales, even after Singapore signaled that it might do just that.

Asian central banks typically buy the dollar against local currencies to slow any export-denting bouts of strength, but then churn the dollars into euros, Australian dollars, and other currencies to spread the risks, so the greenback falls. This 'recycling' of reserves has been at the heart of the dollar's weakness against a range of currencies--including the euro--over recent years.

That relationship came under scrutiny Thursday after the Monetary Authority of Singapore opened up to more currency strength by raising the trading band of the Singapore dollar, initially boosting the currency to a record high against the greenback and dragging other Asian currencies higher with it. Tellingly though, the immediate reaction from Singapore's closest neighbor, Malaysia, was to intervene in the market to stem the rise of its currency--the ringgit--indicating that there is still lot of resistance to allow local currency gains.

Recycling quickly kicked in, and the U.S. dollar plunged, sinking fast against the euro, the Australian dollar, and other major currencies.

Valentin Marinov, a strategist at Citigroup in London, remains of the opinion that emerging-market currencies will be allowed to rise only gradually, maintaining that pressure on the dollar.

'This set-up could be particularly damaging for the dollar against its liquid alternatives in the G-10 world,' he said. 'We think this should continue to generate sufficient upside momentum for the euro and Australian dollar against the greenback,' he added.

Over the past few months, there have been waves of interventions by the central banks of South Korea, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia to arrest the rises of their respective currencies. By keeping their currencies from rising too fast, the central banks want to make sure their exports don't lose competitiveness.

'There is no monetary coordination in Asia, with most policymakers running mercantilist-type policies that favor their own exports via undervalued exchange rates,' Win Thin, New York-based strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman said.

Singapore has been 'more open to currency appreciation in [a] controlled way' than some regional competitors, said Ken Dickson, investment director at Standard Life Investments in Edinburgh, which manages GBP143 billion in assets worldwide.

To some extent, China too has been allowing its currency to rise very gradually as it tries to rein in inflation.

The amount of currency reserves held by Asian central banks has continued to mount, suggesting that the wider market impact of any region-wide change in policy could be huge, even if only a fraction of these reserves are moved in or out of dollars.

At the end of March, China's foreign exchange reserves surged to a record, topping $3 trillion. In Singapore, reserves have been climbing steadily since November, to reach just over $233 billion in March. That indicates that the central banks have been carrying out smoothing operations to keep their currencies within the required trading bands. Data for April will be eagerly awaited for signs that the pace of gains has moderated.

Singapore's move last week means it will be able to trim these smoothing operations, said Dickson at Standard Life.

But as other regional central banks are still loathe to let their currencies rise, the impact of Singapore's action on the U.S. dollar looks set to be drowned out. -By Siva Sithraputhran, Dow Jones Newswires; 44-20-7842-9462; siva.sithraputhran@dowjones.com.

title: 2nd UPDATE: Singapore Tightens Monetary Policy To Fight Inflation As GDP Growth Surges
text:
-- Singapore's central bank tightens monetary policy

-- MAS raises Singapore dollar trading band, leaves slope and width of the band unchanged

-- Government reports GDP growth surged to an annualized pace of 23.5% on quarter from 3.9% in the previous quarter

-- Singapore dollar jumps to fresh record high vs U.S. currency

-- Malaysia ringgit surges, inviting intervention by the Malaysian central bank

(Adds economist comments in paragraphs four and five, Malaysia ringgit reaction in paragraph 11.)

By P.R. Venkat and Gaurav Raghuvanshi

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Singapore tightened its monetary policy Thursday as it posted a sharp acceleration in economic growth for the first quarter, intensifying its fight against inflationary pressures that have continued to build on high global commodities prices.

The central bank's decision to strengthen the Singapore dollar, its main monetary policy lever, sent the currency to a record high against the U.S. dollar, and marked the latest effort by authorities in Asia to try to curb rising consumer prices that have clouded the region's economic outlook.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore's move wasn't as aggressive as its two decisions last year to tighten policy, which set the Singapore dollar on an upward course. But it reflected concern about a surge in inflation, which hit 5.2% in the first two months of the year, and the upside risks from high oil prices and reduced slack in the booming domestic economy.

"It would have been hard for the MAS to ignore the extraordinarily strong first quarter growth number," said Robert Prior-Wandesforde, an economist at Credit Suisse.

"After the latest tightening move, we believe that the MAS will become gradually more relaxed about inflation, which we believe is likely to have peaked. With rising oil prices likely to have an impact (on growth) and the Japan crisis perhaps a bigger issue than most people expect, we doubt the MAS will tighten further in October," he said. But he added: "it's still early days" to think about the October review.

Singapore's economy, a bellwether for the regional economy, grew at an annualized pace of 23.5% in January-March from the previous quarter, accelerating from a 3.9% expansion in the last quarter of 2010 after adjustment for seasonal factors, the Ministry of Trade and Industry said.

The expansion in gross domestic product was much faster than expected by market participants, beating all 11 analyst estimates in a Dow Jones Newswires poll. The median forecast in the poll was for a 12.4% expansion.

The MAS raised its trading band for the Singapore dollar and left the width and the slope of the band unchanged. It recentered the band below the level of the Singapore dollar's nominal effective exchange rate that prevailed before the announcement, a move it said that took into account its policy moves last year.

"This policy will ensure price stability in the medium term while keeping growth on a sustainable path," the central bank said in a statement.

The Singapore dollar rose sharply on the news, surging to a new record against the U.S. dollar. The U.S. currency was quoted as low as S$1.2453 immediately after the announcement, down from S$1.2535 earlier in the morning. At 0420 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at S$1.2491.

The Malaysian ringgit, which closely tracks the Singapore dollar, surged after the MAS decision, prompting Malaysia's central bank intervene to support the U.S. dollar, traders said. The U.S. currency was quoted as low as MYR3.0180 moments after the MAS announcement, though it later recovered to around MYR3.0220.

The MAS has been targeting a "modest and gradual appreciation" of the Singapore dollar against its undisclosed traded-weighted basket of currencies since April last year. Analysts estimate Thursday's move revalued the Singapore dollar by about 1.5% and keeps it on an upward trajectory.

ANZ Bank expects the U.S. dollar to fall to S$1.23 in about a month. DBS forecasts the U.S. currency will reach that level by the end of June. Barclays Capital expects it may take the rest of the year for the U.S. currency to fall that far but said there is risk the slide may be faster.

The MAS guides the local currency within an undisclosed, trade-weighted band, using the exchange rate rather than interest rates as its monetary-policy tool because foreign trade dwarfs domestic demand in island's nearly US$225 billion economy.

Eleven of 14 economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires ahead of the MAS announcement said they expected some form of tightening involving a stronger local currency. Eight of those predicted the MAS would recenter the midpoint of the trading band. Three expected the central bank to hold policy steady.

The move by Singapore comes amid an effort by global central banks to head off inflation, which has been fueled by higher prices of oil and commodities. In Asia, most central banks are well into tightening cycles, with many widely expected to hike interest rates further in coming months. Earlier this month, China raised its interest rates for a fourth time in six months. The European Central Bank last Thursday hiked rates for the first time since 2008.

The MAS said economic activity in Singapore will likely remain high for the rest of the year, though underlying growth momentum will moderate. It warned that cost and price pressures will remain firm and predicted global oil and food prices will remain high.

The central bank said it expects CPI inflation be at the upper half of its 3%-4% forecast this year, while core inflation will be 2%-3%. Headline inflation will likely remain elevated and moderate only gradually to around 3% by fourth quarter of the year, it said.

The MAS, which sets its monetary policy twice a year, tightened at both meetings last year to counter a pickup in inflation as the economy staged a sharp recovery from the global financial crisis. Last April, the MAS re-centered its policy band at a higher level and shifted to its stance of targeting a "modest and gradual appreciation" of the local dollar from zero appreciation. In October, it retained the same language but increased the slope and width of its exchange rate policy band.

DBS Bank said robust sequential growth in GDP suggests that underlying momentum has remained fairly robust despite some near term growth concerns.

The data "further reinforced our long held view that overall GDP growth for this year will remain strong and will most likely exceed the official forecast range of 4-6%," DBS Bank said, adding it expects Singapore's economy to expand 7.0% this year.

"The dollar's slide is losing steam as it's already oversold," says a dealer. Three dealers say Bank Indonesia was suspected of buying around $50 million at the 8,650 level to slow the pair's fall. "The market is somewhat overbought with the recent rally that took the index close to its all-time high, so some consolidation is expected." He tips immediate support at 1545, followed by 1537, the 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the recent 1474 low to the 1576 record high; the Monday high of 1565.04 will likely act as strong resistance. There is plenty for the market to think about, but its coming further down the line." Fed hawk Bullard's comments that he will push for a $100 billion cut in the quantitative easing program are outweighed by Bernanke's commitment on seeing the program through. "The FOMC minutes at the end of the month will be crucial, but there's nothing like that to focus on near-term, except the ECB," the trader adds. 10-year Treasury yields are flat at 3.48% and the June contract is up 0.05 at 118-250. (mark.brown@dowjones.com)

0853 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/PHP hit a 5-month low late Wednesday, weighed by equity-related inflows, remittances from overseas Filipino workers, and also as the EUR advances against the USD. "The central bank surprisingly allowed the dollar/peso to breach the 43.25 major support, so we're expecting further downside tomorrow," says a local bank trader. He tips next support at 42.90 with resistance at 43.25. (rhea.sandique-carlos@dowjones.com)

0845 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/INR is down, but off the nearly six-month low touched earlier in the session, on custodial flows, says a senior dealer with a foreign bank. The pair is at 44.23 after falling as low as 44.175, last touched on Oct. 18, compared with 44.43 late Tuesday. "Apart from the flows, the euro and Asian currencies, like the Korean won, have strengthened, which is helping the INR. Though 44.18-44.20 levels are presenting a good buying opportunity for oil-importing companies," he says. He expects the pair in a broad range of 44.15-44.30 for the rest of the session. (nupur.acharya@dowjones.com)

0841 GMT [Dow Jones] Before its Swiss CPI-fueled collapse early Wednesday, the future looked bright for EUR/CHF. Commerzbank analyst Karen Jones says with the cross breaching its 200-day MA at 1.3145 and also overcoming the 1.3205 February high, a close below here Wednesday evening in Europe, would set the rate up for a move toward the 1.3445 Fibonacci level. However after Swiss March CPI came in at double the 0.5% forecast, EUR/CHF plummeted to 1.3096 from around 1.3220. It now trades at 1.31073. Jones pegs support at 1.3045 ahead of 1.30 and 1.2965 and still favors the upside while the cross trades above 1.2920. (gary.stride@dowjones.com)

0841 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/MYR is a tad lower at 3.0240 vs late Tuesday's level of 3.0250; two traders say Bank Negara Malaysia was suspected of intervening in the market at both the 3.0240 and 3.0250 levels. Our currency has been tracking the Singapore dollar and will likely continue doing that." He tips a 3.0240-3.0300 range for Thursday, with a 2-month target of 3.0150.(ankur.relia@dowjones.com)

title: Asia Central Banks  Intervene  Again As Risk Appetite Boosts Local  FX
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--Central banks in South Korea, Malaysia and Indonesia appeared to intervene in the foreign-exchange market Monday, continuing the fight to slow the rise in their currencies as better risk appetite bolsters purchases of the region's assets.

Big trade surpluses, world-beating economic growth and low interest rates in the U.S. and Europe have pushed a wall of capital into Asia-Pacific economies, driving up currencies to levels that worry the authorities in many export-reliant economies.

Several central banks have responded in recent weeks by selling their currencies for dollars in a bid to tame the rises and keep their economies competitive with those of their neighbors. They're looking over their shoulders at China, where a tightly contained rise in the yuan is putting other Asian exporters at a competitive disadvantage.

Beijing has let the yuan rise 4.4% against the dollar since unpegging the local currency from the greenback in mid-July. In the same period, the Korean won has climbed 11.4%, the Malaysian ringgit 7.8% and the Indonesian rupiah 5.6%.

Most recently, South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand were spotted intervening Thursday, while banks thought to be agents of the Monetary Authority of Singapore have also recently been seen selling the local dollar.

On Monday the Bank of Korea sought to weaken the won at a 30-month high, Seoul traders said, estimating the bank bought $500 million around KRW1,085. The intervention helped lift the dollar to KRW1,086.60 late in the session, but that was still down from late Friday's KRW1,091.10.

"It's like the authorities' warning sign" to keep the dollar well above the KRW1,080 support, said a trader at a local bank trader.

The head of the BOK's currency-market team declined comment.

Seoul looks set to dig in. The government has notified several asset-management firms that it is withdrawing some of the funds it had placed with them, apparently to fund more dollar-buying intervention, the Korea Economic Daily said Monday, estimating the total at KRW2 trillion.

But the central bank and Finance Ministry, like their counterparts elsewhere in Asia, aren't trying to turn the tide in the region's currencies, just slow their advance.

"The weakness of the dollar against the other currencies, except the yen, is the main reason for the won's recent strength," said Byeon Ji-young, a currency analyst at Woori Futures. Unless Seoul shares pull back strongly or risk aversion returns and scares global investors off Asian assets, she said, "Players will likely continue to place short orders on the dollar."

Similarly, Bank Indonesia appeared to sell the rupiah, buying an estimated $50 million at IDR8,675. But the dollar still fell to IDR8,665 late in the day, vs IDR8,690 late Friday.

"The central bank didn't go all out in defending" the initial level, said a local trader. Aldian Taloputra, an economist at Mandiri Sekuritas, expects the dollar to fall to IDR8,600 by the end of the year.

Indeed, the central bank confirmed it's not trying to halt the rupiah's rising trend.

"We still see room for further appreciation of the rupiah," Bank Indonesia Deputy Gov. Budi Mulya told reporters. "The rupiah appreciation is still in line with our fundamentals. Besides that, all currencies in the region are in a strengthening trend, so it's a question of how authorities can maintain stability of their currencies."

The Malaysian central bank appeared to combat the ringgit's surge, buying dollars at MYR3.0250, traders said. The dollar was around that level late in the day, below Friday's MYR3.0255.

-By Jieun Shin, Dow Jones Newswires; 822-3700-1905; jieun.shin@dowjones.com

(Kanga Kong in Seoul, and I Made Sentana, Andreas Ismar and Farida Husna in Jakarta contributed to this item.) [ 04-04-11 1113GMT ]

title: UPDATE: Asia Central Banks  Intervene  As US, France Press China On Yuan
text:
-- South Korea, Malaysia, Thailand intervene to curb gains in their currencies

-- China sets yuan at a record-high against the dollar

-- U.S and France press China to let yuan rise

(Adds Thailand's intervention in the lead and paragraph 11, Korea intervention size in paragraph 4, comments by Korea finance ministry official in paragraphs 5-6, updates forex quotes.)


 
   By Arran Scott and Jieun Shin 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand were seen intervening to slow the rise of their currencies Thursday, as China set the yuan at a record-high while the U.S. and France called for more exchange-rate flexibility--code for wanting Beijing to let its currency rise faster.

The developments highlighted both the reservations in Asian nations about the speed of their currencies' rise and the urgency felt in the U.S. and Europe, where governments argue a stronger yuan is essential to reducing trade imbalances that threaten global economic stability.

Asia's large trade surpluses, a major source of economic growth for the region, has put strong pressure on the local currencies to rise, which authorities have resisted by selling their currencies in foreign-exchange markets. The trade surplus of China, now the world's second-biggest economy, has soared while the U.S. has run a persistent deficit, an imbalance Washington blames in part on an artificially weak Chinese currency.

The Bank of Korea apparently bought $1 billion for won, Seoul-based traders said, citing dollar purchases near KRW1,100 in early trading and additional buy orders at KRW1,095 in the afternoon. It was the first time since March 25 that the BOK was seen intervening.

Korea's Finance Ministry, which sets the country's foreign exchange policy, is closely watching the won and will counter any one-sided moves but isn't targeting a particular level, said Kim Ik-joo, director general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau.

"Capital is flowing into the local financial system with foreigners buying a lot of local shares as they focus more on positive factors. We are closely monitoring the currency market to make sure there aren't any rapid one-sided moves," Kim said.

The dollar ended trading at KRW1,096.7, down from KRW1,104.20 late Wednesday.

Bank Negara Malaysia, similarly, sold ringgit to slow its rise, two Kuala Lumpur dealers said, spotting dollar purchases by the central bank at MYR3.0250. The U.S. currency was at MYR3.0250 in late Asian trade, down from MYR3.0255 late Wednesday.

In Singapore, some traders said there was speculation that the central bank had been in the market, but intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore couldn't immediately be confirmed.

Dealers said banks known to be MAS agents bought U.S. dollars around S$1.2617 in the morning. But the Singapore dollar faced strong upward pressure throughout the trading session, with the U.S. currency falling to a record low of S$1.2592 late in the afternoon, down from S$1.2622 late Wednesday.

Thailand's central bank was suspected of buying $100 million to $200 million around THB30.24-THB30.27, traders said. The U.S. currency was last at THB30.25.

A record-high fixing for the yuan in the morning set a bullish tone for Asian currencies. The People's Bank of China set its dollar parity at CNY6.5564, the lowest ever and down from Wednesday's fixing of CNY6.5586.

The yuan, which ended trading at CNY6.5485 to the dollar in the onshore spot market, has risen 4.2% against since June, when China effectively ended its two-year currency peg and vowed to make the yuan more flexible. Other Asian central banks watch Beijing closely, and to varying degrees have also allowed their currencies to rise against the dollar.

China appeared to be under renewed pressure Thursday to move faster on the currency front at an informal meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of 20 industrial and developing nations held in the former Chinese capital of Nanjing.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner, in prepared remarks at the meeting, argued forcefully for flexible exchange rates, calling the mismatch between fixed and floating exchange rates "the most important problem to solve in the international monetary system today."

"This asymmetry in exchange rate policies creates a lot of tension," Geithner said. "It magnifies upward pressure on those emerging market exchange rates that are allowed to move and where capital accounts are much more open. It intensifies inflation risk in those emerging economies with undervalued exchange rates. And, finally, it generates protectionist pressures."

Geithner didn't mention the yuan in his prepared remarks, but there is little doubt his message was aimed at least in part at China.

French President Nicolas Sarkozy said the global currency system in its current form has fueled growing global imbalances. The world needs to move toward a more flexible exchange rate regime, he said.

China Vice Premier Wang Qishan said Beijing will work with others toward "a more equitable global monetary system" but avoided any reference to the yuan's exchange rate.

-By Arran Scott, Dow Jones Newswires; +65-6415-4042; arran.scott@dowjones.com

title: EM ASIA  FX -Won leads other Asian  currencies  higher as Q1 ends
text:
* Won breaks through 1,100 on exporters, stop-loss dlr sales

* Intervention from S.Korea, Taiwan, Malaysia, Singapore spotted

* Some dealers cautious about near-term correction

(Updates with text, prices)

SINGAPORE, March 31 (Reuters) - The South Korean won rose to a 2-1/2-year high on Thursday, leading other emerging Asian currencies higher, on the back of sustained inflows into the Seoul stock market which will probably spell further gains for the won in the coming quarter.

The won was the biggest gainer among regional currencies in the first three months of the year, advancing 3.6 percent against the dollar, followed by the Indonesian rupiah and the Taiwan dollar.

The dollar's tumble below 1,100 won late in the session spilled over to other currencies such as the Thai baht and Singapore dollar, causing foreign exchange authorities in South Korea, Taiwan and Malaysia to intervene to slow their currencies' gains, dealers said.

Regional currencies are expected to strengthen further in the second quarter, with foreign equity flows to the region rebounding after a selloff earlier in March following a massive earthquake and tsunami in Japan.

"Fears about monetary tightening and inflation risks in the region appear to be easing, with the growth outlook in the region remaining robust," said Mitul Kotecha, head of global FX strategy at Credit Agricole in Hong Kong.

"We look for a soft landing for China's economy, which should also help the positive momentum for capital flows and in turn Asian currencies."

In the near term, though, the recent rallies in some Asian currencies may result in corrective moves lower, some analysts and dealers said.

The won's gains have been bolstered by a 12-day long Korean equity buying spree by foreign investors -- the longest streak since October 2010.

"A correction (in emerging Asian currencies) is possible. I think the recent gains are very over stretched. The whole world is too comfortable with short USD/Asia," a Kuala Lumpur-based dealer said.

In local trade, the dollar/won's 14-day relative strength index fell to 31.548, the lowest since Oct. 2010, indicating the dollar is approaching oversold territory against the won.

The RSI for the rupiah, the second-best performer in the first quarter, has been under 30 since early February.

RUPIAH

One-year dollar/rupiah non-deliverable forwards (NDF)

slid to 9,080, its weakest since June 2007 as speculative investors bet on the rupiah's further appreciation.

"Indonesia's growth will attract more FDI inflows and also possible upgrades of its sovereign rating," said a Jakarta-based dealer, citing reasons for the rupiah's climb.

In the spot market, the rupiah , which had earlier suffered from dollar-short covering, tested 8,700, beyond which would be the strongest since May 2007.

The rupiah may appreciate further in the medium term as the central bank is expected to allow more gains in the currency to fight inflation, and on foreign investors' appetite for the country's bonds.

Foreign ownership of Indonesian government bonds stood at 31.25 percent as of Tuesday.

TAIWAN DOLLAR

The Taiwan dollar rose as exporters bought it for settlements, but its gains were capped as the central bank was spotted buying dollars, especially around T$29.45 and T$29.55, dealers said.

Market players also stayed cautious ahead of the central bank's rate-setting meeting later in the day where it is widely expected to raise interest rates by 12.5 basis points to 1.75 percent.

The currency is expected to maintain its momentum into the second quarter thanks to hopes of growing foreign fund inflows, dealers in Taipei said.

PESO

The peso started local trade at 43.35 per dollar but cut some gains as local banks sold the Philippine currency on behalf of domestic companies.

The peso's support line of 43.50 was no challenged amidst current risk on sentiment. A bullish euro and Australian dollar also provide support the peso.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

The Singapore dollar hit a fresh record high of 1.2590 per dollar on broad weakness in the U.S. dollar and as the firmer won caused investors to keep chasing the Singapore currency.

But Singapore's central bank was spotted buying the greenback to check the currency's gains.
