title: MARKET TALK: China Shares Biased Down; Shanghai Support At 2850
text:
Contact us in Singapore. 65 64154 140; MarketTalk@dowjones.com 
 
 

0104 GMT [Dow Jones] China shares are likely to consolidate with a downward bias amid uncertainty surrounding Japanese nuclear crisis, while investors continue to fret about the impact of Japan's earthquake on China's economy. The benchmark Shanghai Composite Index is expected to consolidate below 2900 after ending down 1.1% at 2897.30 Thursday, analysts say; they put support at 2850. "The scale of Japan's radiation leak is more serious than people had expected" and worries about the Japanese earthquake consequences are still containing the market sentiment, says Shenyin Wanguo analyst Li Xiaoxuan. Also, China's still-high inflation, rising funding costs and a potentially sharp increase in the supply of new shares will also weigh on the domestic stock market, she adds. The Shenzhen Index fell 1.8% to 1284.96. (rose.yu@dowjones.com)

0103 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/PHP may fall as local stocks are expected to rise following Wall Street's advance overnight, while the EUR/USD rises to $1.4000, supporting risk-sensitive Asian currencies. The pair may slide to 43.80 after settling at a seven-week high at 43.92 in late Asian trade Thursday. Traders peg support at 43.70 and resistance at 44. "I think the dollar will be rangebound today. The central bank will likely intervene if the dollar rises to PHP44.00, while banks should start buying the dollar when it slides below 43.80," says a local bank trader. (cris.larano@dowjones.com)

0103 GMT [Dow Jones] Volatility hits the USD/SGD, in line with other regional currencies, on G-7 announcement of joint intervention to force down the yen. But the news overall should be SGD positive, with a trader at a local bank tipping support for the USD/SGD at 1.2650. The risk-on sentiment brought by the G-7 cooperation might bring the carry trade back into Asian currencies, which had slowed as the yen soared, adds the trader; "this should keep the dollar down." The UN security council resolution on airstrikes against Libya adds some risk of oil price shocks, but for the moment this effect is more than outweighed by the yen returning to more normal levels. The pair drops to 1.2753 at 0025 GMT, shortly after the G-7 announcement, and is last trading at 1.2764. The trader eyes resistance at 1.2850. (martin.vaughan@dowjones.com)

0059 GMT [Dow Jones] The AUD/JPY and NZD/JPY gain strongly as the G-7 announces coordinated FX intervention to support the USD against the JPY but volatility continues as people closely watch Japan and Libya, says ANZ Foreign Exchange Manager Murray Hindley. "The joint intervention talk is the reason why these things have rallied and things would suggest they have finished on the downside but it is a $54,000 question," he says. He says markets will be focused on the nuclear situation in Japan and the events unfolding in Libya, "plus we have a Tokyo holiday on Monday that actually might slow things down, or could make the markets even more volatile because of a lack of liquidity." The AUD/JPY is at 80.15 vs 78.025 prior to the announcement and the NZD/JPY is at 58.675 vs 57.305.(rebecca.howard@dowjones.com)

0057 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/MYR is down at 3.0450 from 3.0530 late Thursday in line with regional markets on the G-7 announcement of joint intervention to pare down yen strength. A local trader says the pair is likely to head lower as risk sentiment returns to the market with the yen likely to return to more comfortable levels. He tips support at 3.0400, and says Bank Negara Malaysia is not likely to intervene at these levels. (ankur.relia@dowjones.com)

0057 GMT [Dow Jones] Group of Seven (G-7)'s agreement on joint foreign currency exchange market intervention will likely provide support for the Nikkei in coming sessions after the index suffered in the wake of last Friday's massive earthquake and tsunami, says Hideyuki Ishiguro, investment strategy supervisor at Okasan Securities. The Nikkei is up 2.8% at 9212.13. "The joint intervention shows authorities overseas are also taking the situation in Japan seriously," he says. "The downside risk in the global economy remains on higher crude prices; the G-7 wants Japan to avoid a setback." A report that the Japanese government is planning to issue more than Y10 trillion in earthquake reconstruction bonds (to be bought in full by the Bank of Japan) would, if true, also be supportive of Japan share prices, Ishiguro says. (kosaku.narioka@dowjones.com)

0052 GMT [Dow Jones] The KLCI is expected to open higher, with Wall Street's rebound overnight and stronger Japanese stocks lending support, a local dealer says. Still, he thinks the upside is likely to be limited as investors continue to fret over the impact of Japan earthquake on the global economy and the rising tensions in the Middle East. "Many investors may want to stay away from the market, especially with the weekend approaching, as there are still many unresolved issues outside the country." He tips immediate resistance at 1500, with support at 1474. The KLCI closed 0.35 points lower at 1492.09 Thursday. UMW (4588.KU) may rise after its unit gets a $41.5 million Petronas Carigali contract. (ankur.relia@dowjones.com)

0049 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/TWD is biased down as local shares are likely to rebound following Wall Street's rise overnight, says a local trader. She adds, although the USD/JPY is rising sharply on G-7's joint intervention, the pair is unlikely to follow suit. "Many traders shifted their focus to trade the U.S. dollar against the yen yesterday because they thought it was unlikely to make much profits on trading the U.S. dollar against the New Taiwan dollar," she says. She tips the pair to trade in a 29.450-29.550 band for the day; the pair was at 29.5740 in late Asian trade Thursday. Taiwan shares ended down 0.5% at 8282.69 Thursday; foreign investors were net sellers of NT$9.41 billion worth of local shares. (fanny.liu@dowjones.com)

0049 GMT [Dow Jones] Singapore shares are likely to open higher after a positive session on Wall Street, though ongoing caution amid Japan's woes could limit gains. "Wall Street was green on St. Patrick's Day, so we'll probably get a technical rebound. On the charts, the STI index seems to be sitting on the lower Bollinger Band, so that actually sets the index up for a nice rebound today," says an analyst at a local brokerage. On Thursday, the STI ends down 0.9% at 2942.88. "We'll be watching to see if things continue to be rosy, and there's no more worrying news from Japan; then we may see the index try to fill the gap at 3009 to 3020. However, we also have to note that there may not be very big bargain hunting because the market is still not oversold, that's the danger." All eyes will be on Hutchison Port Holdings Trust (NS8U.SG), which makes its debut this afternoon, after it completed Southeast Asia's biggest ever IPO. (matthew.allen@dowjones.com)

0048 GMT [Dow Jones] The Kospi is up 0.6% at 1971.11 following U.S. stocks gains overnight. Some market fears over damages at the troubled Fukushima Daiichi nuclear-power plants in Japan seem to be easing, analysts say; "the situation in Japan is bad, but there are also hopes that it doesn't get to the worst-case scenario," says Shinhan Investment analyst Lee Sun-yeop. But, he adds, trade could become choppy later due to end-week profit-taking as uncertainties from Japan still remain in the news. He tips a 1975 resistance for the index. Shipbuilders lead gains on continued hopes for more orders with Hyundai Heavy Industries (009540.SE) up 0.7% at KRW474,000 and Samsung Heavy Industries (010140.SE) up 1.3% at KRW37,950. Oil refiners are also up on earnings hopes amid growing refining margins recently; SK Innovation (096770.SE) is up 4.3% at KRW216,500 and S-Oil Corp (010950.SE) rises 1.8% to KRW142,000. (jieun.shin@dowjones.com)

0046 GMT [Dow Jones] February 2012 gold futures on Tocom jump 3.9% from its 0400 GMT close and the contract is trading at Y3,701/gram, roughly $1,415/oz, with volumes at their highest level in 10 months; 106,834 contracts, equivalent to 106.8 tons, changed hands so far. Move matches the USD/JPY's sharp rise; the pair is up 2.3% since 0000 GMT at 81.363. A Tokyo-based trader sees local investors re-entering long positions in gold following recent liquidation on hopes that emergency G7 meeting will lead to weakening of the local currency: "I think investors are looking to that and coming back to precious metal futures in expectation of action." Spot gold is at $1,410.60/oz, up 0.6% since its informal open of $1,402.79/oz at 2200 GMT.(david.fickling@dowjones.com)

0045 GMT [Dow Jones] Malaysia government bonds may fall a tad, taking cues from U.S. Treasurys overnight after the fears over radiation leaks from Japan's damaged nuclear plants eased a little, a local trader says. But he adds the market is likely to be subdued on Friday, as investors may want to stay on the sidelines heading into the weekend. He tips yields on MGS to rise 1-2 bps. On Thursday, the yield on the August 2014 MGS ends at 3.36%, the September 2016 MGS yield ends at 3.53%, the yield on the September 2017 MGS ends at 3.70% and the July 2021 MGS yield ends at 3.99%, all 2 bps lower. (ankur.relia@dowjones.com) [ 03-17-11 2105ET ]

"Investors are cautious and staying on the sidelines as oil prices rise due to the crisis in the Middle East," a local dealer says. He also says the market is likely to remain subdued for the rest of the week ahead of the central bank's rate setting meeting on Friday. He tips 1500 as a strong psychological support in the near term. Market breadth is negative with 512 decliners compared to 146 gainers. Genting Malaysia (4715.KU) is down 2.3% at MYR3.36, Genting Bhd(3182.KU) is down 1.7% at MYR10.16, Malaysian Airline (3786.KU) is down 1.6% at MYR1.84 and AMMB Holdings (1015.KU) is down 1.3% at MYR6.30. Petronas Dagangan (5681.KU) is up 0.6% at MYR14.28. (ankur.relia@dowjones.com)

0625 GMT [Dow Jones] PREVIEW: The BOK is expected to resume monetary tightening Thursday by raising its policy rate for the second time this year after inflation hit a 27-month high last month amid solid exports and retail sales. Eighteen of 23 economists and fixed-income analysts surveyed by Dow Jones expect the BOK to hike the key rate by 25 bps to 3.00%. Remaining five bet on hold but they expect a second hike to come as early as next month; "we expect the BOK to hike rates this time as inflation is rising and growth remains solid," says Nomura economist Kwon Young-sun. "Indeed, oil prices before the Middle East and North African crisis were mostly global demand-driven and higher inflation expectations were already feeding into higher core inflation. All this suggests that further monetary policy normalization looks warranted." He adds, if oil prices were to soar from the current level, the BOK would be faced with a policy dilemma. Domestic inflation hit a 27-month high of 4.5% in February vs 4.1% in January and above the BOK's target range of 2%-4%. Rate decision is due around 0100 GMT Thursday. (In-Soo.Nam@dowjones.com)

0623 GMT [Dow Jones] The Kospi ends down 1.2% at 1980.27, ending its two-session rally as foreigners turn net sellers of KRW56 billion worth of stocks; whether the index recovers the key 2000 level this week will likely be a market focus amid lingering concerns over the unrest in Libya, analysts say. "For a while, foreigners are likely to continue flip-flopping from being buyers to sellers," and vice versa, depending on offshore leads, says Mirae Asset Securities analyst Lee Jin-woo. Though a massive pullout like the one seen in February is unlikely, foreigners aren't likely to provide any strong upward momentum for Korean stocks either, he adds. Airline company stocks were among the biggest decliners amid rising oil prices; Korean Air Lines (003490.SE) ends down 3.1% at KRW61,600 and Asiana Airlines (020560.SE) is 6.1% lower at KRW9,860. Construction plays were mixed after recent weakness, with Hyundai Engineering & Construction (000720.SE) closing up 2.7% at KRW80,300, while Samsung Engineering (028050.SE) falls 4.0% to KRW182,500. (min-jeong.lee@dowjones.com)

0606 GMT [Dow Jones] ASIAN SUMMARY: Regional markets are mostly lower as higher oil prices continue to hurt sentiment, while the resignation of Japan's foreign minister added to Tokyo's gloom; April Nymex crude oil futures rose to their highest level in two and a half years and the contract is trading up $1.66 at $106.08/bbl on Globex. Nikkei is down 1.8%, S&P/ASX is down 1.3%, HSI is 0.3% lower, STI is +0.1% Kospi is down 1.2%, Shanghai Composite is +1.6%, NZX-50 is off 1.4%, Taiex is down 0.7%, Sensex is down 1.8% and SET is +0.5%. In FX markets, the USD/JPY fell as safe-haven demand intensified amid rising crude oil prices and continued political unrest in the Middle East; the USD/JPY is at 82.21 vs 82.30 late Friday in New York. The EUR/USD is at 1.3972 vs 1.3990 and the EUR/JPY is at 114.89 vs 115.10. Chief Cabinet Secretary Yukio Edano will temporarily replace departing Japanese Foreign Minister Seiji Maehara, NHK and other local media reported. The Japanese government took a EUR1.03 billion stake in bonds issued in January by a European bailout fund, making good on its promise to assist European efforts to calm the region's debt turmoil, a government official said. The total number of job advertisements in Australian newspapers and on the Internet rose 1.2% in seasonally adjusted terms in February from the previous month to an average of 193,555 ads per week. The Australian Industry Group Australian Performance of Construction Index rose 4.4 points to 44.6 in February from January. Spot gold is at $1,437.00/oz, up $4.20 vs NY close. (philip.vahn@dowjones.com)

0604 GMT [Dow Jones] Investors will pay attention to ECB President Trichet's speech later in the global day as they look for clues about when the central bank will hike rates, says Kenichiro Ikezawa, a senior fund manager at Daiwa SB Investments. "Though the market consensus on the timing of an ECB rate-hike is somewhere around July, some bullish investors are insisting (it will be) April," he says. Other Tokyo dealers shared a similar view, saying they will focus on whether Trichet will use the phase "strong vigilance" which he often uses a month before a rate-hike. The EUR may move sharply depending on his comments, they say. The EUR/JPY is at 114.92 and the EUR/USD is at 1.3973. (takashi.mochizuki@dowjones.com)

0601 GMT [Dow Jones] March Nikkei 225 futures are down 1.8% at 10,490, off their intraday low of 10,460, as a stronger yen and geopolitical uncertainties weigh on the market. USD/JPY is at 82.24, while EUR/JPY is at 114.95. Investrust CEO Hiroyuki Fukunaga pegs futures' range at 10,350-10,700 for the week. In addition to the effect of high crude prices on the U.S. market, he says conditions for stock market volatility will persist this week unless the Kan administration finds a quick replacement for outgoing Foreign Minister Seiji Maehara following his resignation Sunday. The market is also gearing up for concurrent futures and options settlements at the end of this week, he adds.(judy.lam@dowjones.com)

0600 GMT [Dow Jones] China shares extend gains on the government's reassuring words on inflation control, with coal miners and gold stocks leading gains. The Shanghai Composite Index is up 1.6% at 2989.84, with analysts putting immediate resistance at 3000. "Officials' comments on inflation during the weekend are sending a signal to the market that the country's inflation could be under control, which is prompting investors to chase stocks," says Shi Weixiang, an analyst from Guotai Junan Securities. title: EM ASIA  FX -Officials slow rising  currencies  despite inflation threat
text:
* Indonesian, Thai, Philippine, Malaysian intervention spotted - dealers

 * Won down on intervention caution, importers

 * Central banks not comfortable with speed of currency gains - analysts   (Updates with text, prices)

 By Jongwoo Cheon

 SINGAPORE, Feb 21 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah hit another 3-1/2-year high against the dollar on Monday and dealers said the country's central bank was spotted buying dollars, suggesting authorities were not comfortable with the currency's rapid rise.

 Central banks of Thailand, the Philippines and Malaysia also intervened to curb gains in their currencies and to maintain export competitiveness, dealers said, respectively pushing down the baht, peso and the ringgit.

 The South Korean won was the worst performer on the day among emerging Asian currencies on caution over possible dollar purchases by the foreign exchange authorities, especially as some dealers suspected the authorities intervened via the non-deliverable forward market on Friday in New York.

 The moves by the regional authorities showed their discomfort with the speed of the recent currency gains, even though stronger currencies help mitigate inflation, analysts said.

 "Currency is not the only tool to curb inflation. Other measures are also important," said Philip Wee, a treasury market strategist with DBS in Singapore.

 The rupiah has risen 1.6 percent since the Bank Indonesia raised interest rates on Feb 4, which alleviated some worries that the central bank was letting inflation get out of control.

 RUPIAH

 The dollar/rupiah  came under pressure from sales by custodian banks and leveraged funds ahead of government bond auctions and the central bank was suspected of buying dollars to check the rupiah's strength, dealers say.

 The pair fell to as low as 8,840, the lowest since June 2007 and compared with its previous close of 8,855.

 "State banks (suspected on behalf of the central banks) are actively buying the USD in the market... To anticipate a big flow coming," said an Asian bank dealer based in Jakarta.

 Finance ministry is looking to raise 5 trillion rupiah ($564.7 million) in a regular bond auction selling one year T-bills plus 5-year, 10-year and 20-year government debt.

 WON

 The dollar/won  climbed on importer demand for settlements and caution over possible intervention.

 Some local players also covered dollar-short positions.

 The one-month dollar/won NDF was quoted at 1,117.0/7.5 late on Friday in New York and traded at 1,120.2 as of 0510 GMT.

 "The authorities appeared to manage the closing price of NDFs last weekend, which implies their strong determination to defend 1,110," said a foreign bank dealer in Seoul.

 BAHT

 The dollar/baht  opened at 30.56-30.58 and has given ground right away on catch up selling.

 It hit low of 30.52 as the Bank of Thailand reportedly intervened by selliing dollars.

title: DJ UPDATE: China Fixes Yuan At Record High, Setting Tone For Asia  FX  Gains
text:
-- China fixes the yuan at a record high against the dollar

-- Asian currencies including the Korean won, Taiwan dollar and Thai baht rise

-- Korea and Malaysia apparently intervene to curb gains in their currencies

(Adds forex quotes, context) 


 
   By Arran Scott 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--China's central bank fixed the yuan's exchange rate at a record high against the dollar Wednesday, hours after it raised interest rates to cool its economy, setting the tone for a broad rise in Asian currencies as authorities aim to quell rising inflation pressures.

Central banks in South Korea and Malaysia were again selling their currencies for dollars to keep them from rising too quickly, traders said, indicating the authorities are taking care not to damage the export industries crucial to the region's economic growth.

The People's Bank of China set its parity rate for the dollar at CNY6.5850, down from Tuesday's close of CNY6.5938 in the over-the-counter market and that day's fixing rate of CNY6.5860. China's markets were closed since then for Lunar New Year holidays.

China's currency is now up 3.7% since the PBOC ended the yuan's two-year peg to the dollar in mid-June. Trading in yuan derivatives offshore show investors now expect the dollar to fall to 6.4220/6.4270 in the coming year, compared with the 6.4493/6.4728 implied by one-year nondeliverable forwards before the Chinese holidays.

Other Asian currencies, which have marked modest gains so far this year, continued to rise Wednesday. With China playing such a large role in the region's economy, the rest of Asia watches Beijing's foreign-exchange policy closely, seeking to ensure that their own currencies don't rise so much that their exporters become uncompetitive.

The U.S. currency fell against the Taiwan dollar to a fresh 13-year low in early trading, and slipped against the Thai baht. It was also slightly lower against the Korean won, though the Bank of Korea was suspected of buying dollars, Seoul traders said. Against the Malaysian ringgit, the U.S. currency was steady at Tuesday's closing level of MYR3.0330, where two local dealers said Bank Negara Malaysia defended the dollar.

"China's rate hike should be good for Asian currencies, but the Malaysian ringgit isn't rising because Bank Negara is at the 3.0330 level," said one dealer.

The PBOC raised one-year lending and deposit rates by 25 basis points late Tuesday, to 6.06% and 3.0% respectively, the third hike since October, underscoring policy makers' discomfort with percolating price pressures across the economy. Since the start of 2010, the PBOC has also raised the ratio of deposits that banks must hold in reserve seven times.

Inflation has been picking up in the region, fueled by fast economic growth and soaring prices of food and commodities. In China, consumer prices are expected to keep rising in the first quarter on strong holiday demand and bad weather. The consumer price index rose 4.6% from a year earlier in December, less than November's 5.1% rise, but the central bank appears to be uncomfortable with price pressures and some analysts expect inflation could rise by as high as 6.0% in the first half of the year.

The PBOC was the latest central bank in Asia to tighten monetary policy in recent months. Authorities are gradually moving to remove monetary stimulus that helped spur economic recoveries from the global financial crisis but is now adding to inflationary pressures.

Central banks such as Bank Indonesia have signaled that stronger currencies will be a tool in the inflation fight, and investors appear to be buying into that notion.

The PBOC sets a daily central parity rate for the yuan, allowing the tightly managed local currency to move up to 0.5% either way. Yuan/ringgit and yuan/ruble can as much as 5%, while other currencies are allowed to move as much as 3%.

title: UPDATE: Asian  Currencies  Hit Multi-Year Highs As Risk Appetite Revives
text:
-- Asian FX at multi-year highs on revived risk appetite

-- Expectations grow that central banks will fight inflation with stronger FX

-- Korea, Malaysia suspected of intervening to curb their currencies' rises

(Adds Korea and Malaysia intervention, updates market rates.)


 
   By Arran Scott and Mark Cranfield 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones) Several Asian currencies hit multi-year highs against the dollar Tuesday as revived risk appetite encouraged investors to plow money back into the region.

The authorities in South Korea and Malaysia were spotted intervening in the foreign exchange markets, local traders said, marking the latest interventions by Asian authorities to slow the rise in their currencies.

"Flows are coming back into Asia mainly because investors are betting on the strong (economic) fundamentals in the region," said a trader at a foreign bank in Singapore.

Higher Asia-Pacific share prices, triggered in part by strength on Wall Street overnight and a decline in crude oil prices, set a bullish tone for currencies. Investors appear to be buying into the notion Asian central banks will use a combination of stronger currencies and higher interest rates this year to temper inflation.

The Malaysian ringgit and Taiwan dollar rose to their highest levels since October 1997, when the Asian financial crisis sent regional currencies into a tailspin. The Korean won, which has lagged in the broad Asian currency appreciation last year, struck levels not seen since the Lehman Brothers collapse in September 2008 clobbered Asian currencies.

The Indonesia rupiah added to large gains it has made since Friday, when the country's central bank raised interest rates and signaled it would use a stronger local currency to rein in inflation that has surged above its target band. The rupiah had been hurt by concerns that Jakarta was falling behind the curve in containing inflation, but has now nearly recovered the losses it had logged since mid-November when such worries began to escalate.

With the exception of the Thai baht and Indian rupee, most major regional Asian currencies have posted gains so far this year, with the ringgit, rupiah, won and Taiwan dollar leading a modest appreciation on par with gains marked early last year.

Inflation has been picking up in Asia, fueled by fast economic growth, loose monetary policies and soaring prices of food and commodities on global markets. Central banks across the region have raised interest rates and tried to soak up liquidity that has gushed into the region as investors hunt for higher returns than those available in low interest-rate environments in the U.S. and Europe.

"The final tool in the armory of the region's authorities is FX appreciation," Fiona Lake, an analyst at Goldman Sachs, wrote in a research note. "Korea, Indonesia and Taiwan have shown greater desire for currency appreciation to help tackle inflation."

The won has some catching up to do with Asia's strongest currencies of the past year: the Singapore dollar, the ringgit and the baht. The Bank of Korea has also turned more hawkish in its comments on tackling rising inflation. Economists in a Dow Jones Newswires poll were split on whether the BOK will raise rates again Friday after a surprise rate hike last month. Among those predicting a tightening, Nomura tips a quarter percentage-point increase this week, with similar moves in April and June.

What's more, the U.S. has put the won on its list of currencies for which "there is room for a greater degree of exchange-rate stability and less intervention." The Treasury Department, in its annual foreign exchange report Friday, cited International Monetary Fund calculations that the won is 5%-20% undervalued.

Washington, seeking stronger Asian currencies to put U.S. exporters on a better competitive footing, likely has more leverage with Korea than with China. Sean Callow, a strategist at Westpac, points out that Congress hasn't ratified the U.S.-South Korea free trade agreement signed by Presidents Barack Obama and Lee Myung-bak in December.

The dollar was at KRW1,104.70 Tuesday afternoon in Asia, down from KRW1,107.50 late Monday, tracking the regional decline. But its fall was limited as traders said the BOK bought an estimated $300-$500 million to brake the won's ascent.

Similarly, Bank Negara Malaysia bought an estimated $200 million, traders said, after the U.S. currency carved out a fresh 13-year low against the ringgit, last trading at MYR3.0330. That was down from MYR3.0360 late Monday.

Against the Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency was last at NT$28.9080, after earlier touching NT$28.900, its lowest since October 1997, on foreign capital flows into Taipei stocks on the first trading day after the Lunar New Year holidays. A trader said the market is on the lookout for the Taiwan central bank, which is thought to intervene regularly near the close of trading to smooth out moves in the currency.

Against the rupiah, the dollar was around IDR8,915, down from IDR8,960 Monday and back near the IDR8,890 level at which it traded in mid-November, before concerns over inflation started to permeate the market.

Against the Singapore dollar, which has recently logged record highs, the U.S. currency was at SGD1.2728, down from SGD1.2746 late Monday

The baht and Philippine peso were also higher, helped by the broader rally in Asian currencies.

-By Arran Scott and Mark Cranfield, Dow Jones Newswires; +65-6415-4042; arran.scott@dowjones.com

 By Cheon Jong-woo

 SINGAPORE, Jan 19 (Reuters) - The South Korean won and the  Philippine peso led gains in Asian currencies on Wednesday as  investors reduced dollar positions on a broad weakness in the  greenback.

 Central banks in Taiwan and Malaysia were spotted buying  dollars to cap gains in their currencies while caution over  intervention by Seoul also prevented the won from strengthening  past 1,110 per dollar.

 Asian currencies were expected to stay firm as the dollar  index hit a two-month low, breaking through the bottom of the daily ichimoku chart, dealers said.

 "Look at the dollar index chart, a signal that the market is putting on risk," said a Kuala Lumpur-based dealer.

Currency investors are keeping an eye on a summit between  China and the United States.

 Chinese President Hu Jintao arrived in the United States on  Tuesday for a four-day state visit amid U.S. complaints  about Beijing's currency policies. 

 WON

 The won  rose as one of the country's  shipbuilders announced a big foreign order and market players  cleared dollar-long positions.

 However, caution grew over possible dollar-buying  intervention by the foreign exchange authorities to stem its  strength.

 "Few expect the won to strengthen past 1,110, so offshore are not active buyers around this level," said a foreign bank dealer in Seoul.

 Another dealer said the won may cut gains if the euro falls  or Seoul shares give up rises.

 On the corporate front, Hyundai Heavy Industries  said it had won a 1.14 trillion won order to build two drillships from U.S. offshore drilling contractor Noble Drilling, prompting expectations for more won demand.  

 PESO

 The peso gained 0.4 percent on a jump in the euro and with data showing the country's balance of payment last year hit a record high of $14.4 billion. 

 Credit Agricole expects the peso to strengthen to 41.50 per  dollar at the end of this year as worries about the country's  inflation is groundless and on strong current account surplus.

 Credit Agricole recommended to sell dollar/peso six-month  non-deliverable forwards (NDF).

 "Worries over inflation seem unfounded as the central bank is not behind the curve," it said in a research note. "Monetary  tightening will support the PHP. Strong current account surplus  will put upward pressure on the currency."

 Credit Agricole said it expects two 25-bps rate hike this  year, which will allow policy makers to keep inflation in check.

 TAIWAN DOLLAR

 The Taiwan dollar rose 1.5 percent, but stayed  weaker than T$29 per U.S. dollar as the central bank placed  many bids for the greenback. That made investors and exporters reluctant to sell the U.S. dollars, dealers said.

 A trader at a local bank in Taiwan said exporters might only offer more US dollar next week before the China Lunar new year.

 A Taiwan dollar dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore said he  expected the Taiwan central bank to defend the T$29 for the time being.

title: Emerging-Market Debt Wavers In Strength Against Treasurys
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market debt teetered back and forth in its position against U.S. Treasurys on Thursday as economies carefully gauge potential policy moves to be made by their respective governments.

The risk premium on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, was one basis point wider Thursday, to 279 basis points over Treasurys. The overall index was up 0.06% for the day.

"The market is in a hovering pattern," said Enrique Alvarez, Latin American strategist at IDEAglobal. "There was so much expectation created surrounding the Portuguese refinancing this week and in the end, there was no definitive conclusion coming from that. We're still searching for major price drivers, and we're just not getting them."

U.S. Treasury prices rose Thursday, lifted by Federal Reserve purchases and a bit of support following the 30-year bond auction.

Going into the year, however, Alvarez said country-specific news may become more of a driver.

"There's an underlying trend where the market is beginning to focus more on regional dynamics, where you have a number of different countries entering higher waters related to inflation," he said.

On Thursday, Chile was in focus as participants remained unsure if Chile's central bank will increase its benchmark overnight rate by 25 basis points or keep it steady at 3.25% at its monthly monetary policy meeting. Chile's peso ended slightly stronger versus the dollar Thursday at CLP489.50 to the dollar, compared with Wednesday's close of CLP490.20. While talk of inflation continues to grow, on the Embig, Chile expanded two basis points to 116 basis point over Treasurys. Its index gained 0.05% in price terms.

Ecuador was a prominent gainer on the Embig, tightening 104 basis points to 788 basis points above Treasurys. Its index gained 1.6% on the day. On Thursday, the country's internal revenue service reported that Ecuador collected $7.86 billion in taxes last year, up 17% from 2009.

The Mexican peso weakened again the dollar following a worse-than-expected reading on U.S. jobless claims. The peso recently traded weaker at MXN12.1145 from Wednesday's MXN12.0855, according to Infosel. Mexican sovereign debt gained on the Embig, tightening two basis points to 147 basis points over Treasurys.

"We believe Mexico's economy is stabilizing, which could help the securitization market's recovery," said Standard & Poor's credit analyst Maria del Sol Gonzalez de Cosio, who anticipates fewer negative ratings for the new assets coming into the market.

Elsewhere, Russia's spread gave back tightening that occurred earlier in the day, to remain even on the Embig. On Wednesday, Russian equity indexes made their way to new highs after Prime Minster Vladimir Putin provided official 2010 economic readings, with gross domestic product growth reaching 3.8% and industrial output up by 8.3%.

From Asia, Malaysia contributed to the Embig's expansion, with its individual spread wider by four basis points to 113 basis points over Treasurys. Its index was mostly flat on the day. The Malaysian ringgit, like many other emerging Asian currencies, has faced upward pressure against the dollar. Following the South Korean central bank's surprise 25-basis-point rate increase, Malaysia's own central bank intervened.

Pakistan also fed into the wider Embig, with its own spread up 23 basis points to 811 basis points over Treasurys. Its index fell more than 3%. In addition to the mounting political turmoil, Pakistan's central bank began printing new rupee notes at the start of the year even as the nation faces inflationary pressure that has slashed more than 15% of its currency's value in the past year.

-By Cynthia Lin, Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-4403; cynthia.lin@dowjones.com

title: WSJ: Asian Central Banks  Intervene  as  Currencies  Rise
text:
WSJ: Asian Central Banks Intervene as Currencies Rise

By ARRAN SCOTT, ARIES POON and DITAS LOPEZ

Central banks in South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand are believed to have intervened in foreign-exchange markets Thursday as Asian currencies surged against the dollar on optimism about the region's economic outlook, underscored by strong economic data from China and signals that the yuan will continue to strengthen.

Taiwan, meanwhile, unveiled measures to buttress its banking system against rapid movements in foreign capital, the latest Asian economy to introduce stricter regulations to control the risks posed by such capital flows.

Capital has been flooding into Asia this year, helping finance investments in the fast-growing region. But the influx of foreign money has raised concerns in Asian capitals about the perils of fast-moving capital flows, given the damage the region's economies suffered during the Asian financial crisis of the late 1990s when a previous boom ended suddenly and foreigners rushed for the exits.

Fresh data Thursday from China, the powerhouse of the Asian economy, showed manufacturing growth eased slightly in December but was still at relatively high levels. The HSBC China Manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index, a gauge of nationwide manufacturing activity, fell to 54.4 in December from 55.3 in November; any reading above 50 indicates expansion.

CIMB's Mr. Lum said central banks in emerging markets are looking at tightening monetary policy next year, which means interest-rate differentials between emerging markets and the developed economies of the U.S., Europe and Japan should grow wider. That leaves Asian central banks looking for ways to control inflows of capital chasing higher returns.

In Kuala Lumpur, traders said Malaysia's central bank was suspected of buying dollars to curb a rise in the ringgit, which hit a three-month high Thursday. Bank Negara Malaysia may have bought dollars at around 3.0810-3.0820 ringgit per dollar, dealers said. The dollar was at 3.0846 ringgit in late trade.

Traders in Seoul said they suspected the Bank of Korea entered the market, buying more than $500 million at several intervals between 1,135 and 1,140 won per dollar. The dollar closed at 1,134.80 won, bringing the won's gains against the dollar to 2.6% for the year.

In Bangkok, the dollar was at 30.15 baht in late trade - down from 30.16 baht late Wednesday - with suspected buying by the central bank around that level to limit the downside, two dealers said.

In Taipei, which has been trying to temper gains in the New Taiwan dollar - a favorite among investors seeking exposure to China, given Taiwan's increasingly close economic ties to the mainland - Taiwan's central bank announced new measures to control capital flows.

Starting Saturday, local banks will have to set aside 90% of foreign investors' new deposits as reserves, a leap from the current level of 9.775%.

The central bank also raised its benchmark interest rate by 0.125 percentage point to 1.625%, the third increase this year, as it seeks to normalize lending costs and cool a sizzling property market. Central bank Governor Perng Fai-nan said inflation will likely accelerate next year.

Also Thursday, Taiwan's financial regulator said it will inspect banks' use of foreign funds to determine whether there has been speculative trading in the local currency, after the central bank said it had found "unusual" trading strategies at a small number of banks. "Over the past few days, a small number of authorized foreign-exchange banks have targeted specific times of the day to sell off large quantities of foreign exchange," the central bank said in a statement.

It isn't unusual for Asian central banks to intervene in foreign-exchange markets when volatility in their currencies rises. Many have taken regulatory steps in recent months to try to slow capital inflows and make their banking systems more resilient to movements in foreign funds.

Indonesia's central bank said Wednesday that it would increase the amount of reserves commercial banks must hold at the central bank against foreign-currency deposits, among other steps. Also Wednesday, South Korea said it would announce lower ceilings on banks' foreign-exchange forward positions in January.

 - Joy Shaw in Shanghai, Min-Jeong Lee in Seoul and Ankur Relia in Kuala Lumpur contributed to this article.

title: UPDATE: Malaysia's Interest Rates Accommodative - Zeti
text:
(Recasts, adds more comments from governor, background)

By K.P. Lee

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Malaysia's central bank governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz said Thursday that interest rates in the Southeast Asian country were at an appropriate level, despite a rate increase in neighbouring Thailand a day earlier.

"Our assessment is that interest rates are at an appropriate level at this point in time given the outlook for inflation and the outlook for growth," Zeti said when asked if Malaysia would follow suit. She was speaking at an event in Kuala Lumpur.

Thailand's central bank Wednesday surprised the markets by raising its rate by 25 basis points to 2.0%, the third increase this year, citing potential threats to the economy due to inflation running above policy interest rates. With inflation at 2.8% in November, the Thailand authority said that real interest rates were negative, which could distort market mechanisms.

Early last month, Bank Negara Malaysia in its last rate-setting meeting of the current year kept its policy rate unchanged at 2.75%, after having raised rates by a total of 75 basis points in three increases earlier this year.

Inflationary pressures in Malaysia have remained benign over the last few months, and are expected to remain that way going forward, economists says, the majority of whom don't expect any rate hikes in the first half of 2011. In October, consumer prices in Malaysia rose 2.0% from a year earlier, compared with market expectations of 1.9%.

On the issue of capital controls, Zeti said any moves to curb capital flows should be implemented internationally or regionally. "I do not think any country can (introduce capital controls) successfully without causing instability to others."

The fast-growing economies in Southeast Asia have drawn a surge of capital from slower-growth areas seeking higher returns, fuelling concerns about creation of asset bubbles, stronger currencies that undercut export competitiveness and instability should the inflows suddenly reverse course.

Zeti maintained that Malaysia's central bank will only intervene in the foreign exchange market to maintain "orderly conditions." She said the ringgit will continue to strengthen in line with fundamentals, but the bank won't intervene if the currency's rise is gradual. The central bank "won't intervene to influence underlying trends," she added.

The U.S. dollar was trading at MYR3.1455 at 0700 GMT, down from MYR3.1500 late Wednesday.

title: Malaysia c.bank says orderly  FX  market important
text:
* Central bank says markets have been orderly

* Central bank may intervene in market- economist

* Ringgit has moved within 300-350 bps range of dollar

KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Malaysia's central bank said on Wednesday that an orderly currency market was important, underlining expectations that the authority would continue to conduct smoothing operations to prevent ringgit volatility.

Indeed, currency traders said that Malaysia intervened aggressively in the market on Wednesday to buy dollars. [ID:nSGE6A90B5]

Emerging market currencies are under upward pressure from a flood of capital inflows seeking higher returns compared with developed nations and a number of countries have imposed measures to control the flow.

"We are pleased to say that our foreign exchange market has been very orderly," the central bank's governor, Zeti Akhtar Aziz, told reporters on the sidelines of a business conference.

"We have said from the very beginning there's going to be increased volatility because of increased uncertainty," she said.

"We are on record to say orderly foreign exchange markets are very important for a highly open economy like Malaysia."

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> is Asia's third best-performing currency behind the Japanese yen <JPY=> and the Thai baht <THB=>, with gains of more than 10 percent versus the dollar. It was last at 3.088 per dollar.

Analysts expect Asian currencies to appreciate further, as a second round of U.S. quantitative easing drives capital into emerging economies.

Gundy Cahyadi, an economist at OCBC Bank, said the Malaysian central bank could step into the foreign exchange market to prevent excessive volatility.

"It is important to note that for the most part, we think this is in the spirit of smoothing flows in the market, rather than a draconian measure aimed to stop the ringgit from being stronger," Cahyadi said.

"Bank Negara has previously stated that it may intervene if the market is not orderly, and we think they may just do that, as excessive volatility in the FX market is bad for the economy as a whole."

CIMB's forex strategist Suresh Ramanathan said the ringgit market had been orderly.

"Even with the dollar rallying in the last two days, the ringgit has been declining in an orderly fashion," he said.

The U.S. dollar rallied on Wednesday to its highest level against a basket of major currencies since late October. [ID:nSGE6A905L] (Reporting by Fong Min Hun; Editing by Neil Fullick) ((fong.minhun@thomsonreuters.com; +603-2333-8039; bureau email areuters@gmail.com))

title: UPDATE 1- Malaysia  to  intervene  if ringgit "disorderly"-c.bank
text:
* C.bank will intervene if ringgit becomes "disorderly"

* Sees no inflationary pressures right now

* Economic growth will moderate (Adds details)

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Malaysia's central bank will intervene in currency markets if movements in the ringgit <MYR=> become "disorderly", its governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz said on Tuesday.

The ringgit has risen 10.5 percent against the dollar this year as investors pump cash into higher yielding emerging market assets, making it Asia's third-best performer among the currencies monitored daily by Reuters.

"It (the ringgit) is dependent on the inflows or outflows and the central bank is well positioned to undertake any sort of... intervene in the market if conditions become disorderly or very excessive movements taking place within a very short period of time," Zeti told reporters.

Zeti added there will be volatility and uncertainty in major currencies, not just in the ringgit.

The Malaysian central governor's comments come after the G20 partners pledged that advanced economies would be vigilant against disorderly exchange rate movements. [ID:nTOE69M002]

Japanese Finance Minister Yoshihiko Noda said earlier on Tuesday that Japan would take decisive steps on forex when needed, after Tokyo intervented in mid-September to try to slow the yen's rise. [ID:nTKF107056]

A number of other Asian authorities have also been actively interventing to stem sharp appreciation of their currencies, fearing it could hit exports and stifle economic growth. Some other emerging economies such as Brazil have also taken steps to control foreign inflows. <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Zeti also said the central bank did not see inflationary pressures at this point of time and it had the flexibility to contain any asset bubbles.

The economy would remain firmly on a growth path, but there will be moderation, she said.

On new licences for foreign banks, Zeti said the central bank hoped to announce later this year at least one licence for a mega Islamic bank.

title: FX  ASIA: Malaysian Ringgit May Sail Past  Intervention  Threat
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The ringgit, Asia's best-performing currency so far this year, may rise further ahead of key milestones for Malaysia's economic reform plans -- as long as the country's central bank sticks to its policy of not curtailing currency strength.

The ringgit is up 11% against the U.S. dollar since January, the result of strong foreign inflows to an economy growing at an 8.9% annual pace in the second quarter.

Analysts say the ringgit may receive additional good news next month. The government is expected to present its 2011 annual budget on Oct. 15, including measures that top officials say will lower the deficit significantly from an estimated 5.6% of gross domestic product this year -- one of Asia's highest levels and a significant concern for investors.

Also in October, Petronas Petrochemicals Group Bhd., a unit of Malaysia's government-controlled oil and gas company Petronas, is slated to complete the country's largest initial public offering, surpassing last year's $3.6 billion IPO from Maxis Bhd (6012.KU).

That may be followed by more IPOs later this year, as Malaysia's government implements the New Economic Model it announced in April to boost economic growth.

This is a favorable environment for the ringgit, which on Wednesday hit MYR3.0800 to the dollar, its highest level since the 1997-98 Asian crisis. That followed news that index provider FTSE had re-classified Malaysia as an advanced emerging economy, opening the door for inflows of up to $2.4 billion from managers of indexed funds over the next year, Barclays Capital estimates.

BarCap last week raised its ringgit forecasts and now expects the dollar to trade at MYR2.92 in a year's time, versus a previous forecast of MYR3.05. Some analysts anticipate even faster gains, with the dollar possibly falling to MYR3.0 as early as December.

Standard Bank economist Patrick Bennett recently noted that Malaysia, whose main commodity exports are denominated in dollars, may refrain from intervening in forex markets to cap ringgit rallies. That would be a stark contrast to the concerted forex intervention in East Asian economies that export mainly manufactured products.

Bennett said this suggests the dollar could fall next year toward MYR2.80 -- a level unseen since the height of the Asian crisis.

"The government and central bank have been accommodating of ringgit gains and have no reason to turn back now," Bennett said.

Kuala Lumpur traders say Malaysia's central bank has likely intervened in recent weeks around MYR3.10. But recent data show any intervention has likely been in tiny amounts aimed at smoothing out currency trading, rather than putting a floor beneath the currency as Japan did earlier this month.

Recent data show that as of Sept. 15, Malaysian central bank reserves had risen just 0.7% since the end of August, to $95.9 billion. The small increase is likely explained by the higher valuation of Malaysia's euro-denominated reserves, given the euro's 2.6% rise against the dollar in the period, and implies that few if any dollars were purchased.

title: Malaysia PM: Ringgit Level Now Reflects Fundamentals - CNBC
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Razak said he wasn't worried about the ringgit's strength, CNBC reported Friday, marking a contrast with recent currency intervention by the central bank.

Asked if he was comfortable with the ringgit, which is trading around 13-year highs, Najib said,"Yes, we are," according to CNBC, which said the interview was conducted Thursday.

"But we are monitoring it in terms of both our fiscal and monetary policy to make sure that the ringgit reflects the fundamentals of the economy," he was quoted as saying. "And at the moment, we believe it does and the stronger ringgit doesn't seem to have a negative impact on our exports."

Bank Negara Malaysia has begun to intervene to curb the ringgit in recent days, after staying out of the currency market since April, traders in Kuala Lumpur say. The central bank bought dollars last week and as recently as Wednesday at MYR3.1110-MYR3.1120, the traders said.

title: RPT-INTERVIEW-Malaysia c.bank-no need for change after yuan move
text:
* No plans to intervene after China adopts yuan flexibility

 * Malaysia exports won't suffer from stronger ringgit

 * Monetary policy to support recovery, remove imbalances  (Repeats item first carried late on Wednesday)

 By Gilbert Kreijger

 AMSTERDAM, June 23 (Reuters) - Malaysia's central bank governor said on Wednesday she did not expect to intervene in foreign exchange markets following China's announcement of a more flexible policy on the yuan.

 China said over the weekend it would allow its currency greater flexibility, strengthening Malaysia's ringgit <MYR=> versus the dollar, but Bank Negara Malaysia Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz said that Malaysia would stick to its exchange rate policy and saw limited impact in Asia.

 "This is not expected to have implications on the region in terms of impact on financial markets, including foreign exchange markets, in the region," Zeti told Reuters.

 "We will continue with our exchange rate regime that we have in place. It has served us very well," said Zeti, who was visiting the Netherlands en route to the Bank for International Settlements' annual meeting in Switzerland later this week.

 Zeti said the ringgit's appreciation over the past year -- it is up almost 9 percent to trade at 3.231 to the dollar -- reflects an improvement of Malaysia's economy, which grew by 10.1 percent in the first quarter, the fastest pace in a decade. [ID:nSGE64C0DV]

 "We will promote orderly market conditions. Therefore -- for the most time of course -- it does not involve any interventionist policy," she added.

 Zeti said euro zone debt woes had not posed a threat to market stability and only when there was a potential disruption or disorderly market conditions would Bank Negara consider intervening in the currency market.

 "We were there to stabilise the market condition during that period -- during Lehman's fall and the period that followed. That was to prevent depreciation," Zeti said.

 GLOBAL GROWTH UNCERTAINTY    She said, however, euro zone debt problems and developments in the United States were creating uncertainty for global economic growth.

 Malaysia's central bank has hiked interest rates <MYINTR=ECI> at two consecutive meetings this year, each time by 25 basis points so that its key rate now stands at 2.5 percent, and has repeatedly said that rates must "normalise".

 "There are risks to the external conditions and we do have to take that into account in determining the extent to which further normalisation will take place," Zeti said.

 "We've also said that for the rest of this year monetary policy will remain supportive of the economy and therefore we would not be moving into a tightening phase. This is because we assess inflation will remain modest during this year."

 A low interest rate could push money into "informal sectors" or high-risk activities or create asset bubbles that may hurt the economy when conditions change, Zeti said.

 "The process of normalisation is aimed at removing the risk of a buildup of financial imbalances. We believe such financial imbalances could result in a risk to our growth."

 At the same time, Malaysian exports are not expected to suffer from a stronger ringgit because of their focus on competitiveness, innovation and productivity, Zeti said.

 "Our export sector has also been able to adjust to manage their position better. We have also removed many rules that give them greater flexibility in managing their foreign financial transactions." she said.

 Zeti said the government, which had a 2009 budget deficit of 7 percent of gross domestic product, would have the opportunity to start cutting subsidies on food, petrol, electricity and gas, as it announced last month.

 "The government can take time but it is now that we have achieved stable economic conditions it is good to start the process," she added.  (Editing by Stephen Nisbet)

title: UPDATE:  Malaysia Central Bank :  Forex Intervention  Not Needed Now
text:
(Recasts, adds background on ringgit, comment on stimulus package)

By K.P. Lee

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--The Malaysian central bank said Tuesday it would intervene in the foreign-exchange market to only curb excessive volatility, but it doesn't see a need to do so at the moment despite the recent rapid appreciation of the ringgit.

Although there has been some volatility in the foreign-exchange markets recently, conditions have remained generally stable, Bank Negara Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz said on the sidelines of a conference.

"We are very pleased that we have orderly conditions in the market and, therefore, the need does not arise for central bank intervention. Only when we have excessive adjustments in any particular day that present a risk to orderly market conditions does the central bank come in," she said.

The ringgit has gained more than 3% against a broadly weaker greenback since the beginning of the month. The dollar traded at MYR3.3540 around 0530 GMT, down from MYR3.3730 at the close Monday.

Zeti also said that the government's two stimulus packages totaling MYR67.0 billion ($19.91 billion) are helping the economy recover, and there is no need for a third economic stimulus package to be introduced next year.

"Right now, the economy has shown signs of recovery. Unless there is any further negative development, the current stimulus is already producing results...We are very pleased private consumption is expanding and at the same time, there is some recovery in investment activity," she said.

The Malaysian economy shrank 3.9% on year in the second quarter of this year, but Zeti had earlier indicated that the economy may likely improve in the third quarter and turn positive in the fourth.

-By K.P. Lee, Dow Jones Newswires; (603) 2026 1233; kwan-por.lee@dowjones.com [ 20-10-09 0545GMT ]

title: UPDATE-1-HIGHLIGHTS-Malaysia cbank head on Q1 GDP data
text:
(adds more comments)

KUALA LUMPUR, May 27 (Reuters) - Following are the highlights of Malaysian central bank Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz from her press conference on Malaysia's first quarter GDP data which showed the economy contracted by 6.2 percent in the first quarter.

*****************************************************

"We are now going into the third month of the second quarter, we are almost completing the second quarter and what we see is that the export sector or external demand continued to remain weak and the environment is still challenging.

"Despite early signs of improvement...(second-quarter will be) very similar to the first quarter. But significant improvement will be seen in the third quarter. There is a higher degree of confidence of a positive growth in the fourth quarter." Did the magnitude of contraction in Q1 surprise the central bank?

"The central bank already announced that growth will be significantly affected. We already anticipated a very slow growth as the financial crisis has become more prolonged than earlier expected and the deterioration in global economy was far greater than expected.

"There is a high degree of uncertainty in the global environment, therefore we decided to reduce interest rates and we said we frontloaded it, because the deterioration was far more severe than what we had previously anticipated."

On a new 2009 GDP forecast

The prime minister has mentioned... that he will be announcing (it) tomorrow.

Intervention on the ringgit?

"For us the exchange rate does not represent a policy instrument, therefore we do not target any specific level or band, (we want an) orderly and functioning foreign exchange market...we do not want a situation of too great uncertainty in the foreign exchange market.

But hasn't Malaysia missed its growth target consistently?

"Malaysia has achieved significant progress on two fronts, the domestic economy has become more significant, consumption, for example, has increased (significantly) so consumption demand has become more important.

"We are moving away from an export-dependent economy to become a domestic(ally) significant economy. The domestic sector has been a major driver of growth since 2003, contraction today will be far worse if not for our domestic economy.

"We are moving to a more diversified economy, had we not built and strengthened the services sector, our economic contraction today will be far worse."

Is the '09 inflation forecast maintained at 1.5 to 2 percent?

"Yes."

Are we already in a recession?

"We always look at two quarters of negative growth but it's not constructive to look at this, but to look at the prospects of does Malaysia come out, Malaysia does, we are not facing a financial crisis and we are not overleveraged."

"Stability has emerged in the labour market, the commodity and the stock market and a decline in inflation will improve the purchasing power and the capacity that we have to provide the stimulus package ... all these (and) the prospects of full positive growth going into the final quarter of the year and going into 2010.

As for the budget deficit? What strategy does Malaysia have to counter that?

"State intervention can only be temporary. For others, where they have to repair their financial systems, they are providing life support, for us it is providing support to the economy rather than to the financial system, because our financial system is not facing a crisis. None of the Asian financial systems are facing a financial crisis. Therefore, we anticipate that following this period of uncertainty going into next year, the government can slowly exit from this extensive massive stimulus and that the private sector will assume a greater role in the economy."

So there is no positive growth for Q3 yet?

"There is a great uncertainty. Our assessment is there will be an Improvement. But the extent of the improvement will depend on the external environment as well as the extent to which the domestic environment turns positive arising from all the measurements that have been introduced including the fiscal measures, the cumulative monetary policy measures, the measure to increase the access to financing.

(Reporting by Soo Ai Peng and Loh Lilian, editing by Niluksi Koswanage)

title: WSJA: Asian Shares Drop,  Currencies  Sharply Lower
text:
OF THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA 
 

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Asian stocks were sold off heavily Thursday, knocking many of the region's currencies sharply lower and prompting governments to intervene.

Markets in Tokyo, Hong Kong and South Korea fell in response to a broad selloff overnight in the U.S. Tokyo's benchmark index fell 6.9%, while Hong Kong and Seoul were down 4% and 6.7% respectively. Australia's major benchmark dropped 4.2% and Shanghai fell 1.7%. Mumbai and Singapore were down 4.1% and 2.8% late Thursday. Jakarta was down 2.8% late.

The selling continued in Europe, where the DJ Stoxx 600 index was 3% lower. U.S. stock futures were down 1% to 1.5% in screen trade.

The stock hits reflect fears of deflation in the U.S., a major market for Asia-made goods, and the impact of a slowdown on commodity-rich nations like Australia and Indonesia.

That has led to a flight to safer investments typically denominated in U.S. dollars and the Japanese yen, taking money out of Asian markets and contributing to a drop in local currencies.

"It's part of the wholesale destruction of wealth across the planet," said Patrick Bennett, a strategist with Societe Generale in Hong Kong. "With asset and equity prices tumbling, investors are being encouraged to cut exposure completely."

Weaker currencies can boost big exporting nations because it makes their goods cheaper to sell in other markets. But declining currencies also hit countries with extensive foreign borrowing needs, can drive up inflation by making imports more expensive and can scare off foreign investment.

Among the hardest hit, Indonesia's rupiah and South Korea's won fell to their lowest level against the U.S. dollar since the Asian financial crisis a decade ago.

Thailand's baht fell to its weakest level since March 2007, while Taiwan's dollar hit a three-week low and the New Zealand and Australian dollars also weakened further.

The central banks of South Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore and India intervened to defend their currencies, local traders said. Australia's central bank issued data that showed it plowed A$3.15 billion into currency markets last month to defend the Australian dollar against a sharp decline.

Japan and Hong Kong have defied the trend, the former because its currency is seen as a safe haven and the latter because it is pegged to the value of the appreciating U.S. dollar. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city's de facto central bank, put roughly HK$15 billion into the market Thursday to bring the currency's value within its trading band with the U.S. dollar.

Economists cautioned that the current environment hasn't reached the point of the Asian currency crisis, when domestic funds followed foreign investors as they ran for the exits. Most governments have moved to back bank deposits to reassure consumers. Regional financial institutions have cleaner balance sheets than a decade ago, and bad loans have so far had only a minor effect on regional banks.

Still, continuing hits to currencies continue could erode consumer confidence, leading locals to consider moving their money elsewhere. "The impact on confidence could become a much bigger problem," said Sim Moh Siong, an economist at Citigroup in Singapore. "If this goes beyond how much money foreigners remove from Asia, the situation could broaden out."

In Tokyo, the Nikkei Stock Average of 225 companies ended down 6.9% at 7703.04. Shares of major banks and brokerages were hammered, with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group tumbling 10% to Y281,500 and Nomura Holdings ending down 11% at Y666.

Shares of nonlife insurers dropped after sector companies reported dismal fiscal first half results Wednesday and sharply reduced their earnings forecasts for the full fiscal year ending March.

Although most of the bad news had already been factored in by investors, forecast revisions confirmed the grim outlook. Tokio Marine Holdings went limit-down at Y2,220, and Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance Group Holdings also went limit-down at Y2,035.

Real estate stocks also sank, dogged by credit concerns, with Mitsui Fudosan skidding 14% to Y1,070, and Mitsubishi Estate falling 13% to Y1,077.

In Seoul, the Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, finished down 68.13 points, or 6.7%, at 948.69, based on skepticism over conditions in the U.S., particularly among financials.

Shinhan Financial Group declined 9.7% to KRW26,400, and KB Financial Group plunged by the daily limit of 15% to KRW24,550. Among builders, Hyundai Engineering & Construction and GS Engineering & Construction both dropped by the daily 15% limit to KRW42,100 and KRW45,200, respectively.

In Shanghai, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index, which tracks both A and B shares, ended down 1.7%, or 33.71 points, at 1983.76. Railway companies and insurance companies fell on profit-taking.

China Railway Group Ltd. dropped 4.1% to CNY5.82 after gaining 4.7% Wednesday, while China Life Insurance Co. fell 4.0% to CNY20.24 after rising 6.1% in the previous session.

-By Carlos Tejada, The Wall Street Journal; carlos. tejada@wsj.com

(Takashi Mochizuki and Takashi Nakamichi in Tokyo and Rosalind Mathieson in Singapore also contributed to this article.) [ 20-11-08 0946GMT ]

title: Reuters Southeast Asia News Highlights 0900 GMT Nov 19
text:
- - - -

KUALA LUMPUR - Pirates have hijacked a Thai fishing boat with 16 crew members on board off the Somali coast, said Noel Choong, an official with the Kuala Lumpur-based International Maritime Bureau.

Piracy in the Gulf of Aden, one of the world's busiest sea routes, has surged this year and last weekend pirates captured a Saudi supertanker carrying $100 million of oil, the largest seizure ever.

- - - -

BEIJING - China will start building oil and gas pipelines through Myanmar next year, enabling it to slash the journey time for crude oil imports from the Middle East, state media said, citing an official.

The pipelines into China's southwestern Yunnan province would cut out oil cargoes' long detour through the congested Malacca Strait as well as strengthen China's access to rich energy reserves in Myanmar itself.

- - - -

SINGAPORE - Neptune Orient Lines, the world's seventh largest container carrier, said it will shed 9 percent of its workforce and warned the outlook was grim as the shipping sector faces up to a prolonged downturn.

NOL shares fell almost 3 percent after the firm said in a statement it will cut 1,000 jobs, mostly in North America, as it battles to weather a global economic slowdown.

- - - -

TAIPEI - Indonesia's rupiah dipped to a fresh 7-year low, while the South Korean won and the Taiwan dollar hovered at three-week troughs as concerns over a deepening global downturn and capital outflows hit Asian markets.

The rupiah fell 2.6 percent from the previous day's close to hit a low of 12,060 to the U.S. dollar during Wednesday trade, with the market watching the central bank's moves after it said it would not allow the currency to hit "irrational" levels.

- - - -

BANGKOK - Asian rice prices rose and were expected to stay firm over the next few weeks, supported by a Thai intervention scheme and fresh demand from Iraq and Malaysia for Vietnamese rice, exporters and traders said.

Thailand's benchmark 100 percent B grade white rice rose 9 percent from last week to $580 per tonne as a government buying programme kicked in, exporters said. (Compiled by Carl Bagh; Editing by Jerry Norton)

title: Fitch Revises S Korea Rating Outlook To Negative From Positive
text:
Corrected November 9, 2008 20:31 ET (01:31 GMT) [ 10-11-08 0007GMT ]

Fitch Ratings-Hong Kong/Singapore-10 November 2008: This announcement clarifies the version issued earlier today to highlight that the Outlook on Malaysia's Long-term local currency Issuer Default Rating is Stable. The correct version is as follows:

Fitch Ratings has today revised Korea's rating Outlook to Negative from Stable and the Outlook on Malaysia's Long-term foreign currency Issuer Default Rating to Stable from Positive. At the same time, Fitch has affirmed the sovereign ratings with Stable Outlooks for China, Taiwan, and Thailand. India's Long-term foreign currency Issuer Default rating (IDR) at 'BBB-' (BBB minus) is also affirmed with a Stable Outlook, and the local currency 'BBB-' (BBB minus) IDR is affirmed with a Negative Outlook. All ratings are listed at the end of this announcement.

These rating actions follow the conclusion of a global review of the sovereign ratings of 17 major investment-grade emerging market economies conducted in response to the profound deterioration in the global economic and financial outlook.

"The revision to Korea's Outlook reflects concerns that the de-leveraging of the banking system may contribute to an erosion of the sovereign's external credit strengths, especially if it were accompanied by central bank interventions in the currency market to support the exchange rate," said James McCormack, head of Asia sovereigns at Fitch.

Fitch notes hat the authorities had responded quickly and in a focused manner to the funding distress of the banking system, with a comprehensive package of measures, including a USD30bn foreign-currency swap facility and a USD100bn guarantee programme for new bank debt. Though potential external financing needs are large - a forecast current account deficit (plus outflows of net FDI) for next year of USD35bn plus short-term and liquid foreign liabilities estimated at USD176bn - external financing and liquidity concerns remain moderate given still sizeable Bank of Korea (BoK) foreign exchange reserves of USD212bn at end-October 2008. The BoK also has access to a USD30bn currency swap arrangement with the US Federal Reserve and other swap arrangements that are currently being discussed with the People's Bank of China and the Bank of Japan. Even so, the fiscal and foreign exchange cost of funding the 'de-leveraging' of the banking system against the backdrop of a sharp slowdown in the economy and deterioration in bank asset quality could erode Korea's external credit strengths, especially if the BoK engages in less targeted foreign exchange intervention.

In revising the Outlook on Malaysia to Stable, Fitch took into account the likely impact on the balance of payments of lower oil and other commodity prices, as well as the deterioration in external demand conditions for electronics exports. Malaysia is one of Asia's more open economies and the region's only significant net oil exporter.

To accompany today's global review, the Sovereign group will host a teleconference at 15:00 GMT/ 10:00 EST to discuss the review in further detail. A full list of rating actions and associated rationales are detailed in a special report, 'Rating Review of Emerging Markets', now available at www.fitchratings.com

title: 4th UPDATE: Asian Shares Enjoy A Turnaround; Japan, HK Jump
text:
(Adds quotes, information, updates/adds market levels)

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian stock markets were mostly higher Tuesday with a large intraday recovery in bourses to the north, though some southeast Asian markets suffered as the exodus from smaller emerging markets continued.

Analysts were mixed on where markets might go from here: "Given the 'trading mentality' within Asia, the key question remains how long this change in sentiment will last," said IG Markets dealing head Oliver Stevens.

Intraday trading ranges were very wide and markets were prone to sudden swings, suggesting more volatility ahead.

But CMC Markets dealer Matt Buckland said "there is the mounting belief we may be close to finding the bottom. Asian indices are positive and the simple question as to just how much more value can actually be taken out is certainly worth asking again."

Korea's Kospi Composite shot up 5.6%, aided by buying of blue chips by the nation's pension fund, with Japan's Nikkei 225 ending up 6.4% as a falling yen helped exporter stocks. Pension funds were also supporting.

The Hong Kong Hang Seng Index had rallied 13% after a similar-sized fall on Monday; "if the gains could sustain we are expecting the rebound target for the HSI to be around 16,000 during the fourth quarter of the year" compared to current levels around 12,300, said Ricky Tam, director at Champlus Asset Management.

There was much help for the Hong Kong market from banking heavyweight HSBC, up 12.1% after a 5-day, 30.0% loss.

But some emerging markets were still weak with Indonesia's index down 4.2% and Malaysia lower by 3.8%; "the concern is the whole emerging markets space is in big trouble over the next 12 months," said First NZ Capital Strategist Jason Wong.

The Japanese yen had turned sharply lower and U.S. stock futures were now well higher, with S&P 500 futures quoted up 4% and Dow futures up 243 points.

There was much event-risk on the slate the rest of the week, though, including a Federal Reserve meeting on rates, more earnings from key corporates and an estimate on third quarter U.S. gross domestic product.

Brown Brothers Harriman analysts said the GDP data would be poor, and could be a catalyst for further declines: "Bad news for the U.S. to be sure, but worse news for many other countries whose growth was largely a function of exports to the U.S.," they said.

Macquarie Equities didn't expect global equity markets to bottom until well into 2009, with a wave of earnings downgrades yet to come; "market volatility will continue as short, sharp rallies act as false signals," it said.

Japan's Nikkei 225 made an intraday recovery from a low of 6994.90; the finance minister said the government would immediately tighten regulations on so-called naked short-selling of stocks, about a week ahead of the original schedule.

Fast Retailing gained 7% after Goldman Sachs lifted that stock to a buy rating, while Fanuc gained 9.4%; the maker of factory automation systems and robots cut its full-year forecasts but not by as much as investors had feared.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 ended down 0.4%, though off a four-year low of 3724.8. Miners found support with BHP Billiton up 3.1% and Rio Tinto up 5.6%; financials were weak with National Australia Bank falling 4.3%, Suncorp-Metway down 5.7% and AMP off 5.1%.

The Kospi was aided by domestic institutions, which were net buyers of shares worth KRW320.5 billion, with pension funds purchasing shares worth KRW161.3 billion; among shipbuilders and steelmakers, Hyundai Heavy Industries jumped the daily limit of 15% and Posco soared 13.7%.

Bellwether Samsung Electronics rose 5.8%; UBS raised its rating on the stock to neutral from a sell after a 50% fall in its stock price since May this year.

Taiwan shares ended 0.8% higher after an initial fall of more than 5%; government funds bought "a few billion" Taiwan dollars' worth of shares, traders said, and also bought stock futures.

The STI was up 0.3% after an early fall of more than 6%; "after the steady selling over the past 8 weeks, there must surely be someone tempted to bottom-fish this week," said CIMB analysts.

Thai shares were a standout in southeast Asia, gaining 2.8% after a large fall Monday.

Philippine shares ended 0.6% lower after a 12% fall on Monday while Vietnamese shares ended down 2%; New Zealand shares fell 3.3% to their lowest level since July 2004, after Monday's holiday there.

In currency markets, the yen gave back its early gains. Standard Chartered Bank was tipping imminent intervention by Japanese authorities to sell the yen though there was no sign the day's action involved the Bank of Japan; rather, analysts cited the gain in the Nikkei: "Players are watching only stock price movements. I can't find any other factors," said a senior sales dealer at a major Japan bank.

The U.S. dollar was around Y95.40 from Y92.66 earlier, with the euro at Y119.96 from Y114.43; the euro was around US$1.2576. The Australian dollar was also off its lows, at US$0.6205, with intervention to buy the currency earlier by the central bank there.

Asian currencies were under pressure still; the Korean won ended at its lowest level since April 1998, with official intervention spotted to sell the U.S. dollar in Malaysia and Singapore.

Base metals came off their session lows with the euro on the rise; LME three-month copper was still down $21 at $3,999 a ton but off a low of $3,825. Spot gold was at $730.30 an ounce, up $1.70.

Front-month Nymex crude reversed early falls, even as concerns remained about the demand outlook; it was up 59 cents at $63.81 per barrel on Globex.
