title: Emerging  FX -Asians supported by c.banks as risks rise
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Intervention by central banks in Korea and Malaysia supported their currencies on Wednesday after fears over Lehman Brothers' ability to raise capital stoked a fresh round of risk aversion and selling of Asian stocks.

Trading was however subdued as market participants waited for Lehman to report its quarterly results ahead of the U.S. stock market open. The stock plunged 45 percent overnight on fears it would fail to raise the funds it needs to survive.

But as stock markets globally fell and the dollar gained against the euro <EUR=>, it was obvious that the relief provided by Washington's bailout of mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac this week was wearing off.

MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> fell 1 percent.

The Indian rupee <INR=IN> fell to 45 per dollar, its weakest in nearly two years.

Malaysia's central bank was suspected of selling dollars to defend the ringgit <MYR=> after it fell to 3.47 per dollar, its weakest in a year.

"They know that risk aversion trades are back in the market," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur. He said the Malaysian authorities would be keen to stop the ringgit from reaching 3.50, a level that could psychologically turn the market more bearish. "Also, they are trying to detach the political risk from the FX market so that's why their intervention has been a bit more aggressive these days," he said.

Political tensions have risen in Malaysia where opposition leader Anwar Ibrahim has said he will win over sufficient government legislators and take over from the ruling coalition this month.

Elsewhere, the beleaguered Korean won <KRW=> won some respite from the heavy selling that has driven it down 14 percent this year, mainly on concerns over capital flight from the country.

It rose to near 1,088 per dollar, helped by selling of dollars by the authorities. [nSEO281709]

title: UPDATE 2-Eyes on S.Korea as Asian c.banks defend  currencies
text:
(Updates levels, adds Philippine intervention)

 SINGAPORE, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Central banks in Malaysia, India and elsewhere in Asia defended their weak currencies on Tuesday, but analysts suspected that South Korea's hands-off stance may deter others from standing firmly in the way of their falling currencies.

 The Bank of Thailand said it had sold dollars to put a floor under the baht <THB=TH>, which hit a one-year low of 34.49 per dollar on growing political tensions.

 Thai Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej declared a state of emergency in Bangkok on Tuesday and gave the army control of public order after overnight clashes between pro- and anti-government protesters.

 Market participants also reported interventions in India, Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia as currencies there buckled under the U.S. dollar's broad rally, the latter hitting an 8-month high against a basket of major currencies as oil prices fell.

 "All central banks are trying their best to stop the flood of outflows," a trader in Singapore said.

 In South Korea, where the won <KRW=> has been plumbing multi-year lows, the authorities restricted their efforts to meetings, warnings. Dollar-selling intervention, if any, was light as the volatile currency hit a new 4-year low near 1,134 per dollar.

 No one is sure why the Korean authorities have loosened their grip and let the won weaken, but market participants believe it is either because they want to shore up exports or out of reluctance to spend reserves against an inevitable dollar rally.

 Analysts said Korea's indifference to won weakness could weaken the resolve of other central banks.

 "It's very difficult if one goes, particularly if it's a large and important third-markets competitor for the rest of the region, like Korea," said Simon Flint, a strategist at Lehman Brothers. "It becomes difficult for the others to resist depreciation from a trade-weighted perspective.

 "Secondly, it weakens people's belief in the ability of the central banks to intervene effectively once they have seen one central bank can't do as they have apparently said they will do."

 INDIA ALSO STEPS IN

 The Reserve Bank of India was also spotted selling dollars but the rupee <INR=IN> still continued falling to hit a new 1-½   year low of 44.35 per dollar.

 The Malaysian central bank may have sold dollars at 3.4190 and 3.4180 per dollar, a trader in Kuala Lumpur said, but the ringgit persisted with its decline.

 The rupiah <IDR=> hit a low of 9,196 per dollar, its weakest since Aug. 19. A trader in Jakarta said the central bank sold dollars from 9,190.

 "It's not large. I think they realise that there is no point intervening aggressively in a dollar bull market all over the place," said one trader in Jakarta.

 In the Philippines, the central bank was seen selling dollars as the peso <PHP=> reached 46.60 per dollar, its weakest in almost a year.  (Reporting by Vidya Ranganathan; Editing by Jan Dahinten)

title: Emerging  FX -Asia dips further on credit worries, strong dollar
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The South Korean won hit a fresh four-year low in weaker Asia on Tuesday as the U.S. dollar rose against the euro due to fears of a euro zone slowdown, while renewed concerns over credit markets stoked risk aversion.

The U.S. dollar climbed towards a six-month high against the euro <EUR=> as investors waited for European data releases later in the day for evidence of the health of the euro zone economy. The dollar also neared a two-year high against the pound <GBP=D4> hit on Monday.

The South Korean won <KRW=> fell by 1 percent to 1,089.40 per dollar, its weakest since mid-November 2004, as investors increased their short won positions on growth worries, undeterred by a prospect of intervention.

"Since the market sees that government actions are now useless, everybody is on the (dollar) bid side," a trader in Seoul said.

South Korean authorities were suspected of intervening to support the local currency in recent weeks, but the won is still the biggest loser among the Asian currencies, having lost 14 percent this year.

In Malaysia, traders said the central bank was spotted selling dollars to put a floor under the ringgit <MYR=>.

The ringgit fell as low as 3.393 per dollar to hit a nine-month low against the dollar, hurt by the central bank's decision on Monday to leave rates on hold despite rising inflation.

"CPI is so high but they haven't done anything to contain the inflation while other central banks in Asia are hiking rates," said one trader in Kuala Lumpur.

"And there is the Anwar election today. A lot of event risk," he said, referring to a by-election that opposition leader Anwar Ibrahim is contesting as he seeks to return to parliament.

MORE INTERVENTION

Traders in the Philippines also suspected authorities had intervened to support the peso <PHP=>, which fell 0.8 percent to an 11-month low of 46 against the broadly stronger dollar.

"The central bank was in the market at 45.88 and 45.98 per dollar, and now they are defending 46," a trader in Manila said.

Two other traders in Manila also confirmed the intervention.

"I think there's still demand for dollars. The market would rather hold dollar than peso," a second trader said.

Analysts at Lehman Brothers said they were watching several factors to determine currency movement in the region.

"For the rest of the week the focus will mainly be on testing key central bank intervention levels, the political theatre in Malaysia and Thailand, central bank meetings in Thailand and the Philippines, and slowing growth indicators," they said in a note.

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> extended early losses and dipped 0.6 percent to 1.4263 as market players speculated the central bank may shift its monetary policy away from battling inflation towards one more supportive of growth. "There is a lot of talk that the authorities may change the policy in October," a Singapore-based trader said. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: UPDATE:  Malaysia  Ctrl Bk:  Intervene  Only For Orderly  FX  Mkt
text:
(Adds central bank governor's comments on inflation)

KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Bank Negara Malaysia Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz said Monday that the central bank "continues to monitor" the foreign exchange market and that it will intervene only when necessary to maintain orderly market conditions.

She also said the current weakness in the ringgit, which fell to its lowest this year against the U.S. dollar Monday, reflects the dollar's recent broad strength against many currencies.

"Any intervention that we undertake is to maintain orderly market conditions; that is our priority," Zeti said.

"We will not be intervening to affect the underlying trend of the currency," she said.

Dealers believe the central bank has been intervening in the market for the past one week by selling the dollar to slow the weakening of the ringgit.

The dollar rose to MYR3.3200 Monday, its highest this year, compared with MYR3.2630 a week ago. The greenback has risen against major and regional currencies recently largely due to falling crude oil prices.

On the economy, Zeti said Malaysia's inflation rate, which hit a 26-year high of 7.7% in June, will moderate in 2009 on a likely slowdown in economic growth.

"Moderation in growth will have some dampening effect on inflation...we are already seeing commodity prices retrace," she said.

Zeti said the high inflation experienced recently was part of "the first-round effects."

"What we have to monitor is the second-round effects, and with the moderation in growth, we expect that inflation will moderate next year, particularly in the second half of the year," she said.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia trades narrowly, supported by  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, July 1 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies traded narrowly on Tuesday as investors warily held back following decade-high inflation rates in Thailand and South Korea, while authorities were suspected to have intervened in some currencies.

Foreign exchange authorities in Indonesia, Malaysia, India and the Philippines were suspected to have intervened to support their currencies.

South Korea's annual inflation in June rose to 5.5 percent from 4.9 percent in May, hitting its highest in almost 10 years.

Subsequently, the Korean won <KRW=> weakened to 1,048.75 per dollar, 0.3 percent lower than its previous close of 1,046 <KRW=KFTC>, while market players kept a look-out for possible dollar-selling intervention.

Earlier on, several currencies in the region were buoyed by a pullback in oil prices <CLc1>, which hit a record high above $143 per barrel on Monday, but these currencies gave up gains as oil prices rebounded to around $141 per barrel on Tuesday.

Still, the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> inched up by 0.1 percent to 9,215 against the dollar and held around those levels throughout the day.

Traders in Jakarta said the authorities had sold dollars everyday for the past few weeks to support the rupiah, and were doing the same on Tuesday.

"The government cannot subsidise our local oil, and this has caused higher inflation, so another way to (support growth) is to maintain the dollar/rupiah pairing at a cozy rate so our industries can run well," an Indonesia-based trader said.

Indonesia's annual inflation rate rose to a 21-month high of 11.03 percent in June, due largely to the lifting of fuel subsidies in the country.

The country's policy setting meeting will take place on Thursday, and Robert Prior-Wandesforde at HSBC said he expected a 25-basis-point hike in the present interest rate of 8.5 percent.

"We are expecting another quarter-point move on Thursday and a total of 125 basis points of hikes by the end of this year, taking the policy rate up to 9.75 percent," the economist said.

Thailand's consumer prices in June rose 8.9 percent from a year earlier, higher than the expected 8.5 percent polled in a Reuters survey. However, markets in Thailand were closed for a mid-year holiday.

MORE INTERVENTION CITED

The Indian rupee <INR=IN> fell to a 15-month low of 43.437 on heightened concerns over the impact of rising oil on the economy's growth. Traders said they suspected the central bank had been selling dollars early in the day.

Traders in Manila also cited intervention by the Philippine central bank to support the peso <PHP=>, which hit a 9-month low of 45.02.

"The central bank is protecting the peso around 44.99 to 45 per dollar," a trader said.

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> steadied around its previous closing levels of 3.265 per dollar, and traders said they suspected the Malaysian central bank had sold dollars to support the ringgit at 3.267-per-dollar throughout the day.

"Seems foreigners are not willing to touch this currency in the short term until political news is gone," a trader in Kuala Lumpur said.

Leader of Malaysia's revitalised opposition, Anwar Ibrahim, recently sought refuge at the Turkish embassy following sodomy accusations. The former deputy premier fled to the embassy fearing for his security. [ID:nKLR151860]

title: Emerging  FX -Asia falls on inflation, c.banks move to support
text:
SINGAPORE, June 5 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were weighed down by growing concerns about inflation on Thursday, as the Philippine peso fell to a 7-month low and the Thai baht hit its weakest since February against a broadly stronger dollar.

The Philippine peso <PHP=> fell below a psychologically significant level of 44-per-dollar to 44.10 in early trading on Thursday, marking its weakest level since late October.

Traders in Manila said the central bank was seen selling dollars to support the peso, which fell after the country's annual inflation in May rose to a nine-year high of 9.6 percent, above market expectations.

"Higher inflation is pressuring the peso exchange rate right now, and it is also pressuring the central bank to address the inflation pressures," a trader in Manila said.

The Philippine central bank is due to review its interest rate policy on Thursday, and economists polled were evenly divided over whether the central bank would raise rates or leave them on hold. [ID:nMAN151776]

The Thai baht <THB=TH> fell 0.9 percent to a near 4-month low of 32.885 per dollar, while the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> fell by a similar margin to 3.2660 to the dollar, its lowest since mid-May.

Traders in Kuala Lumpur said they suspected the central bank had intervened to support the currency around 3.2610.

Malaysia and India separately announced fuel price increases on Wednesday in a move to reduce subsidies, which fanned fears of the inflationary impact on economic growth in these countries and contributed selling of the currencies.

"Suffice to say I think inflation risks are on the upside," said Barclay's regional economist Wai Ho Leong, referring to the Malaysian economy.

"Clearly households might be feeling the pinch, because on one hand we don't really see the tangible relief measures being doled out in a systematic way," he said.

In light of the price reforms, economists expected Malaysia's inflation in 2008 to rise to a 10-year high of 4.7 percent, and foresee a rise in the benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 4 percent by the end of the year, a Reuters poll indicated. [ID:nSP162272]

GROWING INFLATION CONCERNS

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> fell by a fifth of a percent to 9,329 per dollar. The Indonesian central bank raised it key interest rate by 25 basis points to 8.5 percent, trumping earlier expectations for a 50-basis-point rate hike.

Analysts warned that other countries in Asia might have to follow Indonesia's lead in raising interest rates as commodity and food prices continue to push inflation higher in the region. [ID:nBNG169466]

The stronger dollar on Thursday, which hit a three-month high against the yen, also pressured Asian currencies lower.

The dollar rose against the euro <EUR=> and other major currencies, extending its gains made the previous day after the Federal Reserve chief Ben Bernanke emphasised inflation concerns, reinforcing views the central bank is done with cutting rates.

Both the Singapore dollar <SGD=> and the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP>, two currencies in Asia which investors are bullish about, fell by 0.4 percent each, with the Singapore currency inching down to a 2-1/2-week low of 1.3710 per U.S. dollar. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0817 GMT

title: UPDATE: Asia Stocks Down,  Currencies  Mostly Up; Oil In Focus
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian stocks remain lower Friday in the wake of a retreat on Wall Street, and as a new record for crude oil and stronger regional currencies add to broad economic concerns.   

"There's very little positive news to hang your hat on today," said Patrick Crabb, senior institutional trader at  Goldman Sachs JB Were in Sydney.   

Despite the risk-averse mood, regional currencies are mostly higher. The Japanese yen has caught its usual safe haven bid, a factor that is weighing on shares of Japanese exporters.   

Staying near multi-year highs are the Malaysian ringgit, Singapore dollar and Taiwan dollar, reflecting the widespread U.S. dollar bearishness now pervading markets.   

Central banks in the region continue to tolerate the moves, in a bid to counter the inflationary pressures many economies are facing due to lofty energy and commodity prices, with their absence from the market on Friday being noted by traders who expect local currencies to keep rising.   

U.S. stock futures are largely flat in screen trade but spreadbetting firms are calling European stocks to open mildly lower.   

In Asia, stocks in Japan are faring the worst, with the Nikkei 225 down 2.6% to 13,558.19. With the yen strengthening, exporters are faring particularly poorly.  Nissan Motor Co. (7201.TO) has fallen 3% to Y961 while  Sony Corp. (6758.TO) is off 4% to Y5010, and  Toyota Motor (7203.TO) down 3.2% at Y5,720.   

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 is down 1.9% at 5518.20 after touching a 5-day low of 5515.60, amid worries about the banking sector after the chief financial officer of the country's second largest bank by market capitalization,  Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA.AU), told a local newspaper that the bank is "feeling enormous pain" from funding costs. Shares of CBA are down 5% to A$41.85, while the S&P/ASX Financials subindex is off 3.7% to 5,183.   

Despite surging commodity prices, resource stocks in Australia are offering the broad market little support, with the materials and metals and mining subindexes each only up about 0.1%.   

Elsewhere, Korea's Kospi Composite is down 1.3% to 1,713.78 while Singapore's Straits Times Index is 1.9% lower at 3,017, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index is down 1.5% to 24,206.96. In India the Sensex is off about 0.6% to 17,709.64 as traders await the country's budget, due later Friday.   

The stock declines follow a retreat on Wall Street amid concerns about U.S. banks, consumers and the impact of rising oil prices. Fueling those concerns, Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke, during a second day of congressional testimony Thursday, noted that small banks could yet fail because of the housing crunch.   

And traders, who fully expect the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates by half a percent at its mid-March meeting, are now wondering if the cut might be as large as 75 basis points. Fed funds futures contracts are pricing in a 28% chance of a cut of that size.   

Those expectations have weighed on the dollar, driving it to multi-year lows against several currencies. The dollar also hit a record low against the Swiss franc; recently it was trading around CHF1.0504 after falling to CHF1.0476.   

The dollar also hit its lowest level against the yen since May 2005, and was recently around Y104.74. The Euro is around Y159.04.   

Among other Asian currencies, the U.S. dollar has fallen to a 10.5-year low of THB31.93, and is trading at 10-year lows of MYR3.1910 against the Malaysian ringgit. "We are seeing strong foreign fund buying of the ringgit, but no signs of central bank intervention as yet," a trader in Malaysia said.   

The U.S. dollar meanwhile has fallen to another 35-month low of NT$30.755.   

Mansoor Mohi-uddin, strategist at  UBS thinks the dollar will settle down in the near term.   

"Euro shorts will be forced to cover. Secondly, oil prices have made record highs, increasing the inflows into dollar-diversifying sovereign wealth funds. Thirdly, the cyclical picture has diverged sharply over the last couple of weeks between America and Europe."   

Still, dollar bulls shouldn't despair entirely, he thinks, with the dollar set for a medium-term rebound as foreign central banks are likely to be forced to cut rates. "Short-term dollar weakness now will give better levels to buy later this year."   

The dollars retreat may be contributing to gains in commodity prices, traders say. Crude oil crossed above $103 a barrel to touch a record high of $103.05 in electronic trading, before pulling back. Most recently crude was closer to $102.58, down a penny from the close of regular trading in New York.   

Spot gold is also robust, quoted up 45 cents from the New York close, at $969.95 per troy ounce, and with some expecting it to test $1,000 before long.   

But the weakening dollar may not be the biggest driver of a recent surge in commodity prices, analysts at  Barclays Capital note.   

The "current emphasis on exchange rates risks diverting attention from both the extent of commodity price increases and the key drivers of recent moves," they wrote to clients. Rather, "supply losses, strong demand and low inventory levels are the key drivers."   

Meanwhile, falling stocks have boosted government bond prices. Futures on Japan Government bonds were recently up 0.59 to 138.28, with the yield on 10-year bonds down five basis points to 1.375%.   

Also, the yield on 2-year Treasury notes was earlier quoted below 1.75%, the lowest point since April 2004, with the spread between the 2- and 10-year notes pushing out to 187.55 basis points, its widest since July 2004. Recently the 2-year yield was around 1.77%.   

Asian credit default swaps have also widened with the Markit iTraxx Asia ex-Japan investment grade index quoted at 162-172 basis points compared with 149-152 basis points Thursday.

title: MONEY TALKS:  Central Bank Currency  Angst On The Rise In Asia
text:
By Rosalind Mathieson   

A Dow Jones Newswires Column   

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian central banks have been getting a bit twitchy as their currencies continue to rise, but that doesn't mean they will try and put an end to it.   

There may be a pickup in spot market intervention, rhetoric or even administrative measures (as evidenced by Taiwan's actions of late).   

This, though, will be aimed at slowing the appreciation in regional currencies, rather than stopping it altogether.   

Governments tend to prefer weaker currencies, given the competitive advantage this provides to exporters.   

Central banks aren't as one-sided, however. Especially in times like these, when they are faced with a slower economic growth outlook but also rising price pressures.   

Letting their currencies gain - in a managed fashion - can help take some of the steam out of inflation (though only to some extent, it can't really do much about domestically-originating inflation pressures).   

So the question becomes one of relativity: Asian central banks are likely to accept some appreciation in their currency, but don't want people trying to capitalize on that by pushing currencies up in wanton fashion.   

The central banks have therefore been making their presence felt of late in several countries, in particular Singapore, Taiwan and Malaysia, where currencies have been especially strong.   

There has been suspected spot market intervention in Singapore, Malaysia and Taiwan, to buy the U.S. dollar.   

There have also been moves by the central bank in Taiwan to curtail speculation in the onshore non-deliverable forwards market, including by exporters who reportedly have been straying from using plain currency forward contracts.   

But there hasn't been the sort of barrage of rhetoric and large-scale intervention that would accompany a bid to halt a trend.   

In some cases, authorities have even cited the higher currencies as a sign of economic strength, i.e. of resilience in the face of the offshore headwinds coming from the U.S.   

And none of the central banks are likely to be silly enough to do something like slap on capital controls. They tend to not work well, for one thing.   

In the medium term, anyway, Malaysia, Taiwan and Singapore may find their currencies do some deflating on their own.   

Some of the momentum in the first two countries right now is tied up with coming elections.   

In Malaysia, that has led to some fairly large spending promises for infrastructure and other developments aimed at luring in foreign investors. Some of those pledges though may turn out to be little more that hot air, once the elections are out of the way.   

In Taiwan, the hype is all about the potential for a change in government, and for that new government to warm up the relationship with Beijing.   

That has led to a level of excitement about the potential for rapid progress in allowing investment between China and Taiwan and greater tourism. But those expectations are also at risk of disappointment - any thawing is likely to come pretty slowly, and the doors aren't going to be swung wide open to a flood of tourists from the mainland, all armed with cash and credit cards to burn.   

For Singapore, the currency is the main policy management tool, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore has been well-concerned about inflation, so authorities would think some local dollar strength is warranted. But the relatively small and export-dependent economy there is heading for a slowdown, and that may yet help bring rents and other costs down.   

Look for continued action from central banks to try and keep a lid on their currencies. But unless it turns into a large speculative attack, the action should remain relatively modest.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia listless amid uncertainty,  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were steady on Thursday as investors held back because of uncertainty over the outlook for the U.S. economy and rate decisions due in Europe later in the day.   

 Traders said the market was also cautious because central banks in the Philippines, Malaysia, India and Singapore were suspected of having intervened this week to curb strength in their currencies.   

 The U.S. dollar recovered against the yen and other major currencies overnight and held near a nine-month high against sterling <GBP=> in Asia.   

 But Asian stock markets <0#.INDEXA>, where foreigners have been heavy net sellers this year, barely moved, giving little direction to currencies.   

 The South Korean won <KRW=> initially rose 0.3 percent to hit 934.0 per dollar as local equities <.KS11> rallied, but it soon pared the gains to trade around 937.   

 A trader in Seoul said the won was stuck between 933 and 945 per dollar.   

 "There's a solid bottom for the dollar at 930 because oil companies are buying more dollars and equity outflows are continuing," the trader said.   

 "But there's also interest from shipping companies to hedge their earnings above 940 and exporters are selling options," she said.   

 Another trader felt the won would weaken to around 970 per dollar over the next few weeks, owing to outflows for dividend payments and  SK Telecom's purchase of a stake in Korean broadband provider  hanarotelecom , valued at nearly $1.2 billion.   

 SK is buying the stake from a consortium led by  American International Group and private equity fund Newbridge Capital.   

 Options traders said there was demand to sell won around 940 for one month and up to 1,000 per dollar through one-year options.   

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> was steady around 1.4310 per U.S. dollar while the Philippine peso <PHP=> fell half a percent from its previous close, backing off the highest level in nearly eight years hit on Wednesday.   

 In a volatile session, the peso rose from a low of 40.78 per dollar to hover around 40.60 before slipping again in late trading as the dollar gained against sterling and the yen.   

 "I think the peso will still appreciate. Any dollar upticks will be sold," a trader in Manila said.   

 But some analysts said the peso's long rally may have run its course for now.   

 They said a report earlier on Thursday showing Philippine exports in November fell 2 percent from a year earlier raised worries the currency's 20 percent appreciation in the past 12 months may be hurting the economy.   

 Many investors kept to the sidelines ahead of meetings by the European Central Bank (ECB) and Bank of England (BoE), and a speech by Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke later on Thursday.   

 Analysts expect the ECB to hold interest rates steady at 4.0 percent but see the BoE cutting rates due to weak consumption, which has sparked fears of a slowdown in the economy.   

 The next Fed rates decision is due on Jan. 30 and market expectations are shifting increasingly towards a cut in the Fed funds rate of as much as 50 basis points, although the majority in a Reuters poll still expected a more modest 25 basis points.

title: Emerging  FX -Asian  currencies  weaker despite stocks rally
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies weakened on Tuesday, yielding ground to a recovering U.S. dollar and failing to find any support from a rally in stock markets as traders groped for direction.   

 The Singapore dollar and Malaysian ringgit led the decline in the Asian currencies.   

 The dollar rebounded sharply from its record lows struck against the euro <EUR=> on Monday after what traders interpreted as G7 indifference towards the currency's weakness. It also climbed back against the yen <JPY=> and other currencies.   

 But trading was marked by confusion, with some looking for bargains in the oversold dollar against the Asians and others returning to risky assets. Some traders also felt the dollar's decline had been overdone -- its trade-weighted basket <.DXY> has fallen nearly 2 percent in two weeks.   

 In Asia, stocks rebounded. MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks outside Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> climbed to 554 from Monday's lows near 540. The index had its steepest fall since Aug. 16 on Monday.   

 At its weakest, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> shed 0.4 percent to hit 1.4678 per U.S. dollar, the ringgit <MYR=> lost 0.3 percent to hit 3.38 per dollar and the high-yielding Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> dropped a quarter of a percent to 9,135 per dollar.   

 The Singapore dollar subsequently rallied to 1.4650, with traders preparing for the currency to appreciate in anticipation of tighter monetary policy as inflation accelerates.   

 "There's marginal downward pressure on U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar due to inflationary pressures," said Standard Chartered Bank's strategist Thomas Harr.   

 "We are in strong end of band already. I see the pair at 1.46 by year-end."   

 Singapore's annual inflation in September was 2.7 percent, softening from a 12-year high hit in August of 2.9 percent. Still, high oil and house prices are expected to keep inflation levels elevated.   

 The currency has come off a 10-year high of 1.4577 hit last week.   

 But it has still risen 2.6 percent in the past month, a rally sparked by the Fed's 50-basis-point rate cut on Sept. 18 and positioning for Singapore's policy review on Oct. 10, when the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) increased the pace of appreciation of the currency.   

 COPYCAT RINGGIT   

 The ringgit has so far dropped half a percent in two sessions. Traders said the ringgit and Singapore dollar were moving in tandem, both undermined by suspected intervention by their respective central banks after hitting decade highs last week.   

 Traders said they would not buy the ringgit against dollars unless there was a big rise in the Singapore dollar as well.   

 "After all dollar/ringgit is negative carry if you sell dollars, so Bank Negara can always afford to buy dollars," a trader in Hong Kong said, referring to the intervention.   

Malaysia's 3.5 percent overnight policy rate is below the fed funds rate at 4.75 percent, making it more profitable to hold dollars.   

 Analysts at  JPMorgan Chase said that in contrast with the Singapore dollar, which was on the strong side of its trade-weighted band, the ringgit was trading about 180 basis points on the weaker side of an estimated informal trade-weighted policy band.   

 They also expect Malaysian inflation data due on Wednesday to show some upward pressure on consumer prices.   

 "Still, the challenge remains that the ringgit is sensitive to risk appetite and the vagaries of equity market sentiment. In this respect, we expect long ringgit positions to experience some downside and volatility this week,"  JPMorgan said.   

 Elsewhere, the Hong Kong dollar <HKD=> tested the upper end of its 7.75-7.85 linked exchange rate system to the U.S. dollar, driven by cash flows into the stock market and speculation that the peg might either be abandoned or recalibrated. [nSHA15826].   

 And the Indian rupee <INR=IN> bucked the weakness in the region, buoyed by the view that foreigners would eventually return to the stock market despite last week's curbs on some derivative investment vehicles. [nBOM232170].  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR   Change on the day at 0821 GMT

title: Emerging  FX -Asia rebounds on Fed move, but caution remains
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Asian currencies bounced back on Monday as regional stocks rallied after the U.S. Federal Reserve cut its discount rate in a surprise move on Friday, but the spectre of a credit market squeeze still weighed on sentiment.   

The Korean won <KRW=> steadied near 943 per dollar after hitting 939.9, which was up about 1 percent from late Asian trade on Friday.   

The high-yielding Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> rose as far as 9,380 per dollar, up nearly 1 percent, although it remains the worst performer in Asia this year with a loss of 4.2 percent versus the dollar.   

A Jakarta-based trader doubted that the rupiah would sustain its rally in the near term, given continuuing jitters about the U.S. subprime market crisis.   

"The subprime issue is still not finished -- there is still some doubt about it. If the subprime woes turn up again, I'm afraid the rupiah will go down again," he said.   

But Indonesia's central bank would want to stop the rupiah falling below the 9,500 level, traders said.   

Last week, central banks in Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines were reported to have intervened to support their currencies as investors fled risk amid credit market turmoil.   

MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> jumped 5.5 percent following a rebound in U.S. stocks on Friday after the Fed cut its discount rate.   

Leading the pack, Indonesian stocks <.JKSE> jumped 6.6 percent, while South Korean shares <.SK11> surged 5.7 percent.   

NOT OUT OF THE WOODS   

Rising local stocks helped drive the Singapore dollar <SGD=> as far as 1.5240 per U.S. dollar, up almost 0.9 percent from late Asian trade on Friday and its strongest in nearly a week.   

Elsewhere, the Thai baht <THB=THB> rose as high as 34.30 per dollar, up more than 0.8 percent, while the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> gained about 0.6 percent to 3.491 to the dollar.   

Philippine markets were closed for a public holiday.   

Many analysts remained cautious as fears of a global credit squeeze persisted, even though the Fed's statement accompanying its discount rate cut fuelled expectations that it could be moving towards lowering its benchmark fed funds rate target.   

Thomas Harr, a currency strategist at Standard Chartered Bank, said he would refrain from telling his clients to buy into Asian currencies for now, despite the recovery in Asian stocks.   

"I think what we are seeing today is obviously a little bit of recovery, which is natural given that the Fed at least did something by cutting the discount rate on Friday," he said.   

"But the feeling in the market is that this may not improve liquidity that much. It's not clear that we are out of the woods yet and we expect the market to be choppy in the coming days." The Japanese yen, which has moved in the opposite direction to most emerging Asian currencies in recent sessions as investors unwound carry trades, eased against the dollar <JPY=> after pulling back from a 14-month high on Friday. title: Emerging  FX -Asian high-yielders buckle under credit fears
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 15 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso, Indonesian rupiah and Singapore dollar hit multi-week lows on Wednesday as investors extended their aggressive sales of risky assets on fears U.S. credit market woes were spreading overseas.   

The high-yielding peso <PHP=> fell 0.8 percent to 46.27 per dollar, a five-week low, while the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, another high-yielder, fell to 9,412 per dollar, its weakest point since June 2006.   

Traders in Jakarta said Bank Indonesia must have sold between $800 million and $900 million as it tried to brake the rupiah's decline and stop it from slipping beyond 9,400 per dollar. Central banks in Malaysia and the Philippines were also suspected of intervening to support their currencies.   

The euro <EUR=>, sterling <GBP=> and Australian and New Zealand dollars fell as investors moved out of higher-yielding assets and bought back the low-yielding yen <JPY=>. The yen hit a 4-1/2-month high against the dollar.   

A Reuters poll showed market participants were pushing back the possibility of a rise in official Japanese rates to September from August. The euro has also been hurt by a paring of the chances of a rate rise by the European Central Bank next month.   

"Indonesia will, of course, be an issue when you have this kind of risk aversion because of the high yields," said UOB Bank strategist Jimmy Koh.   

Koh said he was more worried about other asset markets than about currencies.   

"So far it has been an issue of market sentiment. But it can become a fundamental issue if there is a sharp pullback in liquidity and that introduces a risk premium into other sectors of the economy, thereby dampening consumption," Koh said.   

POSITIONS UNWOUND   

Markets in South Korea and India were closed for holidays. The Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell more than half a percent to the weaker side of 1.53 per U.S. dollar. The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> hit 3.4930 per dollar, its weakest since the end of June. "Currently, we're having a bit more pressure on the Asian currencies as a result of base dollar strength, not so much against the yen but more against European currencies," said Thio Chin Loo, a currency strategist at  BNP Paribas.

"It's just a symptom of unwinding of risk across the board and this has affected Asian currencies as well," she added.   

The flow of bad news from credit markets has not abated.   

Concern grew after a U.S. investment firm wanted to halt redemptions on Tuesday and a Canadian trust couldn't find funds to repay some short-term debt.   

Wal-Mart , the world's largest retailer, cut its profit forecast and Swiss Bank  UBS warned that market turmoil was likely to hit its investment banking business.   

"We continue to see price action driven primarily by crisis management and position liquidation rather than active decision making," said  Bank of America strategist Christy Tan.   

"We're still in the midst of a deleveraging environment," she said.

title: UPDATE 1-FACTBOX-How central banks have acted to inject funds
text:
(Updates with no action from Fed)   

FRANKFURT, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Global central banks are withdrawing much of the extra cash they have injected into banking systems to calm panicky credit since last Thursday.   

Below is a list of central bank actions since the credit markets upheaval turned nasty last week.   

EUROPEAN CENTRAL BANK

Aug 9 - 94.8 billion euros ($129.8 billion) in a one-day tender on Thursday, the largest amount ever.   

Aug 10 - 61.05 billion euros ($83.61 billion) in a three-day tender on Friday to cover the weekend,   

Aug 13 - 47.67 billion euros ($65.29 billion) in one-day money on Monday   

Aug 14 - 7.7 billion in one-day money on Tuesday. The ECB also added an extra 73.5 billion euros in one-week money more than its estimated liquidity needs for banks during its main refinancing operation.   

Trichet also issued a statement on Tuesday calling for investors to stay composed composure in face of market volatility and a repricing of risk.   

The ECB's injections exceed those that it flooded into markets immediately after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks on the United States. At that time, 69.3 billion euro in overnight money was allocated on Sept. 12, 2001, followed by 40.5 billion euros the next day.   

U.S. FEDERAL RESERVE   

Aug 9 - $24 billion during its regular market operations, only slightly above the usual allocation.   

Aug 10 - Added $38 billion through three separate repurchase agreements, its biggest single-day cash injection since Sept. 19, 2001. The repos brought down the federal funds rate, the cost of overnight loans between banks, to the Fed's target rate of 5.25 percent.   

Aug 13 - Added $2 billion of temporary reserves to the banking system through overnight repurchasing agreements.   

Aug 14 - The Fed took the unusual step of refraining from an open market operation at 9:30 a.m. (1330 GMT), when daily operations are usually conducted. In an earlier statement, the Fed said it was evaluating whether or not to conduct an operation at that time and said it stood ready to conduct additional operations later in the day as needed.   

BANK OF JAPAN   

Aug 10 - Added 1.0 trillion yen ($8.45 billion) at its regular money market operation on Friday after a slight rise in the benchmark overnight call rate, the highest amount in about six weeks. Traders said the amount was at the higher end of market expectations, but was not a major surprise.   

Aug 13 - Added 600 billion yen ($5.1 billion) into the banking system in a one-week operation.   

Aug 14 - Drained 1.6 trillion yen ($13.6 billion) in two operations.   

BANK OF ENGLAND   

The Bank of England said banks hit by tough credit conditions could use its emergency lending facility, which is routinely available and priced at 100 basis points above the bank's 5.75 percent policy rate.   

BANK OF CANADA   

Aug 9 - Injected C$1.64 billion ($1.55 billion) on Thursday, saying it was in contact with other central banks on the global situation and stood ready to add money as needed.   

Aug 10 - Injected a total of C$1.685 billion ($1.605 billion)   

Aug 13 - Injected C$670 million.   

THE RESERVE BANK OF AUSTRALIA   

Aug 10 - The RBA added more than twice the usual amount of money into the banking system, injecting A$4.95 billion ($4.19 billion).   

Aug 14 - The RBA added A$2.6 billion ($2.2 billion) in its regular morning money market operation, slightly higher than average.   

SWISS NATIONAL BANK   

Aug 9/10 - The SNB offered banks money at a below-market rate of 2.6 percent on Thursday and Friday, adding a total of 3.1 billion Swiss francs ($2.57 billion) <CHF=>. It since has started to drain the extra liquidity.   

Aug 13/14 - Traders said the SNB drained liquidity as overnight rates remained low after the previous week's liquidity-providing actions.   

CENTRAL BANKS OF MALAYSIA, INDONESIA, PHILIPPINES   

Traders said the Asian central banks intervened in foreign exchange markets on Friday to support their currencies by selling U.S. dollars. Malaysia's central bank chief Zeti Akhtar Aziz said on Monday there was sufficient liquidity in its financial system, but that it was monitoring the situation.   

BANK OF KOREA   

South Korea's central bank said on Friday it was ready to add funds to markets if needed.   

CENTRAL BANK OF NORWAY   

The central bank said Thursday's loan of 45 billion crowns ($7.80 billion) gave ample liquidity to banks and it would continue to ensure orderly operations in the money market.

title: UPDATE 2-Asian c.banks support  currencies , welcome weakness
text:
(adds comments, other central banks)   

SINGAPORE, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Central banks in Malaysia, Taiwan and elsewhere in Asia intervened to sell dollars on Friday to support their currencies during a broad sell-off of riskier assets, but some policy makers openly welcomed the weakness.   

The Indonesian and Philippine central banks were also suspected of selling dollars through state-owned banks to stem falls in the peso and rupiah.   

The Philippine peso <PHP=> fell nearly a percent from Thursday's close before being supported at the day's low of 45.75.   

"I heard they sold dollars at 45.75 and I am still seeing offers at that level," said a trader in Manila, referring to suspected intervention.   

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> continued to hit one-year lows.   

At the same time, Indonesian Vice President Jusuf Kalla told reporters weakness in the rupiah, already Asia's worst performer this year, should be good for the country's exports.   

The Bank of Thailand, which was rumoured to have bought dollars to weaken the currency in the past week, barely flinched during the baht's <THB=TH> quarter percent decline to 34.09 per dollar.   

David Mann, a currency strategist at Standard Chartered Bank, said the Asian central banks were quite possibly intervening just to smooth movements in their currencies.   

"They are happy to see some more two-way risks priced into the market rather than a one-way bet mentality," he said.   

"In my view, they are also quite glad to see a correction in the over-enthusiastic pricing of risk."   

The sell-off in risky assets gathered momentum on Thursday after news French bank  BNP Paribas had frozen funds hit by the troubled U.S. subprime mortgage sector. The European Central Bank pumped funds into European money markets and the U.S. Federal Reserve also injected cash on a smaller scale.   

The Malaysia ringgit <MYR=> fell to 3.48 per dollar, a low point seen at the end of June, before suspected central bank intervention. Traders said the Malaysian central bank sold dollars around 3.4780/90.   

However, a senior Bank of Korea official said the central bank would not supply dollars to ease what it regarded as a lack of short-term supplies in the market.   

Singapore's central bank said it stood ready to supply funds to the market if needed.   

Still, the Asian currencies stayed close to their lows, with the ringgit quoted near 3.48.   

"I think they are in the market to smooth excessive volatility," said Emmanuel Ng, a strategist at  OCBC Bank.

"In this environment, especially with central banks like the ECB, Fed and the BOJ injecting liquidity to forestall any systemic stress, the market is understandably jittery.   

"In such a scenario, further weakness in Asian currencies cannot be ruled out, simply because of risk aversion and the fact that funds may have to be re-channelled," he said.

title: Emerging  FX -Rupee powers to 9-year high, won at 16-week peak
text:
SINGAPORE, April 23 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee extended gains to a nine-year high versus the dollar on Monday, outpacing most other Asian currencies on strong capital inflows.   

 Foreign buying in South Korea's equity market helped push the won <KRW=> to a 16-week high, while the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> tested last week's nine-year peaks before suspected dollar-buying intervention by the central bank pushed the currency down.   

 Asia's other currencies nudged lower, with a rally in the yen encouraging investors to unwind yen carry trades for now. Most regional units have benefited from such trades that involve selling the low-yielding yen to fund investments in assets that offer a higher yield.   

 The rupee <INR=IN> briefly rose to 41.56 per dollar, its highest level since May 1998, helped by a rally in the stock market <.BSESN> and news on Friday that India's annual inflation rate unexpectedly jumped back above 6 percent in early April.   

 It has gained more than 6 percent this year, putting it clearly ahead as Asia's best performing currency against the dollar. This month alone the rupee has jumped 4 percent.   

 "Everybody's looking at the rupee and there has been a sudden surge of interest in the Indian currency," said BNP Paribas currency strategist Thio Chin Loo.   

 "People are searching for value in Asia and the fact that the Indian rupee hadn't moved that much, so traders are looking at the opportunities there."   

INTERVENTION CAUTION   

 Dealers said wariness about central bank intervention to curb rupee strength forced the currency to give up some of its gains.   

 And elsewhere in the region, dealers remained watchful of possible dollar-buying intervention by central banks.   

 A trader in Kuala Lumpur said Malaysia's central bank was suspected of intervening in the market after the ringgit strengthened to 3.42 per dollar -- matching a nine-year high set at the end of last week.   

 "I think they (the central bank) were in the market at 3.42," said the trader. "Given the strong sentiment towards Malaysia, we will break 3.42 soon."   

 The won rose to 925.10 per dollar, its highest level since Jan. 3, amid strong foreign buying of Korean shares.   

 The benchmark KOSPI <.KS11> share index hit a record high on Monday and foreign investors were net buyers for a seventh consecutive session, bringing their total during that period to a net 1.2 trillion won ($1.30 billion) worth.   

 Still, the upbeat won sentiment was tempered slightly by wariness about intervention.   

 On Friday, South Korea warned speculators against piling borrowed foreign funds into the won, and the central bank said monitoring of the currency market had shown excessive speculative trading of foreign currencies by some companies.   

 "We suspect this reflects genuine worries about the possibility of a new surge in exporter selling taking dollar/won still lower," ABN AMRO currency strategist Shahab Jalinoos said in a note to clients.   

 "Exporters such as shipbuilders have been less active in the market than in 2006, but in recent days their presence has been noted."   

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> touched a fresh six-year high at 47.43 per dollar before declining to a session low at 47.67 as investors booked profits on recent peso gains.   

 A trader in Manila said he did not think the central bank had stepped into the market to curb the peso, although it has been suspected of intervention in the last few weeks.   

 "We hit 47.43 and then there was some profit-taking and some short-covering," he said. "It looks like some people were looking to reverse the market."

title: Emerging  FX -Sing dlr pushed off highs, peso hits six-year peak
text:
SINGAPORE, April 10 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar was knocked back from 9-1/2-year highs on Tuesday by suspected central bank intervention, but the Philippine peso climbed to a six-year peak thanks to inflows that had piled up over Easter.   

 Wariness about official intervention to curb currency gains kept other Asian units in a tight range, although sentiment remained positive due to the firm tone in equity markets.   

 Stronger-than-expected economic growth and the central bank's decision to stick to a policy of modest currency appreciation lifted the Singapore dollar to 1.5110 per U.S. dollar <SGD=>.   

 But the gains proved fleeting and it fell as low as 1.5188 on suspected U.S. dollar-buying intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).   

 Still, dealers said the central bank's monetary policy stance and optimism about the economy meant that bullish sentiment towards the local dollar would hold sway.   

 "We definitely had first-quarter GDP on the strong side of expectations, so that would seem to indicate that Singapore is handling the downturn in the electronics cycle quite well," said Magnus Prim, chief strategist for Asia at SEB.   

 "The MAS still has a modest tightening bias and that basically translates into a stronger currency, even though at this point in time we are at the stronger end of the band and that is why we probably saw them intervening."   

 Singapore's economy grew an annualised 7.2 percent in the first quarter, well above forecasts, although a little slower than in the previous quarter.   

 The central bank maintained its policy of a "gradual and modest appreciation" in the Singapore dollar. It uses the exchange rate rather than interest rates to conduct monetary policy and guides the currency in a secret trade-weighted band.   

 "I think the Sing dollar will continue to appreciate against the U.S. dollar but in a slow creeping movement," said Alvin Cheng, a trader at  Fortis Bank Hong Kong Branch.   

 PESO IN DEMAND   

 The peso <PHP=> rose as far as 47.94 per dollar, compared with about 48.05 late on Wednesday, April 4, when Philippine markets were last open before an extended Easter break.   

 "The market is expecting inflows from over the long weekend -- a combination of remittances and equity flows," said a trader in Manila, explaining the peso's rally.   

 "A strong break of the 48 level would lead us to test the 47.50 area."   

 Some traders thought the Philippine central bank had stepped into the market to stall a rapid appreciation of the peso.   

 There was also caution about possible intervention in South Korea and Malaysia.   

 The won <KRW=> held a narrow range between 932 and about 934 per dollar. The ringgit <MYR=> was steady at 3.4455 per dollar, having touched a nine-year high at about 3.4420.   

 Elsewhere, the Thai baht <THB=TH> was little moved at about 34.95 to the dollar in the onshore market.   

 Traders expected the currency to come under pressure after army-appointed Prime Minister Surayud Chulanont was admitted to hospital on Monday for a four-day medical check-up amid rumours he would resign.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia powers ahead as Fed modifies tone
text:
SINGAPORE, March 22 (Reuters) - Asian currencies extended this week's gains on Thursday as the Federal Reserve removed a reference to possible interest rate rises in a policy statement, dealing a blow to the U.S. dollar.  

 However, as the regional currencies rallied, investors grew wary of central bank intervention to cap the gains.  

Malaysia's ringgit <MYR=> hit a nine-year high at 3.4560 per dollar after the country's central bank governor expressed support for a stronger currency late on Wednesday.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose 0.5 percent to a 9-½   year peak at 1.5165 per U.S. dollar, the South Korean won <KRW=> hit a one-month high at about 936 per dollar and the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> jumped 0.8 percent to a three-week high at 9,070 to the dollar.  

 On Wednesday, the Fed left rates steady at 5.25 percent, as expected. But the shift in tone in its policy statement knocked the dollar to a two-year low versus the euro <EUR=>.  

 The statement also triggered a rally in stocks, helping markets to recover further from the beating they took earlier this month on worries that weakness in the U.S. housing sector could spread to the broader economy.  

 Asia's stock markets notched up strong gains <.MSCIAPJ>. Tokyo's Nikkei share average <.N225> rose to a three-week high. The high-yielding Australian dollar <AUD=> briefly touched a 10-year peak against the dollar in another sign of a pick up in risk appetite.  

 "The Fed statement seems to be taken favourably by emerging markets and this is reflected by the weaker yen and stronger Aussie, which is an indication of the return of carry trades," said Bank of America currency strategist Christy Tan.  

 "This puts Asian currencies that have been suffering on the rebound."  

 Asia's high-yielding currencies have seen some of the strongest gains in the region this week. The rupiah, for instance, has risen almost 1.7 percent against the dollar.  

 SPOTLIGHT ON MALAYSIA  

 In Kuala Lumpur, an apparent change in the authorities' long-held view of favouring a cheap currency hogged the spotlight.  

 In the past two days, both the prime minister and central bank governor have expressed support for a stronger ringgit.  

 On Wednesday Malaysia further relaxed foreign exchange rules.  

 But some analysts say that rather than signalling a change in policy, Malaysia is reiterating its tolerance of gradual appreciation in the currency, with the central bank still expected to intervene in the market to limit sharp moves.  

 "They are now warming up to ringgit strength if the currency moves gradually," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur, referring to the government and central bank. "What they don't want is a shock to the market."  

 Still, the latest measures were seen boosting investor sentiment towards the ringgit and paving the way for fresh gains.  

 "Malaysia's currency measures encourage inflows and outflows. But in the current environment they encourage more inflows and this has been endorsed by the central bank, so the ringgit is staged for further appreciation," said Tan at Bank of America.  

CENTRAL BANK SPOTTING  

Malaysia's central bank was suspected of intervening, while dealers said the Philippine central bank was seen buying dollars for pesos around 48.25 <PHP=>.  

 In Singapore, traders said that although there was some caution, the central bank was not expected to intervene just yet given the momentum behind the Singapore dollar's rally.  

 The currency has firmed about 0.6 percent in the past two days.  

 "Dollar/Sing after breaking 1.5240 support should have momentum to 1.5150 and lower," said a trader.  

 "Intervention is just to smooth the fall.. and I don't think the MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore) will be too keen to buy U.S. dollars at this level as the Sing dollar is strong on the crosses."  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR  Change on the day at 0754 GMT

title: *S&PGR Affirms Malaysia Ratings; Outlook Stable
text:
27 Jun 2023 06:27 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Affirms Malaysia Ratings; Outlook Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- As the Malaysian economy recovers from the pandemic-related slowdown, 
we believe its medium-term growth prospects are better than most other 
sovereigns at similar income levels. 
     -- Although its fiscal consolidation plans were delayed, we expect the 
growing economy and conducive policymaking to gradually stabilize government 
finances. 
     -- We affirmed our 'A-/A-2' foreign currency and 'A/A-1' local currency 
sovereign credit ratings on Malaysia. 
     -- The stable outlook reflects our expectations that Malaysia's steady 
growth momentum and strong external position will hold over the next two 
years. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On June 27, 2023, S&P Global Ratings affirmed its 'A-' long-term and 'A-2' 
short-term foreign currency sovereign credit ratings on Malaysia. We also 
affirmed our 'A' long-term and 'A-1' short-term local currency ratings on 
Malaysia. 
 
The outlook on the long-term rating remains stable. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The stable outlook reflects our expectations that Malaysia's steady growth 
momentum and fiscal policy will allow modest improvements in fiscal 
performance over the next two to three years. 
 
Downside scenario 
We may lower the ratings if economic growth suffers a prolonged downturn that 
lowers the trend growth in real GDP per capita to levels in line with that of 
peers. Downward rating pressure could also build if political stability in 
Malaysia deteriorates such that policymaking becomes materially less 
predictable. 
 
Upside scenario 
We may raise the ratings on Malaysia if fiscal outcomes outperform our 
forecasts. Such a scenario may be realized through continuing political 
stability that would narrow deficits sustainably. Consequently, government net 
debt would fall below 60% of GDP or interest payments decline below 10% of 
government revenues. 
 
RATIONALE 
Our ratings on Malaysia are underpinned by the country's strong external 
position and monetary policy flexibility. In addition, its trend economic 
growth rate is faster than sovereigns of similar income level. 
 
Although Malaysia's budget deficits remain high, we expect its growth dynamics 
to offset vulnerabilities associated with an elevated government debt stock 
and weak fiscal performance. Political commitment to resume fiscal 
consolidation post-pandemic also exists, in our view. 
 
Institutional and economic profile: Medium-term growth prospects remain 
healthy; more conducive policymaking environment on abated political risks 
     -- Malaysia's real GDP growth accelerated to 8.7% in 2022, sustained by 
strong exports, high energy prices, and pent-up domestic demand following the 
reopening of the economy. 
     -- Growth in 2023 will moderate to 4% from a high base effect and a 
weaker global growth environment. 
     -- Following the November 2022 elections, the political landscape appears 
to be less fluid with the formation of a new coalition government. 
 
Malaysia's growth momentum from 2022 has continued into this year, with 
first-quarter GDP rising 5.6% year on year. This was underpinned by a further 
improvement in employment, recovery in tourism activity, and continued capital 
investments on both private and public fronts. Nevertheless, we expect 
full-year economic expansion to moderate to 4% as a weakened global growth 
environment takes hold. 
 
The Malaysian economy is well-diversified and has a record of resilience 
following periods of adversity. It has a mature electrical and electronics 
(E&E) sector that supplies components and finished products to major global 
players. We forecast the economy will expand on average 4.5% annually over 
2024-2026. With this, Malaysia's 10-year weighted average per capita GDP 
growth will be 3.6%, which is well above the global median for peers at 
similar income levels. 
 
We project Malaysia's GDP per capita to be about US$12,500 in 2023, lower than 
most peers' in the same rating category but notably higher than that of most 
of its Southeast Asian neighbors except Singapore and Brunei. 
 
After the landmark 2018 elections, which saw the end of United Malays National 
Organisation (UMNO) party's 61 years of uninterrupted rule, Malaysian politics 
entered an era of flux and uncertainty. With no single party able to command 
parliamentary majority, the past five years has seen a number of changes in 
government leadership, parties with wide ideological differences forming 
unstable coalitions, and parliamentarians frequently switching camps. 
 
The general elections in November 2022 resulted in the formation of a new 
coalition government under Pakatan Harapan (PH). Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim 
became the Prime Minister of Malaysia. He is the fifth in five years. Although 
PH won 82 seats, the party did not reach the simple majority of 112 seats 
needed to form government. As a result, the coalition relies on support from 
partners led by UMNO and includes parties representing the East Malaysian 
states of Sabah and Sarawak. 
 
Malaysia's institutions have supported generally effective policymaking for a 
long time. We believe the depth of institutional strength mitigates the risk 
of political instability. Uncertainties regarding policymaking have somewhat 
subsided under the new Anwar administration. The anti-party hopping law, which 
was passed in October 2022, appears to be effective so far in preventing 
lawmakers from jumping ship to destabilize the ruling government. 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: Weak fiscal profile balanced by a solid 
external position 
     -- Deficits will remain elevated in 2023 owing to an expansionary budget 
to support the economy. 
     -- The fiscal position remains weak, but consolidation should resume from 
2024 with economic recovery well on track and a more stable policy environment. 
     -- Malaysia's strong external metrics remain a key anchor of the ratings. 
 
Malaysia's budget for 2023 remains expansionary to support growth momentum and 
alleviate inflationary pressures. That said, with the country in endemic mode, 
expenditure needs are likely to be lower now that COVID-19 support measures 
have ended. Hence, we forecast the net indebtedness of Malaysia's general 
government will rise by 4.4% of GDP in 2023, versus a 5.0% increase in 2022, 
on moderately lower general and central government deficits. 
 
We believe healthy economic growth, alongside fiscal prudence, will be key to 
improving Malaysia's public finances. Net general government debt as a share 
of GDP last year declined to 65.7% from 70.3% in 2021. The double-digit 
nominal GDP growth had outpaced the increase in government indebtedness. 
 
The pandemic has significantly delayed the government's fiscal consolidation 
plans. With the economy now anchored on a sustained growth path, reduced need 
for fiscal stimuli, and a more conducive policymaking environment, we believe 
the government is in a position to resume its consolidation. We forecast net 
general government debt will stabilize at about 68% of GDP in 2023-2026, with 
the annual change averaging 4.1%. 
 
Despite the high energy prices last year, fiscal settings did not fully 
benefit. Increased royalties and duties from higher commodity prices are 
largely offset by generous fuel subsidies to the populace. The Malaysian 
government derives around 20% of its total revenue from petroleum-related 
sources. The single largest component of this revenue is the dividend paid by 
state oil company Petroliam Nasional Bhd. (Petronas). The company paid an 
exceptionally high dividend of Malaysian ringgit (MYR) 50 billion dividend in 
2022 and is budgeted to pay MYR40 billion in 2023. 
 
The PH government replaced the goods and service tax (GST) in June 2018 with a 
sales and services tax, a narrower program that mobilizes less revenue. For 
fiscal consolidation to take hold sustainably, on top of healthy economic 
growth, we believe the government will try to  raise more revenue or reduce 
subsidies or both. Notably, the current administration has begun making 
inroads into a medium-term fiscal framework and enacting a Fiscal 
Responsibility Act. 
 
The Malaysian government identifies guarantees that it has provided for 
various entities that may be unable to service their debt. We have included 
such committed guarantees in our calculation of general government debt due to 
the high likelihood that they will crystallize on the general government's 
balance sheet. 
 
These guarantees include but are not limited to those extended to 
government-linked firms Danainfra Nasional Bhd., Prasarana Malaysia, Malaysia 
Rail-link Sdn. Bhd., and Urusharta Jamaah Sdn. Bhd. We estimate the 
government's total committed direct guarantees at 11.5% of GDP. As such, our 
calculation of the general government's net debt is higher by an equivalent 
amount. We also include legacy liabilities associated with state-linked 
investment firm 1MDB. As of end-2022, the government's 1MDB-related liability 
was MYR18.2 billion, and we incorporate it into the general government's 
balance sheet. By the end of 2023, most of the 1MDB liabilities would be 
extinguished with one remaining MYR5 billion (0.3% of GDP) sukuk maturing in 
2039. 
 
Committed guarantees have consistently risen in recent years, and we believe 
this will remain the case over the next three years as the government 
continues to support key infrastructure projects and associated firms. But as 
a share of GDP, these committed guarantees should hold steady or decline, in 
our view. 
 
We believe contingent liabilities to the government from the banking sector is 
limited. Private sector leverage, as measured by total private sector debt 
(including corporate borrowings from the debt capital markets) to GDP, has 
been gradually building in Malaysia since 2008. Some borrowers may be 
vulnerable to prevailing economic difficulties and rising interest rates. 
However, we expect credit risk for the Malaysian banking system to remain 
manageable, supported by banks' prudent lending and underwriting standards. 

27 Jun 2023 06:27 ET 
Press Release: S&PGR Affirms Malaysia Ratings; -2-


Our Banking Industry Country Risk Assessment for Malaysia is '4' ('1' being 
the strongest assessment and '10' the weakest). 
 
Malaysia's solid external position remains a rating strength. The country has 
had consistent current account surpluses for more than two decades. We 
forecast the current account surplus will stabilize around 3% of GDP over the 
next three years, driven by a gradual recovery in tourism and continued strong 
demand for Malaysian manufacturing exports will support the country's trade 
accounts. 
 
Most of Malaysia's external liabilities are denominated in the domestic 
currency, while external assets--both official foreign exchange reserves and 
other claims on nonresidents--are denominated in foreign currencies. 
 
The Malaysian economy's external position is subject to some market 
volatility. This includes periods of amplified risk aversion, which could lead 
to nonresidents reducing their holdings of local currency government debt. 
Foreign ownership of Malaysian government securities typically accounts for 
15%-25% of the total outstanding stock. We estimate Malaysia's ratio of gross 
external financing needs to current account receipts and usable reserves will 
average 91% over 2023-2026. 
 
The IMF classifies Malaysia's foreign-exchange regime as floating, with 
intermittent intervention in the foreign exchange market. The Malaysian 
ringgit depreciated substantially in 2014-2017 amid the reset in global 
commodity prices. However, pass-through of this depreciation into inflation 
was limited. In part, we believe this reflected relatively well-anchored 
inflation expectations in the country. In our view, the central bank has 
significant independence, which is unlikely to change in the medium term. 
 
The consumer price index in Malaysia had increased in 2022 to 3.4%, in line 
with higher global prices and supply-side constraints. However, we expect CPI 
inflation to come in by the end of this year at a modest 2.8%. This is because 
of the government's generous subsidies on fuel and food staples which cap 
prices. 
 
Malaysia has a deep domestic bond market, which reduces reliance on 
foreign-currency financing. The country's high share of nonresident holders of 
ringgit-denominated government bonds leaves the country's capital markets 
exposed to potential fund outflows. But the market has generally remained 
stable, with limited impact on the ringgit, since the onset of the pandemic. 
This reflects healthy external demand for Malaysian government debt. 
 
We estimate Malaysia's reserve coverage will be 4.6 months of current account 
payments at the end of this year. Although lower than historical levels, it 
remains sufficient, and we expect Malaysia's deep capital markets to support 
financial stability.

The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
     -- On June 27, 2022, S&P Global Ratings revised the outlook on its 
sovereign ratings on Malaysia to stable from negative, while affirming the 
'A-/A-2' foreign and 'A/A-1' local currency ratings. 
     -- We revised the outlook on the long-term foreign currency issuer credit 
rating on Telekom Malaysia Bhd . to stable from negative while affirming our 
'A-' long-term foreign currency ratings on the company and on its senior 
unsecured notes. 
     -- We affirmed our 'A-' long-term local currency rating on Telekom 
Malaysia  with a stable outlook. 
     -- The stable outlook mirrors the outlook on the sovereign rating on 
Malaysia, and our view that the credit profile of the Malaysia-based 
fixed-line operator is intrinsically linked due to its relationship with the 
government. 
 
SINGAPORE (S&P Global Ratings) June 28, 2022--S&P Global Ratings today took 
the rating actions listed above. 
 
We revised the outlook on our foreign currency issuer credit ratings on 
Telekom Malaysia  to stable from negative following a similar rating action on 
the Malaysia sovereign credit rating (foreign currency A-/Stable/A-2; local 
currency A/Stable/A-1). 
 
The company's performance will likely remain sensitive, to some extent, to 
government policies. This is given the government's majority ownership in the 
company--including government-related shareholders, the Malaysian government 
owns more than 60% of Telekom Malaysia . The government also owns a special 
share in Telekom Malaysia  via the Ministry of Finance (Incorporated), which 
enables it to ensure Telekom Malaysia 's direction is in line with government 
policies. Furthermore, the government had previously intervened to improve 
connectivity in the country at the expense of the company's near-term 
earnings. We believe the risk of such intervention will persist in the 
medium-term because Telekom Malaysia  will remain instrumental to the 
government's intent to improve broadband speed and coverage in the country. 
 
The stable outlook on Telekom Malaysia  reflects our view that the company will 
remain the dominant fixed-line player in Malaysia and maintain its 
debt-to-EBITDA below 2.5x over the next 12-24 months. 
 
We may lower the rating if Telekom Malaysia 's debt-to-EBITDA ratio moves to 
2.5x. This could happen if (1) its competitive position or operating 
performance deteriorate materially because of heightened competition or 
regulatory pressures; or (2) the company's capital spending or shareholder 
distributions are much higher than we anticipate. 
 
We may also lower our ratings on Telekom Malaysia  if we lower the sovereign 
ratings on Malaysia. 
 
We may revise Telekom Malaysia 's stand-alone credit profile upward if: (1) the 
company maintains its operating performance and adopts a conservative 
financial policy, as reflected in the ratio of debt to EBITDA staying close to 
1.5x on a sustained basis; or (2) the company significantly improves its 
market position in the wireless segment while maintaining a debt-to-EBITDA 
ratio of about 2x. 
 
The long-term ratings remain constrained by the sovereign foreign currency 
rating.
