title: *S&PGR Revises Malaysia Outlk To Stable; Afrms Ratings
text:
27 Jun 2022 05:47 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Revises Malaysia Outlk To Stable; Afrms Ratings


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- Malaysia is mounting a strong economic recovery from the 
pandemic-driven slowdown and we believe its medium-term growth prospects are 
better than most other sovereigns at similar income levels. 
     -- Though its fiscal consolidation plans were delayed, we expect the 
growth dynamism of the economy and conducive policymaking to gradually 
stabilize government finances. 
     -- We revised our rating outlook on Malaysia to stable from negative. At 
the same time, we affirmed our 'A-/A-2' foreign currency and 'A/A-1' local 
currency sovereign credit ratings on Malaysia. 
     -- The stable outlook reflects our expectations that Malaysia's steady 
growth momentum and strong external position will hold over the next two 
years. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On June 27, 2022, S&P Global Ratings revised the outlook on its long-term 
sovereign credit ratings on Malaysia to stable from negative. 
 
At the same time, we affirmed our 'A-' long-term and 'A-2' short-term foreign 
currency sovereign credit ratings on Malaysia. We also affirmed our 'A' 
long-term and 'A-1' short-term local currency ratings on Malaysia. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The stable outlook reflects our expectations that Malaysia's steady growth 
momentum and strong external position will remain in place over the next two 
years. At the same time, we anticipate the policymaking environment will be 
supportive of restoring fiscal settings to a firmer footing. 
Downside scenario 
We may lower the ratings if economic growth suffers a prolonged downturn that 
lowers the trend growth in real GDP per capita to levels in line with that of 
peers. Downward rating pressure could also build if political stability in 
Malaysia deteriorates such that policymaking becomes materially less 
predictable. 
Upside scenario 
We may raise the ratings on Malaysia if fiscal outcomes outperform our 
forecasts. This would be shown from net debt stock falling below 60% of GDP or 
interest payments less than 10% of general government revenues. 
 
RATIONALE 
We revised the outlook to stable in recognition of Malaysia's consistently 
strong growth trend that is faster than sovereigns of similar income level. 
Though Malaysia's budget deficits remain high, we expect its growth dynamics 
to offset vulnerabilities associated with its weak fiscal settings. In 
addition, political commitment to resume fiscal consolidation post-pandemic is 
strong, in our view. 
Our affirmed ratings on Malaysia reflect the country's strong external 
position, monetary policy flexibility, and record of supporting sustainable 
economic growth. The country's elevated government debt stock and weak fiscal 
performance temper these strengths. 
Institutional and economic profile: Medium-term growth prospects had 
strengthened with strong external demand and COVID-19 contained; more 
conducive policymaking environment on abated political risks. 
     -- With COVID-19 under control, Malaysia has resumed full economic 
activities and reopened its international borders, supporting recovery this 
year. 
     -- Real GDP growth will accelerate to 6.1% in 2022 and 5.0% in 2023, 
sustained by strong exports, high commodity prices and domestic demand 
following reopening of the economy. 
     -- Political landscape remains fluid but more certainty now on 
policymaking with the government reaching a compromise with the opposition. 
 
Following Malaysia's uneven recovery last year, we are projecting a strong 
pick up in its GDP growth to hit 6.1% for 2022. Growth was curtailed in 2021 
(3.1%) by an acute outbreak of the delta variant, which resulted in strict 
countrywide lockdowns and distancing measures. In the first quarter of this 
year, growth surprised on the upside to accelerate to 5% year on year. This 
was driven by solid performance in the manufacturing sector, in particular 
electrical and electronic goods (mainly semiconductors). 
 
We believe this strong growth momentum will persist in the second half of the 
year. Malaysia is a net energy exporter and major producer of crude palm oil 
(CPO). The country is well positioned to benefit from the high commodity price 
environment. Despite pressures from Russia-Ukraine war and global supply-chain 
disruptions, we envisage the easing of domestic COVID-19 restrictions, 
sustained demand, and strong labor market to contribute to economic recovery. 
 
The Malaysian economy is well-diversified and has a record of resilience 
following periods of adversity. It has a mature electrical and electronics 
(E&E) sector that supplies components and finished products to major global 
players. We expect E&E, along with the oil and gas sector taking gains from 
high energy prices, to drive strong exports over the next one to two years. We 
forecast the economy will expand on average 4.7% per annum over 2023-2025. 
With this, Malaysia's 10-year weighted average per capita GDP will be close to 
3%, which is well above the global median for peers at similar income levels. 
 
We project Malaysia's GDP per capita to be about US$11,900 by end-2022, lower 
than most peers' in the same rating category but notably higher than that of 
most of its Southeast Asian neighbors except Singapore and Brunei. 
 
Since the collapse of the Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition in March 2020, the 
political landscape of Malaysia remains fluid. In August 2021, Muhyiddin 
Yassin  who led as prime minister for 17 months after the PH government broke 
up, lost his majority support due to struggles within his Perikatan Nasional 
(PN) coalition. Amid this political leadership crisis, Ismail Sabri Yakoob of 
the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) was appointed prime minister. 
This marked the third new prime minister appointed since the 2018 elections, 
following a 61-year period of uninterrupted rule under UMNO. 
 
Malaysia's institutions have supported generally effective policymaking for a 
long time, and we believe their depth of capacity mitigates the risk of 
instability owing to ongoing political developments. Notably, the government 
proactively introduced stimulus measures aimed at supporting the economy as 
the pandemic raged on over the last two years. The Sabri-led administration 
has also gained recognition for successfully combating COVID-19. On the back 
of rapid deployment of vaccines and booster shots, viral caseloads had come 
down significantly. Domestic COVID-19 restrictions began easing since the 
start of the year and on April 1, the country entered endemicity phase with 
the full reopening of borders and resumption of all economic activities. 
 
Though there remains political fluidity, we believe uncertainties regarding 
policymaking have somewhat subsided. In September 2021, the government signed 
a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the opposition. The MOU addresses 
bipartisan cooperation on Budget 2022, political stability and long-term 
political reforms. Hence, we expect fewer disruptions to policy directions 
until at least the next general elections (which are due by September 2023). 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: Weak fiscal profile balanced by a solid 
external position; Malaysia's fiscal consolidation path to resume 
post-pandemic. 
     -- High energy prices have yet to benefit fiscal revenues and deficits 
will remain elevated in 2022 owing to an expansionary budget to restart the 
economy. 
     -- The fiscal position remains weak, but consolidation should resume from 
2023 with economic recovery well on track and a more stable policy environment. 
     -- Malaysia's strong external metrics remain a key anchor of the ratings. 
 
Malaysia's budget for 2022 remains expansionary to manage the lingering 
effects of the pandemic and restart the economy. That said, with Malaysia 
entering endemic mode, expenditure needs in areas such as healthcare and 
direct fiscal transfers are likely to be lower. Hence, we forecast the net 
indebtedness of Malaysia's general government will rise by 5.1% of GDP in 
2022, versus a 6.4% increase in 2021, on moderately lower general and central 
government deficits. 
 
The pandemic has significantly delayed the government's fiscal consolidation 
plans. With the full reopening of the economy, reduced need for fiscal 
stimuli, and a more conducive policymaking environment, we believe the 
government is committed to resume its consolidation trajectory from next year. 
As a result, we forecast net general government debt will stabilize at about 
70% of GDP from 2022-2025, with the annual change averaging 4%. 
 
That said, despite prevailing high energy prices this year, fiscal settings 
have yet to benefit and remain weak. Increased royalties and duties from 
higher commodity prices are largely offset by generous fuel subsidies to the 
populace. Therefore, historically we had observed a general lag effect from 
high crude oil prices to fiscal revenue boost. The Malaysian government 
derives slightly less than 20% of its total revenue from oil-related sources. 
The single largest component of this revenue is the dividend paid by state oil 
company Petroliam Nasional Bhd . (Petronas ). The company paid a MYR25 billion 
dividend in 2021 and is budgeted to pay the same amount in 2022. In our view, 
upside to fiscal revenues will come on stream in 2023 should Petronas  
experience windfall profits this year and declare a higher dividend next. 
 
The PH government replaced the goods and service tax (GST) in June 2018 with a 
sales and services tax, a narrower program that mobilizes less revenue. For 
fiscal consolidation to take hold on a sustained basis, on top of healthy 
economic growth, we expect the government to make significant efforts to 
restore its revenue-generating framework. Notably, the current administration 
has begun inroads into a medium-term fiscal framework and enacting a Fiscal 
Responsibility Act. 
 
Malaysia's general government balance sheet also carries contingent risks from 
the country's public enterprises and guarantees. These include legacy

liabilities associated with state-linked investment firm 1MDB. We estimate the 
government's 1MDB-related liabilities at MYR17.5 billion at end 2022 and 
incorporate it into the general government's balance sheet. Come 2023, most of 
the 1MDB liabilities would be extinguished with one remaining MYR5 billion 
(0.3% of GDP) sukuk maturing in 2039. 
 
The Malaysian government also identifies guarantees that it has provided for 
various entities that may be unable to service their debt. We have included 
such committed guarantees in our calculation of general government debt due to 
the high likelihood that they will crystallize on the general government's 
balance sheet. 
 
These guarantees include but are not limited to those extended to 
government-linked firms Danainfra Nasional Bhd., Prasarana Malaysia, Malaysia 
Rail-link Sdn. Bhd., and Urusharta Jamaah Sdn. Bhd. We estimate the 
government's total direct liability to these firms at 12.8% of GDP. As such, 
our calculation of the general government's net debt is higher by an 
equivalent amount. 
 
Committed guarantees excluding the 1MDB obligations have consistently risen in 
recent years, and we believe this will remain the case over the next three 
years as the government continues to support key infrastructure projects and 
associated firms. But as a share of GDP, these committed guarantees should be 
steady, in our view. 
 
Malaysia's solid external position remains a rating strength. The country's 
current account achieved a strong surplus equivalent to 3.8% of GDP in 2021. 
We envisage a modest increase in the surplus this year to 4% with strong 
exports from E&E and the energy sector. We forecast the current account 
surplus will stabilize above 3.5% of GDP over the next three years as a 
gradual recovery in tourism and continued strong demand for Malaysian 
manufacturing exports will support the country's trade accounts. 
 
Most of Malaysia's external liabilities are denominated in the domestic 
currency, while external assets--both official foreign exchange reserves and 
other claims on nonresidents--are denominated in foreign currencies. 
 
The Malaysian economy's external position is subject to some market 
volatility. This includes periods of amplified risk aversion, which could lead 
to nonresidents reducing their holdings of local currency government debt. 
Foreign ownership of Malaysian government securities typically accounts for 
15%-25% of the total outstanding stock. We estimate Malaysia's ratio of gross 
external financing needs to current account receipts and usable reserves will 
be about 91.9% in 2022, and gradually fall to about 89.4% by 2025. 
 
We classify Malaysia's foreign-exchange regime as floating, with intermittent 
intervention in the foreign exchange market. The Malaysian ringgit depreciated 
substantially in 2014-2017 amid the reset in global commodity prices. However, 
pass-through of this depreciation into inflation was limited, burnishing the 
central bank's inflation management credentials. In our view, the central bank 
has significant independence, which is unlikely to change in the medium-term. 
 
The consumer price index (CPI) in Malaysia has been edging up recently in line 
with higher global prices and supply-side constraints. However, we expect CPI 
inflation to come in by the end of this year at a relatively modest 2.9%. This 
is because of the government's generous subsidies on fuel and food staples 
which cap prices. 
 
Private sector leverage, as measured by total private sector debt (including 
corporate borrowings from the debt capital markets) to GDP, has been gradually 
building in Malaysia since 2008. Some borrowers may be vulnerable to 
prevailing economic difficulties and rising interest rates, especially in the 
sectors hit hardest by the pandemic. However, we expect credit risk for the 
Malaysian banking system to remain manageable, supported by banks' prudent 
lending and underwriting standards. 
 
Our Banking Industry Country Risk Assessment for Malaysia is '4' ('1' being 
the strongest assessment and '10' the weakest). 
 
Malaysia has a deep domestic bond market, which reduces reliance on 
foreign-currency financing. Malaysia's relatively high share of nonresident 
holders of ringgit-denominated government bonds leaves the country's capital 
markets exposed to potential fund outflows; but the market has generally 
remained stable, with limited impact on the ringgit, since the onset of the 
pandemic. This reflects healthy external demand for Malaysian government debt. 
 
The retention of Malaysian government securities in the FTSE Russell bond 
index has reduced uncertainty for the Malaysian bond market and the associated 
risks of a deterioration in Malaysia's external settings. We also believe the 
central bank is committed to a floating exchange rate, despite financial 
market volatility. 
 
We estimate Malaysia's reserve coverage will be 4.7 months of current account 
payments at the end of this year. Though lower than historical levels, it 
remains sufficient, and we expect Malaysia's deep capital markets to support 
financial stability. Our forecast assumes that reserve coverage will continue 
to decline to 4.3 months through 2025.

title: *S&PGR Affirms Malaysia Ratings; Outlook Negative
text:
22 Jun 2021 05:03 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Affirms Malaysia Ratings; Outlook Negative


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- Malaysia faces continued pressure on its fiscal settings given its 
near-term economic outlook amid a worsened domestic COVID-19 situation and a 
fluid political backdrop. 
     -- The country's solid economic recovery prospects from 2022 onward 
should act as a tailwind for fiscal consolidation. 
     -- We affirmed our 'A-' long-term and 'A-2' short-term foreign currency 
sovereign credit ratings on Malaysia. We also affirmed our 'A' long-term and 
'A-1' short-term local currency ratings. The outlook on the long-term rating 
remains negative. 
 
RATING ACTION 
SINGAPORE (S&P Global Ratings) June 22, 2021--S&P Global Ratings today 
affirmed its 'A-' long-term and 'A-2' short-term sovereign credit ratings on 
Malaysia. We also affirmed our 'A' long-term and 'A-1' short-term local 
currency ratings on Malaysia. The outlook on the long-term ratings remains 
negative. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The negative outlook reflects our expectation that Malaysia faces heightened 
risks to its fiscal and economic recovery prospects over the next 12-24 months 
related to the COVID-19 pandemic and domestic political uncertainty. 
 
Downside scenario 
Our ratings on Malaysia could face downward pressure over the next 12-24 
months if economic growth suffers a deeper or more prolonged downturn than we 
expect, or if we see a weaker commitment to fiscal consolidation. Both these 
situations could result in the faster accumulation of net general government 
debt. Change in net general government debt surpassing 4% on a sustained 
basis, net indebtedness surpassing 80% of GDP, or interest paid by the general 
government exceeding 15% of revenue would indicate such deterioration. 
 
Downward ratings pressure could also build if political stability in Malaysia 
deteriorates such that policymaking becomes materially less predictable, or if 
the country's external position weakens such that the economy's annual gross 
external financing needs surpass current account receipts plus usable 
reserves. 
 
Upside scenario 
We may revise the outlook to stable over the next 12-24 months if the 
Malaysian economy grows considerably faster than we forecast, or the policy 
environment becomes more conducive to credible fiscal consolidation. This 
would in turn produce a stronger fiscal performance than we expect, leading to 
a quicker stabilization of government finances. 
 
RATIONALE 
Our affirmed ratings on Malaysia reflect the country's strong external 
position, monetary policy flexibility, and record of supporting sustainable 
economic growth. The country's elevated government debt stock and evolving 
fiscal policy settings temper these strengths. 
 
The negative outlook reflects enduring pressures on Malaysia's fiscal and debt 
settings, which have been further undermined by a worsening domestic COVID-19 
situation this year. Higher fiscal deficits in 2020 and this year, alongside a 
more muted near-term economic recovery, will keep the Malaysian government's 
net indebtedness close to 70% of GDP. Heightened political uncertainty 
compounds the challenges that the government will face in rapidly 
consolidating its finances over the next two to three years. 
 
Institutional and economic profile: Near-term COVID-19 challenges and 
continued political risk are balanced against healthier medium-term recovery 
prospects 
     -- The serious state of Malaysia's COVID-19 situation and strict 
containment measures will limit the scale of its economic recovery this year. 
     -- Real GDP growth will accelerate to 6.3% in 2022, versus a 4.1% 
forecast this year, supported by vaccine-derived immunity and the gradual 
re-opening of the economy. 
     -- Support for the governing Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition, which has 
been ruling under a state of emergency since January 2021, is difficult to 
gauge. Malaysia's policymaking is clouded by political uncertainty. 
 
We have lowered our 2021 real GDP growth forecast for Malaysia to 4.1% from 
6.2% to incorporate the considerable impact of the tightening of the 
government's Movement Control Order (MCO) since June 1. Though Malaysia's 
severe COVID-19 wave has stabilized over the past two weeks, the broader 
spread of the virus has likely undermined economic activity. 
 
We expect the majority of the impact to economic activity to be felt in the 
second quarter of 2021. The recovery will likely be gradual in the third 
quarter owing to the cautious reopening that the government has indicated. 
Critically, some economic sectors are allowed to operate with strict safety 
procedures, subject to approval under a positive listing process. As such, 
activity will not be affected to the same extent as during the first MCO in 
the second quarter of 2020. 
 
We expect Malaysia's economic recovery to gain pace as the government's 
inoculation drive progresses, and targets are met for a broader reopening of 
activities. Near-term targets include a decline in national daily positive 
cases to less than 4,000, improvement in the capacity utilization of key 
healthcare infrastructure, and 10% inoculation of the population. 
 
The Malaysian economy is well-diversified and has a record of resilience 
following periods of adversity. The country's manufacturing sector is 
well-oriented to take advantage of a global surge in demand for electronics. 
Malaysia has a mature electrical and electronics sector that supplies 
components and finished products to major global players. We expect this 
sector to drive strong exports over the next one to two years, in particular. 
 
The Malaysian economy is likely to grow at an above-trend rate in 2022 and 
2023, before settling toward a more sustainable long-term rate of expansion in 
line with its historical performance. 
 
We project Malaysia's GDP per capita to be about US$11,100 by end-2021, lower 
than most peers' in the same rating category but notably higher than that of 
most of its Southeast Asian neighbors except Singapore and Brunei. 
 
Malaysia's PN coalition has been in power since March 2020, following the 
collapse of the Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition. PN is anchored by 
representatives of the Bersatu party, as well as the Barisan Nasional (BN) 
coalition, including key constituent party United Malays National Organization 
(UMNO). This marked Malaysia's second change of government in less than two 
years, following a 61-year period of uninterrupted rule under BN up to 2018. 
 
Malaysia's institutions have supported generally effective policymaking for a 
long time, and we believe their depth of capacity alleviates the risk of 
instability owing to ongoing political developments. Notably, the government 
proactively introduced stimulus measures aimed at supporting the economy as 
the pandemic worsened in 2020. However, Malaysia's COVID-19 situation has 
worsened considerably this year, and the government is facing pressure from 
various constituencies, including some within the PN coalition itself. 
 
Fissures within the government, as well as the broader parliament, appear to 
be material, calling into question the longevity and strength of PN's mandate. 
 
Further changes in government are increasingly likely once the current state 
of emergency, implemented in January of this year, is lifted. 
 
BN leaders have indicated that the coalition will not work with the broader PN 
coalition, nor key constituent party Bersatu, when the next set of elections 
are held. 
 
The high level of political uncertainty in Malaysia undermines clarity 
regarding the government's fiscal policy trajectory, and elevates the risk 
that fiscal consolidation targets will not be met over the coming years. 
 
The Malaysian government has introduced numerous stimulus packages since 
February 2020. The latest "Permerkasa+" package announced prior to 
reinstatement of the heightened MCO measures is worth Malaysian ringgit (MYR) 
40 billion. This takes the total value of stimulus measures, inclusive of PH's 
first package in February 2020, to MYR380 billion. Direct fiscal injections, 
budgeted at MYR65 billion in November 2020, account for only a fraction of 
this total, but we believe that this component could increase further 
depending on the severity of the pandemic, and concomitant economic 
difficulties. 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: Malaysia faces a steepening road to 
fiscal consolidation 
     -- Malaysia's fiscal deficit will remain elevated in 2021 owing to a 
weaker economic outlook. 
     -- A higher shortfall this year will make consolidation over the next two 
to three years more challenging as the government balances fiscal restraint 
against the need to support the nascent economic recovery. 
     -- Malaysia's fiscal consolidation also faces policy risks related to the 
country's uncertain political landscape. 
 
We forecast the net indebtedness of Malaysia's general government will rise by 
6.6% of GDP in 2021, versus a 6.3% increase in 2020, on slightly higher 
general and central government deficits, and continued accumulation of 
committed guarantees. 
 
The much wider scale of Malaysia's COVID-19 situation this year will play a 
key role in the government's fiscal performance. The containment measures will 
hit revenue generation, and expenditure needs are likely to be higher than 
programmed in areas such as healthcare and direct fiscal transfers. As a 
result, we forecast net general government debt will average 70% of GDP from 
2021-2024, with the annual change averaging 4.8%. The general government's 
fiscal deficit this year is likely to be its highest since the global 
financial crisis in 2009. 
 
The Malaysian government derives slightly less than 20% of its total revenue 
from oil-related sources. The single largest component of this revenue is the 
dividend paid by state oil company Petroliam Nasional Bhd . (Petronas). The 
company paid a MYR34 billion dividend in 2020. This reduced the downward 
effect on government revenue from much lower oil prices in 2020.

However, Petronas' dividend to the government for 2021 is likely to be much 
lower. It is currently budgeted at MYR18 billion, partially reflecting adverse 
business conditions in the previous year. Despite higher prevailing oil 
prices, this will limit upside prospects for Malaysia's revenue growth in 
2021. 
 
The PH government's decision to zero-rate Malaysia's goods and services tax 
(GST) in June 2018 weakened the government's revenue generation capacity; GST 
previously contributed nearly 20% to government revenue. We believe the GST 
helped the government to maintain sound fiscal metrics following the 2014-2015 
global collapse in commodity prices, and considerably reduced the government's 
dependence on commodity revenues. The PH government replaced the GST with a 
sales and services tax, a narrower program that mobilizes less revenue. Amid 
heightened uncertainty around how long the current government will last, as 
well as the pandemic, it remains to be seen what efforts the government can 
make to restore its revenue-generating framework. 
 
To cap its fiscal deficit at about 6% of GDP this year, the government will 
need to achieve savings through the rationalization of operational and capital 
expenditure. It may also require additional support from some 
government-related entities, while higher commodity prices should help to 
alleviate the impact on government revenues stemming from strict COVID-19 
containment measures and a slower economic recovery in the second quarter of 
2021. 
 
The strong financial performance of companies such as Petronas and Khazanah 
Nasional Bhd . lends some additional flexibility to the government's fiscal 
profile, though aggregate dividends are likely to be lower than in 2020. 
 
Malaysia's general government balance sheet also carries contingent risks from 
the country's public enterprises and guarantees. These include legacy 
liabilities associated with state-linked investment firm 1MDB. We estimate the 
government's 1MDB-related liabilities at MYR31 billion and incorporate it into 
the general government's balance sheet. 
 
The Malaysian government also identifies guarantees that it has provided for 
various entities that may be unable to service their debt. We have included 
such committed guarantees in our calculation of general government debt due to 
the high likelihood that they will crystallize on the general government's 
balance sheet. 
 
These guarantees include but are not limited to those extended to 
government-linked firms Danainfra Nasional Bhd., Prasarana Malaysia, Malaysia 
Rail-link Sdn. Bhd., and SRC International Sdn. Bhd. We estimate the 
government's total direct liability to these firms on a net basis at more than 
10% of GDP. As such, our calculation of the general government's net debt is 
higher by an equivalent amount. 
 
Committed guarantees excluding the 1MDB obligations have consistently risen in 
recent years, and we believe this will remain the case over the next three 
years as the government continues to support key infrastructure projects and 
associated firms. 
 
Malaysia's solid external position remains a rating strength. The country's 
current account achieved a solid surplus equivalent to 4.4% of GDP in 2020. We 
envisage a moderate decline in the surplus this year as imports, income 
accounts, and transfers begin to normalize. We forecast the current account 
surplus will stabilize modestly above 3% of GDP over the next three years as a 
gradual recovery in tourism and continued strong demand for Malaysian 
manufacturing exports will support the country's trade accounts. 
 
Most of Malaysia's external liabilities are denominated in the domestic 
currency, while external assets--both official foreign exchange reserves and 
other claims on nonresidents--are denominated in foreign currencies. 
 
The Malaysian economy's external liquidity requirements, on a gross basis, are 
considerable; its external liquidity is therefore subject to market 
volatility. This includes periods of amplified risk aversion, which could lead 
to nonresidents reducing their holdings of local currency government debt. 
Foreign ownership of Malaysian government securities typically account for 
15%-25% of the total outstanding stock. We estimate Malaysia's ratio of gross 
external financing needs to current account receipts and usable reserves will 
be about 93.9% in 2021, and gradually fall to about 92.6% by 2024. 
 
We classify Malaysia's foreign-exchange regime as floating, with intermittent 
intervention in the foreign exchange market. The Malaysian ringgit depreciated 
substantially in 2014-2017 amid the reset in global commodity prices. However, 
pass-through of this depreciation into inflation was limited, burnishing the 
central bank's inflation management credentials. 
 
The consumer price index (CPI) in Malaysia has been edging up recently in line 
with higher global prices and supply-side constraints. We expect CPI inflation 
to moderate to 3.3% by the end of this year. In our view, the central bank has 
significant independence, which is unlikely to change under the current 
government. 
 
Although high household debt remains a risk for the banking system and the 
broader economy, it has been gradually declining relative to GDP. We believe 
risks are contained by banks' strong capitalization and a generally sound 
regulatory framework. Household financial assets are also ample. 
 
Private sector leverage, as measured by total private sector debt (including 
corporate borrowings from the debt capital markets) to GDP, has been gradually 
building in Malaysia since 2008. Some borrowers may be vulnerable to 
prevailing economic difficulties, especially in the sectors hit hardest by 
pandemic restrictions. However, we expect credit risk for the Malaysian 
banking system to remain manageable, supported by banks' prudent lending and 
underwriting standards. 
 
Banks' exposure to segments that are most at risk amid the weakened economy is 
manageable, in our view. These segments include lower-income households, 
micro, small, and midsize enterprises, and some corporate sectors that are 
most vulnerable to COVID-19, such as commercial property developers and 
hospitality. 
 
Our Banking Industry Country Risk Assessment for Malaysia is '4' ('1' being 
the strongest assessment and '10' the weakest). 
 
Malaysia has a deep domestic bond market, which reduces reliance on 
foreign-currency financing. Although Malaysia's relatively high share of 
nonresident holders of ringgit-denominated government bonds leaves the 
country's capital markets exposed to potential fund outflows, the market has 
generally remained stable, with limited impact on the ringgit, since the onset 
of the pandemic. This reflects healthy external demand for Malaysian 
government debt. 
 
The retention of Malaysian government securities in the FTSE Russell bond 
index has reduced uncertainty for the Malaysian bond market and the associated 
risks of a deterioration in Malaysia's external settings. We also believe the 
central bank is committed to a floating exchange rate, despite financial

The Malaysian central bank  has in recent years typically maintained a sizable

We estimate Malaysia's reserve coverage will be 4.7 months of current account

financial stability, our forecast assumes that reserve coverage will continue

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Thai baht firms on cenbank  intervention  doubts,  Malaysia  shares climb
text:

    * Indonesian markets closed for a holiday
    * Baht hovers near key support level
    * Malaysia's Public Bank announces bonus share issue

    By Anushka Trivedi
    Dec 9 (Reuters) - The Thai baht hit a near one-year high on
Wednesday as traders sold dollars amid expectations that the
Bank of Thailand will intervene to stem the currency's rapid
rise, while Malaysian equities jumped more than 1%, lifted by
Public Bank.
    The baht firmed 0.2% to 30.04 against the dollar
and has now recouped most of its losses made this year since a
breakthrough in coronavirus vaccine in November brightened the
outlook for the trade and tourism-reliant Thai economy.
    The Bangkok index is on track to gain over 2% in two
sessions after the country eased curbs on tourist arrivals,
while foreign equity inflows have added to the baht's strength,
which Thai exporters on Tuesday urged the central bank to curb
at 30.0 per dollar mark.
    "There was 'panic USD selling' among exporters once baht
rose beyond 30.15 on expecting support from Bank of Thailand ...
and given no currency briefing by BoT as previously expected,
some exporters may be in wait and see mode and could rush to
sell dollars more once baht rises above 30 level," said Poon
Panichpibool, markets strategist at Krung Thai Bank.
    The Bank of Thailand, which cancelled a planned briefing on
currency measures, may not intervene at this level but could use
unconventional tools like quantitative easing as well as debt
monetisation to limit the baht's gains, Poon added.
    Other Asian currencies rose against a softer greenback
, with the Taiwanese dollar leading gains at 1%
stronger.
    However, the Indian rupee failed to capitalise,
dropping 0.1%, on suspicions the country's central bank was
mopping up inflows to prevent its rise.
    In the equity markets, Malaysia's index scaled a
16-month peak after the country's second-largest lender Public
Bank Bhd announced a bonus share issue, which
brokerage MIDF Research said would improve the bank's liquidity
and the stock's affordability.
    Positive sentiment from a strong finish at Wall Street on
progress in coronavirus vaccines spilled over to Asia as most
stock markets made big gains.
    South Korea's KOSPI rose 1.4% and Singapore shares
 advanced 0.6%.
    Financial markets in Indonesia were shut due to a public
holiday.
 
    HIGHLIGHTS

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Indonesia, Malaysia among Asia's top pct losers; rupiah slides again
text:
* Bank Indonesiaintervenes in spot market
    * Petronas units among losers in Malaysia as oil prices drop
 
    * Malaysia central bank meets on Thursday 
    * Graphic: World FX rates http://tmsnrt.rs/2egbfVh

    Sept 9 (Reuters) - Indonesian, Malaysian and Philippine
stocks led declines in Asia's emerging markets on Wednesday, as
a global sell-off in technology stocks helped the dollar find
some support, which in turn weighed on regional currencies.
    Moving into afternoon trade, currencies were mostly lower
with Indonesia's rupiah falling the most, which forced
the central bank to intervene.
    The currency has fallen nearly 1.5% over the past week and
lost another 0.5% on Wednesday, as concerns about government
influence over its central bank dominated headlines.
    In Malaysia, the listed units of state-run oil and gas group
Petronas were among the top percentage losers, while in Jakarta,
Medco Energi Internasional plunged the most as oil
prices fell below $40 a barrel on worries over demand.
    Indonesia's main index fell 2% to a one-month low,
while the Malaysian index dropped as much as 1.9% to its
lowest since the end of June.
    A slim majority of economists expect Bank Negara Malaysia to
shave 25 basis points off its main rate on Thursday, bringing it
to a record low of 1.5% to help offset the impact of the
coronavirus crisis and jump start its economy.
    The central bank has already slashed rates by 125 bps this
year, but ING economist Prakash Sakpal argued that the ringgit's
 4% rise against the dollar since June should give the
bank more room for manoeuvre. 
    The ringgit dipped 0.2% against the dollar.
    A top Indonesian minister told Reuters that the country must
synchronise monetary and fiscal policies better to tackle the
economic fallout of the pandemic, but said the government does
not back a proposal for a monetary board to oversee Bank
Indonesia.
    The rupiah is suffering from concerns over the proposed
changes to the central bank charter as well as selling of
Indonesian bonds, which are among the region's favourite
high-yielding carry trades for foreign investors, said Wei Liang
Chang, a macro strategist at DBS.
    The country's external debt was $408.6 billion in the second
quarter, the central bank said https://www.bi.go.id/en/ruang-media/info-terbaru/Pages/Utang-Luar-Negeri-Indonesia-Triwulan-II-2020-Meningkat.aspx("https://www.bi.go.id/en/ruang-media/info-terbaru/Pages/Utang-Luar-Negeri-Indonesia-Triwulan-II-2020-Meningkat.aspx")#
 in August, adding up to 37.3% of gross domestic product.
    A bi-weekly bond auction on Tuesday raised 22 trillion
rupiah, but total bids fell to their lowest in more than four
months.

    ** Indonesian 10-year benchmark yields up 2.4 basis points
to 6.907%​​
    ** Top percentage losers on Malaysia's benchmark index
 were Top Glove Corp and Hartalega Holdings

    ** Malaysia's 3-year benchmark yield up 0.5 basis points to
1.859%

stocks led falls in Asia's emerging stock markets on Wednesday,
as a tech sector sell-off drove a wave of global selling and a
drop in oil prices added to the pain for Malaysia's
state-controlled oil companies. 
    Currency markets across the region were more resilient,
although Indonesia's rupiah again suffered after a week
dominated by concerns about government influence over its
central bank, forcing the bank to intervene again in markets.
    In Kuala Lumpur, the listed units of state-run oil
and gas group Petronas were among the top losers as oil prices
fell below $40 a barrel for the first time since June on worries
over demand.
    The index fell as much as 1.9% to its lowest since the end
of June.
    With central banks across the region cutting interest rates
to offset the impact of the coronavirus crisis, a slim majority
of analysts expect Bank Negara Malaysia to shave another 25
basis points off its main rate on Thursday, bringing it to a
record low of 1.5%.
    The central bank has already slashed rates by 125 bps this
year but ING economist Prakash Sakpal argued that the ringgit's
 4% rise against the dollar since June should give the
bank more room for manoeuvre. 
    The ringgit dipped 0.2% against the dollar in morning trade.
    The rupiah has fallen more than 1% in the past week
and it was down another 0.5% on Wednesday, with the central
bank's head of monetary management telling Reuters it had
intervened to calm spot currency markets.
    Wei Liang Chang, a macro strategist at DBS, said the rupiah
was continuing to suffer from concerns over proposed changes to
the central bank charter as well as selling of Indonesian bonds,
among the region's favourite high-yielding carry trades for
foreign investors.
    A bi-weekly bond auction on Tuesday raised 22 trillion
rupiah, but the total bids fell to their lowest in more than
four months.
    A top Indonesian minister told Reuters that the country must
synchronise monetary and fiscal policies better to tackle
economic pressures caused by the pandemic, although the
government does not back a proposal for a monetary board to
oversee Bank Indonesia.

title: *S&PGR Revises Malaysia Outlook To Neg; Ratings Affirmed
text:
26 Jun 2020 06:13 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Revises Malaysia Outlook To Neg; Ratings Affirmed


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- The economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, combined with depressed 
oil prices and fiscal stimulus, will weaken the Malaysian government's debt 
position for the next few years. 
     -- We are revising our outlook on Malaysia to negative to reflect 
additional downside risk to the government's fiscal metrics, owing to the weak 
global economic climate and heightened policy uncertainty. 
     -- We are affirming our 'A-' long-term and 'A-2' short-term foreign 
currency sovereign credit ratings on Malaysia. We are also affirming our 'A' 
long-term and 'A-1' short-term local currency ratings. 
     -- Our ratings on Malaysia balance the country's strong external 
position, monetary policy flexibility, and track record of supporting 
sustainable economic growth, against its elevated government debt stock, and 
evolving fiscal policy settings. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On June 26, 2020, S&P Global Ratings revised its outlook on Malaysia's 
long-term ratings to negative from stable. We affirmed our 'A-' long-term and 
'A-2' short-term foreign currency sovereign credit ratings, as well as our 'A' 
long-term and 'A-1' short-term local currency ratings on Malaysia. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The negative outlook reflects our expectation that Malaysia faces heightened 
risks of a further deterioration in its fiscal settings, related to the 
COVID-19 pandemic, over the next 24 months. 
 
Downside scenario 
Our ratings could face downward pressure if economic growth suffers a deeper 
or more prolonged downturn than we currently expect, or if we see a weaker 
commitment to fiscal consolidation, either of which could result in the faster 
accumulation of net general government debt. Downward ratings pressure would 
arise if Malaysia's annual change in net general government debt surpasses 4% 
on a sustained basis, or interest paid by the general government exceeds 15% 
of revenue. Downward ratings pressure could also build if political stability 
deteriorates such that policymaking becomes materially less predictable. 
 
Upside scenario 
We may revise the outlook to stable over the next 24 months if the economy 
grows considerably faster than we forecast and, in turn, produces a stronger 
fiscal performance than we expect, leading to a quicker improvement in 
government finances. 
 
RATIONALE 
We revised the outlook to negative to reflect pressures on Malaysia's fiscal 
and debt settings, which have been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. 
Higher fiscal deficits this year and next, alongside a forecast contraction in 
real GDP this year, will likely lead to the Malaysian government's net 
indebtedness surpassing 60% of GDP. Against an unforgiving global 
macroeconomic backdrop, heightened domestic political uncertainty is adding 
downside risks to the government's fiscal position. We weigh these risks 
against Malaysia's strong external position, sound long-term growth prospects, 
and well-established monetary policy credibility. 
 
Institutional and economic profile: The economy faces a steep downturn in 
2020, and will likely stabilize from 2021 onward 
     -- We forecast a 2% contraction in the Malaysian economy in 2020, 
reflecting the deep effects of the pandemic. 
     -- The economy will likely begin to stabilize thereafter, and we forecast 
a strong recovery to 7.5% growth in 2021. 
     -- Malaysia faces heightened political uncertainty owing to marginal 
support for the ruling Perikatan Nasional coalition in parliament. 
 
We forecast real GDP growth contracting by 2% in 2020 as COVID-19 hits 
Malaysia's trade flows, investment, and private consumption. Strict domestic 
containment measures against the virus were introduced in March, and have been 
gradually lifted since May. Although the measures appear to have been 
successful in preventing a much more serious local epidemic, they will have 
significantly curtailed economic activity in second-quarter 2020, and it will 
take some time for the economy to recover from the lockdown. Like many 
economies around the world, this will be Malaysia's worst economic performance 
in many years--underscoring the deep effects of the global economic and health 
crisis. There could be additional downside risk to this forecast should the 
pandemic last longer than expected, or if the global economy does not 
meaningfully recovery in 2021. 
 
Nevertheless, the Malaysian economy is well-diversified and has a long track 
record of resilience following periods of adversity. In 2021, we expect a 
strong rebound in growth largely on base effects. Over the medium term, we 
expect the Malaysian economy to return to its trend growth rate of 4%-5% 
annually, with a slightly stronger performance in 2022 as lost output is 
further recovered. 
 
We project Malaysia's GDP per capita to be about US$10,400 by end-2020, lower 
than most peers' in the same rating category but notably higher than most of 
its Southeast Asian peers except Singapore and Brunei. We forecast Malaysia's 
real GDP per capita growth to average approximately 2.8% per year over 
2020-2023. 
 
Malaysia's Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition government came to power in early 
March, following the collapse of the Pakatan Harapan coalition. PN is anchored 
by representatives of the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition, including key 
constituent party UMNO, as well as the Malaysian United Indigenous Party 
(PPBM), which crossed the aisle from the PH government to form PN. This marks 
Malaysia's second change of government in two years, following a 61-year 
period of uninterrupted rule under BN up to 2018. 
 
Malaysia's institutions have supported generally effective policymaking for a 
long time and we believe their depth of capacity will help to alleviate the 
risk of instability owing to ongoing political developments. Notably, the 
government proactively introduced stimulus measures aimed at supporting the 
economy as the COVID-19 pandemic worsened in recent months. 
 
Nevertheless, marginal support for PN in parliament has led to challenges by 
prominent members of the PH opposition, including former Prime Minister 
Mahathir Mohamed, as well as opposition leader Anwar Ibrahim . Uncertainty 
regarding the level of support for either coalition could result in further 
changes in government, or snap polls, thereby undermining the predictability 
of policymaking at a crucial juncture, in our view. In particular, this 
undermines clarity regarding the government's fiscal policy trajectory, and 
elevates the risk that fiscal consolidation targets are not met over the 
coming years. 
 
To try and mitigate the severe economic impact of the pandemic the PN 
government has expanded the stimulus measures first introduced by the PH 
government in February. The total value of stimulus measures, inclusive of 
PH's first package in February, is now about Malaysian ringgit (MYR) 295 
billion (20.3% of GDP). Only MYR45 billion (3.0% of GDP) of the package is 
expected to be borne directly by the government, largely comprising measures 
that aim to support employment and protect the most vulnerable segments of 
society. Other measures not borne by the government include a roughly MYR100 
billion, six-month moratorium on repayments of loans to banks by households 
and businesses, overseen by Bank Negara Malaysia  (BNM), as well as a scheme to 
provide as much as MYR50 billion in government guarantees on lending to firms 
facing working capital difficulties. The latter scheme will be administered 
through government-linked company Danajamin Nasional Bhd. 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: The higher debt stock and deficits 
reflect a weaker fiscal profile 
     -- Malaysia's fiscal deficit will rise to 6% of GDP this year, owing to 
fiscal stimulus measures and weaker revenue generation. 
     -- Net general government indebtedness will surpass 60% of GDP on a 
sustained basis, as a result of higher fiscal deficits and lower nominal GDP 
growth. 
     -- Malaysia's fiscal consolidation trajectory could be affected by 
political uncertainty. 
 
We have revised our general government deficit forecast up to 6.0% of GDP in 
2020, versus our previous expectation of 4.1%. Greater expenditure on stimulus 
measures, in combination with weaker revenue generation against the backdrop 
of a shrinking economy, are the key contributors to the higher deficit. As a 
result of these evolving dynamics, we now forecast net general government debt 
will average 62.8% from 2020-2023, with the annual change in net general 
government debt averaging 3.9%. 
 
The Malaysian government derives slightly less than 20% of its total revenue 
from oil-related sources. The single largest component of this revenue is the 
dividend paid to the government by state oil company Petroliam Nasional Bhd . 
(PETRONAS), which we expect to be maintained at MYR24 billion, as allocated in 
the government's original 2020 budget. This dampens the potential downward 
effect on revenue from much lower oil prices. However, future budgets may see 
less support from Petronas in the form of its annual dividend transfer, if oil 
prices remain lower for longer. 
 
The former PH government's decision to zero-rate Malaysia's goods and services 
tax (GST) in June 2018 has weakened revenue generation capacity; the GST was 
previously responsible for nearly 20% of government revenue. We believe the 
GST was instrumental in the government's ability to maintain sound fiscal 
metrics following the 2014-2015 global collapse in commodity prices, and that 
it considerably reduced the government's dependence on commodity revenues. The 
PH government replaced the GST with a sales and services tax, a narrower 
program that mobilizes significantly less revenue. Amid heightened uncertainty 
around how long the current government will last, as well as the pandemic, it 
remains to be seen what efforts the government can make to restore its 
revenue-generating framework over time, in our view. 
 
In order to cap its fiscal deficit at 6% of GDP this year, the PN government

will need to achieve savings through the rationalization of operational and 
capital expenditure items, as well as through additional support from some 
GLCs, including Petronas, KWAP, and Khazanah. The strong financial performance 
of these firms lends some additional flexibility to the government's fiscal 
profile. Still, the government's targeted fiscal deficit will likely be its 
highest since the global financial crisis in 2009. 
 
In view of these developing dynamics, we forecast that the general 
government's net debt stock will rise sustainably above 60% of GDP. We expect 
net debt to GDP to average 63.4% through 2023, and to fall to 61.1% by the end 
of our forecast period, from a high of 66.1% this year. The rise in the 
government's debt stock is also likely to require Malaysia to revise its 
long-standing fiscal rule of limiting central government debt stock to less 
than 55% of GDP. We expect officials to raise this ceiling in the near future, 
as government operations could otherwise be affected if the debt stock were to 
breach that level. 
 
Malaysia's general government fiscal position also carries contingent risks 
from its public enterprises and financial sector. These include guarantees on 
debts and letters of support (including the US$3 billion letter of support for 
1Malaysia Development Bhd . [1MDB], which we regard as a direct financial 
obligation of the government). 
 
The former PH government announced that it was committed to provide support 
for government guarantees for various entities that may be unable to service 
their debts. We have included such committed guarantees in our calculation of 
general government debt, due to the high likelihood that they will crystallize 
on the general government's balance sheet. 
 
These guarantees include but are not limited to those extended to 
government-linked firms Danainfra, Prasarana, Malaysia Rail-link Sdn. Bhd. 
(MRL), SRC International Sdn. Bhd., and 1MDB. We estimate the government's 
total direct liability to these firms on a net basis at more than 10% of GDP. 
As such, our calculation of the general government's net debt is higher by an 
equivalent amount. We note that some of these state-linked vehicles carry 
significant assets which, if liquidated, will likely be used to repay maturing 
debt. We expect committed government guarantees to gradually decline over the 
next three-to-four years assuming that the government does not undertake 
significant new off-budget capital expenditure projects. 
 
Malaysia's solid external position remains a ratings strength. Its current 
account remains in modest surplus at about 3.4% of GDP in 2019. We envisage a 
moderate decline in the current account surplus this year, to 1.9% of GDP, 
largely on a deterioration in Malaysia's terms of trade. However, we expect 
the surplus to stabilize above 2% of GDP from 2021 onward as global trade 
conditions normalize. 
 
Most of Malaysia's external liabilities are denominated in the domestic 
currency, while external assets, both official foreign-exchange reserves and 
other claims on nonresidents, are denominated in foreign currencies. 
 
The Malaysian economy's external liquidity requirements, on a gross basis, are 
considerable; its external liquidity is therefore subject to some degree of 
market volatility. This includes acute bouts of risk aversion, which could 
lead to nonresidents reducing their holdings of local currency government 
debt. Foreign ownership of Malaysian government securities typically account 
for 15%-25% of the total outstanding stock. We estimate Malaysia's ratio of 
gross external financing needs to current account receipts and usable reserves 
at about 96.3% in 2020 although we forecast this will gradually fall to about 
93% by 2023. 
 
We classify Malaysia's foreign-exchange regime as floating, with intermittent 
intervention in the foreign exchange market. The Malaysian ringgit depreciated 
substantially in 2014-2017 amid the reset in global commodity prices; 
pass-through of this depreciation into inflation was limited, however, 
burnishing the central bank's inflation management credentials. More recently, 
consumer price inflation has been very low partly because of the zero-rating 
of GST in 2018. In our view, BNM has significant independence and we do not 
expect this to change under the current government. 
 
Malaysia has a deep domestic bond market, which reduces its reliance on 
foreign-currency financing--although the development of this market has led to 
somewhat greater volatility in nonresident capital flows. BNM has made some 
policy adjustments over recent years. Most notably, these include the stricter 
enforcement of a ban on offshore forward trading in the ringgit and a decrease 
in foreign-exchange amounts exporters are allowed to hold. These policies may 
have contributed to a sell-off in nonresident holdings of ringgit-denominated 
government securities, particularly in early 2017. The central bank actively 
supported dollar liquidity conditions in the local market during this period, 
however. This reflects the sufficiency of its foreign exchange reserves as 
well as the efficacy of its policy levers. 
 
Although high household debt levels remain a risk for the banking system and 
the broader economy, relative to GDP these levels are gradually declining. We 
believe risks are contained by strong capitalization and a generally sound 
regulatory framework. Household financial assets are also ample. 
 
Private sector leverage, as measured by total private sector debt (including 
corporate borrowings from the debt capital markets) to GDP, has been gradually 
building since 2008 and could exacerbate the effects of the downturn. Overall, 
however, we expect the credit risk of Malaysian banks to remain manageable, 
supported by prudent lending and underwriting standards. Banks' exposure to 
the lending segments most at risk to the weakened economy--including lower 
income households and commercial property developers--is manageable in our 
view. Our base case is for an incremental increase in credit losses and 
impaired loans owing to the economic downturn. Our Banking Industry Country 
Risk Assessment for Malaysia is '4' ('1' being the strongest assessment and 
'10' the weakest). 
 
Malaysia's relatively high share of nonresident holders of ringgit-denominated 
government bonds leaves the country's capital markets exposed to the potential 
for a sudden fund outflow. Nonresident holders of ringgit-denominated 
government bonds have previously pared their holdings of these bonds over 
short periods, but the market has generally remained stable with limited 
impact on the ringgit. This position carries additional vulnerability to the 
outstanding decision by FTSE Russell regarding the potential exclusion of 
Malaysian government securities from its bond index. We do not anticipate a 
material deterioration in Malaysia's external settings, either way the final 
decision goes. We also believe the central bank is committed to a floating 
exchange rate, despite financial market volatility. 
 
BNM in recent years has typically maintained a sizable amount of reserves sold 
forward; we subtract this quantum under our assessment of the bank's useable 
reserves, which excludes items not readily available for foreign exchangeoperations. 
 
Malaysia's reserve coverage stood at an estimated 4.6 months of current 
account payments at the end of 2019. Although this level remains sufficient, 
it is near a multi-year low. While Malaysia's deep capital markets should 
provide support for financial stability, our forecast assumes that reserve 
coverage will continue to decline through 2023 to nearly 4.0 months.

title: SE Asia Stocks-Philippines, Indonesia rise as U.S., China allay trade war fears
text:
* Thailand nearly flat as energy, banking stocks drag
    * Indonesia snaps four sessions of losses

    By Soumyajit Saha
    Aug 7 (Reuters) - Philippine and Indonesian shares gained
more than 1% Wednesday, after Beijing and Washington stepped up
to ease escalating trade war tensions, while Malaysia fell
dragged down by consumer stocks.    
    Chinese authorities intervened to steady the yuan on Tuesday
after letting it slide to its lowest in over a decade on the
previous day, which had sparked accusations of currency
manipulation from the United States and threatened to spread the
trade war into the currency space.
    U.S. President Donald Trump then played down fears of a
protraction in the trade war, tweeting that "massive amounts of
money from China and other parts of the world" were coming into
the U.S. economy.
    "Acceleration towards an all-out trade war between the U.S.
and China appears to have been averted, at least for the
moment," said Stephen Innes, managing partner at VM Markets Pte
Ltd. 
    Real estate and banking stocks pushed up Philippine's
benchmark more than 1%. Property developer SM Prime
Holdings rose 1.7%, while lender BDO Unibank advanced
1.4%.
    Philippines' trade deficit narrowed as imports fell 10.4%,
while exports grew 1.5%.
    The banking sector helped Indonesian shares gain,
with lenders Bank Central Asia and Bank Rakyat
Indonesia (Persero) rising 1.6% each.
    Meanwhile, the Malaysian index fell, hurt by losses
in the consumer cyclical sector.
    Tourism company Genting Malaysia Bhd and related
group Genting Bhd fell 10.8% and 5.3%, respectively,
after Genting Malaysia decided to acquire and privatise the
loss-making Empire Resorts Inc.  
    Thai stocks also edged marginally lower, hurt by
losses in the energy and banking sectors.
    Lender Bank of Ayudhya fell 1.3%, while oil
explorer PTT Exploration and Production lost 1.2%.
    Thailand's central bank is widely expected to hold its
benchmark rate steady in a meeting later today, a Reuters poll
showed, despite slowing growth and easing moves by its regional
peers.
    Energy stocks were also hurt by the a drop in oil prices
overnight, as escalating trade war fears had ignited worries
over demand.

title: Malaysia's Mahathir proposes common East Asia  currency  pegged to gold
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, May 30 (Reuters) - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad on Thursday mooted the idea of a common trading currency for East Asia that would be pegged to gold, describing the existing currency trading in the region as manipulative.

Mahathir said the proposed common currency could be used to settle imports and exports, but would not be used for domestic transactions.

"In the Far East, if you want to come together, we should start with a common trading currency, not to be used locally but for the purpose of settling of trade," he said at the Nikkei Future of Asia conference in Tokyo.

"The currency that we propose should be based on gold because gold is much more stable."

He said under the current foreign exchange system, local currencies were affected by external factors and were manipulated. He did not elaborate on how they were manipulated.

Mahathir has long been a critic of currency trading, and once famously accused billionaire George Soros of betting against Asian currencies.

During the Asian financial crisis, Mahathir pegged the ringgit currency at 3.8 to the dollar and imposed capital controls. That peg was scrapped in 2005.

Mahathir served a 22-year term as prime minister before stepping down in 2003. He was re-elected in May last year in a shock election, defeating the Barisan Nasional coalition that had ruled Malaysia for the six decades since independence.

Earlier this week, the Trump administration said no major trading partner met the criteria required to be placed on the U.S. Treasury Department's list of its currency manipulators but named Malaysia among nine countries that required close scrutiny.

In response, Malaysia's central bank said on Wednesday its intervention in currency markets was limited to managing excessive volatility.

(Reporting by Rozanna Latiff, writing by A. Ananthalakshmi; Editing by Sam Holmes)

title: BUZZ-COMMENT-Asia c. banks ignore yellow card from US Treasury
text:
The US Treasury reached the same conclusion as it did in its October semi-annual report to Congress: that no major trading partners are manipulating their currencies. But it highlighted six Asian countries for more scrutiny - China, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, and Vietnam. The report said China's intervention has been limited over the past year . The crux of the issue is that the US doesn't want trading partners to intentionally devalue their currencies for export advantages, but in reality, no one's doing that. Instead, Asian central banks have been busy over the past month preventing their currencies from falling too fast. China's persistent management of the daily USD/CNY benchmark is one example, but also South Korean authorities' suspected selling of USD in the spot market to bolster the KRW. The Monetary Authority of Singapore has also likely been active recently, keeping USD/SGD rallies in check.

Malaysia's central bank is well-known to restrain USD/MYR, sometimes through draconian measures involving deployment of monitoring personnel at banks' trading desks. Indeed, the US may be right about FX manipulation, but it's clear why they're not about to hand out red cards to Asian central banks - they're all playing on the same side.

(Editing by Sam Holmes)

title: *Fitch Affirms Malaysia at 'A-'; Outlook Stable
text:
14 Aug 2018 05:12 ET  Press Release: Fitch Affirms Malaysia at 'A-'; Outlook Stable


 
 
The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings : 
 

Fitch Ratings-Hong Kong-14 August 2018: Fitch Ratings has affirmed Malaysia's Long-Term Foreign-Currency Issuer Default Rating (IDR) at 'A-' with a Stable Outlook.

A full list of rating actions is at the end of this rating action commentary.

KEY RATING DRIVERS

- Malaysia's Long-Term IDRs are supported by solid economic growth and a net external creditor position built up from a record of current-account surpluses. These strengths are offset by elevated government and private sector debt, and low per capita income and World Bank governance scores relative to rating peers. The affirmation not only takes into consideration measures such as the rollback of the goods and services tax (GST), but also the stated intention to reduce fiscal deficits and improve governance. The agency has raised its estimate of central government debt at end-2017 to around 65% of GDP, from 50.8%, following the government's recognition that it will need to service a large share of explicitly guaranteed debt. This estimate may be further revised as more details become available.

The Pakatan Harapan coalition, which won the May 2018 election, has moved ahead on many of its key election promises, notably repealing the GST. It also plans to continue fuel subsidies in place since early 2018, although they will be made more targeted. Fitch views these measures as negative for the credit profile. However, the government aims to implement offsetting fiscal measures and has indicated its intention to contain the central government deficit. There are risks to achieving this target, such as lower-than-Fitch-expected growth - which could limit room for expenditure cutbacks - as well as delays in implementing planned revenue measures.

The authorities expect to meet the original budget deficit target of 2.8% of GDP for 2018 through offsetting measures, including a review of large infrastructure projects and the reintroduction of the sales and services tax with full-year revenue of 1.6% of GDP that had been replaced by the GST (full-year revenue of 3% of GDP) under the previous government. The authorities also expect additional oil revenue of 0.4% of GDP due to higher global oil prices and dividends from government-linked enterprises providing an additional 0.3% of GDP in revenue. On the expenditure side, the authorities plan to cut operational and development spending by MYR10 billion (0.7% of GDP) in 2018.

We expect the deficit to continue falling to around 2.5% of GDP by 2020 under our baseline assumptions through a combination of subsidy rationalisation, further capital spending cuts, new revenue measures and better tax compliance. Central government debt is likely to decline to around 59% of GDP by 2020, although the decline could be more rapid if the government chooses to sell off public assets and use the proceeds for debt reduction. More details on some of these measures could be announced in the budget, which is due on 2 November. However, there are also upside risks to debt as a part of contingent liabilities related to public-private partnerships of 14.9% of GDP may migrate to the sovereign balance sheet.

Malaysia's structural indicators, such as GDP per capita, standards of human development and governance remain below the 'A' category median. One of Pakatan Harapan coalition's notable campaign promises was a royal commission inquiry into recent corruption scandals, such as that surrounding the state investment fund, 1Malaysia Development Bhd . The investigation could help raise governance standards over time, although improvements may take time to eventuate. Malaysia ranked in the 61st percentile on the World Bank governance indicator, compared with the 'A' category historic median's 75th percentile.

We expect GDP growth to slow to 5.2% in 2018, 4.8% in 2019 and 4.6% in 2020, from 5.9% in 2017, as the government seeks to constrain recurrent spending in line with its narrower revenue base. In addition, public capital spending is being held back by a review of large infrastructure projects and exports are likely to moderate from slowing external demand. However, Malaysia's average GDP growth for the five years to 2018 will remain above peer medians. Downside risks to our growth projections could materialise from accelerated spending cuts, disruption to capital projects or slowing investment in the event of prolonged policy and political uncertainty.

Intervention by the Central Bank of Malaysia (BNM) to smooth currency volatility in the midst of large capital outflows between April and June 2018 contributed to a decline in foreign-exchange reserves of about USD5 billion, to USD105 billion, at end June-2018. We expect BNM to limit its intervention and allow sufficient currency flexibility to preserve foreign-exchange reserves at a reasonably healthy level of around five months of current external payments. Although short-term external debt is high, foreign-exchange reserves continue to cover over 100% of this debt.

We expect Malaysia's current account surplus to remain between 3% - 4% of GDP between 2018-2020, supported by higher oil-related exports and slightly slower import growth, which should counter our forecast moderation in exports of electronics. Imports are likely to slow from the new government's review of major infrastructure projects. However, given Malaysia's high degree of trade openness, it remains vulnerable to negative external developments, such as rising trade protectionism. The country is also vulnerable to shifts in external investor sentiment due to high levels of short-term external debt and foreign holdings of government debt, especially against the backdrop of rising US interest rates. Foreign holdings of treasury bills, Malaysian government securities and government investment issues were around 28% of total central government debt in 1Q18.

Banking soundness indicators remain steady, with a system-wide common equity Tier 1 ratio of 12.7% and liquidity coverage ratio of 140% continuing to indicate adequate capital and liquidity buffers. Pockets of risk remain within certain over-supplied property sub-segments, highly leveraged lower-income households and high corporate debt. However, household credit growth has eased over the last few years, and we expect the banking sector to be resilient in case of a moderate correction in the property market.

SOVEREIGN RATING MODEL (SRM) and QUALITATIVE OVERLAY (QO)

- Fitch's proprietary SRM assigns Malaysia a score equivalent to a rating of 'BBB+' on the Long-Term Foreign-Currency IDR scale.

In accordance with its rating criteria, Fitch's sovereign rating committee decided not to adopt the score indicated by the SRM as the starting point for its analysis, because the SRM output has migrated from 'A-' to 'BBB+', but in our view this is potentially a temporary deterioration.

Fitch's SRM is the agency's proprietary multiple regression rating model that employs 18 variables based on three-year centred averages, including one year of forecasts, to produce a score equivalent to a Long-Term Foreign-Currency IDR. Fitch's QO is a forward-looking qualitative framework designed to allow for adjustment to the SRM output to assign the final rating, reflecting factors within our criteria that are not fully quantifiable and/or not fully reflected in the SRM.

RATING SENSITIVITIES

- The main factors that, individually or collectively, could trigger a positive rating action are:

- Narrowing of structural weaknesses relative to peers, including per capita GDP and governance standards.

- - Material reduction in government debt ratios or contingent liabilities, accompanied by improved transparency.

The main factors that, individually or collectively, could trigger negative rating action are:

- Increase in the debt-to-GDP ratio, for example, from a failure to reduce the fiscal deficit or from crystallisation of additional contingent liabilities.

- - External financing pressures that strain macroeconomic stability.

- - Instability in the financial system, possibly triggered by excessive credit growth and a rise in household debt.

KEY ASSUMPTIONS

- - The global economy performs broadly in line with Fitch's global economic outlook.

The full list of rating actions is as follows:

Long-Term Foreign-Currency IDR affirmed at 'A-'; Outlook Stable

- Long-Term Local-Currency IDR affirmed at 'A-'; Outlook Stable

title: Malaysia Vote Shocks Investors -- WSJ
text:
This article is being republished as part of our daily reproduction of WSJ.com articles that also appeared in the U.S. print edition of The Wall Street Journal (May 11, 2018).

Heavy selling looms in Malaysian assets when markets reopen next week, after the country's opposition coalition pulled off a shock victory in Wednesday's election.

A U.S.-listed exchange-traded fund of Malaysian stocks slumped 6% on Wednesday, its biggest decline since 2011, while the dollar has risen more than 2% against the ringgit in the derivatives market.

Incoming Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad earlier declared two days of national holidays after his Alliance of Hope coalition secured a parliamentary majority following the vote in the Southeast Asian nation.

The "huge upset" over Najib Razak "ranks up there with Brexit and [U.S. President Donald Trump's] election," said Aninda Mitra, senior sovereign analyst at BNY Mellon Investment Management.

While anticipating short-term volatility in Malaysian markets next week, "a long-term fix of governance, institutions and public life is now in sight," he said. Still, he added, near-term policy uncertainty will be high, taking a toll on the country's currency, the ringgit, for now.

Malaysia's currency and stocks had started falling ahead of the election, as signs emerged that Dr. Mahathir's opposition party was gaining momentum. His party has offered few details on its economic policy plans, although its campaign manifesto proposed scrapping the country's goods-and-services tax and reintroducing fuel subsidies.

Such moves could have a negative impact on Malaysia's credit rating without offsetting measures to raise fiscal revenues, Moody's Investors Service warned in a statement Thursday. It currently rates the country at A3, four steps above the investment-grade rating threshold.

Malaysia's election upset comes at a time of heightened stress in global emerging markets.

Argentina has tapped the International Monetary Fund for financial backing, the latest drastic step policy makers have taken as they seek to stem the peso's depreciation. The central bank last week boosted interest rates to 40%.

Meanwhile, Turkey's markets have continued to swoon over concerns about its economy. Standard & Poor's Global Ratings recently slashed the country's sovereign-debt rating further into junk territory, and the International Monetary Fund has warned that Turkey's economy is at risk of overheating.

The central bank of Malaysia's neighbor Indonesia has intervened in the foreign-exchange market in recent weeks to shore up its currency, the rupiah, while foreign investors have been running from its stocks and bonds. Markets there are closed Thursday for the Ascension Day holiday.

Investors had been positive on Malaysia's market at the start of 2018, with the ringgit and equities outperforming regional peers: The country's main stock benchmark briefly topped its 2014 record high last month.

However, the ongoing corruption scandal surrounding Mr. Najib and state-owned investment fund 1Malaysia Development Bhd., which is subject to investigations in multiple countries, has clouded investor sentiment.

The yield on a 10-year bond from 1MDB that matures in 2023 surged to 9.54% on Thursday morning, according to IHS Markit, up from 6.1% on Wednesday. Bond yields rise when their prices fall.

The cost of insuring Malaysian government debt has also risen, with the price of 5-year credit default swaps up nearly 9% on Thursday.

The Malaysian election results also weighed on neighboring Singapore's stock market. Equities there had been underperforming of late -- with Malaysia -- and the Straits Times Index was lower most of the day, though little changed heading into the last hour of trading Thursday amid broad gains for Asia-Pacific stock indexes.

Meanwhile, Malaysia's central bank went ahead with its previously scheduled policy meeting and as expected kept interest rates at 3.25%.

The policy statement only had one mention of the election.

"The domestic economic outlook remains positive, the financial sector is strong and monetary and financial conditions are supportive of economic growth in the post-election environment," it said. That could signal central bank confidence that the markets can weather uncertainties created by the change in government.
