title: China Shares Fall Amid Doubts Over Beijing's Rescue
text:
Chinese stocks fell Tuesday, casting doubt on the government's ability to stem the slide.

Over the weekend, Beijing took its most aggressive action yet to boost its markets, suspending initial public offerings  and lending cash to investors to buy stocks. China's brokers vowed to buy shares until the Shanghai Composite hits the 4500 level.

But the market fell 1.3% Tuesday to 3727.12, putting it down 27.9% from its peak and 17.2% below the promised 4500 level. More worrying is that the market performed worse than the index makes it seem.

China's smaller Shenzhen stock market fell for the second straight day, putting it down 5.3% for the week while the ChiNext board, composed of smaller cap stocks, and dropped 11.2% to 2352.01. Both indexes are off more than a third from June highs.

Hong Kong's market also sank, with the Hang Seng Index falling 1% and a gauge of Chinese companies listed offshore in the city, known as H-shares, falling 3.3% during the trading day to enter a bear market—defined as a drop of more than 20%—compared with highs reached in May.

The performance in Shanghai showed how government efforts to boost the market are playing out. Just 55 companies rose Tuesday while 864 names fell, according to Chinese data provider Wind Info. Those gainers were the market's heavyweights, which the brokers pledged to buy. Companies such as Bank of China Ltd., China Construction Bank Corp. and Ping An Insurance (Group) Co. of China rose the maximum 10% trading limit.

Beijing's policy changes to stabilize the stock market seemed unlikely to produce a durable recovery, even if the market is able to rebound in the short term, said Arthur Kwong, head of Asia-Pacific equities at BNP Paribas Investment Partners, which has €548 billion ($605.86 billion) in assets under management. He says he remains wary of Chinese domestic shares even after the selloff during the past month.

"We'd only be excited when the market has a turnaround in terms of fundamentals," he said. What's more, policy moves so far have shown limited effectiveness in improving economic growth. "A lot of the bullets are already shot," he added. "How many more rate cuts can they do?"

Some analysts attribute Tuesday's losses in China to margin calls , when brokerages call in money owed by investors who borrowed to buy shares. "The pressure on margin calls remain heavy," said Qian Qimin, an analyst at Shenyin Wanguo Securities. While some highly leveraged Chinese investors have already been forced to liquidate margin positions in small and midcap stocks, the selloff could continue.

"The entire clearance process, in our view, may last a few more weeks," said Nomura in a research report.

China has rolled out a steady stream of measures to arrest the selling frenzy that knocked $2.4 trillion in value from China's equities over the past three weeks. According to data from FactSet, 514 stocks are suspended in Shenzhen and 162 in Shanghai. Despite the recent rout, Shanghai shares are up 81% over the past year, and 15.2% since January. Shanghai recovered modestly Monday, which some investors and analysts attributed to heavy buying of blue-chip stocks by state-backed funds.

That buying looks set to continue. Chinese brokerage Haitong Securities Co. on Tuesday said it would boost the amount it invests in blue-chip exchange-traded funds by 15 billion yuan ($2.42 billion). The announcement follows an agreement over the weekend among 21 brokerages to invest in a stock-rescue fund.

Other measures include halting new initial public offerings, raising quotas for foreigners to buy stocks and an initiative by the central bank to provide funds to help investors borrow to buy shares.

Some brokerages are encouraged by Beijing's efforts: "Chinese monetary and fiscal easing policies, combined with further reform measures, should support [mainland] A-share indexes to new highs in 2016," says Raymond So, co-head of research at Chinese broker CCB International Securities. A number of sectors stand to benefit from the Beijing-backed call to buy, including financials, property developers, health care, utilities and telecoms, he added.

Still, China's volatility is starting to spill into global markets, as Beijing's moves to arrest stock selloffs  have darkened the outlook for the world's second-largest economy. Oil prices tumbled nearly 8% Monday , their biggest single-day decline in more than three months, amid fresh fears about weaker demand from China, one of the world's largest consumers of raw materials. The sharp falls moderated Tuesday, with Brent crude gaining 1.6% to $57.43.

Hong Kong's market has risen strongly but was never gripped by the mania that sent Chinese stocks soaring. While it is considered a more mature market with far more institutional investors, Hong Kong has hundreds of mainland Chinese companies, mostly large state-owned banks and heavy-industry companies, which account for 44.1% of the market capitalization of all stocks listed on the city's exchange.

Elsewhere, Asian markets mostly rose as investors appear hopeful that a resolution between Greece and its creditors is still within reach.

"It seems that investors either believe that 'Grexit' can still be avoided, or that, if it does happen, the contagion will be limited," analysts from Capital Economics wrote in a research report.

Greece's vote on Sunday to reject creditors' demands, including pension cuts and tax increases, could put Greece closer to exiting the eurozone. That led markets in Europe and the U.S. lower, though the declines weren't as dramatic as expected. The euro fell 0.7% against the U.S. dollar and 0.5% against the yen.

The Nikkei 225 Stock Average rose 1.3% while South Korea's Kospi Composite fell 0.7%.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rose 1.9%, its strongest one-day gain since mid-February, with falling oil expected to lower operating costs for energy-intensive commodity producers. The Reserve Bank of Australia kept benchmark interest rates on hold at 2.00%.

Meanwhile, banks warned that Malaysia's financial markets could come under further stress, after the country's currencyfell to its weakest level since the Asian financial crisis  Monday. The oil-exporting nation has been hit by falling commodity prices, which have nearly halved since July last year. Malaysia's stocks are down 1%.

The ringgit strengthened 0.3% to 3.8151 against the dollar amid speculation that Malaysia's central bank may be intervening to buoy the currency, traders say. The ringgit is down 8.2% for the year, making it one of Asia's worst-performing currencies.

"Among Asian financial assets, Malaysia's are the most exposed to oil," analysts from ING wrote in a research note. Efforts to strengthen the ringgit "will give way if oil prices continue to decline," the bank added.

Malaysia's currency also has come under pressure as political strain builds against the country's prime minister. The Wall Street Journal earlier reported that Malaysian government investigators looking into the activities of state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Bhd ., or 1MDB, had traced almost $700 million in deposits into what they believe are Mr. Najib's personal accounts. Mr. Najib has denied wrongdoing.

On Tuesday, Malaysian authorities said they have ordered six bank accounts to be frozen ("http://www.wsj.com/articles/malaysia-authorities-order-six-bank-accounts-frozen-tied-to-probe-of-alleged-transfers-to-prime-minister-najib-1436253593")in connection with an investigation into alleged fund transfers to bank accounts of Mr. Najib.

Anjie Zheng, Yifan Xie and Dominique Fong contributed to this article.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Risk aversion weighs on Asia  FX , won falls with  intervention  spotted
text:
* Won falls as S.Korea intervention spotted
    * Ringgit down on corp dollar bids; higher oil cuts losses
    * Rupiah skids, intervention limits slides

 (Adds text, updates prices)
    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SINGAPORE, March 26 (Reuters) - Most emerging Asian
currencies eased on Thursday as military action against rebels
in Yemen and losses on Wall Street undermined risk sentiment.
    The South Korean won fell as foreign exchange
authorities were spotted intervening to curb its strength,
traders said.
    Malaysia's ringgit and Indonesia's rupiah 
slid on corporate dollar demand. The Philippine peso 
eased ahead of the central bank's policy meeting later in the
day when the authority is expected to keep interest rates
unchanged. 
    Asian stocks skidded as Saudi Arabia and its Gulf Arab
allies started a military operation in Yemen. 
U.S. equities on Wednesday also lost ground with the Nasdaq
 suffering its largest decline in nearly a year.
    Regional currencies showed muted reactions to the dollar's
weakness after data showing spending on U.S. durable goods fell
for a sixth consecutive month in February. 
    "Asian currencies saw more impact from risk aversion than
the dollar," said Yuna Park, a currency and bond analyst at
Dongbu Securities in Seoul.
    "However, they may find some relief as money printing in 
China and Japan, as well as stabilisation in major currencies,
could spur more carry trades in Asia," Park added.
    
    WON
    The won fell as South Korea's foreign exchange authorities
were spotted defending the 1,100 per dollar level, traders said.
    The South Korean currency has chart resistance levels at
1,099.7, a 55-day moving average and 1,099.4, a 100-day moving
average. The unit has been closing the local daily market weaker
than the 100-day average since Sept. 5.
    "From 1,100, the authorities was suspected of pulling up
(dollar/won)," said a foreign bank trader in Seoul.
    The authorities were also seen keeping the won weaker than
9.2000 against the yen, traders said.
    The won weakened to near 9.3000 to the yen from the previous
close of 9.2110. South Korea and Japan compete in overseas
markets for various products such as electronics and cars.
    Meanwhile, the Bank of Korea said it boosted the ceiling on
its key loan facility for small-to-medium sized businesses by
5.0 trillion won as part of its push to boost the economic
recovery at home. 
    
    RINGGIT
    The ringgit slid on quarter-end dollar demand from local
companies.
    The Malaysian currency pared some of its losses as oil
prices jumped. The Saudi Arabia-led strike on Yemen rebels could
pose risks to the security of oil shipments.
    Malaysia is a net oil exporter and the recent slide in crude
prices boosted concerns over their impact on the country's
current and fiscal accounts.
    Given those worries, the ringgit was the worst-performing
Asian currency so far this year with a near 5 percent loss
against the dollar, Thomson Reuters data showed.
    
    RUPIAH
    The rupiah skidded with month-end corporate dollar demand
increasing.
    The official Jakarta Interbank Spot Dollar Rate,
which the central bank introduced in 2013 to manage exchange
rate fluctuations, was fixed at 13,003 rupiah per dollar, weaker
than Wednesday's 12,932.
    Indonesia's central bank expects the rupiah to remain under
pressure through June as dollar demand rises for dividend
payments, its chief said on Wednesday. 
    The central bank was spotted intervening to support the
ailing unit, but the official support was not seen as
aggressive, traders said.
    "It just gave some liquidity for the market," said a
Jakarta-based currency trader.
    Providing some long-term relief was news Japanese companies
will invest $5.6 billion in Indonesia, the head of Indonesia's
investment board said, following President Joko Widodo's visit
to Tokyo.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Won turns up after 20-month low as further rate cut views wane
text:
* Won ends up as no further S.Korea rate cut seen in 2015
    * Bank of Korea lowers rates to record low 1.75 pct
    * Intervention caution supports most emerging Asia FX

 (Adds detail, updates prices)
    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SINGAPORE, March 12 (Reuters) - South Korea's won ended
local trade firmer, recovering slightly  from a 20-month trough
hit on Thursday when the central bank unexpectedly slashed
borrowing costs to a record low.
    Expectations of another interest rate cut anytime soon
vanished, with a snap Reuters poll of analysts finding the
surprise cut now viewed as the central bank's last easing, at
least for this year. 
    The Bank of Korea slashed its base rate by 25
basis points to 1.75 percent at its monthly policy meeting.
 
    The won closed at 1,126.4 per dollar after
falling to 1,136.4 per dollar, its weakest since July 10, 2013,
compared with Wednesday's close of 1,126.5. 
    Traders rushed to cover the short positions they had built
up on expectations of further easing, and treasury bond futures
 pared back much of their gains they made after the rate
cut. 
    Finance Minister Choi Kyung-hwan told reporters after a
scheduled meeting that Thursday's rate cut was a pre-emptive
move and would help revive the economy. 
    The Bank of Korea's rate cut is unlikely to spur sharp
portfolio outflows as foreign investors have been happy to
accumulate Korean debt, said Jonathan Cavenagh, senior FX
strategist with Westpac in Singapore.
    "However, as the U.S. gets closer to raising rates the
attractiveness of investing in Korean debt may start to become
more questionable," he added.
    Meanwhile, most emerging Asian currencies rose as caution
set in over possible intervention by authorities to stem
excessive currency weakness. 
    
    RINGGIT
    Malaysia's ringgit gained as nerves over possible
intervention to support the ailing currency prompted investors
to cover short positions.
    Traders scrambled for the Malaysian currency when it
strengthened past 3.6900 per dollar.
    The government has sold 4.0 billion ringgit ($1.1 billion)
in bonds maturing in 2025 with bid-to-cover ratio of 2.23 times
at an average yield of 3.955 percent, the central bank said
earlier. 
    Most government bond prices and Kuala Lumpur shares 
rose.
    
    BAHT
    The Thai baht edged up even though the Bank of
Thailand unexpectedly cut borrowing costs on Wednesday.
 
    The baht slid to as low as 32.92 per dollar earlier on
Thursday, its weakest since Jan. 7.
    The currency firmed, analysts said, because the rate
reduction is unlikely to undercut the baht against regional
peers.
    "We do not think this knee-jerk reaction to the rate cut
will necessarily cause the THB to reverse all of its recent
outperformance versus most Asian currencies," said Dominic
Bunning, senior FX Strategist at HSBC, in a client note.
    The baht has gained 0.1 percent against the dollar so far
this year, making it the third best-performing Asian currency,
according to Thomson Reuters data.

title: Ringgit Revisits Its Past as 3.8000 Appears on Horizon -- Market Talk
text:
0418 GMT [Dow Jones] Malaysia's ringgit briefly traded at 3.7000 to the U.S. dollar Tuesday, says a trader, for the first time since March 2009. The new 6-year low has evoked memories of the ringgit's pre-2005 pegged value of 3.8000 to the U.S. dollar. The currency peg was abolished in July 2005 - the same day China announced its own liberalisation of the yuan. But could the ringgit again trade at its old pegged level? lost ground on Monday after stronger-than-expected U.S. job data
boosted expectations that the Federal Reserve may raise interest
rates in the middle of this year, hurting regional
attractiveness of higher yields.
    Adding to depreciation pressure, China's imports in the
first two months of the year fell more than 20 percent from a
year earlier, indicating persistent weakness in the world's
second-largest economy. 
    The Indonesian rupiah hit a near 17-year trough as
bonds and stocks slid. The Malaysian ringgit touched a
six-year low, while the Singapore dollar stayed around
its weakest since July 2010.
    South Korea's won slid to a three-month low as
offshore funds sold the currency.
    U.S. nonfarm payrolls rose 295,000 in February, beating a
market forecast for a 240,000 increase, data showed on Friday.
The jobless rate last month fell to 5.5 percent, the lowest
level since May 2008. 
    Those healthy numbers sent the dollar to a fresh
11-year high against a six major currencies and lifted U.S.
Treasury bond yields.
    "The strong jobs data helped the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield
rise above 2.2 percent despite lower oil prices. That indicated
markets were pricing in an earlier interest rate hike," said
Yuna Park, a currency and bond analyst at Dongbu Securities in
Seoul.
    "The dollar's strength and volatilities in emerging
currencies will intensify, especially in the second quarter,"
Park added.
    The benchmark U.S. note yield stood at 2.2289
percent on Monday in Asia. The yield on Friday in New York
posted their biggest rise since November 2013.

weakest since August 1998, on dollar demand from local
companies.
    The currency also slid in non-deliverable forwards

weakest since the launch.

worst-performing Asian currency so far this year around the
session's low, traders said.
    However, the authority did not seem to be defending specific
levels, they added.
    
    RINGGIT

weakest since March 2009.
    The Malaysian currency came under further pressure as oil
prices slid, underscoring concerns that falling crude will hurt
the country's current account surplus and widen its fiscal
deficit.
    The central bank was spotted intervening to support the
currency, traders said.

title: Peso Stable After Three-Day Papal Closure of Markets -- Market Talk
text:
0143 GMT [Dow Jones] The peso is stable at around 44.72 versus its last close of 44.68 as Philippine financial markets reopen after the three-day closure due to the Pope's visit. USD/PHP is below the base of the daily Ichimoku Cloud support zone--a mild bearish chart signal--but is inching higher and away from the Bollinger downtrend channel at 44.61. A range of 44.61-44.77 formed by the Bollinger downtrend channel and the 20-day Bollinger mid resistance may trap the pair on an intraday basis. Although the greenback is stronger on escalating risk aversion in Asia, the U.S. dollar may struggle to rally while yields on U.S. government bonds stay below 2.00%. (ewen.chew@wsj.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0142 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/KRW is turning higher as risk aversion brews, lifting the safe haven U.S. dollar in Asia and threatening to end the bearish technical bias which was established Monday. A Tuesday close above 1,084 would nullify the daily Bollinger downtrend channel and place USD/KRW back inside the daily Ichimoku Cloud consolidation zone. Risk appetite is poor following a sharp fall in Chinese equities on Monday which could be exacerbated by a likely weak China 4Q gross domestic product report due at 0200 GMT. But sustained upside for USD/KRW may be fleeting while the yield on the benchmark U.S. 10-year Treasury note remains below 2.00%. USD/KRW is now 1,084.0 from its Monday close of 1,078. (ewen.chew@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: KLH 
 

0131 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/IDR is inching higher and out of its consolidation range of 12,550-12,650 as risk aversion looms before China's gross domestic product data due at 0200 GMT. A weak reading might exacerbate investor anxiety sparked by China's stock market crash on Monday. A disappointing number below the consensus forecast of 7.2% could trigger more risk aversion-related U.S. dollar-buying. The greenback is likely to stay up at least until Thursday when the European Central Bank is expected to announce another easing of monetary policy that would depress the euro. Fundamentally though, the rupiah could look more attractive to investors in the medium term as the government seeks to channel budgetary savings from its fuel-subsidy cut into infrastructure development. title: 1MDB Crisis Won't Wound Malaysia Government: Eurasia Group -- Market Talk
text:
0738 GMT [Dow Jones] The Malaysian government will not be significantly damaged by an ongoing crisis at 1Malaysia Development, Eurasia Group reckons. The state-owned fund, which is known as 1MDB and is charged with developing the economy, reportedly missed a payment in December to a group of Malaysian banks on a $560 million loan, raising questions about its management. But Prime Minister Najib Razak's administration will benefit from the fact that the issue "is unlikely to resonate with the majority of voters in the country," writes analyst Ambika Ahuja. She notes that she expects the government to arrange an extension of loans for the fund. Looking at the year ahead, Malaysia--a net oil exporter--will suffer from falling global oil prices, but Najib is likely to move forward with fiscal reforms regardless. The implementation of a goods-and-services tax is expected in April. (newley.purnell@wsj.com; Twitter: @Newley)

Corrections & Amplifications

This snippet was corrected at 04:13 a.m. EST because the fund was misstated as 1MBD in the headline.

However it will be several months before the final ruling is made, according to analysts at Helaba, by which time the ECB will probably have taken action with many analysts looking for fresh stimulus details at the Jan. 22 ECB meeting. "China still lacks a popular green movement like in the West," the firm said, adding that its survey of Tesla buyers there show they bought the car because it is trendy or cool rather than for environmental reasons. That puts it in competition with other brands and with other types of luxury products, JL Warren says. The firm also cited signs of a gap between the number of Teslas imported to China and the number registered to drive, as well as turnover in Tesla's China management. (carlos.tejada@wsj.com; Twitter: @CRTejada) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0637 GMT [Dow Jones] As oil markets tumble, U.S. power generators are usually pretty quick to switch their energy supply to natural gas from coal, says Whitehaven Coal (WHC.AU) chief executive Paul Flynn. But, he says, Asia's thermal-coal market doesn't face the same pressures. "The price of gas is a lot higher in Asia" and would have to fall much more sharply here to displace coal as the cheapest energy commodity, thereby prompting substitution, says Flynn. "And I wouldn't expect to see that happen in the short term," he says. Asian benchmark gas prices are around three times higher than U.S. natural gas. Flynn also doesn't think surplus U.S. coal will make its way into Asia--which would add to an oversupply and weigh on prices--even with declining freight costs. "It is just not a viable alternative," he says. (rhiannon.hoyle@wsj.com; Twitter: @RhiannonHoyle) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0633 GMT [Dow Jones] There's been winners and losers from the sliding Australian dollar. For Whitehaven Coal (WHC.AU), which exports coal to countries including Japan, it's undoubtedly eased some of the pressure of weak energy markets, according to chief executive Paul Flynn. "For us, it is a benefit," says Flynn. "Australian-dollar coal is much better off than it was six-to-12 months ago," he says. Exactly how much of a boost to earnings it's providing will become clear when the miner reports its half-year results later this month. To be sure, Citi earlier Wednesday cautioned that depreciating exporter currencies may lower the cost of production, thus lowering the natural price support level for coal, and Flynn agrees it could prolong an oversupply in the market. However, he argues the surplus isn't as big as it used to be and that Whitehaven is better equipped to deal with soft prices after sharply lowering its operating costs. (rhiannon.hoyle@wsj.com; Twitter: @RhiannonHoyle) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0610 GMT [Dow Jones] Malaysia's ringgit has chalked up a 5.5-year low of 3.5950 to the U.S. dollar as the price of Brent crude oil fell 1.1% to $46.08 a barrel. The Malaysian currency has lost 2.8/% against the dollar this year. In the last two months of 2014, the ringgit depreciated 5.9% due to oil prices collapsing. The USD/MYR psychological trading barrier of 3.6000, if breached, could trigger stoploss orders to sell more ringgit. Malaysia's central bank might intervene to prevent a sharp fall in the currency, but according to one onshore trader, this seems less likely given Bank Negara Malaysia has not been active in the spot market recently. The USD/MYR is now at 3.5950 versus its Tuesday close of 3.5920. (ewen.chew@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: FLS 
 

0557 GMT [Dow Jones] The Hong Kong government's plans to start talks with joint venture partner Walt Disney (DIS) on the Phase Two expansion of Hong Kong Disneyland come just months before the scheduled opening of Disney's Shanghai theme park, which will be bigger and will draw tourists away from the Hong Kong resort. Hong Kong Disneyland, which opened in 2005, remains the smallest of Disney's global theme parks, and struggled in its early years partly because attendance was lower than expected. It turned its first profit in fiscal 2012, as newer attractions helped boost attendance. A large plot of reclaimed land adjacent to the theme park--that's been earmarked for Disneyland's expansion--still sits vacant. (jeffrey.ng@wsj.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0556 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/JPY falls below 117, briefly touching 116.99 on EBS amid Nikkei weakness (now down 1.8%) and tumbling copper prices, says a Japanese bank dealer. "There are no fresh cues but (the pair) also lacks buying incentives," says the dealer. Focus is now on whether the pair can stay above 117. If the pair falls well below that mark, as possible option-related stop loss orders just below 117 kick in, there may be no downside support until 115.50, the dealer says. The USD/JPY is now at 117.10. (hiroyuki.kachi@wsj.com)

0525 GMT [Dow Jones] The plunge in copper prices in Asia is "red meat to Aussie dollar bears," says Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac. Callow says there is a significant risk that the Australian dollar will extend its losses to below US$0.8000 soon. Pair now US$0.8091. (james.glynn@wsj.com; Twitter @JamesGlynnWSJ) 


 
Editor: KLH 
 

0524 GMT [Dow Jones] The Aussie's stubbornness relative to falling copper prices in the North American time zone, gave way in Asia as copper continued to plummet, says David Forrester, currency strategist at Macquarie Bank. While copper is a small weight in Australia's commodity export basket (about 2%) it punches above this weight when it comes to influencing the Australian dollar, given its importance as an indicator for global commodity demand from global manufacturing and construction activity. (james.glynn@wsj.com; Twitter @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1Malaysia Development, a state-owned fund, is also known as 1MDB. "1MBD Crisis Won't Wound Malaysia Government: Eurasia Group -- Market Talk," at 0738 GMT, incorrectly referred to the fund as 1MBD in the headline.

0901 GMT [Dow Jones] Tumbling oil prices and spare capacity in the Indian economy should keep wholesale inflation subdued in the coming months, says Shilan Shah, an economist at Capital Economics. That would strengthen the case for the central bank to loosen monetary policy despite wholesale inflation becoming less important, he adds. "Today's data provide more evidence of subdued price pressures and bolster the case for the Reserve Bank of India to begin loosening policy over the coming months." India's official data showed wholesale prices in December edged 0.11% higher from a year earlier, after remaining unchanged in November. (anant.kala@wsj.com)

The opinion said the ECB has "broad discretion" when implementing monetary policy and that the program is "necessary." There's a lot of legalese in this, but nothing that would appear to handcuff the ECB in launching a QE program later this month. (brian.blackstone@wsj.com)

markettalk@wsj.com 

0858 GMT [Dow Jones]--ECB president Mario Draghi's comments in a German press interview support market expectations that the ECB will launch QE at its Jan. 22 meeting. In an interview published by Germany's Die Zeit newspaper, Mr. Draghi said the ECB is united in its determination to deliver on its 2% inflation target, and that it doesn't have many options left to achieve this. brian.blackstone@wsj.com 


 
Contact us in London. +44-20-7842-9464 
markettalk@wsj.com 

0855 GMT [Dow Jones]--The seeming certainty of a new record low borrowing cost at Germany's launch of a new 10-year Bund might lead to weak demand. Should this be the case, there's no need to worry, says ING Bank strategist Padhraic Garvey. German auctions with a lower amount of bids than the offer size are not unusual. "Initiations can struggle in terms of bid/offer but we'd not read much into this should that be the case," Mr. Garvey says. Grey market levels indicated a yield for the new Bund at 0.51%. markettalk@wsj.com 
 

0849 GMT [Dow Jones] Japan's economy, which fell into a recession in the second and third quarters of 2014, is likely to see a recovery in 2015, Nomura Securities says. Tomo Kinoshita, the brokerage's chief economist, says private consumer spending should rise steadily on the back of a decline in oil prices and the rise in real income from higher nominal wages and the sales tax hike delay. He also says private investment is likely to rebound from the 2014 fourth quarter. Exports, which started an upward trend in September last year, should rise gradually, he adds, driven primarily by the U.S. economic recovery. "On growth strategies, the government is likely to intensify its efforts after the ruling coalition won the Lower House election last December," he says. (bradford.frischkorn@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: FLS 

0828 GMT [Dow Jones]--Credit Suisse strategists see little risk premium in the EUR price from the impending European Court of Justice opinion on the legality of the European Central Bank's Outright Monetary Transactions program. markettalk@wsj.com 

0822 GMT [Dow Jones]--Germany is set to launch the new 0.50% February 2025-dated Bund at auction Wednesday, with a new record low borrowing cost that may well hit demand, says KBC Bank. "From an absolute point of view, the record low German yield isn't enticing," the banks' analysts say. They expect a difficult auction which they say "can only be saved" by the fact that demand tends to be relatively higher at the beginning of the year. Results of the EUR5 billion auction are due at 1030 GMT. Grey market levels show the new Bund at a yield of 0.51%. Any yield below 0.74% at an auction would represent a new record low German 10-year borrowing cost. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha) 


 
Contact us in London. +44-20-7842-9464 
markettalk@wsj.com 
 

0816 GMT [Dow Jones] China's government bonds are higher after a report saying the central bank injected liquidity into commercial banks. The seven-year government bond yield is down 3 basis points at 3.52%. The Shanghai Securities News reported Wednesday that the PBOC injected 280 billion yuan ($45 billion) into the Chinese banking system through its medium-term lending facility, and lenders including China Citic Bank Corp. (601998.SH) and Shanghai Pudong Development Bank Co. got infusions of cash on Tuesday. The finance ministry also auctioned one-year government bonds at 3.14% versus an expectation of 3.23%, which also lifted interest in the bonds. But Shenyin Wanguo Securities says the MLF injection doesn't signal further easing of PBOC policy. "We need to pay attention to the net injection of MLFs...Tuesday's MLF is simply a renewal of maturing ones and is designed to maintain liquidity at normal levels," it adds. (wynne.wang@dowjones.com)

0815 GMT [Dow Jones]--Russia's economy minister Alexei Ulyukayev is rather pessimistic about the country's sovereign rating. On Wednesday, he said that the probability of a rating downgrade to junk is "rather high," Russian news agencies reported. S&P warned late last year it may cut Russia's rating below investment grade and the revision is likely either this or next week. (andrey.ostroukh@wsj.com) 


 
Contact us in London. +44-20-7842-9464 
markettalk@wsj.com 
 

0804 GMT [Dow Jones] China's economy likely grew 7.2% in the fourth quarter of 2014, down from 7.3% in the third, according to the median forecast of 17 economists surveyed by Dow Jones. Gross domestic product growth for the year as a whole will likely come in at 7.3%, the same poll indicates. That would make for the lowest quarterly figure since 2009, and the lowest annual one since 1990. "Both production and investment have slowed to their weakest levels in at least five years, as China enters its 'new norm' of economic growth," says Jianguang Shen of Mizuho Securities. "We believe China is ready for additional monetary easing amid deflation concerns." The GDP data are due to be released, along with a clutch of others - industrial production, fixed-asset investment and retail sales--at 0200 GMT on Tuesday. (richard.silk@dowjones.com) 


 
Editor: KLH 
 

0803 GMT [Dow Jones] The Bank of Japan will likely tone down its language on prices in a monthly economic assessment due at a January 20-21 policy meeting, people close to the central bank said. First, it will moderate its "around 1%" language in a sentence that currently says the core consumer price index is rising at a pace of "around 1%,"--adjusted for a sales tax increase--to something more bearish. Second, the BOJ will change another sentence on prices that talks about the likely path of the core consumer price index for the coming several months; it currently says "The year-on-year rate of increase in the CPI is likely to be at around the current level for the time being." Making those changes may be natural considering a falling inflation rate driven down by oil prices, but such a move would add to speculation of additional easing, which many economists think will come sometime this year. (Takashi.nakamichi@wsj.com)

    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SINGAPORE, Dec 3 (Reuters) - Most emerging Asian currencies
skidded lower on Wednesday as the dollar climbed to a seven-year
high against the yen, buoyed by higher U.S. Treasury yields on a
more bullish outlook for the world's top economy.
    Malaysia's ringgit hit a near five-year low as a
rebound in oil failed to ease concerns over the impact of lower
crude prices on the country, a net oil exporter and major palm
oil producer.

its weakest since December 2008, amid the global financial
crisis, on local corporate dollar demand.
    South Korea's won tracked the yen's slide. 
    The dollar index, a gauge of the greenback's
performance against six major currencies, stayed around 4-1/2-
year high, on stronger U.S. bond yields.
    The dollar was supported by comments earlier this week from
New York Fed President William Dudley and Vice Chair Stanley
Fischer who both provided a mostly rosy outlook for the U.S.
economy. 
    "Asia FX will stay weaker as everybody agrees on a strong
dollar trend," said Jeong My-young, Samsung Futures' research
head in Seoul.
    "We may see some profit-taking from the dollar, but it is
hard to reverse the trend unless U.S. economic data is bad or
other economies show a solid picture of health."

 lost 0.8 percent, well underperforming other Southeast

downside, traders said.

text:
* Ringgit may head to 3.4295/dollar
    * Malaysia intervention spotted to curb ringgit loss-traders
    * Won to see longest monthly losing streak since 2008 crisis

 (Adds text, updates prices)
    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SINGAPORE, Nov 28 (Reuters) - Malaysia's ringgit led losses
among emerging Asian currencies, hitting a near five-year low on
Friday as oil prices tumbled, while regional units were poised
to suffer depreciation in November.
    The ringgit lost as much as 0.8 percent to 3.3720
per dollar, its weakest since March 2010, as offshore funds
dumped the currency on fears that lower oil prices may hurt
Malaysia, a net oil exporter and major palm oil producer.
    Brent crude fell close to a four-year low touched in
the previous session after OPEC decided not to cut oil output to
support prices. 
    "The sharp drop in oil prices will weigh on the fiscal
position and the trade balance position," said Jonathan
Cavenagh, senior FX strategist with Westpac in Singapore.
    "Only central bank intervention stands in the way of further
USD/MYR strength."
    Malaysia's central bank was spotted intervening to limit the
ringgit's losses, traders said. Still, spot ringgit is seen
weakening to 3.4295, the 61.8 percent Fibonacci retracement of
its appreciation from 2009 to 2011, analysts said.
    The country narrowed the fiscal deficit to 3.9 percent of
gross domestic product in 2013, and Prime Minister Najib Razak
wants to further trim the gap to 3.5 percent this year and to 3
percent in 2015, heading toward a balanced budget by 2020.
    Malaysia's exports in September rose 2.0 percent from a year
earlier, missing market expectations, government data showed on
Nov. 7. 
    The ringgit was the No. 3 worst-performing emerging Asian
currency with a 2.8 percent loss against the dollar so far this
year, according to Thomson Reuters data.
    "We remain unconstructive on MYR," said Sacha Tihanyi, a
senior currency strategist for Scotiabank, said in a research
note.
    "Though USDMYR has traded through our end of year target of
3.30 rather rapidly in November, we continue to see further
weakness and will likely be revising up our USDMYR forecasts for
2015 and 2016."
    South Korea's won and Taiwan's dollar 
underperformed the ringgit on concerns that a weaker yen 
will reduce competitiveness of those countries' exporters.
    
    WON DOWN FOR 3RD MONTH
    The won has fallen 3.5 percent so far in November, a third
consecutive monthly depreciation and the longest monthly losing
streak since the November 2008 global credit crisis, Thomson
Reuters data shows.
    Adding to the gloomy outlook, South Korea's industrial
output in October unexpectedly fell, data showed on Friday.
 
    The South Korean currency led a monthly slide in emerging
Asian currencies.
    "Given very weak October data and our expectation of a fall
in November exports, we cannot rule out the possibility of a
25bp rate cut on 11 December, though this is not our base case,"
Nomura economist Young Sun Kwon wrote in a research note.
    The ringgit has lost 2.4 percent so far in November, which
would also be a third straight monthly slide. The Taiwan dollar
has eased 1.5 percent.
    Singapore's dollar has fallen 1.3 percent, which
would be a fifth consecutive monthly depreciation, the longest
monthly losing spree since March 2013.
    The Indonesian rupiah has lost 1.0 percent, while
the Indian rupee has slid 0.9 percent.
    The Chinese yuan has fallen 0.6 percent, which
would be the largest monthly loss since April.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Global economic recovery signs lift Asia  FX , yuan jumps
text:
* Won near 6-year high on stock inflows; intervention limits
    * Baht gains to pre-coup level on offshore, local investors
    * Ringgit around 7-month high as hedge funds buy NDFs

 (Adds text, updates prices)
    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SINGAPORE, June 9 (Reuters) - Emerging Asian currencies rose
on Monday as U.S. and China data pointed to a strengthening
global economic recovery, while the yuan jumped after the
central bank fixed the daily midpoint surprisingly higher.
    The South Korean won touched a near six-year peak
on sustained stock inflows, although intervention by the foreign
exchange authorities capped its upside.
    Malaysia's ringgit hit a near seven-month high,
tracking its strength in non-deliverable forwards (NDFs)
 on hedge funds demand.
    The Thai baht advanced to levels seen before the
May 22 military coup on demand from both offshore and local
investors as public protests against the junta dwindled.
 
    U.S jobs data on Friday showed nonfarm payrolls increased
217,000 last month, bringing employment back to its
pre-recession level and validating the view that labour
conditions are improving. 
    In China, exports in May gained steam, even though an
unexpected drop in imports indicated weaker domestic demand in
the world's second-largest economy, weekend data showed.
 
    Those signs of global recovery came as the European Central
Bank last week eased its monetary policy to prevent deflation in
the euro zone.
    With those policy step, investors have been expected to
chase higher-yielding assets in emerging Asia.
    "The U.S. nonfarm payrolls data came in at a 'sweet spot'
for Asian FX," Scotiabank said in a client note.
    "This combined with the Chinese trade data over the weekend
has set a positive tone for EM Asia at the outset of the week,
and should help bolster even underperforming Asian currencies,"
it added. 
    
    WON
    The won advanced 0.3 percent to 1,017.0 per dollar, its
strongest since August 2008, as foreign investors were set to
extend their buying spree in Seoul shares for an 18th
consecutive session.
    They have bought a combined net 3.15 trillion won ($3.10
billion) worth of stocks during the period, the Korea Exchange
data showed.
    The won also found support from catch-up demand as South
Korean financial markets were closed on Friday for a holiday
when other Asian currencies gained on the ECB's easing and a
stronger yuan.
    The foreign exchange authorities were, however, spotted
intervening to curb the won's appreciation as the currency also
hit a near six-year high against the Japanese yen.
    South Korea's major companies compete with Japanese peers in
key overseas markets and industries.
    
    BAHT
    The baht rose as much as 0.5 percent to 32.42 per dollar,
its strongest since May 22 when Thailand's military seized 
power.
    Army chief and coup leader General Prayuth Chan-ocha on
Saturday declared himself the head of the Board of Investment,
paving the way for the approval of a 700 billion baht ($21.6
billion) pending investment projects.
    The number of protesters against the coup also dwindled
although the junta kept thousands of troops and police ready to
deal with any public demonstrations. 
    Last week, foreign investors bought a combined net 8.04
billion baht in Bangkok shares.
    
    RINGGIT
    The ringgit rose as much as 0.6 percent to 3.1930 per
dollar, its strongest since Nov. 21.
    Hedge funds bought one-month NDFs, traders
said.
    A senior Malaysian bank trader in Kuala Lumpur said spot
ringgit has room to strengthen to 3.1700-3.1800.
    Malaysian exports surged by nearly a fifth in April, beating
market forecasts and increasing expectations that the central
bank may raise interest rates next month. 
    
    RUPIAH
    The rupiah gained on its strength in overnight NDFs
 market.
    The official Jakarta Interbank Spot Dollar Rate, which
Indonesia's central bank launched last year in an effort to
manage exchange rate fluctuations, was fixed at 11,790 per
dollar, stronger than the previous day's 11,823.
    The Indonesian currency, however, gave up some of earlier
gains on dollar demand linked to dividend payments, traders
said.
    The rupiah NDFs on Monday turned slightly weaker on renewed
worries about the country's current account deficit and
uncertainty over July's presidential election.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Indonesia trade deficit hits rupiah; Asia  FX  weaker
text:
* Indonesia Apr trade balance at -$1.97 bln vs +$0.22 f'cast
    * Won falls on foreign selling, intervention caution
    * Ringgit slides as stocks underperform

 (Adds text, updates prices)
    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SINGAPORE, June 2 (Reuters) - The rupiah hit its weakest
level in more than three months on Monday after Indonesia
unexpectedly reported a trade deficit, leading losses among
emerging Asian currencies as investors took profits on May's
gains amid broad strength in the dollar.
    Regional units came under further pressure as the Australian
dollar was hit by data showing Australian building
approvals in April fell more than expected. 
    The South Korean won fell as foreign investors
sold the currency amid caution over possible intervention by the
foreign exchange authorities to stem its appreciation.
    Malaysia's ringgit slid on weaker domestic stocks
.
    "The market appeared to adjust positions on the Australian
dollar's weakness," said Jeong My-young, Samsung Futures'
research head in Seoul.
    "Still, Asian currencies have more positive factors given a
recovery in China's economy and the ECB's further easing," Jeong
added.
    Chinese factory activity expanded at the fastest pace in
five months in May due to rising new orders, official data
showed on Sunday, increasing hopes that the economy is regaining
momentum in the second quarter. 
    The European Central Bank is expected to deliver economic
stimulus on Thursday via monetary easing.
    The speculation has caused investors to seek higher yields
in emerging Asia, helping most regional currencies enjoy monthly
gains.
    
    RUPIAH
    The rupiah fell as much as 0.7 percent to 11,750
per dollar, its weakest since Feb. 24.
    Indonesia reported a surprise $1.97 billion trade deficit in
April, against the market forecast of a $0.22 billion surplus
and following two consecutive months of surpluses, official data
showed earlier. 
    The rupiah is seen staying weaker in June as inflationary
pressure and imports could pick up on rising consumption ahead
of Ramadan, traders said.
    A Jakarta-based trader said the currency may also come under
pressure from dollar demand linked to dividend payments.
    
    WON
    The won slid as mounting caution over possible intervention
caused investors to cut holdings in the currency.
    Last week, the foreign exchange authorities were spotted
buying dollars to prevent the won from strengthening beyond
1,020 to the greenback, traders said.
    Foreign investors bought dollars in the futures market,
traders said.
    South Korean exports in May suffered their worst decline in
eight months due to a drop in Chinese demand and fewer working
days. 
    
    RINGGIT
    The ringgit fell as Kuala Lumpur shares lost 0.6
percent, underperforming most regional stock markets.
    Investors also covered dollar-short positions on the
Australian dollar's slide.
    Still, traders expected the ECB's potential easing to
support the ringgit, as the monetary policy may spur more
capital inflows to Asia.
    "It is just market squaring up for mega events this week
such as the ECB meeting," said a senior Malaysian bank trader in
Kuala Lumpur, referring to the ringgit's daily loss.
    The trader said he was looking to buy the ringgit around
3.2350 per dollar on dips.

    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SINGAPORE, May 7 (Reuters) - The South Korean won hit a near
six-year high on Wednesday, leading gains among emerging Asian
currencies, as U.S. Treasury yields fell ahead of Fed Chair
Janet Yellen's congressional hearings later this week.
    The baht, however, dipped as Thailand's
Constitutional Court is believed almost certain to rule against
Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra on an abuse of power charge
later in the day. 
    The won rose on catch-up plays after holidays.
Traders said the foreign exchange authorities have not yet been
spotted intervening.
    Malaysia's ringgit advanced on offshore funds'
demand in non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets and a
wider-than-expected trade surplus in March. The Taiwan dollar
 gained on capital inflows.
    The U.S. dollar stayed around its lowest since
October against a basket of six major currencies as Yellen is
widely expected to maintain a dovish stance at congressional
hearings on Wednesday and Thursday.
    "As it stands no radical departure from the script is
expected by the market," OCBC Bank said in a client note.
    "Coupled with net portfolio inflows, we note that a wobbly
dollar has continued to afford relative resilience for the Asian
units," the bank added.
    By contrast, Asian shares fell as Ukraine's worsening
chances of slipping into civil war dented risk sentiment.
    Regional currencies have not been hurt much yet by mounting
geopolitical tension there as some traders saw its impact on
Asia as limited.
    Some big global investors are riding out the
stomach-churning drops seen in Russian assets this year,
refusing to join a stampede to the exits on the belief that any
retaliation against Moscow for its role in Ukraine will fade and
prices will rebound. 
    
    WON
    The won rose as much as 0.4 percent to 1,026.0 per dollar,
its strongest since August 2008.
    Most of its NDFs to the greenback strengthened
on Monday and Tuesday when South Korea's financial markets were
closed for holidays.
    Trade was subdued on growing caution over possible
intervention by foreign exchange authorities to stem the
second-best performing emerging Asian currency so far this year.
    Some traders took profits as Seoul shares fell on
foreign investors' continuous selling.
    The dollar/won's 14-day relative strength index also fell to
29.4, below the 30-threshold, indicating dollar/won is oversold.
    
    RINGGIT
    The ringgit gained as much as 0.4 percent to 3.2400 against
the dollar, its strongest since April 21.
    Malaysia reported a 9.6 billion ringgit ($3.0 billion) trade
surplus in March, higher than a forecast of a 7.4 billion
ringgit. 
    Some offshore funds earlier bought the Malaysian currency in
one-month NDFs, traders said.
    "I prefer to sell (dollars)," said a foreign bank trader in
Singapore.
    "As long as U.S. rates continue to stay low, dollar/Asia are
more in tandem to this," the trader added, referring to overall
dollar/emerging Asian currency pairs.
    Domestic corporates such as importers, however, bought
dollars for payments on dips, limiting the ringgit's upside,
traders said.
    The ringgit is seen having chart resistance at 3.2384, the
61.8 percent Fibonacci retracement of its depreciation in April.
    
    TAIWAN DOLLAR
    The Taiwan dollar advanced on inflows from foreign financial
institutions but the flows were slowed by softer local shares
 - limiting the Taiwan dollar's gains.
    Caution increased over potential intervention by the central
bank to cap the currency's further appreciation as it threatens
to strengthen past 30.100 per U.S. dollar, a "warning zone,"
traders said.
    Authorities have has not been spotted buying the greenback
yet, the traders added.

The AUD has been something of a liquid proxy for a number of less liquid emerging-market Asian currencies, such as the CNY. This adds to worries over the ongoing protest against a cross-Strait service trade pact and the Federal Reserve's possible rate hike by mid-2015, triggering recent foreign fund outflows. Currency traders have were spooked into buying back U.S. dollar shorts on the unexpectedly hawkish tone of the U.S. Federal Reserve at its Wednesday policy meeting. Fed chief Janet Yellen said that interest rates could rise as soon as six months after the Fed's bond-buying program is completely removed, sparking a two-day surge in the U.S. dollar. Knee-jerk optimism for the rupiah that arose early this week from the nomination of presidential candidate Joko Widodo - which also rallied local stocks - appears to be fading for now. The aftershock of the U.S. Federal Reserve's hawkish tone at its Wednesday policy meeting is triggering a tsunami of dollar-buying across Asia. Overnight, medium-term investors--who typically hold larger positions--were said to be buying USD/Asia broadly. In order not to drive the dollar up too high too fast--which raises their average cost of buying the dollar--these macro funds usually spread out their orders over a few sessions. title: EM ASIA  FX -Won leads Asia  FX  losses on China, Fed worries
text:
* Won down on offshore funds, stocks; exporters relieved
    * Philippine peso lower on dollar short-covering
    * Ringgit falls; Malaysia Jan inflation at 27-month high

 (Adds text, updates prices)
    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SINGAPORE, Feb 20 (Reuters) - The South Korean won led
slides among emerging Asian currencies on Thursday, hit by
worries about a slowing Chinese economy and as the U.S. Federal
Reserve is seen scaling back its stimulus at the current pace.
    The won fell on continuous stock selling by
foreign investors and worries over China's economy as the
country is South Korea's top export market.
    The Philippine peso weakened on selling from
offshore funds and dollar-short covering.
    Activity in China's factories tumbled again in February as
employment fell at its fastest pace in five years, a private
survey showed earlier, indicating a mild slowdown in the world's
second-largest economy continues. 
    The minutes of the Fed's Jan. 28-29 policy meeting showed
several policymakers wanted to emphasize that its asset-buying
programme would be trimmed in predictable, $10-billion steps
unless the economy's performance surprises them. 
    "It is time for Asian currencies to see more corrections as
China's numbers are inconsistent, increasing uncertainties over
the economy," said Yuna Park, a currency and bond analyst at
Dongbu Securities in Seoul.
    "Asian currencies will fall further if U.S. data improves
after the impact of the cold weather wanes," Park added.
    Most emerging Asian currencies have risen so far in February
as some solid data from China earlier this month eased concerns
over the country's economic slowdown. The U.S. dollar also eased
on the recent sluggish U.S. data.
    
    WON
    The won slid as offshore funds sold the currency amid
continuous foreign selling in Seoul's main stock market.
    A senior executive at Moody's Investors Service said a
sharper-than-expected slowdown in China's growth poses a greater
threat to South Korea and the ongoing tapering by the Fed.
 
    Local exporters, however, chased the won for month-end
settlements when the South Korean unit was weaker than 1,070 per
dollar, traders said.
    It has the 50.0 percent Fibonacci retracement at 1,074.1 of
its appreciation in February.
    "The won is likely to stay weaker than 1,070 for now, but it
will depend on how much exporters sell the dollar above the
level," said a foreign bank trader in Seoul.    
    
    PHILIPPINE PESO
    The peso fell as offshore funds and local banks covered
short positions in the dollar.
    Investors expect dollar demand from local companies for
month-end payments.
    "As long as dollar/peso stays above 44.69-71, I will try to
go long targeting 44.85," said a Philippine bank trader in
Manila.
    
    RINGGIT
    The ringgit eased against the U.S. dollar in thin trade
after data on Wednesday showed Malaysia's inflation in January
hit a 27-month high. 
    The Malaysian currency also fell against the Singapore
dollar.
    Still, investors stayed wary of possible intervention by
Malaysia's central bank to stem its weakness.

The ringgit is weaker Thursday as the greenback rebounded against the emerging market currencies overnight after the U.S. Federal Reserve again reduced its monthly bond buying program by $10 billion, sparking a bout of risk aversion in global stock markets. 0145 GMT [Dow Jones] PREVIEW: The Philippine economy likely slowed in 4Q, dragged by destruction wrought by natural calamities, particularly Typhoon Haiyan. The median forecast of 11 economists polled by the Wall Street Journal projects 4Q gross domestic product growth at 6.0% on year, a slower pace than the 7.0% posted in 3Q. "Private consumption and public spending should remain supportive of overall growth," says Bernard Aw, research analyst at Forecast Pte. The government is confident GDP growth will be at the higher end of the 6.0%-7.0% growth target, with the strong performance of the economy in the first three quarters cushioning the weakness in the last three months of the year. Full-year and 4Q GDP data are due 0200 GMT Thursday. (cris.larano@dowjones.com)

0139 GMT [Dow Jones] The rout in emerging markets is a bit of a misnomer, DBS says. The bank notes that the currencies of Turkey, Latin America and Russia are being hit, but Asian currencies for the most part are not. "On the currency front, for example, the Turkish lira, Argentine peso and Russian ruble are down (against the dollar) by 29%, 10% and 6.5% from average Dec 2013 levels. Most Asian currencies are off by 1% to 2% over the same time frame. In the currency world, that's practically nothing; just noise (market price vibrations), the bank says. DBS also pointed out that the Canadian dollar, hardly an emerging-market currency, is down by 4.5%, while China's yuan--the biggest emerging market currency of all--is stronger against the dollar than it was back in December. (jerry.tan@wsj.com)

0135 GMT [Dow Jones] Crude-oil futures are slightly higher in early Asian trade Thursday as investors weigh Fed tapering and a rise in U.S. oil stockpiles. Oil inventories rise by 6.4 million barrels to 357.6 million barrels in the week ended Jan. 24, EIA data show, compared to an expected gain of 2.2 million barrels. "The advance in stocks was despite the opening of the southern leg of the Keystone pipeline which allows improved access to Cushing stocks. The rise in crude inventories was balanced by a large decline in distillate inventories, which declined 4.6 million barrels, more than double forecasts," ANZ says. Oil markets also have support from the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to cut bond purchases by another $10 billion. "The decision to taper was unanimous and it shows the confidence Fed officials have towards the sustainability of their country's economic recovery," Philip Futures says. Nymex crude is up 25 cents at $97.62/bbl, ICE Brent is up 1 cent at $107.86/bbl. (eric.yep@wsj.com)

0131 GMT [Dow Jones] BMD CPO futures are headed for a choppy session on Thursday as investors may square off positions ahead of the Lunar New Year holiday. Market participants say negative technical cues point to more downside for the tropical oil that is used to make everything from chocolates to cookies and lipsticks. CPO's downside target remains at MYR2,505/ton, says AmInvestment Bank. Benchmark April CPO ended up MYR15 at MYR2,544/ton Wednesday. (shie-lynn.lim@wsj.com)

A mitigating factor that could help the Singapore dollar hold up is the safe-haven status of the currency relative to regional emerging-market currencies. If risk aversion escalates, the Singapore dollar could see more demand as investors seek stability and USD/SGD could thus be weighed lower. USD/SGD is now at 1.2768 from its Wednesday close of 1.2767. (ewen.chew@wsj.com)

The benchmark KLCI is down 0.3% at 1783.57. "There might be some profit taking going on ahead of long Chinese New Year holiday," brokerage house JF Apex says, and tips support at 1775. (abhrajit.gangopadhyay@wsj.com)

USD/JPY is now at 102.17 against 103.33 before the Fed announcement. "The Wednesday 2.7% market rise was overdone given prevailing global market conditions, as the turmoil in emerging markets does not look like it's close to dying down," says Yoshihiro Okumura, general manager at Chibagin Asset Management. "While the continuation of the Fed's tapering program implies higher U.S. interest rates, a stronger dollar and a weaker yen--all of which are fundamentally positive for Japan stocks--the 'risk-off' investor mood and jolt to the world's growth markets is trumping these facts." All 33 subindexes are lower, with SoftBank (9984.TO) off 5.6% at Y7,387, extending its losing streak to seven days. Fast Retailing (9983.TO) is also down 3.4% at Y38,010. Canon (7751.TO) falls 1.6% despite posting a net-profit increase Wednesday of 5% for Apr-Dec. Sumitomo Mitsui FG (8316.TO) falls 5% despite announcing a 28% rise in Apr-Dec. net profit. Nintendo (7974.TO) rises 0.9% at Y13,000 after announcing a share buyback. (bradford.frischkorn@wsj.com)

0022 GMT [Dow Jones] Worries about emerging markets could start to weigh on base-metal prices as China heads into its week-long Lunar New Year holidays that starts Friday. "Unwinding the US Federal Reserve's quantitative easing programme was never going to be easy and it has barely started and some emerging market countries are already running into trouble," Justin Pugsley, markets analyst at MahiFX, says in a report. The two big external factors as to whether recent emerging-market currency volatility is just a wobble or the beginning of a bigger crisis will be the pace of global economic growth and China, the world's biggest consumer of industrial metals. Slowing China growth has already triggered a fall in copper prices in the past six sessions on the Comex. LME 3-month copper ends 0.2% lower at $7,127/ton Wednesday, while aluminium closes 0.7% lower at $1,741/ton after touching $1,735.25/ton--the lowest price since July 2009. (arpan.mukherjee@wsj.com)

He says USD/JPY may fall to 101.50 during Asian trading from 102.32 currently. There appear to be few ways to stave off another selloff now that rate hikes from the Turkish and South African central banks on Wednesday failed to restore stability. "This trend is likely to continue for a while," he says. Meanwhile, the Fed decided to cut its monetary stimulus more, which doesn't help riskier assets. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com)

17:05 EST - A 25 bps interest rate hike in March by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, absent a significant escalation of emerging-market tensions, now looks like a strong bet, said Darren Gibbs, strategist at Deutsche Bank. He says while the market might toy with the possibility of a 50 bps hike in March, DB views this as exceptionally unlikely. Instead, firm sees authorities following through with three further 25 bps hikes, most likely in April, June and either September or December. Gibbs adds that given the present global environment, there is no need for more aggressive action by the RBNZ. (james.glynn@wsj.com)

16:40 EST - Buying the Australian dollar against the New Zealand dollar might be the trade of choice now that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand has decided to hold interest rates steady, said Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac, based in Sydney. This trade might become even more attractive if the Reserve Bank of Australia removes its easing bias at a policy meeting on Tuesday. With recent 4Q inflation data in Australian surprising to the high side, there is a strong chance the RBA will change views, ditching plans to cut rates further. The Australian dollar was trading in early Asia at NZ$1.067, up from NZ$1.0575 before the RBNZ announcement. (james.glynn@wsj.com)

title: EM ASIA  FX -Rupiah leads Asia  FX  gains; ringgit higher before budget
text:
* Rupiah to see best week since Sept 2009 on inflows * Malaysia PM Najib's budget speech eyed * Won dips on intervention caution, exporters limit losses (Adds text, updates prices) By Jongwoo Cheon SINGAPORE, ct 25 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah hit a near eight-week high on Friday, leading gains among emerging Asian currencies, as expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve will maintain its bond-buying programme through early next year kept the dollar pressured. The rupiah is poised to enjoy the best week in more than four years on capital inflows and demand from real money funds. The Malaysian ringgit gained on hopes the government will announce later in the day measures to cut the fiscal deficit. The dollar stayed around a nine-month low against a basket of major currencies as a disappointing U.S. jobs data earlier this week cemented views that the Fed's plans to taper its stimulus won't start until next year.

 "With the market pushing out the timing of Fed tapering until March 2014, further portfolio inflows into emerging Asia can be expected in the near-term," ANZ said in a client note. Even before the U.S. September payrolls number, most emerging Asian currencies had gravitated to the view that the recently-ended 16-day U.S. government shutdown will likely prompt the Fed to delay a shift in policy.


    The rupiah took top honours in emerging Asia this week,
making the most out of the dollar's dour near term outlook.   
    The Indonesian currency has risen 3.0 percent against the
dollar, the largest weekly gain since the week ended on June 5,
2009, according to Thomson Reuters data.
    The rupiah is seen as one of the most vulnerable to the


Fed's tapering due to Indonesia's sizable current account deficit. It remains the worst-performing Asian currency of the year. Last week, central bank Governor Agus Martowardojo said the current account deficit is likely to ease to less than 3 percent of gross domestic product. The gap hit 4.4 percent in the second quarter. The ringgit has also gained 0.4 percent so far this week, while the Taiwan dollar has risen 0.2 percent. The Singapore dollar is up 0.1 percent. The South Korean won took a different path, turning weaker for the week with a 0.1 percent loss after the foreign exchange authorities on Thursday were spotted buying dollars after earlier warning against "excessive" won moves.


    
    RUPIAH
    The rupiah rose as much as 1.6 percent to 10,970 per dollar,
its strongest since Sept. 2, on demand from custodian banks.
    The forward onshore market, or Jakarta Interbank Spot Dollar
Rate (JISDOR), was fixed at 11,142 per dollar,
compared with Thursday's 11,268.
    Five-year Indonesian government bond yield fell
to 6.896 percent, the lowest since July 10. Three-year yield
 also slid to 6.631 percent, the lowest since June 25.
    Domestic shares eased, but the market enjoyed
foreign buying in the previous two sessions.
    A Jakarta-based trader said the rupiah may strengthen to
10,700.
    
    RINGGIT
    The ringgit advanced on hopes that the government may
announce steps to tackle Malaysia's fiscal deficit when Prime
Minister Najib Razak unveils the 2014 budget.
    "Our fundamental view is mildly bullish on the budget and we


expect price to head towards 3.0770 should the budget meet expectations," Maybank said, referring to the ringgit's value to the dollar, in a note. Still, local investors took profits to guard against any disappointment from the prime minister's proposals. The Malaysian currency has a chart resistance at 3.1410, a 200-day moving average.


    
    WON
    The won edged down as offshore funds sold the currency on
heightened caution over possible intervention by the
authorities.
    Foreign investors were poised to report their first selling
day in Seoul's main stock market in 41 sessions.
    Still, the won found relief from exporters' month-end demand
for settlements, traders said.
    South Korea's economy grew 1.1 percent in the third quarter
from the previous three months, the central bank estimated,
slightly beating market expectations. 
    "The authorities are likely to keep the won around the


current level. The won's resistance is seen firmer if foreigners stop a buying spree in the stock market," said a foreign bank trader in Seoul. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0430 GMT

title: FX  CHAT: Resilience of North-Asia  Currencies  Continues; Won Gains.
text:
Contact us in Singapore. 65 64154 140; MarketTalk@dowjones.com 
 
 

0646 GMT [Dow Jones] The South Korea won bucks the trend of falling currencies in Asia while China's yuan and the Taiwan dollar bob about. The won is up on Wednesday ending stronger at 1,115.4 versus its Tuesday close of 1,116.3 as the Kospi reverses its earlier 1.2% loss to close nearly flat. China's yuan is just a little weaker at 6.1228 to the dollar against its Tuesday close of 6.1217 while the Taiwan dollar is roughly unchanged. The tale of two cities continues to play out in Asia where the countries with current-account deficits suffer disproportionately in this bout of global risk aversion sparked by fear of the U.S. stepping into the Syria situation. India's rupee hit a new low of 68.75--3.6% weaker than its Tuesday record of 66.30. Malaysia and Indonesia continue to extend their multiyear lows as they remain under pressure owing to their deteriorating current-account deficits. (ewen.chew@wsj.com)

0614 GMT [Dow Jones] Asia has a high exposure to oil, and there are numerous channels through which rising oil prices can impact Asian economies, including worsening trade balances, weakening fiscal positions, squeezed profit margins, higher inflation and weaker domestic consumption, analysts at Nomura say in a note. They say Thailand, South Korea, the Philippines and India are the largest net importers of oil and petroleum products as a percentage of GDP, and a rise in oil prices would hurt their current account balances the most. A $10/bbl rise in oil prices would lower Asian GDP growth by 0.4% and weaken Asia's current account positions by 0.6% of GDP, Nomura says, citing the IMF. Nymex WTI crude is up $2.64 at $111.65/bbl, ICE Brent crude is up $2.02 at $116.38/bbl. (eric.yep@dowjones.com)

PREVIEW: South Korea's exports in August likely expanded 4.0% from a year earlier, following a 2.6% rise in July, a survey of seven economists polled by Dow Jones shows; imports likely increased a median 2.9% on-year in August, compared with a revised 3.2% gain in July. Daishin Economic Research Institute senior economist Kim Yoon-gee says growth in South Korean exports will likely accelerate in the second half on growing shipbuilding orders and economic recovery in the U.S. and Europe. The Dow Jones survey forecasts a trade surplus of $2.8 billion in August, compared with a revised surplus of $2.54 billion in July. The trade ministry is due to issue August data at 0000 GMT Sunday. (kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com)

PREVIEW: South Korea's industrial production likely expanded 1.0% on-year in July, reversing the 2.6% on-year contraction in June, a median forecast of seven economists polled by Dow Jones shows; on a month-on-month basis, output likely grew 0.4% in July, remaining unchanged from the preceding month. Hana Daetoo Securities economist Kim Doo-un says the output growth likely had support from increased shipments of IT goods on new product releases as well as South Korea's shipbuilding industry picking up on Europe's economic rebound. July's output data will be released at 2300 GMT Thursday. (kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com)

0603 GMT [Dow Jones] South Korea's year-on-year inflation likely remained at 1.4% in August, unchanged from the previous month, according to the median forecast of seven economists surveyed by Dow Jones. On a month-on-month basis, the consumer price index likely gained 0.4% in August after a 0.2% rise in July. Hyundai Securities economist Lee Sang-jae says the year-on-year inflation will likely remain subdued at a mid-1% level through the year. August's CPI data are due Sunday at 2300 GMT. (kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com)

0513 GMT [Dow Jones] Fed tapering fears have taken a back burner Wednesday to concerns surrounding a possible U.S. military strike against Syria, although the question that has dominated markets for months surely isn't far from investor minds with a key meeting of the central bank's policy makers just weeks away. Over at Daiwa, the firm says the Fed's verdict on whether or not to start winding down its easing program is a "close call for September" but it continues to believe the central bank will stick to its current program until at least October. "We suspect that officials will not have enough information one month from now to ease their concerns about the economic outlook," the firm adds, noting the impact of rising interest rates on housing activity as one area that may merit further review at the Fed. (mia.lamar@wsj.com)

0445 GMT [Dow Jones] Australian shares are likely to rise as domestic political uncertainty abates after the Federal Election on Sept. 7, though investors may tend to wait for the Federal Reserve meeting on September 17/18 before significantly adding to their portfolios, says Martin Lakos, Macquarie Private Wealth division director. "Investors are cognizant of risks from Syria, but there's certainly no panic by any stretch of the imagination," he adds. "They are actually focusing more on what's happening domestically and what they should be doing after the Sept. 7 election. It's been a very long election campaign and I think the domestic market will benefit from a recovery in consumer and business confidence once that's out of the way." The S&P/ASX 200 index is down 1.1% at 5083.4. (david.rogers1@wsj.com)

There still appears to be no end to the rupee's slide, as the dollar once again rises due to global risk aversion to a new record high of 67.63 versus Tuesday's high of 66.30. In addition to the dumping of risk assets on fear of the U.S. being drawn into the Syria conflict, the possibility of capital flight from India is also pushing the USD/INR higher. Though the government said last week there are no plans to install capital controls, India has a poor track record of consistency in its policy, hence rupee investors are still jittery and looking to take their money out while they can. The USD/INR is recently at 67.59. (ewen.chew@wsj.com)

0410 GMT [Dow Jones] The Philippine economy likely slowed in the second quarter after 7.8% on-year growth in the first--the fastest in Asia for that period. The median forecast of 10 economists project gross domestic product growth in the April-June quarter at 7.5% on year. GDP data is due at 0200 GMT Thursday. Eternal trade weighed on growth in the second quarter, ANZ economist Eugenia Victorina says. "We expect consumption to have gotten a boost from election-related spending in the first two months of Q2," she adds. (cris.larano@wsj.com)

0359 GMT [Dow Jones] Gold is little-changed in Asia after rising to a three-month high overnight as investors flee risky assets amid escalating geopolitical tensions in Syria. The metal may continue its upward trend in the coming sessions thanks to a combination of its safe-haven status amid Middle East instability and macroeconomic variables out of the U.S., traders say. Nonetheless, the decline in the rupee will almost certainly raise fresh doubts about Indian gold demand going into the wedding season, especially now that the impact of a weaker currency is being magnified by sharply higher gold prices, IntlFC Stone senior analyst Edward Meir says. In the physical markets, the SPDR gold fund reported another modest inflow as of last Friday and there are many more days where increases are taking place as opposed to withdrawals, perhaps an indication that fund money is finally wading back into the complex, Mr. Meir adds. Spot gold is at $1,417/oz. (yue.li@dowjones.com)

The NZD/USD is likely to remain under pressure as the market "is waiting with bated breath" to find out whether there will be military action in Syria, says HiFX dealer Michael Johnston. "The path of least resistance for it (the NZD) is lower." Over the last 24 hours there has been tough rhetoric from the U.S. and its allies on Syria, which has raised the specter of military action and seen investors move towards currencies perceived traditionally as safe. The pair is at 0.7788 vs 0.7795 this morning. Johnston says support around 0.7800 has been difficult to break convincingly, with further support sitting at 0.7750. (lucy.craymer@wsj.com)

0342 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/MYR is a little higher at 3.3315 vs 3.3300 late on Tuesday in Asia supported by continued equity-related outflow; the benchmark KLCI is down 1.2% mainly on concerns over possible U.S. intervention in Syria. Comments from the Malaysia central bank governor on Tuesday could boost the pair towards 3.3500 "sooner than we thought," Maybank IB says. Bank Negara Malaysia governor says it doesn't focus on any specific level for the ringgit and intervenes only when the foreign-exchange market is "highly disruptive and disorderly." (jason.ng@wsj.com) [ 28-08-13 0646GMT ]
