0246 GMT [Dow Jones] Brent crude oil prices may surge to $120-$125/bbl either in anticipation of an attack on Syria or in reaction to headlines that an attack has started, analyst Michael Wittner at Societe Generale says in a note. "In our base case, we assume an attack begins in the next week. If it takes longer, and there are no signals that an attack is imminent, the oil price uplift from the entire Syrian situation will start to fade," Wittner says, adding that an attack is likely within the next week, but not before the weekend. However if the conflict spills over and results in supply disruptions then Brent could briefly spike to $150/bbl, he says. The big worry is Iraq where attacks on oil installations may be moving south and disrupt the 2 million barrels a day of Basrah grade crude oil exported through the Basrah port complex on the Persian Gulf. Nymex WTI crude is up $1.46 at $110.46/bbl, ICE Brent crude is up $1.59 at $115.95/bbl. (eric.yep@dowjones.com)

0223 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/PHP, currently at 44.54, could be on the way to 45.00 as risk aversion shifts into higher gear following the overnight surge in demand for U.S. Treasuries as an investment safe harbor. High-yielding assets, such as emerging market currencies, are being dumped and money is being parked in U.S. dollars as risk aversion exacerbates due to the U.S. possibly entering the Syrian conflict. While the Philippines is not deemed as risky as say, Indonesia or India, the large speculative bets on the peso -- which accumulated earlier this year on expectations of the country getting an investment grade rating from all three major credit rating agencies -- could now potentially be reversing. (ewen.chew@wsj.com)

0151 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/MYR hit a second consecutive 3-year high of 3.3340, topping Tuesday's 3.3300, as global risk aversion goes into full swing, marked by strong buying of U.S. Treasuries - typically considered the safest investment. USD/MYR may be on its way to the top of the weekly Bollinger uptrend channel at 3.3500 next. The greenback will likely remain well-bid despite the overnight slippage in the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield - which had a positive correlation with the dollar up till this week - simply because the flight to safe haven assets will send investors away from risky ones such as the Malaysia ringgit. USD/MYR is now 3.3290.(ewen.chew@wsj.com)

0148 GMT [Dow Jones] Crude-oil futures extend gains in Asian trade Wednesday as tensions in Syria build up, with Nymex WTI trading at its highest level in 18 months and ICE Brent at its highest in six months. "While the events in Syria have little impact on oil prices in isolation, the potential impact flowing through to the rest of the region is high while sectarian violence continues in Iraq and supplies from Nigeria, Libya and Sudan continue to disappoint," ANZ said in a note this morning, adding that a larger-than-expected build in US crude inventories was largely ignored in the face of escalating Middle East tensions. The API, a trade group, said late Tuesday that its data showed crude oil stockpiles rose by 2.5 million barrels. Nymex WTI crude is up 71 cents at $109.72/bbl, ICE Brent crude is up 92 cents at $115.28/bbl. (eric.yep@dowjones.com)

0145 GMT [Dow Jones] Taiwan shares are down 0.6% at 7773.43, tracking losses on Wall Street, on concerns over escalating tensions in Syria, says Horizon Securities analyst Benson Huang. "There are too much uncertainties, such as the QE tapering, the development in Syria, and the impact from the government's decision to raise power prices in October," he says, but adds buying from government-backed funds is providing some support. He tips the Taiex to trade in a 7810-7760 band for the session. Hon Hai (2317.TW) falls 1.0% to NT$79.20 and HTC (2498.TW) is down 1.0% at NT$148.50; TSMC (2330.TW) rises 0.1% to NT$95.70. MediaTek (2454.TW) rises 0.5% to NT$369.00 after the company announced late Tuesday its merger with MStar (3697.TW) was conditionally approved by Chinese regulators. (fanny.liu@wsj.com)

The Singapore dollar may weaken further, dragged by other currencies in the vicinity, which continue to weaken against the U.S. dollar. USD/SGD is rising within the daily Bollinger uptrend channel, eyeing the top of the channel at 1.2876. Speculative traders have been buying the U.S. dollar broadly, in anticipation of further emerging market carnage, thus sending several Southeast Asia currencies to multi-year lows. The Sing dollar, which notched a 1-year low of 1.2859 Tuesday, has reacted much less to risk aversion than its direct neighbors, Malaysia's ringgit and Indonesia's rupiah. But traders are now buying more USD/SGD, anticipating the pair to catch up with the rest of Southeast Asia in due course. USD/SGD is now at 1.2826. (ewen.chew@wsj.com)

The dollar remains strong in Asia, despite U.S. yields slipping overnight because investors bought more U.S. Treasurys -- the ultimate safe-haven asset -- amid risk aversion related to the possibility the U.S. may enter the Syria conflict. While data Tuesday showed U.S. consumer confidence improved markedly and U.S. home prices rose -- though at a slower pace -- which suggest the Fed could indeed reduce its pace of bond purchases next month, the focus now is on dumping risky assets for safer ones, which could therefore see the U.S. Treasury yields continue to slip. (ewen.chew@wsj.com)

0120 GMT [Dow Jones] Shares of Japanese exporters are leading the broader market down as the dollar and euro continue their descent against the yen, with the dollar last at Y97.15. Canon (7751.TO) and Nikon (7731.TO) hit new year lows, down 1.4% at Y2,959 and down 1.1% at Y1,667, respectively. "Investors see the risk in both issues, with the fall in the dollar and the euro and the pair's exposure to overseas markets for their digital cameras," says Okasan Securities Strategist Hideyuki Ishiguro. "The market may yet worsen for Japan shares as U.S. stocks look overbought against the background of Syria tensions, Fed tapering, and re-kindling debate over raising the U.S. national debt ceiling, which together pose a threat to stocks," says Tachibana Securities market advisor Kenichi Hirano. (bradford.frischkorn@wsj.com)

USD/KRW falls to 1,118.40 from an earlier Wednesday high of 1,119.80, but is still higher than Tuesday's onshore close of 1,116.30. Lee Seung-sik, Hana Bank FX analyst, says there is upward pressure on the pair due to traders selling risk currencies because of concerns the U.S. plans military intervention in the Syrian civil war but that force is tempered by expectations that South Korean firms will be making their usual end-of-the-month conversions of foreign currency-denominated assets into the won. Lee tips the pair in a 1,115-1,123 range Wednesday. (jeyup.kwaak@wsj.com)

0023 GMT [Dow Jones] The recent copper rally may be about to run out of steam. After rising more than 6% this month, Barclays says it's skeptical the market's uptrend can continue. Its argument: the rally has been merely the result of short covering from a period of extreme bearishness, rather than any notable demand from market bulls on signs of economic stabilization in China. Base metals are "still facing a sluggish global growth environment with unimpressive demand trends," Barclays analysts say in a note. The bank forecasts copper to move into a clear surplus by 4Q13, as demand for copper cable for China's power-grid infrastructure slows and mine supply rises. "Our new trade recommendation," the Barclays analysts say, "is to short copper above US$7,200 a ton." LME three-month copper is trading US$1.25 lower at US$7,313.75 a ton. (rhiannon.hoyle@wsj.com) [ 28-08-13 0342GMT ]

"Opposing forces are shaping oil market fundamentals on both sides of the Atlantic, with the WTI-Brent spread reflecting this shift in balances," the bank said, adding that the factors boosting WTI crude are easing while large supply shortfalls and heightened geopolitical tension support crude prices outside North America. The house says Brent crude is also facing a shrinking pool of supplies in the North Sea implying better support in the long run. "The deep seated problems underlying recent export shortfalls from Libya look intractable in the short term and, in our view, the oil market will need to get used to increased variability in Libyan supply," Barclays says. If EUR/USD drops out of the uptrend channel - a possibility as dollar strength builds ahead of the September FOMC meeting - the euro could retreat to $1.3329 where the 20-day Bollinger mid-support lies. (ewen.chew@wsj.com)

0250 GMT [Dow Jones] Singapore's industrial production likely grew 1.5% on year in July, helped by a lower base of comparison, according to the median estimate in a Dow Jones Newswires poll of seven economists. That compares with a 5.9% fall in June. Measured on month in seasonally adjusted terms, industrial production likely contracted 0.3% in July after falling 3.1% in June. Economists point to purchasing managers' index data from Singapore showing an improvement in the manufacturing sectors and a mild increase in industrial output could be "in line with our modest recovery theory," says Selena Ling, the head of treasury research at OCBC. The data are due at 0500 GMT on Monday. (gaurav.raghuvanshi@dowjones.com)

0215 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/CNY falls, in response to the Chinese central bank's guidance to lead the pair's fixing lower. A Shanghai-based local bank trader says corporate dollar selling may push the pair down further for the session, tipping a nearby support at 6.1100. Near-term, the pair may consolidate with a downward bias around 6.1200, the trader adds. The USD/CNY is at 6.1186, vs 6.1210 late Friday, while the central parity is set at 6.1680 vs 6.1710 Friday. Offshore one-year USD/CNY is at 6.2350/6.2400 vs 6.2440/6.2470 late Friday. (yue.li@wsj.com)

USD/IDR NDF contracts continue to trade at an exorbitant premium to the spot contract, a sign that dollar liquidity in the onshore market is still thin and investor confidence is low. The 1-month NDF contract--the most liquid in the offshore market--trades at close to IDR600 over the spot price. In 'normal' market conditions, the premium over the spot price is around IDR30-IDR50. Once the NDF premium begins to decline, which traders see as a sign of improving investor confidence and a return of appetite for high-yielding assets, we could see the rupiah stage a more significant recovery. USD/IDR is now 11,380--IDR600 over the current spot price. (ewen.chew@wsj.com)

USD/KRW falls for a second straight session, to 1,113.5 from 1,116.9 late Friday. Samsung Futures analyst Jeon Seung-ji says it is likely to be a directionless week for the pair amid a tug of war between month-end export settlement and a number of USD-supporting uncertainties; "Fear that the Fed could taper its stimulus measures soon, jitters over destabilizing emerging markets, and BOK's possible intervention all are providing a firm support." She tips a 1,110-1,117 band for Monday and 1,110-1,127 range for this week. (kanga.kong@wsj.com)

USD/CNY - consolidation. Technical signals suggest a mild downside bias if the USD/CNY pair stays within the Bollinger downtrend channel that caps now at 6.1224. Traders have recently started speculating again that the Chinese authorities might implement a rate cut or reduce the reserve ratio requirement that banks must hold, in order to stimulate growth to meet the government's GDP target of 7.5%. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support for USD/CNY is at 6.1200 (psychological support), then at 6.1143 (base of Bollinger downtrend channel), before 6.1090 (record low). Immediate resistance is likely at 6.1224 (top of daily Bollinger downtrend channel), then at 6.1306 (20-day Bollinger mid), before 6.1387 (daily Bollinger uptrend channel).

USD/TWD - upside bias. USD/TWD appears bullish on the chart, hovering just above the Ichimoku Cloud zone which provides support at 30.060. The dollar is likely to stay in demand as a September withdrawal of U.S. monetary stimulus looms. Traders will be averse toward shorting the dollar due to the elevated U.S. 10-year Treasury yield. Taiwan industrial production data, released Friday, surprised much stronger and bodes well for 3Q growth, which could further insulate the Taiwan dollar from the selloff in emerging Asia currencies. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support is at 30.060 (daily Ichimoku Cloud support and 20-day Bollinger mid), then at 30.000 (psychological support), before 29.940 (daily Bollinger downtrend channel). Immediate resistance is likely at 30.180 (daily Bollinger uptrend channel), then at 30.300 (top of daily Bollinger uptrend channel).

USD/KRW - consolidation. USD/KRW may be supported near the daily Bollinger downtrend channel as the dollar opens lower Monday at 1,113, gapping down from its Friday close of 1,116.9. The reaction might be due to the slight pullback in the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield Friday. Although most traders expect some form of tapering to occur after the U.S. Federal Reserve meets in September, the upside for the dollar may already have been priced in to some extent and the greenback may hence give up some gains ahead of the FOMC. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support is at 1,112 (daily Bollinger downtrend channel), then at 1,110 (psychological support), before 1,108 (base of daily Bollinger downtrend channel). Immediate resistance is at 1,117 (20-day Bollinger mid), then at 1,120 (psychological resistance), before 1,121 (daily Bollinger uptrend channel).

USD/SGD - upside bias. USD/SGD has dipped to the bottom of the Bollinger uptrend channel at 1.2775 and may consolidate here for a bit, but as long as this key support is intact at the end of the day, further dollar upside looks likely. The greenback slipped as the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield subsided a little Friday, but there may be buying-on-dips expected as the market is leaning toward a September Fed tapering of QE. Singapore releases industrial production data for July at 0500GMT. Recent intervention by the Malaysia central bank did little to deter dollar-buying, though it did slow the pace of the move higher last week, which could be part of the reason traders are reducing their long-dollar positions. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support is at 3.2800 (psychological support), then at 3.2650 (20-day Bollinger mid support), before 3.2500 (psychological support). Immediate resistance is at 3.2870 (daily Bollinger uptrend channel), then at 3.3000 (major psychological barrier), before 3.3090 (top of daily Bollinger uptrend channel).

USD/THB - consolidation with upside bias. USD/THB may retreat slightly as the dollar eases against most other South East Asia currencies. The daily chart suggests a slightly overbought situation that might require a pullback to 31.72 to relieve some of the skew in market positioning. When speculative positioning is more balanced, there could again be more room to the upside. The pair could range within a 31.72-32.00 band for now. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support is at 31.80 (psychological support), then at 31.72 (daily Bollinger band standard deviation 2), before 31.50 (psychological support). Immediate resistance is at 32.00 (psychological resistance), then at 32.17 (Thursday's 3-year high), before 32.49 (monthly Bollinger uptrend channel).

USD/PHP - closed.

USD/IDR - pullback lower. USD/IDR could pullback toward 10,500 as the market reacts to the moves announced by the government Friday. The Indonesia finance ministry decided to temporarily scrap the mineral export quota, as well as to increase taxes on imported cars. Additionally, the government said it will open more industries to foreigners, all in an attempt to increase inflows, improve trade balance and therefore bring down the current account deficit. The rupiah has been under immense selling pressure due to its burgeoning deficit problem. The USD/IDR NDF contracts continue to trade at an exorbitant premium to the spot contract, a sign that dollar liquidity in the onshore market is still thin and investor confidence is low. Once the NDF premium begins to decline, we could see the rupiah stage a more significant recovery. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support for spot USD/IDR is at 10,700 (psychological support), then at 10,640 (daily Bollinger band standard deviation 2), before 10,500 (psychological support). Immediate resistance is at 10,800 (psychological resistance), before 11,000 (major psychological barrier).

USD/INR - reversal lower. Technical signs suggest the USD/INR could reverse lower, possibly to the base of the daily Bollinger uptrend channel at 61.74. The long-tailed doji candlestick Thursday followed by the bearish engulfing candlestick Friday confirms the reversal signal. The rupee has been able to salvage some of its losses after the government said there are no plans to install capital controls to stop the currency's freefall. This calmed the market, which had been anticipating a larger exodus of investors taking flight in fear of capital controls to come. The multitude of problems facing India, beginning with its chronic current account deficit, have seen it collapse to an all-time low of 65.56 to the dollar. Dow Jones technical analysis suggests immediate support is at 63.00 (psychological support), then at 62.50 (psychological support), before 62.00 (psychological support). Immediate resistance is at 63.50 (psychological resistance), then at 64.00 (psychological resistance), before 65.00 (psychological resistance).

title: Malaysian c.bank says rarely  intervenes  in ringgit
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Feb 23 (Reuters) - Malaysia has largely adopted a hands-off approach in managing the ringgit since it removed the currency's peg to the dollar, mostly leaving it to market forces to determine its level, the central bank chief said.  

Malaysia freed the ringgit <MYR=> in July 2005 from its seven-year-old dollar peg in favour of a managed float, but economists and currency dealers said the authorities had still kept a grip on the currency to protect its exporters.  

Central bank chief Zeti Akhtar Aziz, who rarely comments on day-to-day management of the ringgit, told Reuters in an interview late on Thursday there had been minimal intervention since Malaysia abandoned the peg of 3.8 per U.S. dollar.  

"At some points in time when there are excesses, this does occur but it has been very few in number," Zeti said.  

"For the most part, it has not required intervention operations and the rate has been market-determined. But we have been transparent in always mentioning that orderly market conditions are important and that our policy will be guided by that."  

The ringgit is one of Asia's best-performing currencies so far this year, with a gain of about one percent.  

However, it defied expectations of a large, immediate appreciation when it was untied from the dollar in mid-2005, holding a tight range until early 2006, which raised suspicions of intervention.  

Dealers say the central bank eased its tight grip on the ringgit last year, allowing more fluctuation.  

At the same time, they say, it has made its presence felt in capping sharp gains -- for instance, buying dollars through agent banks in January to prevent a rapid appreciation through 3.5 per dollar.  

Zeti said the central bank could step in when trading volumes were thin and market movements exaggerated.  

"Certainly, one of the criteria is if the market is very thin and a very small transaction results in a very large movement," she said.  

Philip Wee, senior currency economist with Singapore's DBS Bank, said Malaysia had loosened its hold on the ringgit on occasions.  

"After the Thai capital controls, they were keen to differentiate themselves from Thailand to build up investor confidence," Wee said.  

"Given the broad international push for more market-driven currencies, nobody -- except for Thailand -- would like to declare in a loud way that they are controlling the currencies."  

The ringgit traded at about 3.4920 per dollar on Friday.

title: Malaysia 2nd Fin Min: "Very Happy" About Fund Inflows
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Malaysia is "very happy" with the recent inflow of foreign funds into the country, Second Finance Minister Nor Mohamed Yakcop said Tuesday, a day after Asian central bankers warned that rising regional capital flows pose a major challenge.  

"No. We are not concerned at all, we are very happy with the capital inflows," he told reporters when asked whether the government was concerned about the inflows. "We will carry on with the policy to encourage portfolio inflows - that is the policy."  

Asian central bankers meeting in Tokyo Monday said that large capital inflows into the region posed a policy challenge because of its impact on economic and foreign-exchange policy.  

Malaysia's central bank has been intervening in the foreign exchange market, apparently to smoothen rising capital flows after Thailand recently introduced capital controls.  

The second finance minister also reiterated that the government is confident that last year's gross domestic product growth probably exceeded the government's 5.8% target. The economy expanded by 6% in the first three quarters.

title: US Treasury:China Moving To Flexible Yuan But Too Slowly
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--The U.S. Treasury Department on Tuesday again declined to designate China as guilty of currency manipulation in a report, noting the government in Beijing is moving steadily, though slowly, toward a flexible foreign exchange regime.  

"The Department of Treasury concluded that no major trading partner of the U.S. met the technical requirements for designation," according to the closely watched and overdue report to Congress on international exchange rate policies during the first half of 2006.  

Treasury outlined steps China is taking to loosen restrictions on capital moving in and out of the country and develop new financial instruments, such as currency futures, to prepare for a freely floating currency. In recent months, the government has allowed the value of the Chinese yuan to fluctuate more and the pace of appreciation has picked up. This progress made it difficult to say that China is managing its currency regime with the intent of gaining a trade advantage, a senior Treasury official told reporters on condition of anonymity.  

Nonetheless, China is moving too cautiously and the pace of reforms are too slow, Treasury said.  

"China's cautious approach to exchange rate reform continues to exacerbate distortions in the domestic economy and impede adjustment of international imbalances," Treasury said. "Clamping down on exchange rate fluctuations has increased pressures in other parts of the economy."  

Treasury's decision, originally due Oct. 15, was widely expected. The department has refused to call China a currency manipulator in recent reports. And since the last report, released in May, China has allowed the yuan to appreciate more rapidly. The yuan strengthened 0.5% against the U.S. dollar in the second half of 2005 and another 1.0% in the first half 2006. Since China abandoned the dollar peg in July 2005, the yuan has risen just under 6.0%.  

This is far too little, say U.S. manufacturers and their representatives in Congress, who argue the yuan is undervalued by as much as 40%. Indeed, China's central bank continues to accumulate massive foreign exchange reserves as a result of currency market intervention to prevent faster yuan appreciation.  

Treasury will be under fire from those critics, who say the Bush administration hasn't been tough enough on China, when Congress returns for a new session in January. They got a boost last week when Federal Reserve Board Chairman Ben Bernanke, in the prepared text of a speech, called the undervalued yuan an export "subsidy."  

Members from both the House and the Senate are working on legislation to overhaul the foreign exchange reporting requirement and develop new laws, mostly directed at China, to pressure countries that limit currency appreciation. A measure backed by Sens. Max Baucus, D-Mont., and Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, would target currency "misalignment" rather than "manipulation," taking the question of intent out of consideration of whether Treasury should call out a country for problematic currency policy.  

Treasury officials have said repeatedly that they believe diplomacy will be far more effective in getting China to reform than trade sanctions. Last week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson led a delegation including almost half of President George W. Bush's cabinet for talks with senior Chinese officials on economic relations between the two countries.  

The meeting yielded some modest agreements, such as for sharing environmental and energy technology and pledges to work on an agreement protecting investment flows. At the close of the meeting, Paulson said the currency issue will remain "at the core" of U.S.-China engagement.  

In the report released Tuesday, Treasury noted China's average monthly accumulation of foreign exchange reserves was $20.4 billion in the first half this year. That measure fell to $15.6 billion in the third quarter, coinciding with a pick-up in the pace of yuan appreciation.  

The burden of intervention on the central bank has hindered its ability to control interest rates and inflation, Treasury said. It has also impeded rebalancing of Chinese growth away from investment and exports in favor of more consumption, a stated goal of the Chinese government.  

For its part, the U.S. should help reduce global trade imbalances, which economists warn could spark financial market instability, by encouraging its citizens to save more and by cutting budget deficits.  

Turning to other trading partners, Treasury said tepid economic growth in Europe and Japan has contributed to global trade imbalances.  

"Europe and Japan each need to achieve higher rates of growth of domestic demand on a sustained basis," Treasury said, noting that it is uncertain whether Europe's brighter economic outlook will last. Growth in Japan is already decelerating from last year's recovery, Treasury said.  

Most important U.S. trading partners have floating currency regimes in place. Japan, whose trade-weighted yen is at its weakest level in two decades, hasn't intervened in currency markets since March 2004.  

Malaysia - noted in previous Treasury reports for its large and growing current account surplus - like other oil-exporting countries would benefit from more currency flexibility, Treasury said.  

Trade surpluses among major oil exporters are now outpacing those of Southeast Asia's developing economies, inflated by higher oil prices. Russia's current account surplus totaled $56.5 billion in the first half 2006, or equal to just over 11% of gross domestic product. Russia's central bank intervenes to manage the pace of ruble appreciation against the dollar, 6% in the first half 2006.  

Saudi Arabia, like other Gulf countries, pegs its currency to the U.S. dollar. Between 2004 and 2006, Saudi's oil revenue almost doubled to just under $200 billion. A portion of this money returns to the U.S. for investment, raising the U.S. capital account surplus, a mirror image of the current account deficit.  

Treasury said the oil producers could help sustain global economic growth and reduce global trade imbalances by investing more in oil production capacity, investing more in their economies, and moving to a more flexible currency.  


  -By Elizabeth Price, Dow Jones Newswires; 202-862-9295; Elizabeth.Price@dowjones.com

title: Emerging  FX -Asia higher, won shrugs off  intervention  fears
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 6 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies extended gains against a weak dollar on Wednesday as optimism about the region's economic picture offset worries about official intervention to curb currency strength.  

The South Korean won <KRW=>, backed by the yen's <JPY=> gains, jumped 0.9 percent and went as high as 915.9 per dollar, its strongest since October 1997.  

It has gained about 10 percent this year.  

The U.S. dollar slipped towards a four-month low against the yen and inched nearer a 20-month trough versus the euro due to expectations that its interest rate advantage would be eroded further.  

"I think it's still a weak dollar story -- Asian currencies that are backed by strong fundamentals are able to catch up," said UBS currency strategist Nizam Idiris. "The won is following the dollar story, but it's not that alarming for the Bank of Korea for now."  

The won's strength in recent days has been underpinned by dollar sales by exporters, despite caution over possible intervention by the Bank of Korea.  

Malaysia's ringgit <MYR=>, which jumped 0.8 percent on Tuesday, rose another 0.4 percent on Wednesday to 3.544 per dollar, its highest level in nearly nine years.  

On Tuesday a leading Malaysian think tank predicted it could rise to 3.5 in the first quarter of 2007 and called for the central bank to loosen its grip on the currency, which was depegged from the dollar in July 2005.  

It has gained about 6.7 percent so far this year but has underperformed other regional currencies, such as the Singapore dollar, South Korean won, Indonesian rupiah and Thai baht.  

FUNDAMENTALS MATTER  

A renewed rally in Asian currencies in recent weeks has sparked a wave of verbal and actual intervention by regional central banks to curb their strength to protect exporters.  

"The symptoms of excessive liquidity remain, with regional bonds and equities rallying and showing an increasing mistrust of the dollar, despite all the policy makers' attempts to cajole the market into buying the dollar," Claudio Piron and Yen Ping Ho at JPMorgan said in a research note.  

Sustained foreign capital flows into the region's equity markets and solid economic fundamentals, including large trade surpluses, are providing support for Asian currencies despite worries over a possible slowdown in the U.S. economy.  

The Thai baht <THB=>, which took a hit on Monday when the Bank of Thailand announced measures to tighten foreign exchange rules, rose a quarter of a percent on Wednesday, while the Indonesian rupiah traded between 9,094 and 9,115 per dollar.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Intervention  as won, Sing dlr hit 8-year highs
text:
SINGAPORE, May 3 (Reuters) - The currencies of South Korea, Singapore and Malaysia hit their highest levels in more than eight years on Wednesday, prompting central bank intervention, as the U.S. dollar fell on speculation U.S. interest rates would stop rising soon.  

The won <KRW=> hit a high of 933.2 per dollar, its strongest level since October 1997.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose as high as 1.5730 per dollar, its highest since November 1997, while the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> hit 3.6049 per dollar, a level last seen in April 1998.  

Traders said central banks across the region stepped in with dollar purchases to stifle further gains in their currencies. Some central banks intervened through state lenders.  

"The state-run banks have been buying dollars aggressively," said a Singapore currency dealer at a foreign bank.  

The dealer said investors held off from bidding the Singapore dollar higher after seeing the authorities intervene at 1.5730/35 levels. The currency could retreat to levels around 1.58 before traders pushed it higher again, dealers said.  

Similar intervention was noted in South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand.  

Asian authorities are worried that stronger currencies, could hurt Asian exports to the United States, Europe and Japan, particularly when China is keeping the yuan on a tight leash.  

Data on Wednesday indicated that the South Korean authorities had been intervening in the foreign exchange market since April. The country's foreign exchange reserves jumped $5.55 billion last month to $222.89 billion, the fourth largest in the world.  

"The authorities are afraid of the pace and further appreciation of the won. That's why they came into the market to support the dollar. But the intervention is a smoothing operation -- they want to moderate the pace and not stop the trend," said Roh Sang Chil, a currency trader at Kookmin Bank in Seoul.  

Swiss bank UBS said concerns about the record U.S. current account deficit, attempts by central banks to diversify their reserves away from the dollar and expectations that the Fed may end its rate-rise cycle after another increase this month were likely to dominate currency markets.  

It expects the yen <JPY=> to strengthen to 108 per dollar in three months from about 113.25 now. The euro <EUR=> could climb to $1.3 from about $1.26 over the same period, it said.  

TAIWAN INFLOWS  

The bearish dollar outlook and a surge in foreign investment in Taiwan's stock market helped push up the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> to a nine-month high of 31.59 per U.S. dollar.  

Foreign investors continued with their purchases of Taiwan stocks, picking up a net T$11.7 billion worth on Wednesday. They bought T$170 billion worth in April, the highest monthly total since December.  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> jumped more than half a percent to 51.32 per dollar, its strongest level in two weeks.  

The currency had tumbled to an eight-week low last week on concern about record high oil prices and the likely impact on the country's fiscal deficit but some analysts reasoned that strong remittances from overseas Filipino workers were likely to offset the outflow of dollars caused by soaring crude oil import costs. New York oil futures <CLc1> traded close to $75 per barrel, near last week's record high of $75.35.

title: Malaysia Ringgit Up Late, Sets New 8-Yr High; Bonds Mixed
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--The Malaysian ringgit was higher late Wednesday versus the U.S. dollar, after achieving yet another new eight-year peak earlier in the day, traders said.  

As was the case with other regional currencies including the Singapore dollar, traders attributed the ringgit's rise to underlying dollar weakness.  

"Basically, the whole world is selling dollars, against ringgit and other currencies," said a trader at a big local bank.  

Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara, intervened intermittently to slow the dollar's decline, traders said.  

The central bank doesn't comment on its currency market activities.  

"They were the only bidder in the market but they weren't very serious" about defending the dollar, said the trader.  

On Tuesday, central bank governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz indicated Bank Negara is comfortable with the ringgit's rise, saying its rise so far has been orderly.  

"Non-dollar currencies have strengthened across the board, so this in essence is an expected development," Zeti said in a Business Times daily report Wednesday.  

"The word I use, stability of the currency, means that it's orderly; that the movement remains orderly, and orderly movement of the currency is important," she said.  

The ringgit has risen nearly 4.9% so far this year against the dollar.  

At 0830 GMT, the dollar was at MYR3.6070, far lower than Tuesday's MYR3.6140. It traded between MYR3.6050 - an eight-year low - and MYR3.6135 Wednesday.  

Traders remained confident the ringgit will extend its gains Thursday.  

"I think tomorrow we will shed another big figure, and fall to the 3.59 level," said the chief dealer of a local bank.  

Non-deliverable forwards declined, in line with the dollar's fall in the spot market. The one-month rate was MYR3.5930, down from MYR3.6000 Tuesday. The three-month rate was MYR3.5710, from Tuesday's MYR3.5760.  

Government bonds were mixed in relatively narrow trading as investors focused on the ongoing sale of a MYR500 million seven-year bond by Germany's state-owned KfW (KFW.YY).  

The bond was indicated at a yield of 4.55% to 4.60%, about 30 basis points higher than notional seven-year Malaysian Government Securities yields.  

Short-term government paper, the focus of trading in the past few days, was also relatively inactive as investors preferred to participate in two tenders of government paper earlier Wednesday.  

The central bank sold MYR500 million of three-month negotiable notes at an average yield 2.47% in an auction that drew a subscription rate of 4.4 times, higher than 2.3 times at the previous tender.  

A tender to sell six-month MYR500 million Bank Negara bills drew bids totaling 2.3 times the amount on offer, higher than the 1.4 subscription rate of an earlier auction. The six-month paper was sold Wednesday at 2.98%.  

The April 2011 Malaysian Government Securities yield rose 2 basis points to 4.14%, and MYR370 million were traded.  

The April 2009 Islamic Government Investment Issue yielded 4.00%, down 2 basis points, and MYR360 million changed hands.  

The Band 4, or 68- to 91-day, Bank Negara note yielded 2.31%, down 30 basis points with MYR346.6 million done.

title: Malaysia Zeti: Will Moderate Major  FX  Moves As Needed
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Malaysia's central bank will intervene in foreign-exchange markets to moderate any major outflows, particularly if such moves don't reflect economic fundamentals, Bank Negara Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz said.  

Although the currency has been in a strengthening trend, it has in the past been susceptible to outflows of speculative money.  

"We would moderate any excessive movement, especially if those movements are being determined by short term flows. Such excessive movements would not reflect the fundamentals of the economy," Zeti told Dow Jones Newswires in a recent interview when asked how the central bank would react if the ringgit comes under downward pressure.  

Her comments follow a central bank report Wednesday, which signaled that Bank Negara will allow "market conditions" as well as economic fundamentals to determine the value of the ringgit, now under a managed-float regime after the central bank in July dismantled a peg against the U.S. dollar.  

Market participants read the comment to mean the central bank is now comfortable with a stronger ringgit, which has gained 2.5% this year after appreciating just 0.5% from July to December 2005.  

At 0146 GMT, the dollar was quoted at MYR3.6930.  

Despite the overall gain in the currency since the peg was dismantled, the central bank's reserves dropped sharply late last year as speculators sold short term securities, with some MYR20 billion leaving the country in September to November before Bank Negara raised the overnight policy rate for the first time in seven years.  

Data released this week show a net outflow of MYR11.9 billion in Malaysian short-term money market and debt securities in 2005 compared with an inflow of MYR33.8 billion in 2004 when there was anticipation that the ringgit would gain after it was unpegged from the dollar.  

On the economy, Zeti said Malaysia's external sector would be a key support for growth in 2006.  

"The external sector is going to do better," she said. "The external environment has become more favorable in 2006. If you look at world trade, it is projected to increase from 7% to 7.4%. We expect the external sector to do very much better than in 2005."  

Bank Negara expects Malaysia's gross domestic product to grow by 6% this year, faster than the 5.3% expansion last year and despite a likely moderation in domestic demand and private-sector consumption.

text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies slipped in holiday-thinned trading on Tuesday, weighed down by profit-taking after their sharp rises in the past week and the anxiety about possible central bank intervention.  

 Markets in Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia were closed for a Muslim festival holiday. That kept trading volumes thin.  

 The won <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> closed local trade around 982 per dollar, just off Monday's high of 975 which was the currency's strongest level since the Asian financial crisis in 1997.  

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> fell to 52.645 per dollar, off Monday's peak of 52.25 which was its highest level since May 2003.  

 The Thai baht <THB=> gave up some ground, easing to 39.93 from Monday's 8-month high of 39.69 a dollar.  

 "Seems like some players took profit, but when we were back up above 39.90 some exporters came to sell dollars," said a baht trader based in Bangkok.  

 Regional currencies slipped as the dollar staged a slight rebound from three-month lows struck the past couple of sessions against the euro <EUR=> and yen <JPY=>.  

 Also, markets paused to see the extent to which central banks around the region would intervene to cap their currencies, which have risen sharply since the start of the year.  

 South Korean authorities kept up their normal run of comments.  

 The Vice Finance Minister said the won had risen too fast and steps would be taken as necessary, soon after a Bank of Korea official said the currency had risen above an equilibrium range against the dollar but authorities would not force it lower.  

 "Korean authorities clearly are not comfortable with either the pace of the move or the rate of the won," Richard Yetsenga, HSBC's currency strategist, said.  

 "But it unlikely that they will be successful in preventing the won moving at all."  

 Shahab Jalinoos, currency strategist with ABN AMRO Bank, said in a note the comments suggested there would be no concerted attempt to cap the won.  

 "This backs our view that strong growth means Korea will not want to risk the liquidity headaches implied by concerted intervention. Korean intervention in 2006 will be tactical rather than  strategic," he said.  

 That view would be confirmed if the Bank of Korea raised interest rates at its policy meeting on Thursday, he said.

title: Malaysia's Zeti: Rate Increase Likely If 3Q GDP Improves
text:
FRANKFURT (Dow Jones)-Malaysia's central bank is likely to raise interest rates if third-quarter economic data improve over the second quarter, Bank Negara Malaysia Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz hinted over the weekend.  

"If growth improves in the third quarter, we can expect a monetary policy response," Zeti told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview.  

Malaysia's second-quarter gross domestic product growth was 4.1% on year. Most economists expect third-quarter growth to come in at around 4.6%. Third-quarter data may be released as early as this week.  

"In the second quarter, we saw slower growth amid an environment of rising prices, and at that time the risk of slower growth and higher inflation was about in balance," Zeti said.  

Zeti added that the third quarter's performance will give a clearer picture of underlying growth potential and the degree of inflationary conditions.  

"The future direction of interest rates would thus depend on whether the risk of slower growth diminishes while the current inflationary trend continues," Zeti said.  

Bank Negara Malaysia has said that inflation is likely to remain above 3% until April of 2006, after rising to 3.7% in August, the highest level since 1999.  

And economists are eyeing a possible increase in fuel prices, as the government cuts back on fuel subsidies next year to rein in fiscal spending. In addition, observers say the government could grant national utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd. leeway to increase electricity rates, adding upward pressure to prices.  

Malaysia has kept its key overnight policy rate steady at 2.70% since its introductin in April 2004, when it replaced the previous intervention policy rate.  

Economists are upbeat about Malaysia's growth outlook for the third quarter due to a recovery in cyclical demand for electronics, higher exports, and strengthening industrial output.  

The government has said the economy will expand by around 5% this year, after achieving 5.8% on year growth in the first quarter, followed by 4.1% in the second quarter.  

In mid-November, the Malaysia-based U.S. electronics manufacturers' group said third-quarter export sales rose 14.6% on year to MYR18.96 billion. Exports from this industry group accounted for around 19% of Malaysia's total manufactured exports in 2004.  

Malaysian exports as a whole rose 7.4% on year in September after a surprisingly strong 12.5% jump in August.  

Most observers expect a gradual increase of rates at between 25 to 30 basis points, but have been divided over whether the timing of the move will be this year or next.  

"We think Bank Negara may...go ahead with a 30 basis point rate hike...," Chua Hak Bin, an economist at DBS Economic Market Research, said in a research note last week, citing an acceleration of capital outflows.  

"We think the capital outflows represent more than simply foreign funds exiting, and include domestic funds capitalizing on higher interest rates abroad and the recent liberalization of capital controls," Chua added.  

Malaysia is gradually adopting greater flexibility in its exchange rate regime after removing the ringgit's $1=MYR3.80 peg to the dollar earlier this year. The currency peg, in addition to restrictions on domestic investment abroad, were put into place in September 1998 and were aimed at limiting capital outflows in the wake of the Asian financial crisis.  

Last week, Fitch Ratings affirmed Malaysia's A- long-term foreign currency rating.  

"Fitch's rating balances Malaysia's robust international liquidity position and declining external debt profile against the scope for further improvements in public finances," Ai Ling Ngiam, associate director at Fitch's sovereigns team in Asia said Friday. She emphasized Malaysia's external finances as a fundamental rating strength and said Malaysia's current account position will likely remain above 12% of GDP this year.  

Fitch also said it expects Malaysia's economic growth to be around 4.9% this year, rising to 5.3% in 2006.

title: Malaysian ringgit at weakest since July de-peg
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 15 (Reuters) - The Malaysian ringgit on Tuesday eased to its weakest level since its peg against the dollar was abandoned in July, as outflows from local markets pushed the currency lower.  

The ringgit <MYR=> <MYR=D1> fell to about 3.7815 per dollar, moving closer to the 3.8 level at which it was pegged to the dollar for seven years before the July 21 currency reform, dealers said.  

It has dipped about one percent since early August with further weakness prevented by central bank intervention in the currency market, dealers said.  

Second Finance Minister Nor Mohamed Yakcop played down the weakness in the currency, telling reporters in Kuala Lumpur the ringgit levels reflected the strength of the U.S. dollar and that capital outflows were not a cause for concern.  

But dealers said disappointment with a lack of currency appreciation since the dollar peg was dropped meant foreign investors were likely to continue to exit Malaysia's bond and stock markets, keeping the ringgit under pressure.  

"Ahead of the depeg, a lot of foreigners had taken strong positions on the local markets and after the move they saw that there isn't too much currency appreciation coming through," said Deutsche Bank currency strategist Mirza Baig.  

"A lot of positions taken up in the bond market have not been rolled over. Investors have been taking out their speculative capital from Malaysia and this has added to ringgit weakness."  

A dealer in Kuala Lumpur said expectations for rising U.S. interest rates would weigh on the ringgit.  

The key U.S. interest rate is at 4.00 percent and has been raised 12 times since mid-2004.  

Malaysia's benchmark rate has been at 2.70 percent since it was introduced in April 2004, but some analysts expect a rate rise by the end of the year to curb inflation.  

"Interest rates in the U.S. are expected to continue to rise into the first quarter of next year and that in itself will fuel the outflows going into the end of the year," the dealer said.  

"I don't see this trend of outflows reversing itself."  

He added that intervention by Malaysia's central bank was likely to prevent the ringgit weakening beyond 3.8 per dollar.  

Analysts said central bank intervention has led to a drop in Malaysia's foreign exchange reserves, which stood at $77.1 billion on Oct. 31 -- down 2.9 percent from $79.4 billion on Oct.14.  

"The central bank has been in the market for the last two months," the trader said. "They won't allow the ringgit to touch 3.8. That won't look good four months after the unpeg."

title: INTERVIEW: Malaysia Anwar: New Ringgit Regime Like A Peg
text:
TOKYO (Dow Jones)--Malaysia's former Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim Friday said Kuala Lumpur's move last week to abandon its peg to the dollar and move to a managed float was basically a peg under a different name, though he welcomed the new regime.  

The former finance minister, who was sacked a day after then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad imposed the peg in 1998 as part of capital controls during the Asian financial crisis, also reiterated his call for a free float of the ringgit to prevent speculation on the currency and to make the economy more competitive.  

Similar to a move by China last week, Malaysia delinked the ringgit, which had been fixed at 3.80 to the dollar since September 1998 and was widely viewed as undervalued. Since the move, the ringgit has risen about 1.3% against the dollar but has stayed relatively stable since Tuesday.  

Currency traders said the relatively slight strengthening was largely due to aggressive dollar buying by the Malaysian central bank, Bank Negara.  

"Notwithstanding that they were compelled to change after the revaluation of the yuan, I would certainly see this as a positive move," he told Dow Jones Newswires and CNBC Asia-Pacific in an interview. CNBC will broadcast portions of the interview Monday.  

But "when you look at the details - the devil is in the details - substantially nothing has changed," he said. "What they would call a managed float is actually a re-peg and it's unfortunate that the band or latitude is so limited to the extent that Bank Negara has to intervene immediately after the so-called unpegging."  

Anwar said Malaysia has "adequate enough protection" - possibly referring to the nation's $75 billion in foreign exchange reserves and strong growth - to fully float the currency, though he said there would be some initial volatility.  


 
   Foreigners Delaying Investment 
   

A former Mahathir protege, Anwar has been critical of the policies of current Prime Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi and has said the tight currency controls have caused Malaysia to lose its attractiveness for foreign investment and its competitiveness.  

The medium- to long-term sustainability of an economy is a crucial determinant of where multinational corporations invest, he said, saying Malaysian leaders must stop blaming China and India for siphoning off investment.  

"That is why I have called on the prime minister, who is also the minister of finance, to take a more decisive position vis-a-vis the pegging issue," he said. "People invest in a big way when they are confident about the sustainability."  

Before Kuala Lumpur's decision last week, the Malaysian Institute of Economic Research had said the country's large trade and current account surpluses suggested a serious exchange rate misalignment, and warned the peg was already hurting the economy as seen in large speculative inflows in the money market, a soaring import bill and rising inflation.  

It noted some foreign investors were delaying investments pending anticipated exchange rate changes and warned that competitiveness based on a cheap currency can't be sustained.  

Anwar was sacked and arrested in 1998 after a fallout with Mahathir and was later convicted and sentenced to 15 years in jail for corruption and sodomy. But Malaysia's highest court overturned the sodomy conviction last September and freed Anwar because he had completed the corruption sentence. But the politician is barred from active politics until 2008 under rules regarding those who have been convicted.  

He says he was framed in a conspiracy to block him from challenging Mahathir for power. Mahathir, who retired in October 2003, has denied plotting against his former deputy.  

Anwar accused Mahathir of imposing the peg at the time to "protect the interest of his cronies and companies" mired in heavy debt.  

He was in Tokyo to speak at a United Nations University conference and to meet with the media and politicians, including the head of Japan's largest opposition party, Katsuya Okada of the Democratic Party. Anwar currently is a visiting fellow at the School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins University in Washington DC.  

-By James Simms, Dow Jones Newswires; 813-5255-2929; james.simms@dowjones.com

title: Currency  speculators buy up Malaysian bonds
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, July 25 (Reuters) - Currency speculators dived into Malaysia's bond market on Monday, betting on further strengthening of the ringgit after the currency's peg to the U.S. dollar was severed last week, bond traders said.  

"Everyone believes that the ringgit is going to appreciate," a bond trader with a local bank said, as bond prices rose across the board, four days after Malaysia scrapped the seven-year-old peg and followed China in moving to a managed-float currency.  

"It's going to lead to more speculation," he added.  

The yield curve on Malaysian government paper took a step down, with the yield on the five-year bond due February 2009 falling to a new all-time low of 3.13 percent, and the benchmark 3-year bond down seven basis points to yield 3.05 percent.  

"Investors are buying in anticipation of further strengthening in the ringgit. We see more downside to yields in the near term," said a dealer with another local bank.  

But local share prices fell, with most speculative capital heading for the government debt market and many local share investors taking profits after the benchmark Composite Index <.KLSE> hit a five-year closing high on Friday.  

"Foreign hedge funds are taking a three-to-six month view, where they are less likely to lose money on the fixed-income side, especially during a short term period," said a fund manager with a leading local asset management firm in Kuala Lumpur.  

"Their principal will be protected, and (the hope is) they will just make on the currency. Whereas in equities it'll be a hell of a ride, for example in a 2-3 percent move either way."  

The ringgit, fixed for seven years at 3.8 to the dollar until last Thursday night, is widely viewed by economists to be about 10 percent undervalued.  

Since Malaysia switched to a managed float, minutes after China made a similar move with the yuan, the ringgit has strengthened by about 1 percent against the dollar.  

Malaysia's central bank is suspected to have intervened in the currency market to prevent a rapid appreciation, but local bond dealers said the ringgit would find it difficult to resist further strengthening as long as the yuan continued to appreciate.  

"My own personal view is they will perhaps let it go to the level that we have seen the yuan appreciate, which is about 2 percent," HCBC Malaysia treasurer John McGowan said.  

The central bank says it will use a trade-weighted basket of currencies as a guide to managing the ringgit, but declines to give details on its new policy, other than to say the currency was already around fair value at the old, fixed rate of 3.8.  

"They say we are tied to a basket of currencies but as I see it we are tied to the yuan," a dealer said.

title: RPT-UPDATE 1-Malaysia says wants stable ringgit, no trade band
text:
(Repeating story issued on Sunday) (Adds quotes, background)  

By Liau Y-Sing  

KUALA LUMPUR, July 24 (Reuters) - Malaysia aims to keep its currency stable and has not set any trading band for its value, the country's second finance minister said on Sunday, three days after Malaysia moved to a managed float of the ringgit.  

"The central bank's rule in the managed float is, of course, to make sure that there is stability, there is no undue volatility in any single period," Nor Mohamed Yakcop, a principal architect of the ringgit's old peg to the dollar, told reporters.  

"And the central bank is very well equipped to do it. The government does not fix the rate any more, it is just more of ensuring that there is stability, not too much volatility. Certainly the exchange rate should reflect the fundamentals."  

He said there was no undisclosed official level or trading band for the ringgit.  

On Thursday the central bank scrapped the seven-year-old peg of 3.8 to the U.S. dollar and followed China in moving to a managed float. But the bank has not given any other specific guidance other than to say 3.8 was already around fair value.  

The ringgit was last quoted on its first day as a managed-float currency on Friday at 3.778 to the dollar, less than 0.6 percent stronger than its old, fixed rate. Traders said the central bank had intervened to prevent a rapid appreciation.  

Malaysia fixed the ringgit to the dollar in September 1998, at the height of Asia's financial crisis, and the tactic helped the country weather the crisis, but it is now widely thought by economists to be about 10 percent undervalued.  

As the U.S. dollar weakened and Malaysia's trade surplus ballooned last year, the cheap ringgit threatened to push up import costs and exacerbate inflation, already under pressure from soaring crude oil prices.  

Inflation is now running at six-year highs.  

'GOOD FOR EVERYBODY'  

Nor Mohamed, speaking after opening a new customs centre, described the move to a managed float as good for the economy and said that even the impact on major exporters would be muted.  

"In the long run, it's good for everybody. In the short run, certainly there are more winners than losers," he said.  

"The net effect for the economy, now that we have gone into this managed float, is very, very positive," he added. "Exporters will not be badly hit because many of the exports in Malaysia also have large amounts of import content. In the electronics sector for example, 85 percent of the exports is import content."  

Electronics make up about half of total exports, the main driver of the economy.  

Nor Mohamed confirmed there was no plan to lift controls on offshore trading in the ringgit, a legacy of the fixed-rate regime seen by the authorities as vital for currency stability.  

"There is no specific programme to internationalise the ringgit. There is no intention," he said.  

The prospect of a ringgit revaluation drew in large inflows of foreign capital in domestic bond and stock markets last year, with speculators betting that Malaysia would move once China led the way and allowed the yuan to appreciate.  

But, fortunately for Malaysia's central bank, some gave up the wait for a change in ringgit policy and sold their Malaysian holdings, so there was no big wave of profit-taking when the move finally came late last Thursday.  

Instead, the share market hit a five-year closing high on Friday and foreign investors also bought into local treasury bills, dragging down short-term yields, on hopes of further ringgit appreciation in the days and weeks ahead.

title: RPT-UPDATE 3-Malaysia cenbank curbs  currency  after dropping peg
text:
(Adds dropped work in first paragraph)  

KUALA LUMPUR, July 22 (Reuters) - Malaysia's ringgit rose on Friday after the government abandoned a policy of fixing the exchange rate with the dollar, but it defied predictions of sharp gains on suspected central bank intervention.  

Malaysia dropped the seven-year old peg of 3.8 per dollar and followed China's move to a managed float, but dealers said the central bank spent heavily on the first day of trading on Friday to keep a lid on speculative buying of the currency.  

"They have been there all morning, bidding at 3.795," a trader said, adding the central bank had bought at least $1 billion against the ringgit, which is viewed as undervalued.  

The central bank declined to comment.  

Foreign investors have been ploughing money into Malaysian bonds and stocks over the past year, betting the ringgit would be revalued once China relaxed its policies to allow the yuan to rise.  

They were right on the chain of events -- Malaysia moved immediately after Beijing late on Thursday -- but Friday's ringgit gains were not enough to spark profit-taking and a flight of capital, which had been a key concern facing the central bank.  

The ringgit <MYR=>, still banned from offshore trade, firmed by about 0.7 percent to trade late in the day at 3.7750 per dollar, an intraday high.  

But derivatives markets offshore that settle only in U.S. dollars were factoring in an 8 percent rise in the value of the ringgit over the next year.  

Economists said a firmer ringgit can help curb inflation, which hit a 6-year high in June, and keep interest rates low.  

But speculators could continue to pile potentially destabilising funds into the country if they believe the currency is undervalued, they said.  

"The fact that the ringgit has appreciated so little from its original rate could attract more speculative inflows as investors bet on continued appreciation in coming weeks," said Sani Hamid, economist with Singapore's Forecast Private Ltd..  

China revalued the yuan by 2.1 percent to 8.11 per dollar on Thursday from 8.28 per dollar. However, the currency fell back slightly to 8.1111 per dollar in trading on Friday.  

Yields on Malaysian treasury bills tumbled on Friday, partly as foreign investors bought bonds. Yielding less than U.S. treasuries, they offer little attraction to foreigners apart from potential currency gains, economists said.  

"We are seeing some further interest from the offshore in our domestic treasury bills," HSBC Malaysia treasurer John McGowan said. "My own personal view is that it (ringgit) will gradually appreciate on an ongoing basis, from day to day," he added.  

'READY FOR ANYTHING'  

With a war-chest of $75.2 billion in foreign currency reserves, the central bank is considered well armed to deal with existing speculators.  

Malaysia's prime minister vowed late on Thursday the country was "ready for anything" speculators could throw at the ringgit.  

Exporters, probably the biggest beneficiaries of an undervalued ringgit, are unlikely to be badly hurt, since cheaper imports can reduce their costs, economists said.  

Malaysian exporters rely heavily on imported raw material. Electronics, which make up about half of total exports, have an import content of about 80 percent, economists say.  

Shares in exporters, from electronics to oil-palm plantation firms, fell in early trade on Friday, but partially recovered as it became clear the ringgit was standing its ground.  

But overall, foreign investors, who had long chafed against the ringgit peg and related capital controls, applauded the move and helped push the stock market <.KLSE> to close at a six-month high.  

Malaysian Pacific Industries Bhd , the nation's biggest chip maker, and Kuala Lumpur Kepong Bhd, an oil palm planter, recovered from early losses to close 2.5 percent and 1.4 percent down, respectively.  

Companies with big foreign debts to service, such as power utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd , would benefit. Tenaga rose 4.6 percent on Friday.

title: 2nd UPDATE:USD/MYR Falls, Short-End  Malaysia  Paper Soars
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Suspected intervention by Malaysia's central bank and the continued exclusion of offshore players Friday helped restrain the dollar's fall against the ringgit, a day after the country embraced a managed float system and dropped its 7-year-old fixed-rate regime.   

"The central bank has been in (the market) since this morning," said a trader at a foreign bank. "It's just an onshore market so activity will be limited."   

The Association of Banks Malaysia, an industry grouping, late Friday echoed this sentiment, saying, "...as the ringgit remains non-tradeable offshore, this would allow Bank Negara to maintain a tightly managed band for the ringgit."   

Earlier Friday, the dollar was bid as low as MYR3.7700 compared with the previous MYR3.8000 fixed rate, which was abandoned in lockstep with China's yuan revaluation. Late in the day, the dollar trimmed its losses and was bid at MYR3.7750.   

Bank Negara said late Thursday the ringgit would be allowed to operate on a managed-float basis, with economic fundamentals determining its value. "Bank Negara Malaysia will monitor the exchange rate against a currency basket to ensure that the exchange rate remains close to its fair value," the bank said. Prior to this, the ringgit had been fixed at MYR3.80 to a dollar since September 1998.   

Friday, Bank Negara declined to comment on whether it had intervened in the foreign exchange market. Traders said the central bank bought dollars earlier in the day via several banks, but was largely absent by the afternoon.   

In its regime change statement Thursday, the central bank didn't specify a particular value for the ringgit, but the Association of Banks expects the ringgit to rise about 2% against the dollar.   

"We expect the ringgit to appreciate in tandem with the yuan, i.e. by about 2.0% against the U.S. dollar," the industry group said in a statement.   

Government bonds trimmed losses after earlier plunging in a kneejerk reaction to the ringgit regime change. The early weakness in bonds was due to fears the change could prompt a reversal of foreign funds that have flowed into the market since late 2004, traders said.   

Short-end debt has since recovered, with most tenors closing higher compared with Thursday, on renewed foreign buying. Some speculators set up new positions on hopes of more ringgit appreciation going forward, traders said.   

"Someone must be buying heavily. Six- and three-month government paper are yielding 1%," said a trader at a local bank. Six- and three-month central bank paper had been yielding 2.36% Thursday.   

Goldman Sachs Regional Economist Adam LeMesurier warned that the inflows could spark the central bank's wrath.   

"We would watch for any potential Bank Negara moral suasion to the local banks against intermediating foreign inflows into the domestic bond market," LeMesurier said in a research report.   

"This could be a sign that Bank Negara is becoming upset with the level of inflows," he said.   

Meanwhile, the key composite stock index soared 1.9% to end at 969.69, just shy of the year's high of 940.94 achieved in January. The market's biggest stocks in capitalization terms - Malayan Banking (1155.KU), Telekom Malaysia (4863.KU), and power utility Tenaga Nasional (5347.KU) - all benefitted handsomely from renewed optimism after the peg's removal. Maybank surged 4.5% to MYR11.60, Telekom rallied 5.7% to MYR11.20 and Tenaga gained 4.6% to MYR11.30.   

Mayban Securities economist Saifuddin Morat attributed the market's initial surge to the "feel-good factor" from the regime change.   

"With the ringgit peg removed, the equity market's greater attractiveness to foreign funds means that the KLCI could trade at the higher range of our target of between 940 and 970 for this year," Saifuddin said.   

Still, analysts and traders are split over the medium-term impact of the regime change on the dollar/ringgit rate.   

"We will expect the initial value to overshoot, but thereafter for the (dollar) to settle around MYR3.50," said Standard Chartered Bank economist Joseph Tan.   

DBS Bank's Chua Hak Bin thinks the ringgit's rise will be modest initially. "We expect the ringgit to appreciate by only about 2% or 3% in the immediate term," he said.

title: Malaysian rate hikes, peg move seen in 2005 - DBS
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, July 5 (Reuters) - Malaysia is expected to raise interest rates and abandon its ringgit peg this year to fend off rising inflation and close a widening interest rate gap with the United States, Singapore's DBS Bank said on Tuesday.  

Malaysia may lift its overnight policy rate by 25 basis points in the third quarter and another 25 basis points in the fourth quarter, economist Chua Hak Bin said in a report.  

The overnight policy rate, Malaysia's benchmark interest rate, has been at 2.70 percent since it was introduced in April 2004. In that time, the U.S. federal funds rates has risen to 3.25 percent from 1.00 percent.  

Bank Negara, Malaysia's central bank, has said it may keep interest rates low to support growth even if oil prices stay high, but investors expect inflation to lead to tighter policy.  

Malaysian inflation has been trending higher, as higher oil prices drive up food and transport costs. Inflation hit 3.1 percent in the year through May, the biggest rise since a 3.2 percent gain in the year through March 1999.  

Chua said Malaysia might also abandon its ringgit peg of 3.8 per dollar for a managed float in the second half of 2005.  

Markets expect a revaluation of China's yuan would trigger a ringgit move, but Chua said this carried a risk for Malaysia.  

"Such an event could trigger a wave of speculative capital inflows, requiring huge sterilised intervention on the part of Bank Negara Malaysia to prevent a collapse in interest rates," Chua said.  

"We think Bank Negara Malaysia would want to avoid such an ugly scenario, shifting to a managed float before a (yuan) move."  

Authorities can issue debt securities to mop up the excess cash, a process known as sterilisation.  

Speculation of a revaluation has sucked short-term money into Malaysian bonds and shares, raising concern about destabilising capital flows and possible inflationary pressures.  

Bank Negara Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz said last week that Malaysia would review its foreign exchange policy when China revalued its yuan.

title: TABLE-Asia ex-China reserves dip $4.6 bln in May
text:
SINGAPORE, June 9 (Reuters) - Asian holdings of foreign exchange reserves excluding China fell $4.6 billion in May, central bank figures show, a fall which currency analysts said reflected a rally in the dollar against the euro <EUR=>.   

Including China's holdings as at the end of March -- it has not released figures for April and May -- Asian central banks hold $2.53 trillion in foreign exchange reserves.   

Analysts expect the net change in Asian reserves during May would be positive if China's reserves were included, suspecting that the speculation of a yuan revaluation led to inflows of foreign money into the country in April and May.   

They said the fall in reserves for other economies was mostly due to the U.S. dollar's gains against the euro and other major currencies in May, driven by a strengthening U.S. economy, the euro zone's economic woes and uncertainty that culminated in French and Dutch voters rejecting a new EU constitution.   

The euro fell almost 4.5 percent against the dollar in May. With an estimated 20 percent share of world reserves, the euro's fall would have caused revaluation losses for reserve-holders.   

Japan, Indonesia and India suffered the biggest falls in reserves in dollar terms, each losing over $1 billion in May.   

The region's reserves have grown by $83.5 billion so far in 2005. The largest foreign flows have been into China, Malaysia, South Korea and Taiwan, although dollar-buying intervention by central banks has been far lower than in 2004, analysts say.   

Asia ex-Japan's reserves increased by $173 billion in the last quarter of 2004, which analysts said was a record quarterly jump. China's reserves alone rose over $95 billion in the final quarter of 2004 to a record $609.9 billion.   

Amidst the euro's descent and the steep rise in U.S. Treasury prices since March, there has been renewed talk about whether Asian central banks are diversifying their dollar holdings.   

Over 60 percent of global central bank reserves were held in dollar assets at the end of 2003, IMF figures show.   

Some traders believe the euro's decline has been exacerbated by talk Asian central banks may be less inclined to buy the weakening currency. Others felt this was an opportune time for euro-buying by the central banks.   

"What would make logical sense in terms of currency allocation is to be buying the euro when it comes off like this," said James Malcolm, currency strategist with Deutsche Bank in Singapore.   

"But that is not the way it seems to work in practice."   

Besides fitting in with their longer term investment mandates, such central bank buying could help restrain the volatility in the euro and in U.S. Treasuries, he said. Latest foreign exchange reserve holdings:

title: IMF Lowers Malaysian 2003 GDP Forecast To 4.2% From 5%
text:
KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- The International Monetary Fund has revised down its economic growth forecast for Malaysia this year to 4.2% from a previous estimate of 5% made in April. 

 In its World Economic Outlook report issued Thursday, the IMF also revised down its 2004 forecast to 5.3% from the 5.8% projected in April. 

 The IMF attributed the lower forecasts to weaker domestic demand resulting from the outbreak of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome earlier this year, and from uncertainties related to the Iraq crisis. 

 The IMF expects Malaysia's average inflation to remain modest this year at 1.7%, which is a bit above the government's forecast of 1.1%. 

 "For the most part, the policy response to weaker growth has been appropriate," the IMF stated, referring to the region as a whole. "With inflation contained, monetary policy has been eased in a number of countries, though the continued buildup of official reserves suggest that reforms to increase exchange rate flexibility remained largely on hold." 

Malaysia lowered its key intervention rate - used by banks to calculate prime lending rates - to 4.5% in May from 5%, as part of an economic stimulus package, which included 1.7 billion ringgit ($1=MYR3.80) in on-budget fiscal expenditures. 

 In its annual economic report issued with the budget last Friday, the finance ministry reiterated that the ringgit's peg to the dollar, currently MYR3.8, that was introduced in 1998 remains supported by economic fundamentals. 

 Earlier this week, the central bank Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz said the government would only review the peg if there was a structural and fundamental shift in foreign exchange conditions. 

 Observers say the country is highly unlikely to tinker with the peg ahead of the power transition end-October, when Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad hands the scepter to his deputy Abdullah Ahmad Badawi, nor in the near term thereafter. 

 In its report, the IMF reiterated calls on countries to make exchange rates more elastic in order to even out imbalances between countries' economies. 

 "From a policy standpoint, moreover, further exchange rate flexibility would confer a number of benefits - including reducing risks of future crises, making domestic growth less dependent on the vagaries of the global cycle, lower holding costs of official reserves, and raising consumption opportunities for local residents in cases where exchange rates may be undervalued - while also helping to resolve global imbalances," the report said. 

 The IMF report also noted that the accumulation of international reserves in the region in 2002 "was well in excess of that warranted by fundamentals." 

 It also cited the need for current account surpluses in emerging markets in Asia in order to share in the adjustment of the unsustainable U.S. current account deficit "to prevent an undue burden of adjustment in other countries." 

 As at end-August, Malaysia's international reserves stood at $38.7 billion, sufficient to finance six months of retained imports and around 4.3 times short-term external debt.

title: POLL-Malaysia's interest rate hike unlikely till H2 '04.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 13 (Reuters) - Malaysia is unlikely to
tighten monetary policy until the second half of 2004, a
Reuters poll showed on Wednesday, with inflation in check and
global interest rates expected to remain low.
With the U.S. Federal Reserve signalling that it would keep
interest rates low for a long time, economists saw no immediate
pressure to lift Malaysian interest rates.
The poll of 10 economists ruled out a move in the first
quarter of next year, and on average saw a three percent chance
of a rate hike in the second quarter.
A Reuters poll in mid-July predicted that central Bank
Negara would hold rates steady for the rest of 2003.
"I don't think there'll be any hurry (to increase rates),"
said David Cohen, director of macro-forecasting at MMS
International.



"The inflation picture is under control and interest rates
around the world will remain within the low range."
Malaysia's monthly consumer price index, the official
barometer of inflation, has stayed below two percent since the
start of the year.
As concerns about the domestic economy abate, with growth
expected to accelerate in the second half of the year, focus
has turned to a possible hike in borrowing costs.
The last interest rate movement was in May when Malaysia
trimmed the intervention rate by 50 basis points to 4.5
percent.
Economists saw a relatively bigger probability -- albeit



only a modest 17 percent chance on average - of a rate hike



going into the second half of 2004, as an anticipated global



economic recovery gained ground.



Those who expected a hike saw the intervention rate being
increased by 25 or 50 basis points.
The overall chance of an interest rate movement was small,
economists said, as Malaysia makes few interest rates changes,
although the ringgit currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar.
The Federal Reserve has cut rates 13 times since January
2001, slicing 5.50 percentage points off its key short-term
interest rate, now at one percent.
In contrast, Malaysia has only cut rates twice during the
period -- in September 2001 and May this year.
Reuters asked 10 economists to estimate the percentage
chance that the central bank would raise interest rates in the
