title: Malaysia Ctrl Bk: Banks Urged To Curb Deposit Rate Moves
text:
KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- Malaysia's central bank governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz reiterated Thursday that Bank Negara has asked commercial banks to make only minimal changes to deposit rates, following a cut in the monetary authority's intervention rate Wednesday. 

 "We have urged banks to minimize adjustments (to deposit rates)," she told reporters after delivering a speech at an economic seminar. 

 Commercial banks are required to follow Bank Negara Malaysia guidelines in determining deposit rates which gives banks only limited leeway to tamper with rates. 

 Details on the central bank's guidelines weren't available. 

 Zeti's remarks reiterate those in a statement from the central bank Wednesday. 

 "Liquidity operations by Bank Negara Malaysia will ensure that the interbank rates are maintained at current ranges. This will minimize the adjustment to deposit rates," the central bank said Wednesday in a statement. 

 Bank Negara Malaysia Wednesday cut its intervention rate, used by banks to calculate their prime lending rates, to 4.5% from 5%, as part of the government's economic stimulus package. 

 Zeti later clarified that any change in deposit rates will be of a smaller magnitude than base lending rate adjustments. 

 On Wednesday, the central bank noted that the ceiling for base lending rates for commercial banks has fallen to 6% from 6.42%, and for finance companies to 6.94% from 7.46%. 

 Changes to deposit rates won't be of that magnitude, she said. Any decline in deposit rates "should be less than the adjustment in the base lending rate, which is around 40 basis points," Zeti said Thursday. 

 "Do not expect the one-month fixed-deposit rate to be below 3%," she added. At present, the average one-month fixed-deposit rate stands around 3.20%. 

 For other deposit rate maturities, adjustments won't be more than 30 basis points, Zeti said. 

 In the speech, Zeti dismissed concerns of a deflationary economy. 

 "Our policy is to promote consumption and investment activity ... (and that is) expansionary rather than deflationary," Zeti said in her speech. 

 She noted the country's interest rate cut will strengthen private consumption growth, which rose 4.2% in 2002 and is projected to rise 6.9% this year, and cited signs of healthy consumer demand. 

 "Therefore, we don't view our circumstances as a deflationary situation," she said. 

 On Wednesday, the statistics department said consumer prices rose 1% year-on-year in April, continuing a benign inflationary trend seen over the past several years. 

 Turning to the U.S. dollar, Zeti reiterated the ringgit peg has served Malaysia well in mitigating external currency volatility. 

 She noted that the dollar has depreciated against major currencies to around the levels of when the peg was first introduced in 1998. 

 "The objective of our policy has never changed," she said. "We want the best mechanism that will facilitate trade and investment," adding that the peg continues to support significant amounts of both.

title: Malaysia  Unlikely To Cut  Intervention  Rate Soon - Banker
text:
KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- Malaysia is unlikely to cut its intervention rate any time soon, as lower rates may not necessarily boost lending and spur the local economy, a senior banker said Monday. 

 Analysts have been speculating the central bank may soon slash the intervention rate - which is used by commercial banks to calculate their own lending rates - to stimulate the economy as prospects of a war in Iraq mount. The rate is currently at 5%, a historical low. 

 However, Bumiputra Commerce Bank Bhd. Executive Vice President Nik Hassan Nik Mohd Amin said such a move was unlikely. 

 "A cut won't result in additional investments and it may cause deflation which is more difficult to cure," he told reporters. 

 Bumiputra-Commerce Bank is a unit of Malaysia's second-biggest financial group Commerce Asset-Holding Bhd. (P.CAH). 

 Nik Hassan said the government's recently announced measures to boost the domestic capital market, coupled with a coming fiscal stimulus package in April, will be sufficient to cushion the economy from a global economic slowdown, should there be war in Iraq. 

 Amid the global uncertainties, Malaysians are placing their money in banks rather than spending or investing, Nik Hassan noted. 

 Last year, total deposits in banks in the country increased 5.6% or by 2.1 billion ringgit ($1=MYR3.80) from a year earlier, he said. 

 Meanwhile, Commerce Asset Director Rozali Mohamed Ali said the group remains optimistic about its financial performance this year despite the risk of war in Iraq. 

 "We will focus on areas we have identified and hope to continue to perform well this year," Rozali said but declined to elaborate. 

 Commerce Asset is due to announce its 2002 financial results by Friday. Analysts have forecast an average net profit of MYR514.70 million for the year ended Dec. 31, 2002, up 34% from 2001. 

 The release of Commerce Asset's 2002 results has been delayed because of its recent acquisition of Indonesia's PT Bank Niaga. 

 For this year, analysts expect the banking group to post a net profit of around MYR674 million. 

 Earlier Monday, Bumiputra-Commerce Bank signed a $200 million one-year syndicated term loan facility agreement to finance the operations of its overseas and offshore branches. 

 The group has about MYR6 billion outstanding in U.S. dollar and other foreign currency loans, Rozali said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Find a footing, but vulnerable.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 13 (Reuters) - Asian currencies settled in narrow bands against the U.S. dollar after early some choppiness on Thursday, but analysts said there was high risk of them falling sharply if the tensions over Iraq or North Korea rose. 

 The Singapore dollar and the Korean won were hemmed in after having rallied from two-month lows this week, while the Thai baht and the Taiwan dollar have been rising after revisiting their end-2002 lows this week. 

 The U.S. dollar see-sawed against the yen in Asia, pressured by worries over the Iraq stand-off and rumours the United States might again raise its security alert level, while the yen benefitted from Japanese exporter sales and fund repatriation. 

 Traders said Asian currencies were expected to hold their ground until Friday, when U.N. weapons inspectors report on Iraq's compliance with a directive to disarm. 

 "From now until Friday, Asian regionals will be hovering in a range. But the bias will be weak on account of geopolitical risks, the yen, and intervention by the regional central banks," said Jimmy Koh, currency strategist at United Overseas Bank. 

 Koh said the Korean won would be most susceptible. The won weakened at the open after North Korea was declared in breach of the United Nation's atomic safeguards and the matter was referred to the U.N. Security Council, but it then headed back towards Wednesday's close. 

 "Clearly, this is the next flash point to watch for - North Korea had said that if further sanctions are imposed, that would be tantamount to a declaration of war - but we take the view that the actual military confrontation is extremely unlikely," JP Morgan currency strategist James Malcolm said in a note. 

 SING DOLLAR, BAHT RECOVER 

 The Singapore dollar weakened as far as 1.7592 as the yen softened towards 121.50 per dollar, and then rallied. 

 But analysts said the currency is still quite expensive in trade-weighted terms, implying it had substantial room to move lower. They also said trade in regional crosses, involving short Sing dollar positions against the won or Thai baht, was keeping it on the defensive. 

 The baht found support around 43 per dollar, and on Thursday was the only regional currency to be stronger than its 2002 close against the U.S. dollar. 

 It touched a six-week low of 43.20 on Tuesday, but analysts say the central bank will use any regional downtrend to buy dollars as the early reprepayments of IMF loans begin. 

 On Friday, Thailand will repay $950 million of an IMF-arranged loan, leaving $3.85 billion outstanding. The government intends to clear the loans by July. 

 Meanwhile, analysts were mixed about the impact of a decision by the influential California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS) to review investments in the region. 

 Earlier this week, a CalPERS consultant recommended the fund put Thailand and Malaysia back on its list of approved investments and drop the Philippines. 

 Analysts said the amounts the fund had previously invested in these countries was quite low, and the impact, if any, would be on sentiment rather than flows into these currencies. 

 PESO STILL VULNERABLE 

 The Philippine peso slipped slightly to end at 53.95, raising concern it may head back to last week's 18-month low of 54.10 per dollar, from where it was pulled away by central bank warnings on dollar hoarding and some suspsected intervention. 

 It got some brief respite from selling after reports that the January budget deficit was around 15 billion pesos, under the government target of 16.8 billion for the month. 

 But the country's budget problems and worries about a sovereign ratings downgrade, combined with its exposure to global oil prices, placed the peso under considerable stress, analysts said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was volatile, moving close to Tuesday's six-week lows of 8,980 per dollar and then rallying to 8,938. Traders said there was no central bank intervention.

title: UPDATE 2-INTERVIEW-Sakakibara sees Japan crisis, no contagion.
text:
PANGKOR LAUT, Malaysia, Sept 6 (Reuters) - Japan's leaders should not intervene in the falling stock market as that would not prevent an "unavoidable" financial crisis from hitting the economy, former financial diplomat Eisuke Sakakibara said on Friday 

 Japan's ex-vice finance minister for international affairs told Reuters an economic crisis was looming for his country as current leaders muddled through, but added that problems were domestic and should not cause damaging ripples around the world. 

 Sakakibara, whose every word used to be dissected by foreign exchange dealers when he was in office, said he expected the yen to trade between 116 and 121 to the dollar. 

 He said Japan had exhausted all possible macroeconomic solutions, adding that only aggressive, structural reforms targeted at cutting its huge debts could help. 

 "A financial crisis is unavoidable," Sakakibara said in an interview on the Malaysian resort island of Pangkor Laut, where he is due to address an international conference. 

 "It could happen this month, three to six months time, but sooner or later it will happen," he added. 

 Sakakibara, who had a reputation for aggressive intervention when he was at the Ministry of Finance, said existing leaders lacked the resolve to push through necessary reforms. 

 "Only structural reforms can help, but the current leadership does not have the resolve. They are just muddling along," he said. 

 "We can solve it ourselves but the leaders must have the power and will to break out of the existing mould." 

 HARD TO SAY WHICH THE WEAKER 

 Sakakibara said it was difficult to say whether the yen or the dollar was weaker, and expected the yen to stay ranged until "the market decides". 

 "It is funny, both are weak and nobody is quite sure which is worse," he said. 

 "But among the majors, the euro has the most strength because the economy there is still doing alright." 

 So far, little impact has been felt in the forex market, though dealers warned further falls in Japanese equity prices could prompt liquidation of overseas assets by Japanese investors, generating yen buying against other currencies. 

 On Friday, the yen was around 118 to the dollar and was changing hands at a four-week low against the euro, weakened by a fall in Japan's key Nikkei share average to 19-year trading lows. 

 The Nikkei closed down 1.01 percent at 9,129.07. 

 Known as "Mr Yen" because of his reputation for aggressive intervention in the forex markets, Sakakibara is still seen as an influential figure in Japan's foreign exchange policy. 

 He left the ministry in 1999 and is now a professor at Keio University. 

 MUDDLING THROUGH 

 Sakakibara said Japan's economy was in a mess and that short-term measures to shore up the stock market were futile. 

 While strong exports helped Japan's economy grow 0.5 percent in the April-June quarter, consumer spending continues to languish, depressed by years of profit-crushing deflation. 

 Beleaguered Japanese firms are still more ready to fire rather than hire, and unemployment stands at 5.4 percent, just shy of its post-war high. 

 "Japan has already exhausted all macro policies," he said, adding that there were no longer any effective weapons to combat the long-lived problem of deflation. 

 He also said investors should not hope for a reprise of February, when government steps prised the market off 18-year lows in the face of a fiscal year-end banking crisis. 

 "They have already done it once, you can only do it once." 

 The Nikkei has now lost more than three-quarters of its value since 1989 when Tokyo's shares were worth more than the rest of the world's equity markets combined, and a Reuters poll of eight analysts last week suggested it could bottom out between 8,400 and 9,000.

title: Malaysian interest rates seen steady for now.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 15 (Reuters) - Malaysian interest rates are expected to remain steady in the near term although there is still room for a further cut, analysts and money market dealers said on Thursday. 

 Talk of a lowering of Malaysia's central bank intervention rate had surfaced in the market after earlier speculation that the U.S. Federal Reserve could slice another 50 basis points off the benchmark federal funds rate. 

 However, the Fed left the rate unchanged at 1.75 percent, a 40-year low, at its monetary policy meeting on Tuesday, but warned that economic risks have tilted toward weakness in a step that may foreshadow rate reductions ahead. 

 "There is no pressing need for a rate cut at this point. Any cut would send a confusing signal to the market,"Suresh Kumar, a currency analyst with Standard & Poor's/MMS, said of Malaysian rates. 

 Bank Negara last cut its three-month intervention rate to 5.0 percent on September 20, days after the September 11 attacks on the United States that jolted global markets. 

 Anthony Dass, head of research at SJ Securities, said with the inflation rate still benign, the current accommodative monetary policy was expected to remain intact. 

 "This means the 5.0 percent slapped on the three-month intervention rate will remain," he said. 

 A cut in the intervention rate would also hurt bank profits, analysts said. 

 "We estimate that bank earnings would decline by about 5.0 percent for every 50 basis point reduction in the intervention rate," said one banking analyst. 

 ROOM FOR RATE CUT 

 But analysts did not rule out lower interest rates going forward if the United States cut rates by another 50 basis points and if the weak external economic outlook was prolonged. 

 "Bank Negara is looking at U.S. rates for an indication on domestic interest rates. Based on the current domestic and offshore interest rates, we believe there is room for some revision," said Franklin Tan, head of research at OCBC Securities in Malaysia. 

 "Secondly, the gap between domestic interbank rates and the present intervention rate is still rich at 180 basis points. As such, there is a strong possibility of a 50 basis point cut." 

 The benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) currently stands at 3.24 percent. 

 The intervention rate was introduced in September 1998 to rein in runaway interest rates, which reached as high as 18 percent at the height of the Asian financial crisis. 

 As the base lending rate (BLR) is pegged to the intervention rate, a 50 basis point rate cut will lower the BLR for banks to a new all-time low of six percent from the current 6.4 percent. 

 Banks' net interest income margins will be squeezed as liabilities are locked at higher rates and cannot be re-priced immediately. 

 Deposit rates range between 3.20 percent and 4.0 percent for a period spanning one month to one year. 

 Thus banks with a high proportion of floating rate loans and high loan-deposit ratios could be hard hit. They include Commerce Asset and RHB Bank. 

 But top lender Malayan Banking would be among those least affected, OCBC's Tan said. 

 Money market dealers said the central bank could also be looking for other ways to lower borrowing costs to keep rates steady given the excess liquidity in the banking system. 

 Options included reverting back to using the three-month KLIBOR in determining the base lending rate instead of the intervention rate, they said. 

 But dealers said such a move was unlikely as it would result in a big drop in interest rates given the 176 basis point differential between KLIBOR and the intervention rate.

title: Malaysia To Maintain Loose Monetary Policy
text:
KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- Malaysia will maintain its loose monetary policy as a means to boost economic growth, the finance ministry said Friday in its annual 2001/2002 economic report. 

 The annual economic report, released in conjunction with the budget presentation to parliament, noted such a stance is needed to "mitigate the slack external demand," given the expected prolonged economic slowdown in the U.S. and Japan. 

 Looking ahead to 2002, the finance ministry said monetary policy "will continue to remain accommodative" as a way to complement the government's fiscal stimulus measures. 

 Global easing of interest rates has given the country greater flexibility for maintaining a loose monetary stance, the report noted. 

 In tandem with rate cuts around the world following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the U.S., Bank Negara Malaysia Sept. 20 lowered its key three-month intervention rate to 5% from 5.5%, the first cut in more than two years. However, central bank Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz said last month that any further monetary measures this year would be "less visible" than the interest rate cut. 

 Banks use the intervention rate to calculate their base lending rates, or prime rates. The move was accompanied by a lowering of deposit rates to help banks cope with an expected margin squeeze. 

 Malaysia has maintained a regime of low interest rates since the Asian financial crisis to sustain economic recovery. So far, low inflation hasn't pressured Bank Negara to alter that stance. 

 The economic report projects average annual inflation of just 1.3% for this year, and the rate is likely to remain benign at below 2% in 2002. Nevertheless, the report cautioned external pressures following the events on Sept. 11 could cause consumer prices to edge upward next year. 

 "The recent hike in freight rates, insurance premiums and other transport-related costs is of concern, as they may translate into higher costs," the report said. 

 Also, higher domestic demand could "generate inflationary pressures" if supply shortages, particularly for food, aren't resolved. 

 "Given these risks, the government will remain vigilant to take the necessary measures in containing inflation," the report said, adding that these include boosting local food production and reducing the cost of doing business. 

 Turning to the ringgit peg, the economic report praised the fixed currency system for providing stability during this period of global economic uncertainty, implying the peg won't be changed any time soon. Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad has repeatedly stated there are no grounds for Malaysia to remove or to alter the peg. 

 "The ringgit peg continues to provide an environment of stability and predictability to facilitate economic activities," said the finance ministry. Mahathir also holds the finance portfolio, after announcing the retirement of his former minister Daim Zainuddin in early June. 

 Malaysia pegged the ringgit at 3.80 to the dollar in September 1998 in the midst of the Asian economic crisis as part of its capital controls to stem the currency's decline. 

 The government hasn't altered the level of the peg, despite calls to do so earlier this year when regional currencies weakened. 

 "The ringgit peg will be closely monitored against both domestic and external developments to ensure that it remains consistent with macroeconomic fundamentals," the report said, adding that since the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the U.S., the ringgit has depreciated by 0.2% to 3% against major and regional currencies. 

 "What should give us confidence regarding the ringgit peg...is the acceptance of the ringgit value by all parties, and (that) there is no black market in the ringgit," Mahathir said in his preface to the report. 

 -By Tara Patel, Dow Jones Newswires; 60-3-2692-5254; Tara.Patel@dowjones.com

title: INTERVIEW-Malaysia sees inflation at 1.8 pct in 2000.
text:
BANDAR SERI BEGAWAN, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Malaysia's inflation rate is likely to dip to about 1.8 percent in 2000 from 2.8 percent last year, despite a proposed hike in petroleum prices, Deputy Finance Minister Shafie Salleh said on Sunday. 

 Shafie told Reuters in an interview the subdued inflation outlook would help banks to keep lending rates at low levels in the near-term. 

 "Based on present trends, it is anticipated that the inflation rate would be about 1.8 percent in 2000 as a whole, considering that excess capacity still exists in the economy and monetary policy continues to be accommodative to support economic growth," he said. 

 Shafie is leading the Malaysian delegation at the seventh APEC finance ministers meeting in the tiny oil-rich sultanate of Brunei. 

 Malaysia's inflation rate, measured by the consumer price index, rose by just 1.5 percent year-on-year during January-July, compared with 3.1 percent in the year-ago period. 

 The government plans to increase the price of petroleum for the first time in nearly two decades. The move has raised concerns about the impact on overall prices. 

 But the minister said an increase in petroleum's price would have a minimal impact on the inflation rate. 

 LOW RATES TO REMAIN 

 "As monetary policy will continue to remain accommodative to firmly support growth, it is likely that the 3-month BNM (Bank Negara Malaysia) intervention rate will remain at the current 5.5 percent," Shafie said. 

 The central Bank Negara's three-month intervention rate is used by banks and financial institutions as a benchmark to set their prime lending rates. 

 Last month, Malaysian commercial banks and financial institutions raised deposit rates by 25 basis points, fuelling fears of a hike in interest rates. 

 But Shafie allayed such fears saying the banks had sufficient money available to ease any upward pressure on lending rates. 

 "Given the ample liquidity emanating from both domestic loan growth and current account surplus in the balance of payments, banks will have sufficient funds to lend without pressure for lending rates to increase," he said. 

 BUOYANT GROWTH 

 Shafie said the economy, spurred by strong exports and buoyant domestic demand, was likely to expand more than the official estimate of 5.8 percent in the current year. 

 "While official estimates stand at 5.8 percent, growth in GDP is expected to be higher, given that growth in the first half was 10.3 percent. Private analysts estimate growth at between 6.0-8.0 percent," he said. 

 A recent Reuters poll forecast the economy to grow by 8.6 percent in 2000 and moderate to 6.2 percent in 2001. 

 Malaysia's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 8.8 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2000 against 11.9 percent in the first quarter. 

 Shafie said Malaysia's economic recovery was now broad-based and domestic demand was gathering steam in response to the government's expansionary fiscal and monetary policy. 

 RINGGIT PEG TO STAY 

 He said there was no need to adjust the two-year-old ringgit currency peg, which was in line with economic fundamentals and benefitted the economy. 

 "Currently, the degree of undervaluation is very small and the stable exchange rate has a positive impact on economic activity," he said. 

 "However, if circumstances occur which cause a gross misalignment of the ringgit exchange rate, then Bank Negara Malaysia will, of course respond accordingly." 

 Malaysia imposed capital controls and pegged its ringgit currency at 3.8 to the U.S. dollar in September, 1998, to stem the outflow of short-term capital during the Asian economic crisis in 1997-98.

title: Tame Malaysia inflation mirrors weak domestic demand.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 15 (Reuters) - Malaysia on Monday announced a benign inflation rate which analysts said indicated weak domestic demand and excess capacity in many industrial sectors. 

 The Statistics Department said consumer prices were 2.1 percent higher in October over the same month in 1998. The consumer price index was unchanged at 118.8 points in October from the preceding month. 

 Average prices in the first 10 months of the year rose 2.9 percent compared with the same period a year earlier. 

 "The two main groups, food and gross rent, fuel and power together accounted for 75.6 percent of the overall increase recorded in the current period," the Statistics Department said in a statement. 

 WEAK DEMAND CAPS INFLATION 

 "Domestic demand is weak and growth is mainly due to external demand," said Ng Bok Eng, senior economist at Daiwa Research Institute of Research in Singapore. 

 "It is also partly because of the base factor. Last year, at this point, it was higher because of the currency crisis effect." 

 Analysts said that strong foreign demand for imports, mainly electrical and electronic goods, sparked the recent recovery. 

 Malaysia expects gross domestic product to expand 4.3 percent in 1999 and 5.0 percent in 2000 after shrinking 7.5 percent in 1998. 

 "There is lot of slack in the economy and people are still cautious on spending," said an economist at a Malaysian bank. 

 Eddie Lee, regional economist at Vickers Ballas in Singapore, said demand in many sectors had started picking up but was still below the buoyancy witnessed before the Asian financial crisis erupted in mid-1997. 

 Analysts forecast a low inflation rate over the next six months and expected it to average around 3.0 percent in 1999. 

 BALANCING INTERESTS OF SAVERS AND BORROWERS 

 Subdued inflation and excess liquidity provided the government with the leeway to lower interest rates, analysts said. 

 But Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's ruling coalition, facing its toughest electoral battle in four decades, was keen to balance the interests of savers and borrowers. 

 The government recently unveiled plans to issue 2.0 billion ringgit worth of savings bonds to people above 55 and not employed on a full time basis to ease the impact of low bank deposit interest rates on their incomes. 

 "Interest rates are very, very low. There has to be a balance between savers and borrowers," Ng said. 

Malaysia's central Bank Negara has brought the key intervention rate down in 50 basis point stages, from 7.0 percent in April to 5.5 percent. The last cut came on August 9. ($1 = 3.8 ringgit) ((Kuala Lumpur newsroom +60 3 2275 6846, fax +60 2 232 6752, kuala.lumpur@reuters.com)).

title: FACTBOX - Chronology of financial crisis.
text:
LONDON, June 28 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of the financial crisis in emerging markets, first triggered by devaluation of the Thai baht two years ago. 

 1997 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest ever single-day point loss. 

 Oct 31 - IMF unveils Indonesia's $40 billion aid package, of which $23 billion is front-line defence. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won. 

 1998 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 March 23 - Indonesia nearly doubles interest rates to boost the rupiah and control inflation. 

 May 21 - President Suharto of Indonesia steps down under strong pressure and is succeeded by former deputy president B.J. Habibie. 

 June 5 - International lenders and Indonesian companies reach a deal to reschedule the country's massive corporate debt. 

 June 10 - China's central bank governor warns that the weak yen is having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade. 

 In Taiwan, the local dollar hits new 11-year lows and the Australian dollar plummets past 59 U.S. cents. 

 June 29 - South Korea closes banks for the first time, shutting five ailing operations in a major step towards meeting the mandate of the IMF rescue package. 

 July 13 - Japanese Prime Minister Hashimoto resigns. 

 August 17 - Russia sets a 90-day partial debt moratorium on foreign credits, says short-term rouble debt will be restructured. Government abandons floor value for rouble of 7.13 to the dollar, saying new lower limit is 9.5. 

 August 25 - Rouble suffers its worst one-day fall in nearly four years. Government announces rouble debt restructuring with terms which foreign investors say amount to default. 

 August 28 - Rouble trade is suspended indefinitely on the main Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX). 

 August 31 - Wall Street suffers its second-largest points loss in history, plunging 6.37 percent and sparking another series of stock market routs in Asia. 

 September 2 - Russian Central bank abandons support for the rouble. 

 Malaysia announces that the ringgit will be fixed at 3.80 to the dollar indefinitely. 

 Wall Street stages its second-largest comeback in history, sparking a rally in Asian markets. 

 September 3 - Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is sacked. 

 September 9 - Russian Central bank chief Sergei Dubinin quits. 

 October 2 - Russian exporters start selling half of their hard currency revenues at MICEX under a central bank order aimed at supporting the rouble. Shares hit all-time lows. 

 October 28 - Brazil unveils a 28 billion reals ($23.5 billion) austerity plan of budget cuts and tax hikes to shore up the economy. 

 November 6 - The Russian government and foreign banks agree in general on terms to restructure short-term rouble debt. 

 November 13 - The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and rich nations announce a loan package totalling more than $41 billion for Brazil to avoid a financial meltdown in Latin America. 

 1999 

 January 13 - Brazil plunges deeper into crisis and sends world markets tumbling when it devalues the real. 

 June 15 - Mexico unveils a $23.7 billion financing programme designed to fireproof its economy. 

 March 10 - Brazil's lower house of parliament passes a bill raising a financial transaction tax, a key measure in its anti-crisis austerity plan. 

 April 28 - The IMF agrees to lend Russia $4.5 billion over 18 months but insists several reform proposals must be passed by its parliament before the money is released. 

 June 15 - Mexico unveils a $23.7 billion financing programme designed to fireproof its economy. 

 June 17 - Russia's State Duma votes against a petrol tax bill considered vital to win IMF cash promised in April. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: Malaysia Target Of 8% Bank Loan Growth Out Of Reach
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Despite prodding from the central bank, Malaysian banks aren't likely to achieve the 8.0% growth in lending this year that has been targeted by the government, analysts said. 

 Several positive factors, such as government-sponsored home-ownership campaigns, a possible further interest rate cut, and the recent surge in Malaysian share prices, haven't encouraged banks and consumers to step up the pace of new loans by that much. Analysts say loan growth of around 4.0% is the most that the banks are likely to achieve this year. 

 Banks remain reluctant to lend and consumers remain reluctant to borrow until the economy shows more definite signs of a recovery. 

 "The economy has to start going before loan demand comes in," says Pong Teng Siew, assistant research manager at Kuala Lumpur based securities firm KAF Seagroatt & Campbell Sdn. Bhd. 

 Even so, Malaysia should still be able to achieve its target of 1.0% growth in gross domestic product this year, analysts said. Robust exports will make up for any shortfall in bank lending, providing enough of a boost to the general economy. 

 But Malaysian officials continue to insist that a revival in loan growth is both necessary and achievable. Bank Negara Malaysia Governor Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman said last Tuesday he is confident stricter banking rules announced in April coupled with current low interest rates will spur fresh lending to meet the government's 8.0% growth target by the year end. He noted that some local banks have achieved loan growth rates of around 20% so far this year. 

 He also said 8.0% lending growth is imperative for the country's gross domestic product to expand 1% this year. 

 But government officials have had a poor record of getting domestic banks to increase their lending, since the crisis that erupted after the currency devaluations of July 1997. 

 At the end of March, the latest figure available, total loans in Malaysia's banking system rose only 1.3% year-on-year. Compared to February, loans grew at a measly 0.1%. And despite an 8.0% loans growth target for 1998, lending contracted 1.8% year-on-year. In comparison, lending grew 21.3% in 1997 and 26.3% in 1996. 

 Analysts said banks will continue to lend cautiously as long as they remain mired in nonperforming loans. 

 "Banks are still in the midst of restructuring after the recent (regional financial) crisis. They are wary of over-extending themselves," says Sani Hamid, regional economist at Standard & Poor's MMS in Singapore. 


1999 Loans Growth Seen Up To 4%, Lower Than 8% Target



A reduction in bad loans is expected to encourage lending this year,
but not significantly.



By June, Malaysia's asset management company, Danaharta Nasional Bhd.
is expected to reach its target of absorbing up to MYR40.0 billion from
an estimated MYR100.0 billion in bad loans from the banking system.



Danaharta was set up last June to buy bad loans from Malaysia's banks,
and has since taken over MYR8.0 billion worth of bad loans from 39
financial institutions, and is managing another MYR11.0 billion for two
banks.



But even with fewer problem loans, banks will remain reluctant to lend
as long as the economic recovery is tentative. The economy remains
plagued by oversupply in the manufacturing, property and services
sectors, holding back the pace of recovery and making banks cautious
about new lending, analysts said.



It will take at least a year before these problems are resolved,
analysts said.



The recent rally in the stock market will help to bolster consumer
demand in Malaysia, but won't be enough to raise lending levels to the
government target.



The spectacular rally in the Malaysian stock market in the last two
months has pushed up the benchmark Kuala Lumpur Composite Index to
743.34 points Monday, from only 498.57 on March 30.



Even a second home-ownership campaign, to be launched in Kuala Lumpur
this Thursday, won't propel many Malaysians to apply for loans, analysts
said.



Many prospective house buyers have already made a home purchase during
the first campaign in January, when property sales reached MYR3.79
billion.



A poor outlook due to an oversupply in residential properties is also
expected to keep away buyers, analysts said.



"We have already seen the bulk of house buyers during the first
campaign. Whether they can entice more this time around is left to be
seen," said Sani at MMS.



GDP Target Can Be Achieved on Sustained Trade Surplus



Also, there will be fewer buyers this time around since many people
believe they should wait until the central bank cuts interest rates
further.



And a further reduction in the central bank's intervention rate is
unlikely to sharply boost lending activities.



Last week, junior finance minister Mustapa Mohamed said in Tokyo that
interest rates in Malaysia have not bottomed out, indicating that an
intervention rate cut was imminent. The intervention rate is used by
commercial banks to compute their prime rates.



The central bank last cut its intervention rate - the rate at which it
borrows or lends in the interbank market - to 6.00% from 6.50% on May 3,
in line with expectations of a lower inflation rate.



Far more important for loans than rates at this point are job
security, business confidence, consumer sentiment and political
stability, analysts said.



Although the increase in layoffs has eased, thousands of Malaysian
employees are still retrenched each month.



Business confidence remains skittish as listed companies continue to
post losses.



And political concerns now focus on long-serving Prime Minister
Mahathir Mohamad's successor and when the 73-year-old Mahathir will step
down.



Mahathir has said recently that his deputy Abdullah Ahmad Badawi will
succeed him within the next four years, but analysts say Abdullah has
yet to prove himself as capable leader and lacks the vision and tenacity
of his boss.

0900 GMT - Asian regional currencies pared early losses as 

 the yen recovered some ground on growing talk Japan might have

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Regionals soft as yen droops.
text:
0030 GMT - Asian regional currencies were looking soft in 

 early trade with the yen still depressed against the dollar but 

 off its worst on light profit-taking. 

     Dealers said the dollar showed potential to trade higher in 

 the near term, with firm support expected around 121 yen. 

     U.S. stock prices surged overnight, signalling new investor 

 confidence in America's robust economy and sparking dollar 

 buying. 

     Japanese Finance Minister Kiichi Miyazawa said Monday's 

 "tankan" survey of business sentiment showed the worst is over 

 for the Japanese economy. 

     *** Bank Negara Malaysia cut its three-month intervention

 rate to 6.5 percent from 7.0 percent late on Monday. 

     It said the maximum base lending rates of commercial banks 

 were expected to drop to 7.67 percent from 8.04 percent. 

     The central bank last cut the intervention rate, the 

 benchmark for commercial bank lending, on November 10 when it 

 was lowered to 7.00 percent from 7.5 percent. 

     The latest rate cut was not unexpected as interbank rates 

 have been falling over the past few days due to excess 

 liquidity in the money market. 

     The bank said the latest cut reflects the downward trend in 

 the expected inflation rate and is also aimed at sustaining 

 positive developments in the economy. 

     It said last week the consumer price index was expected to 

 fall below four percent this year from 5.3 percent in 1998. 

     *** Malaysian business groups said the ringgit was 

 undervalued at 3.80 to the dollar and could make imports 

 expensive and debt servicing burdensome. 

     Leading trade associations urged Trade Minister Rafidah 

 Aziz to adjust the ringgit exchange rate, saying an upward 

 revision would also give a psychological boost to investors. 

     *** The peso was steady after gaining ground from dollar 

 inflows on Monday. 

     Finance Secretary Edgardo Espiritu said the Philippines 

 received $1.03 billion in loans from Japan and funds from bond 

 issues in March. 

     He also said the benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate may 

 fall below 11 percent in April if inflation declines further. 

     March inflation data is due at 0100 GMT. 

     A Reuters poll of five economists last month showed 

 inflation could drop to 9.28 percent in March from February's 

 9.9 percent. 

     Moody's Investors Service said overnight the Philippines' 

 stable foreign currency ratings outlook reflects recent 

 improvements in the balance of payments and external payments 

 position as well as past progress in fiscal adjustment and 

 structural reform. 

     *** The Korean won opened lower after a three-day break as 

 the market played catch-up with a weaker yen. 

     But Seoul shares made strong headway on persistent 

 institutional buying of blue chips. 

     The Finance Ministry said on Monday the number of Korean 

 companies forced to close their bank accounts after defaulting 

 on debt rose to 656 in March from 555 in February. 

     It said the increase was mainly due to a higher number of 

 new start-ups and noted that the debt default ratio was still 

 low compared with last year. 

     The number of firms in default on debt reached a peak of 

 1,226 in January 1998.

title: FOCUS - Malaysia sees dim light at end of tunnel.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, March 31 (Reuters) - Malaysia's central bank on Wednesday delivered a cautiously upbeat outlook for 1999, predicting the economy will recover modestly this year from Asia's financial crisis and its first recession in 13 years. 

 Bank Negara said gross domestic product is expected to expand by one percent in 1999 after contracting by 6.7 percent last year - the worst battering since 1985. 

 Analysts were split over whether the economy will grow even modestly this year but said authorities had scope to push down interest rates and prime the spending pump to stimulate growth. 

 They also said that whatever Malaysia does, its decision last year to slap controls on foreign exchange flows has left a bad taste in foreign investors' mouths and will make it more difficult for the nation to attract overseas investment. 

 "Malaysia has to make up its mind whether it wants to take part in this global economy," Raymond Lim, group chief economist with ABN Amro Asia in Singapore, told Reuters Television. 

 "As long as it has doubts and it is arrogant in a vociferous manner, it will continue to put off foreign capital and that will definitely affect Malaysia's growth as the region recovers." 

 Bank Negara said economic growth will be marginal in the first half of 1999 in view of high inventory build-up since early last year, then would pick up in the last six months. 

 "There are indications that the trough in the growth cycle has been reached in the third quarter of 1998 and prospects are for a gradual recovery in 1999," Bank Negara governor Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman said in the foreword to the 291-page report. 

 Barring a global economic setback, the bank said GDP growth could inch closer to two percent in 1999 as dozens of banks and companies hit by the crisis are overhauled. 

 But it said the prospects for continued export growth were uncertain and the main growth engine would be domestic demand. 

 "Fewer people dispute that Malaysia is doing something right," said Margaret Chin-Wolf, senior fund manager at Pauli Investment Management in Singapore. "They are tackling their problems." 

 Tan Chong Koay, chief executive of Pheim Asset Management Sdn Bhd in Kuala Lumpur said: "The worst is over." 

 But Geoffrey Dennis, Deutsche Bank's global emerging markets equity strategist, said Malaysia was being overly optimistic in projecting one percent GDP growth in 1999. 

 "We think one percent is still somewhat optimistic. We're arguing growth will probably be negative. Malaysia's not in the forefront of the recovery stories in Asia at this point." 

 Analysts agreed Malaysia, with a burgeoning current account surplus and subdued inflation, could continue to cut interest rates to help stimulate growth. 

 "What was a surprise is that they did not lower interest rates," said C.T. Yeo, country treasurer for Bank of America Malaysia Bhd in Kuala Lumpur. 

 "We thought they should have taken the opportunity to lower the intervention rate down to six percent from seven percent." 

Malaysia imposed capital controls and fixed its ringgit exchange rate in September against a backdrop of mounting economic and political tension. 

 Bank Negara governor Ali gave a robust defence of the capital controls, saying they had provided the stability needed to ensure recovery. 

 "Malaysia is a separate case until they free those capital controls up," Dennis said.

text:

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Rupiah and peso gain, others steady.
text:
0800 GMT - The regional currencies had a quietly steady day 

 as dollar/yen held in a narrow range, but the rupiah firmed as 

 aid dollars flowed across the foreign exchanges. 

      Dollar/yen was little changed from Friday's late Asian 

 level but it was up a little on Friday's New York close. 

     Japan's still acute banking sector problems will tend to 

 prevent the yen moving any higher but for now most traders do 

 not see it dipping below the 120 per dollar level. 

     The dollar did get some support from news that European 

 leaders believe the conditions are right for interest rate 

 cuts. 

     *** The rupiah stood out with another good gain but its 

 recent rally does seem to be slowing and many in the market do 

 not see it moving substantially higher from here. 

     The rupiah has rallied some 35 percent this month and has 

 more than doubled in value against the dollar since its June 

 low of around 17,000. 

     The move higher has been fuelled by the conversion of aid 

 dollars into rupiah and despite the apparently spectacular 

 rally it is still almost 70 percent down on levels seen before 

 the Asia crisis kicked-off in July 1997. 

 Indonesia's central bank has no plans to intervene on the 

 rupiah in coming months but will aim to create conditions which 

 prevent excessive volatility. 

 "We will let the rupiah move in accordance with market 

 laws. Bank Indonesia will not intervene," Bank Indonesia 

 director Achyar Iljas was quoted as saying by the official 

 Antara news agency. 

 The rupiah did gain some support from a local newspaper 

 report that the central bank might reimpose an intervention

 band. 

 *** In Malaysia trouble flared at the weekend with two 

 policemen and 12 protesters injured and 241 arrested as crowds 

 clashed with police. 

 Supporters of the detained former deputy prime minister 

 Anwar Ibrahim threw rocks and petrol bombs around a mosque in 

 the Moslem Kampong Bharu district. 

     Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad condemned his opponents 

 saying his government would not be intimidated. 

     Away from his political problems, Mahathir's budget on 

 Friday received only a lukewarm response from analysts. 

     There was some praise that it would help stimulate the 

 economy but there is concern over just how Malaysia would fund 

 its projected budget deficit of 6.1 percent of GDP in 1999. 

     Analysts say there is no way the funding for next year's 

 budget can come from domestic sources and foresee aid from 

 outside the country being necessary. 

     Mahathir proposed more than four billion ringgit ($1 

 billion) be spent on the transport sector and offered tax cuts 

 for exporters, local manufacturers of consumer durables and 

 investors in unit trusts. 

 Malaysia's Second Finance Minister Mustapa Mohamed said the 

 government will not have any problem funding a projected 1999 

 budget deficit. 

 He told Reuters Television that capital controls imposed in 

 September have been a success, and Malaysia would consider the 

 competitiveness of its neighbours' currencies before scrapping 

 the controls. 

 *** The peso was another bright spot on continued 

 speculation that dollars from direct investment will make their 

 way across the foreign exchanges. 

 Traders said there was talk that proceeds from the sale of 

 San Miguel Corporation's stake in Nestle Philippines Inc and 

 Coca-Cola Beverages were finding their way into the market. 

 San Miguel sold its 45 percent stake in Nestle last August 

 for about $695 million. In July, it sold its stake in Coca-Cola 

 for 339.6 million sterling or around 24 billion pesos. 

     The Philippine Lower House on Sunday approved a proposed 

 1999 national budget of 579.5 billion pesos ($13.8 billion). 

     The proposed appropriation is 9.7 percent higher than this 

 year's budget and targets a lower budget deficit of 17.9 

 billion pesos from this year's projected deficit of 40 billion 

 pesos. 

 The budget bill will go through a third reading for a final 

 vote when Congress reconvenes next month, although this is 

 considered a mere formality. 

 *** The Taiwan dollar closed at a seven-month high against 

 its U.S. counterpart amid U.S. dollar selling in form of 

 non-delivery forward and central bank selling. 

     *** The Korean won and the Singapore dollar both eased 

 slightly. 

     Singapore CPI fell 1.4% in September on a year-on-year 

 basis and was down 0.3% from August. This followed a 0.8% 

 year-on-year drop in August. CURRENCIES

title: HK welcomes stable markets, but wants results.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Hong Kong residents, shell shocked by deflated stock and property values, high interest rates and rising unemployment, on Tuesday welcomed the promise of relief from new government measures to stabilise local markets. 

 But political analysts warned that the territory's leaders will face mounting public pressure if the new regulations and a costly stock market intervention fail to produce results. 

 "Any kind of draconian measure will be accepted because Hong Kong people are infused with the desire to avoid an economic meltdown," said political observer Lau Siu-kai. 

 "But in the long-term, people will want results. How can you put in billions of dollars and not see results?" said Lau, who is also a sociology professor at the Chinese University. 

 Starting in mid-August, the government has spent more than HK$100 billion (US$12.9 billion) on stock and futures to foil market manipulators it accused of attacking the local dollar to drive interest rates up and stock prices down to take profits on short stock positions. 

 Since then, Hong Kong's struggle with economic recession has become intertwined with the government's fight against market speculators and its defence of the territory's U.S. dollar-linked exchange rate. 

 Local media have described the government's actions as a "war" with international hedge funds who are preying on Hong Kong's open economy and regional economic instability. 

 Editorial cartoons and even front-page newspaper graphics have depicted Hong Kong Monetary Authority boss Joseph Yam and other officials in sword fights with dark-suited figures labeled "speculators" in defence of the dollar peg. 

 Discussion of the government's measures and the strength of the dollar peg - viewed as unimpeachable just a few months ago - now dominate talk among business people and non-investors alike. 

 Residents have largely voiced support for the actions, saying they may prevent the territory from suffering the same type of economic meltdown plaguing neighbouring countries, such as Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia. 

 "Market intervention is necessary. Speculators who come here can create trouble," said retiree Lo Kam-seng, 55. "If the government doesn't intervene, the stock market will fall even more." 

 Lo added that during "normal times," intervention would not be good for the economy. 

 The HKMA announced over the weekend seven measures to strengthen the currency board and on Monday the government unveiled a 30-point plan to tighten rules and improve transparency in stock and futures markets. 

 But while many approved of the measures, the applause was muted as some wondered if Hong Kong, which has prided itself as one of the world's most open economies, might perhaps be paying too high a cost, both monetarily and in damage to its free-market reputation. 

 "The money would have been better spent on education, welfare or to lower the unemployment rate where more people would stand to gain," said Chris Chan, a working mother. 

 Political analyst Sonny Lo, an associate professor of politics at the University of Hong Kong, said there would be more domestic pressure on leader Tung Chee-hwa's administration after this spate with foreign speculators. 

 "This issue has polarised Hong Kong society, with some agreeing that fighting speculators is right and must cost money, while the other camp wants the government to concentrate on domestic issues, such as welfare," Lo said.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Regionals wilting, Sing dlr downcast.
text:
0420 GMT - Asian currencies were tending to droop despite 

 the dollar sliding below 138 yen as fears of another missile 

 strike by North Korea and Malaysia's retreat from world markets 

 turned investors off the region. 

     Dollar/yen was off its lows below the 137 level, but making 

 slow progress after Japan's "Mr Yen", Eisuke Sakakibara said 

 the yen's excessive weakness had not yet fulling corrected and 

 a senior Finance Ministry official said Japan was ready to 

intervene on forex if necessary. 

     *** Malaysia's radical new foreign exchange controls 

 continued to cast a shadow over the region, with the shock 

 sacking of Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar 

 Ibrahim late on Wednesday, deepening the market's gloom. 

     Anwar, seen as one of the last market-friendly members of 

 the Malaysian government, is due to hold a news conference at 

 0700 GMT. 

     Some analysts say his removal means the cabinet is now 

 united behind Prime Minister Mahathir, and likely to have more 

 success in implementing current policy. 

     The Malaysian government is due to hold an emergency 

 Cabinet meeting to name Anwar's successor today. 

     Malaysia's central Bank Negara, eased monetary policy 

 further by cutting its intervention rate (the three-month 

 interbank rate) to eight percent from 9.5 percent. 

     It said it expects the maximum base lending rate of 

 commercial banks and finance companies to moderate to 9.06 

 percent and 10.76 percent, respectively, following the 

 reduction in the intervention rate. 

 The liquid asset ratio of commercial banks will also be 

 reduced to 15 percent from 17 percent of total eligible 

 liabilities from September 16 and commercial banks will no 

 longer be required to maintain vostro balances of foreign 

 banking institutions with Bank Negara from Thursday. A vostro 

 account is a foreign bank's account maintained in a domestic 

currency. 

 Ringgit forward markets were still trying to unravel 

 positions ahead of the complete end to offshore trading in the 

 ringgit. 

 Bank Negara said in a circular to chiefs of banks that it 

 would introduce mechanisms to allow for settlement of 

 outstanding ringgit transactions after September 9. 

 On Wednesday, Bank Negara said the ringgit's exchange rate 

 would be fixed at 3.80 to the dollar for an indefinite period, 

 but dealers said there was already talk of a black market, with 

 the dollar being quoted above 4.50 ringgit. 

 "The Malaysian government is taking a lot of risk by fixing 

 the exchange rate," the head of regional currencies at a 

 European bank in Singapore said. 

 *** Singapore's Foreign Exchange Market Committee has 

 agreed on a rate of four Malaysian ringgit to one U.S. dollar 

 for the settlement of outstanding ringgit positions in the 

 offshore market. 

 The Singapore dollar was among the biggest losers in the 

 region, falling within a whisker of the 1.78 level from a 

 morning high of 1.75, as players sold it as a proxy for the now 

 untradeable ringgit and illiquid baht and rupiah. 

     "Everybody just wants to catch hold of dollars at the 

 moment.wants to buy," the European bank dealer said. 

     He said the Sing dollar had also been hit by speculation 

 that oil-rich Brunei might abandon its currency link with 

 Singapore, but added that this seemed unlikely in the current 

 volatile environment.

 companies for foreign debt payments. 

     The government said merchandise exports rose 19 percent in 

 the first seven months of 1998, compared with a year ago. 

     Exports rose 20.9 percent year-on-year in July. 

     Budget Secretary Benjamin Diokno said the IMF had expressed 

 concern over whether the government can meet its revenue goals. 

     The government has projected a deficit of 40 billion pesos 

 for the year, but Manila newspapers said the IMF expected a 

 higher deficit of 50 billion pesos.

title: Malaysia moves to cut interest rates again.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Malaysia cut interest rates again Thursday, barely 24 hours after dismissing its finance minister, who had favoured keeping rates high, and two days after imposing tough foreign-exchange controls. 

 The central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, said it eased monetary policy by cutting its intervention rate, which serves as a benchmark for commercial bank lending, to 8.0 percent from 9.5 percent. 

 The easing was the fourth reduction in the rate in the past month as part of a government plan to revive the recession-hit economy. 

 Bank Negara said it expects the maximum base lending rate of commercial banks and finance companies to moderate to 9.06 percent and 10.76 percent, respectively. The key base lending rate quoted by the country's biggest bank, Malayan Banking Bhd, is currently at 10.3 percent, after it sharply reduced the rate from 10.9 percent from Tuesday. 

 The central bank also said the liquid asset ratio of commercial banks will be reduced to 15 percent from 17 percent of total eligible liabilities from Sept. 16. Dealers said the move will bring down banks' cost of funds. 

 The rate cut came barely 24 hours after the dismissal of Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, who had repeatedly blamed high interest rates for the sharp contraction of the economy. 

 Malaysian gross domestic product shrank by 6.8 percent in the second quarter of this year from the year-earlier period, sinking the country into its first recession in 13 years. The economy contracted by 2.8 percent in the first quarter. 

 Anwar's ouster followed the double resignations of Bank Negara's governor and deputy governor last week over differences with Mahathir on how to manage the economy. 

 Dealers said Malaysia has room to lower interest rates after shielding its ringgit currency from fluctuations by imposing controls on the convertibility of the currency. Expectations of a big inflow of ringgit from offshore accounts would also allow for the lowering of interest rates, they said. 

 Mahathir said Tuesday that ringgit notes must be brought home by the end of this month, making the ringgit held outside Malaysia worthless as of Oct. 1. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: ASIA FOCUS - Chronology of Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 3 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of Asia's financial crisis. 

 1997 

 Jan 23 - Leading South Korean steel maker Hanbo Steel Corp defaults on loans, the first of a string of major corporate failures in 1997. 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency comes under attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate 1-percentage points to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thai finance minister. Resignation has immediate impact in the Philippines, where the overnight deposit rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". 

 The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bail-out package, bringing it to $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 20 - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad tells delegates of IMF/World Bank conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Around this time the South Korean won also begins to slump in value. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over on to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest single-day point loss ever. 

 Oct 31 - Indonesia's IMF package is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - Indonesia shuts down 16 troubled banks. 

 Nov 5 - IMF approves a $10 billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won, which rapidly falls to 1,000 to the dollar. 

 Dec 4 - IMF approves a $21 billion loan for South Korea, part of a bail-out package that will total nearly $60 billion. 

 Dec 8 - Thailand closes 56 of 58 previously suspended finance companies. 

 1998 

 Jan 8 - Representatives of the IMF and South Korea agree to a 90-day rollover of short-term debt. 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. Shares fall sharply in Hong Kong, China and Singapore. 

 Jan 15 - IMF managing director Michel Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 Jan 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing. 

 Jan 28 - International creditor banks and the South Korean government say they have agreed on a plan to exchange $24 billion of short-term debt for new loans maturing in one, two and three years. 

 Jan 30 - U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warns Asia's financial crisis could spread. 

 Feb 14 - The IMF threatens to cut off the bail-out fund for Indonesia over its plans to introduce a currency board. 

 Feb 26 - Indonesia's borrowers and lenders begin negotiations on rescheduling at least $70 billion in private off-shore debt. 

 March 1 - Indonesian President Suharto says reforms prescribed by the IMF have not worked. 

 March 4 - The IMF approves release of the third tranche payment from Thailand's package and commends the Thai government for its economic reforms. 

 March 6 - IMF says its board will not discuss Indonesia's economic reform programme before April, effectively delaying a $3 billion payment initially expected by March 15. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: FOCUS-Malaysia imposes  forex  controls.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Malaysia slapped controls on currency trade on Tuesday to shield the battered ringgit against global instability and speculators, long blamed by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad for Asia's financial woes. 

 The central bank, Bank Negara, said the controls would insulate Malaysia's recession-hit economy from the global financial "crisis", allowing cuts in interest rates without affecting the business of traders and investors. 

 "The overriding objective of the new measures is to regain monetary independence and insulate the Malaysian economy from the prospects of further deterioration in the world economic and financial environment," Bank Negara said in a statement. 

 "In the process, the nation would be adequately prepared to minimise the impact of a possible global economic crisis and a breakdown in the international financial system." 

 The range of measures threw the foreign exchange market into confusion but the ringgit strengthened dramatically, rising to about four per U.S. dollar at 0614 GMT from 4.18 late on Monday. 

 Mahathir, who has repeatedly pointed a finger of blame at speculators for Asia's troubles, was set to take questions from a panel of three interviewers over nationwide television at 3 p.m. (0700 GMT). 

 The central bank said the measures would affect some types of short-term capital flows but current account transactions and foreign direct investment would be unaffected. 

 It said foreigners now needed the central bank's approval to convert ringgit into foreign exchange. 

 The measures would limit speculators' ability to deal in the ringgit, which has lost nearly 40 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since the outbreak of Asia's financial crisis in mid-1997. 

 Dealers said the move would virtually put an end to speculative trade in the ringgit but also undermine Malaysia's reputation as having one of the most open economies among developing countries. 

 "Overall, although the ringgit is likely to strengthen as a result of this as speculators are effectively wiped out from the market, Malaysia's efforts in financial liberalisation have experienced a considerable setback," markets consultancy I.D.E.A. said. 

 Bank Negara's governor and deputy governor, who officials said opposed the currency controls, submitted their resignations last week, exposing a rift in the government. 

 The central bank said on Tuesday that Malaysia was still committed to the free market and the trend towards liberalisation, but there were limits to its commitment. 

 "The benefits of the market can only be realised in an environment of stable and efficient global financial markets," it said, adding that it would withdraw the controls once there was a "discernible normalisation" of the financial markets. 

Malaysia's moves were the latest example of a government intervening to shield the economy and followed efforts by Hong Kong, Taiwan and Russia to protect their markets. 

 Bank Negara chastised the international community for failing to tackle the risks linked to globalised markets. 

 "While arguments have been put forward for emerging economies to undertake economic and financial reforms," the central bank said, "of greater urgency is the need to reform the international financial system to better cope with the changed international financial environment." 

 Mahathir has repeatedly railed against currency speculators, accusing them of undermining the gains that Malaysia made during a decade of eight percent or more annual economic growth. 

 Malaysia's economy shrank 6.8 percent between the second quarters of 1997 and 1998. Since it had also fallen 2.8 percent during the year to the first quarter, the economy is now formally in its first recession in 13 years. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Bank Resignations/Malaysia -2: Zeti As Acting Governor
text:
"Unless someone has managed to convince him otherwise, he is leaning to some form of controls," says a Singapore-based economist with close links to Bank Negara. This economist and financial executives say Dr. Mahathir's decision not to attend the Non-Aligned Movement summit meeting in South Africa this week indicates that the 73-year-old prime minister is considering drastic economic measures. 

 It remains unclear what shape exchange controls might take. Many economists say that altering Malaysia's liberal capital policies would hurt a country that relies heavily on global trade and foreign investment, because international investors want to be able to move capital around the world freely. 

 In recent months, Dr. Mahathir and Daim Zainuddin, the minister appointed in June with a brief to get the economy moving, have said Malaysia will pursue an easier monetary policy and government will spend more. But many economists say that route is extremely risky because it puts further pressure on the currency and on an already stretched financial system. 

 "What the country needs is to put its banking system in order and get foreign money into the system," says a Singapore-based commercial banker. "The resignations of two respected government officials just add more uncertainty." 

 Formerly chief executive of the country's largest banking group, Malayan Banking Bhd., Ahmad was appointed central-bank governor in 1993 and is widely credited with repairing Bank Negara's sullied reputation after it lost billions of dollars trading currencies in the early 1990s. Ahmad won praise from Malaysia's banking community in recent months for resisting government intervention in the running of the central bank. 

 Since the Asian economic crisis erupted a year ago, Ahmad has rebuffed Dr. Mahathir's entreaties to lower interest rates to help companies that couldn't afford to borrow. Instead, with Finance Minister Anwar, the central-bank governor argued that Malaysia needs high interest rates to attract investors to the ringgit and keep a lid on inflation. 

 "The government has never agreed to the idea that we should have high interest rates and dry up credit, because it will cause a contraction, and we have seen it in the second quarter," Dr. Mahathir told reporters on Saturday, referring to the 6.8% contraction in Malaysia's economy in the second quarter after a 2.8% drop in the first. 

 The government appointed the assistant governor of the central bank, Zeti Akhtar Aziz, as acting governor. As the bank's chief economist, Zeti has been a strong proponent of the policies advocated by her predecessor but isn't regarded as being as forceful.

title: ASIA MARKETS -  Currencies  calm but stocks surge.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 20 (Reuters) - A mostly quiet day on the 

currency front in Asian markets but stocks made a splash with 

 another day of strong gains on indexes in Hong Kong, Korea and 

 Malaysia. 

     Both Hong Kong's Hang Seng index and Malaysia's KLSE were 

 benefitting from actual or rumoured government intervention, 

 while bank merger deals helped Korea's KOSPI. 

     However, Tokyo's exchange, the region's largest, closed 

 slightly lower, with the market little impressed by a media 

 report of a government plan to support a merger between the 

 troubled Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan Ltd and Sumitomo Trust 

 & Banking Co Ltd, traders said. 

    The Nikkei average had initially suffered profit-taking, 

 triggered by a setback in Wall Street stocks overnight, but the 

 losses were mostly offset later by the yen's surge, they said. 

    The 225-share Nikkei average finished down 14.93 points or 

 0.10 percent at 15,391.41 while the dollar sank more than one 

 yen in late trade. 

      HONG KONG STOCKS END FIRM WITH DOWNSIDE SEEN LIMITED 

     The Hang Seng index closed up 1.57 percent at 7,742.53 

 after peaking as high as 7,880 in early trade -- its highest 

 level this month. 

     But dealers are concerned the market is being artificially 

 supported by government buying. They say investors are jumping 

 on the bandwagon but nobody knows when the intervention will 

 stop. 

     Brokers expect the government to continue squeezing short 

 sellers until the August Hang Seng Index futures expire on Aug 

 28. 

     MALAYSIAN STOCKS GET A BOOST FROM ANWAR 

     In Kuala Lumpur, the KLSE moved from strength to strength 

 as a key resistance at 368 was breached on local buying. 

     Fresh buying was sparked by Deputy Prime Minister Anwar 

 Ibrahim's comments that drastic measures were being planned for 

 the economy. 

     Anwar also expanded on Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's 

 Tuesday comments that the Moslem pilgrims fund could enter the 

 market to buy shares in the local stock market without waiting 

 for a government directive. 

     Anwar said only stocks deemed halal -- acceptable to Islam 

 -- such as companies not dealing in gaming, liquor and tobacco 

 production could be bought. 

     But dealers say the market is becoming sceptical at how 

 long the market can sustain the government-linked rally. 

     SINGAPORE POSTS DROP IN JULY IN NON-OIL DOMESTIC EXPORT 

     Singapore posted weaker July non-oil domestic exports, 

 reflecting deteriorating Asian consumption and slowing demand 

 in key markets. 

     Non-oil domestic exports fell in July by 2.3 percent 

 year-on-year in nominal terms to 7.59 billion Singapore 

 dollars, after rising 6.1 percent in June, according to the 

 Trade and Development Board. 

 Economists and analysts said the July fall was expected 

 because of Asia's economic crisis and oversupply in the global 

 electronics market. 

     Electronics account for 70 percent of Singapore's non-oil 

 domestic exports, and more than 50 percent of manufacturing. 

     TAIWAN CHALKS UP HUGE 2ND QTR CURRENT ACCOUNT SURPLUS 

     Taiwan's current account posted a surplus of $753 million 

 in the second quarter of 1998 compared with a surplus of $1.408 

 billion in the second quarter of 1997, the central bank said. 

     The second-quarter current account surplus was more than 

 twice as big as analysts expected. A Reuters Poll of economists 

 on August 17 yielded an average forecast of US$311 million. 

     Taiwan's merchandise trade surplus shrank to $2.535 billion 

 in the second quarter, compared with a surplus of $3.612 

 billion a year ago, the central bank said. 

     The central bank attributed the year-on-year decline in 

 current account surplus to Southeast Asia's currency crisis 

 eating into the island's exports. 

     Taiwan stocks ended marginally off but were well-supported 

 on continued optimism over the government's planned 

 market-stimulus measures. 

     The Securities and Futures Commission announced yesterday 

 it was drafting proposals to help stabilise the stock market 

 following President Lee Teng-hui's call to ensure investor 

 confidence. 

 The Taiwan cabinet adopted a 193.7 billion Taiwan dollar 

 stimulus plan for the 1999-2000 fiscal year on Thursday, but 

 dealers were still cautious after Wall Street's overnight 

 losses. 

     JAKARTA SHARES WEAK AS NEW BANKRUPTCY CODE BECOMES 

 EFFECTIVE 

     Jakarta stocks fell as a new bankruptcy law came into 

 effect. Investors are worried this could be the start of a slew 

 of bankruptcies that might even claim some listed companies. 

     The bankruptcy law is designed to give creditors more power 

 to force debtors to restructure and pay off their debts. Firms 

 that seek bankruptcy protection will have 270 days to 

 restructure and work out their payment plan with creditors. 

 After that, they can be liquidated. 

 KOREAN STOCKS AIDED BY BANK MERGER PLANS 

 South Korea's stock market index, the KOSPI, rose by nearly 

 five percent, helped by a stronger yen and aggressive foreign 

 buying. 

 Blue chips remained bullish on arbitrage buying and bank 

 shares came into the spotlight mainly due to a merger deal 

 between Hana and Boram banks, they said. 

 The Korea Stock Exchange composite stock price index shot 

 up by 4.87 percent, or 14.69 points, to close at 316.59, 

 recovering from the day low of 301.76. Gainers led losers by 

 638 to 155 with 123 stocks going limit up. 

 "Foreign investors became net buyers for the first time 

 since August 11. The amount of their buying is really big," 

 said Kim Kyung-hack, a market analyst at the Korea Stock 

 Exchange. 

     The exchange said foreign investors bought a net 13.9 

 billion won and individual investors 29.1 billion. 

     Brokers said heavy buy orders poured in for bank shares as 

 investors believed a wave of bank restructuring was in the 

 offing with the Hana-Boram merger and the Commercial-Hanil bank 

 merger announced last month. 

 The banking sub-index rose 3.96 percent to 76.62 points. 

 A senior official at Hana Bank said the presidents of the 

 two banks agreed on a merger deal Wednesday night and a formal 

 signing of the letter of intent was expected soon. 

 The Korean won was also firmer, breaking through the 1,300 

 level by midday trade. Dealers said dollar selling from Kia 

 Motors and the strong yen helped prop up the currency. 

 Prospects for the won remained good with the weekend ahead 

 and export negotiations lined up for next week.
