title: FOCUS-Malaysia explores ways of shoring up shares.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Tuesday the government was considering supporting the ailing stock market by buying shares and barring banks from selling stock. 

 Mahathir told reporters in the capital that money from a government-run fund for Moslem pilgrims might also be used to shore up the stock market, which slumped to a new 10-year low on Tuesday. 

 He also said that the government was considering cutting taxes. 

 "It's quite difficult to raise taxes during these trying times. In fact we should lower taxes," he said. 

 Mahathir, who relishes verbal combat, earlier on Tuesday told a workers' rally that speculative attacks on currencies of emerging markets had reached a dangerous level and might prompt countries to retaliate. 

 He said, apparently in jest, that he feared attacks on the rouble might tempt Russia to use its nuclear weapons. 

 "The attacks by currency traders have reached a dangerous stage and are totally irresponsible," he said in a speech. 

 "I worry if the attacks continue on emerging markets, it may hit countries that have the capability to fight back. I worry, for example, if Russia continued to be pressured and they have nuclear bombs, then they may want to drop the bombs on those who attack them," he said, prompting laughter from some listeners. 

 "For us, we will continue to defend our country. We do not have atomic bombs or nuclear bombs. But I'm confident Malaysians can fend off all attacks mounted by any quarter." 

 Malaysia's stock market and currency have fallen sharply since the start of Asia's economic crisis in July 1997, and Mahathir has repeatedly blamed foreign currency traders. 

 Earlier on Tuesday, the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's benchmark index, which has dropped by more than 70 percent since July 1997, fell to a new 10-year low of 312.90. 

 The index ended the day barely changed at 315.66 after Mahathir's comments. But the ringgit currency was not impressed, closing the day slightly lower at 4.23 to a dollar against Monday's finish of 4.22. 

 Analysts said any moratorium on the sale of shares by banks could hammer bank stocks and in the long run lead to an increase in banks' sour loans. 

 The proposal would mean banks which are holding onto shares as loan collateral might no longer be able to force the sale of the shares if the loan was in default, said markets consultancy firm S&P's MMS International in Singapore. 

 "If this is the case, it could trigger additional investor fright, as the move would essentially mean that corporate risk is now transferred to the banking sector, which may well cause the collapse of more banks under a mountain of 'uncollectible' bad debts," it said. 

 There were also questions about how the government planned to finance market intervention. 

 Mahathir said Malaysia and other countries whose currencies had been driven down by speculators had to take measures to protect their economies. 

 In Hong Kong, for example, the territorial government had to step into the market to buy shares but it was accused of interfering with free market, he said. 

 "You look at other countries, Hong Kong for example. There are some specific measures and of course they will get attacked by the foreign media and the others," he said. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority intervened in the stock and futures market on Friday to support sagging prices. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: ASIA MARKETS - Yen and yuan worries hurt markets.
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Most Asian regional currencies fell on Monday in line with a weaker Japanese yen, which was trading close to 146.5 per dollar after nearing an eight-year low of 146.75 earlier. 

 Dealers said a test of 146.75 could come soon. 

 Persistent worries about the Chinese yuan also weighed on markets, despite comments over the weekend by China's Jiang Zemin pledging support for the currency. 

 HONG KONG STILL A CONCERN, DESPITE CALMER DOLLAR 

 Concerns about the resiliency of the Hong Kong dollar peg after a series of speculative attacks last week as well as worries about the Chinese yuan were likely to keep the dollar strong against the yen, traders said. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was under less pressure on Monday, with forward spreads narrowing and interest rates falling. By mid-afternoon, the three-month forward rate was at 1050/1120 points compared with 1400/1500 at Friday's close. 

 Sentiment had improved but they said the local dollar was still susceptible to attack, dealers said. 

 Moreover, there were worries the Hong Kong government's next defence of the peg would not be so easy. Last week, the government's purchases of Hong Kong dollars were funded with sales of U.S. dollar assets from fiscal accounts, skirting the currency board system and keeping a lid on interest rates. 

 While most Asian stock markets were lower on Monday because of the weakening yen, Hong Kong's blue-chip Hang Seng Index was mildly firmer on the back of easier local interest rates. The index ended up 0.23 percent at 7,034.62. 

 CHINA INTERVENES, AGAIN 

Central bank intervention kept the Chinese yuan at 8.2800 to the dollar at the close on Monday, little changed from Friday's close. Dealers said the central bank intervened to keep the currency at that level. 

 On Sunday, Chinese President Jiang Zemin repeated that Beijing was determined to avoid devaluing the yuan. 

 China's share markets slumped to new lows. Shanghai's hard currency B shares ended down 3.44 percent at a record-low close of 27.634 points due to falls in domestic A shares. The weaker yen and poor corporate interim results were blamed for the fall. 

 The Shenzhen B share index also closed at a record low, down 3.66 percent at 55.46 points. 

 MALAYSIA CUTS INTEREST RATES 

Malaysia's Bank Negara cut its three-month intervention rate by 50 basis points to 10 percent, its second cut in a week. The ringgit eased modestly on the move. 

 The currency already had taken an early hit with the market still worried about the state of the country's banking and corporate sectors. 

 Malaysia on Friday announced the creation of a new committee to help companies restructure debt without seeking customary court protection. 

 The ringgit also was hurt by the Kuala Lumpur stock index, which opened 2.5 percent lower on Monday and later hit a new nine-year low. By 0833 GMT, the KLSE index was down 3.13 percent to 352.66, off a low of 351.47. 

 OTHERS ASIANS MIXED 

 The Singapore dollar took a big hit, falling by nearly two percent on the back of a weaker yen. Trade was quiet, however, with Singapore markets closed for a holiday. 

 The rupiah was relatively unscathed and down only slightly, with traders looking for it to firm because of the large amount of U.S. dollars which are due to flow into the country. 

 The baht bucked the region's weakening trend, gaining a bit on local demand. But traders said they were awaiting the announcement of a package to help the country's ailing banking sector. 

 In North Asia, the Korean won and the Taiwan dollar were down amid worries over the yen as well as the Hong Kong and Chinese currencies. 

 With the exception of Hong Kong's market, most regional stock markets were weaker on Monday, weighed down by softer currencies. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Malaysia seen cutting rates further to spur growth.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Malaysia is likely to cut interest rates further this year in a bid to keep the economy from sliding deeper into recession, analysts said on Tuesday. 

 Some analysts expect the key three-month interbank rate to fall by another 100 to 200 basis points by the end of the year, from around 10.5 percent now. 

 "Overall, the environment is relatively conducive for rate cuts," said Simon Flint, regional economist at Singapore-based financial consultancy I.D.E.A. 

 "However, given Malaysia's record on structural reform and the risks of further regional ructions, the central bank will have to proceed cautiously. It seems likely that Bank Negara will cut gradually, observing the reaction of the market at each juncture," he said. 

 He expects the three-month interbank rate to fall to 9.0 percent by year-end. 

 In a major policy shift, Bank Negara Malaysia, the central bank, on Friday cut the three-month intervention rate to 10.5 percent from 11 percent. 

 With inflation contained and the current account swinging into surplus, the "fundamental trends provide Malaysia with the room for a cautious easing of monetary policy to minimise the severity of the downturn in (the) domestic economy", it said. 

 The move marked a policy shift for the central bank, which for months had stood by tight money as the best way to defend the ringgit currency and pave the way for economic recovery. 

 Malaysia's gross domestic product shrank by 1.8 percent in the first quarter this year compared with the same period in 1997, its first contraction in 13 years. 

 The once-vibrant economy is officially forecast to contract by one to two percent in 1998, but analysts reckon that it could shrink by as much as four percent. 

 "Another (rate) cut before the end of the year is necessary to revive the economy. But I don't expect it to be so soon after the recent cut," said Chia Woon Khien, head of Asian research at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken. 

 Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and Special Functions Minister Daim Zainuddin have campaigned for lower rates to help businesses survive the recession. 

 Bank Negara also cited slowing money supply and credit growth as one of the reasons for the monetary easing. 

 Broad money, M3, expanded by 7.1 percent year-on-year in June against 9.6 percent in May, while annual lending growth slowed to 10.3 percent at the end of June from a year earlier, compared with 12 percent at the end of May. 

 On Monday and Tuesday, five banks cut their base lending rates to 12 percent from 12.1 percent. 

 Analysts said currency stability was also prompting the authorities to cut rates. 

 The ringgit, which has lost nearly 40 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since July last year, has kept to the 4.10-4.20 a dollar range in the past two weeks. 

 "Cautious easing of monetary stance is seen as a positive move but only as long as inflation and the ringgit remain under control," Standard & Poor's MMS International said in a commentary. 

 "The next move hinges on forthcoming macro economic figures with another 100 basis points off the three-month rate by end-1998 likely," it said. ((Kuala Lumpur newsroom, +60 3 201-4813 fax +60 3 232-6752, kuala.lumpur.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Policy makers change course as deflation hits Asia.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Government policy makers across Asia are steadily changing direction as a new threat emerges to their already embattled economies - the prospect of serious deflation. 

 Since mid-year the authorities have been loosening the tight monetary policy screws in place since the peak of the Asian crisis, and making plans to boost government spending to try to head it off. 

 In taking this new direction, analysts say, governments have been given a green light by the International Monetary Fund. 

 "Deflation is the watchword in Asia at this point," said Tim Condon, regional economist at Morgan Stanley in Hong Kong. 

 No less a figure than Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji openly admitted the existence of deflation in China's economy just this week. 

 "In view of the current situation in which there is deflation, the central government has decided to take more active fiscal policies to raise more capital and strengthen infrastructure investment," Zhu told a local newspaper on Monday. 

 Economists define deflation as a sustained reduction in the general level of prices. It is often, though not always, accompanied by declines in output and employment. 

 This is certainly happening across Asia now and governments appear to have decided that, since exports are not going to provide the needed stimulus to avoid deflation, they have to step in. 

 "It's a question of economic survival," said Chia Woon Khien, head of Asian research at SE Banken in Singapore. 

 Over the past few weeks finance ministers and central bank governors regionwide have been announcing broadly similar measures. 

 Taiwan cut commercial banks' reserve requirements, resulting in a drop in passbook deposit rates by half a percentage point. The move was designed to spur the economy and bolster money market liquidity. 

Malaysia cut its central bank intervention rate by 50 basis points to 10.5 percent, effective on Monday, leading at least one bank to cut its base lending rate. It had already announced a major fiscal stimulus package amounting to around three percent of GDP. 

 South Korea's Finance Minister Lee Kyu-sung said he planned to lower interest rates steadily and said the country plans to expand fiscal spending to create jobs. 

 Thailand's central bank governor, Chatu Mongkol, said this week there was room to stimulate the economy via monetary expansion and lower interest rates. 

 The Thai government is also in meetings with the IMF this week at which it has said it plans to seek permission for a much larger budget deficit. The government wants to double the fiscal deficit to two percent of GDP from a planned one percent target. It's likely the IMF will agree. 

 Even in Singapore's secretive money markets, some dealers say the authorities have been adding liquidity at the short end over the past couple of weeks by selling the Singapore dollar in a bid to get domestic interest rates down. The government announced a $1.2 billion economic stimulus package at the end of June. 

 The only major country not being threatened by deflation at the present time is Indonesia. This week it posted an inflation rate for the year to July of nearly 70 percent, although output and employment are certainly declining. 

 Analysts say the switch to expansionary economic policies is inevitable but worry that it may not be enough. 

 "We're seeing countries go from extremely tight economic policies to moderately tight ones. But it still may not be sufficient to boost domestic demand," said Morgan Stanley's Condon. 

 Condon also warns that the price for such policies would normally be a further weakening in currency rates leading to a worsening of the situation for countries with large amounts of foreign debt. 

 But SE Banken's Chia said many of the economic problems that led to the original currency crisis, such as inflexible exchange rate systems and high current account deficits, have now largely disappeared and there is now much less reason for speculators to sell down Asian currencies.

title: Malaysia  cuts  intervention  rate to 10.5 pct.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, July 31 (Reuters) - Malaysia's central bank said on Friday that it will cut the three-month intervention rate to 10.5 percent from 11 percent effective August 3. 

 Bank Negara Malaysia said in a statement that there was "room for a cautious easing of monetary policy to minimise the severity of the downturn in (the) domestic economy". 

 "The judgement is made that this monetary easing can be made without the risk of breaching the inflation objective," Bank Negara said. 

 The central bank said there was an absence of inflationary pressures and the current account deficit was expected to turn around to a surplus position. 

 It said leading and lagging indicators such as sales and service tax collections, car sales, credit card spending and import demand were sharply down, and there was an absence of wage pressures. 

 "Similarly, the sharp downturn in equity prices and the softening of the property market have eliminated the inflationary potential of the asset markets," it said. 

 The growth of money supply and credit has slowed sharply to levels that are below the ceilings projected under the credit plan. 

 Inflation in developing countries was expected to remain subdued, with the moderation in petroleum prices supporting this trend, it said. 

 The central bank said that increases in the consumer and producer price indices essentially reflected the pass-through effects of the depreciation of the ringgit or were for certain specific items such as food due to supply factors. 

 "The adjustments resulting from the depreciation have, however, for the most part already been priced into current prices," it said. 

 "The price increases due to the currency depreciation have in effect been partially offset by dampening demand," it said, noting that Malaysia had one of the lowest rates of inflation in the region. 

 Bank Negara said the improved current balance and long-term commitments in the form of foreign direct investment have supported the currency. International reserves have hovered at about $20 billion, enough to cover 3.5 months of imports. 

 "These fundamental trends provide Malaysia with the room for a cautious easing of monetary policy to minimise the severity of the downturn in domestic policy," it said. 

 The central bank last adjusted the intervention rate in February when it raised it to 11 percent from 10 percent. 

 It also cut banks' statutory reserve requirement (SRR), or funds required to be kept interest-free with the central bank, to 10 percent from 13.5 percent. 

 Earlier this month, it cut the SRR again, to eight percent from 10. ((Kuala Lumpur newsroom, +60 3 201-4813 fax +60 3 232-6752, kuala.lumpur.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: ASIA FOCUS - Chronology of Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 2 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of Asia's financial crisis. 

 1997 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". 

 The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bail-out package, bringing it to $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 20 - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad tells delegates of IMF/World Bank conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Around this time the South Korean won also begins to slump in value. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over on to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest single-day point loss ever. 

 Oct 31 - Indonesia's IMF package is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - Indonesia shuts down 16 troubled banks. 

 Nov 5 - IMF approves a $10 billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won, which rapidly falls to 1,000 to the dollar. 

 Dec 4 - IMF approves a $21 billion loan for South Korea, part of a bail-out package that will total nearly $60 billion. 

 Dec 8 - Thailand closes 56 of 58 previously suspended finance companies. 

 1998 

 Jan 8 - Representatives of the IMF and South Korea agree to a 90-day rollover of short-term debt. 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. Shares fall sharply in Hong Kong, China and Singapore. 

 Jan 15 - IMF managing director Michel Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 Jan 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing. 

 Jan 28 - International creditor banks and the South Korean government say they have agreed on a plan to exchange $24 billion of short-term debt for new loans maturing in one, two and three years. 

 Jan 30 - U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warns Asia's financial crisis could spread. 

 Feb 14 - The IMF threatens to cut off the bail-out fund for Indonesia over its plans to introduce a currency board. 

 Feb 26 - Indonesia's borrowers and lenders begin negotiations on rescheduling at least $70 billion in private off-shore debt. 

 March 1 - Suharto says reforms prescribed by the IMF have not worked. 

 March 4 - The IMF approves release of the third tranche payment from Thailand's package and commends the Thai government for its economic reforms. 

 March 6 - IMF says its board will not discuss Indonesia's economic reform programme before April, effectively delaying a $3 billion payment initially expected by March 15. 

 March 23 - Indonesia nearly doubles interest rates to boost the rupiah and control inflation. 

 April 1 - Japan begins steps aimed at liberalising its financial markets to make them "free, fair and global" by 2001. Tokyo share prices fall, the yen dips and Japan's central bank governor pronounces every economic indicator bad. 

 April 2 - The chairman of electronics giant Sony, Norio Ohga, says the Japanese economy is on the verge of collapse. 

 April 3 - U.S. ratings agency Moody's lowers its outlook on Japan's sovereign debt to negative from stable. Asian currencies fall sharply on the news. 

 May 7 - Fears that riots in the Indonesian city of Medan will spill over into a wider social crisis send regional stocks into retreat. 

 May 11 - India stuns the world with announcement of three underground nuclear tests. Pakistan stocks tumble 3.52 percent while India's National Stock Exchange index slides 2.55 percent. 

 May 13 - The United States imposes economic sanctions on India and Japan suspends some loans. 

 May 14 - Mobs rampage through Jakarta and students demand Suharto's resignation. Indonesia's worsening crisis takes centre-stage for Asian markets, several of which suffer sharp losses. 

 May 15 - Suharto returns home from Egypt amid signs he is losing his 32-year grip on power. 

 May 21 - Suharto steps down and is succeeded by former deputy president B.J. Habibie. Markets enjoy a limited rally. Jakarta stocks surge more than three percent. 

 May 25 - South Korean shares plummet 6.78 percent despite a lifting of foreign ownership limits on stocks. Most other Asian markets shrug off Seoul's fall. 

 May 26 - Seoul's KOSPI share index continues to dive, losing a further six percent, hurt by a looming recession and labour unrest. 

 May 27 - Asian markets are hammered as the yen falls against the dollar and amid mounting fears of economic recession. Hong Kong stocks plunge more than five percent after Chief Executive Tung Chee Hwa warns of possible recession. 

 May 28 - Pakistan conducts nuclear tests. 

 May 29 - The dollar rockets to a seven-year high of 139 yen on fears of a possible nuclear arms race in Asia and after news that Japan's unemployment rate hit 4.1 percent in April, its highest level since the end of World War Two. 

 Recession looms in much of Asia. Hong Kong reports that its gross domestic product contracted two percent in first quarter of 1998. About the same time Indonesia and Malaysia also report their economies contracted in the first quarter. 

 June 1 - Pakistani stocks plunge 12.38 percent as traders get their first chance to react to sanctions imposed after the country's nuclear tests. Asian markets are hit as nuclear tension adds to a cocktail of domestic problems. 

 June 5 - International lenders and Indonesian companies reach a deal to reschedule the country's massive corporate debt. 

 June 8 - The yen falls past 140 to the dollar, sending a shudder through Asian markets. Signs that Japan and other leading economies are unlikely to intervene to support the unit sap confidence further. 

 June 10 - China's central bank governor warns that the weak yen is having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade, raising fears that China may devalue its yuan currency. Markets across Asia tumble, led by a near five percent fall on Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index. 

 In Taiwan, the local dollar hits new 11-year lows and the Australian dollar plummets past 59 U.S. cents. 

 June 11 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin all but rules out the possibility of joint intervention by major industrial powers to bolster the yen. He says the weak yen reflects the state of the Japanese economy. 

 June 12 - Economic Planning Agency says Japan's gross domestic product fell by an annualised rate of 5.3 percent in the first quarter, signalling recession. The yen dives towards 145 to the dollar as hopes fade of official intervention. 

 June 17 - The U.S. joins Japan in selling the dollar in favour of the yen. 

 The action takes markets by surprise and the yen rises to a high of around 134 at one stage from a level of some 142.50 prior to the intervention. 

 June 19 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin tells Reuters he is not expecting high level meetings in Tokyo to produce specific new action plans on the economy. His statements puts further pressure on the yen. 

 June 20 - Top finance officials from the Group of Seven meet in Tokyo and vow to cooperate as appropriate in the currency markets. 

 June 23 - Michel Camdessus calls the yen fall a "crisis within the crisis". 

 June 25 - Indonesia and the IMF sign another letter of intent - the fourth. The letter says that Indonesian GDP is expected to contract by at least 10 percent in 1998 and says the rupiah will stabilise at around 10,000 by the last quarter of 1998. 

 June 26 - Malaysia cuts bank statutory reserve requirements to eight percent from 10 percent. 

 June 29 - For the first time, South Korea closes banks, shutting five ailing operations in a major step towards meeting the mandate of the massive IMF rescue package.

title: FOCUS-Bank Negara cuts statutory reserves further.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, June 26 (Reuters) - Malaysia's central bank on Friday announced a further cut in the statutory reserve requirement for banks that would release 8.0 billion ringgit ($2 billion) into the liquidity-strapped banking system. 

 Bank Negara said it was cutting the requirement, or funds required to be kept interest-free with the central bank, to 8.0 percent of total deposits and other liabilities from 10 percent, from July 1. 

 It will be the second such cut this year. On February 16, Bank Negara lowered the requirement to 10 percent from 13.5 percent. 

 The central bank said a sharp deceleration in monetary and credit growth and a slowdown in economic activity in the first half of the year prompted the latest move. 

 It earlier announced that broad M3 money growth had fallen to 9.6 percent year-on-year in May compared with 12.2 percent in April and 20.1 percent in the same month a year ago. 

 "Over the same (one-year) period, credit growth of the banking system slowed down from 30.4 percent at end-June 1997 to 12 percent at the end of May 1998," it said. 

 It said the reserve requirement cut was part of a series of measures that will be taken to ensure the "Malaysian economy does not spiral into a major economic slowdown". 

 Malaysia's gross domestic demand (GDP) sank 1.8 percent in the first quarter of this year, its first contraction since the 1985 recession. 

 Some analysts questioned whether the 8.0 billion ringgit would be enough to bring down rates, now hovering around 11 percent. 

 "The shortage itself is suspected to be much larger," said Sani Hamid, markets analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS. 

 Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim said recently that 32 billion ringgit had flowed out of the banking system between January and May this year. 

 "The intention is of course to help provide funds for the system, thereby lower BLR, and help ailing corporates stay afloat," market consultancy firm I.D.E.A. said in a commentary. 

 "No doubt this will help provide support for the ailing corporate/banks, thereby the entire economy, but the cost of bailing out the banking sector is really exorbitant," it said. 

 The Bank Negara announcement came on the day Daim Zainuddin was sworn in as minister with special functions in charge of economic development. 

 Daim, a former finance minister, has spearheaded a drive to force banks to bring down lending rates. 

 His campaign, backed by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, has stoked tensions with the central bank, which has cautioned that funds would flow out of the country, undercutting the already weak ringgit, if rates are pushed too low. 

 Bank Negara said a two percentage point reduction in the reserve requirement would reduce the base lending rate of commercial banks by 0.21 percent and that of finance companies by 0.27 percent. 

 It said "the liquidity in the interbank market will be closely monitored and the three-month Bank Negara Malaysia intervention rate will continue to remain unchanged". 

 Bank Negara's three-month intervention rate is 11 percent. 

 Sani of MMS said he expected the SRR cut to have little near-term impact on the ringgit "as market accesses Daim and eyes possible fallout with Bank Negara over monetary policy". 

 The Malaysian unit fell below 4.00 per dollar on Friday, losing about 38 percent of its value against the U.S. currency since a regional financial crisis erupted last July. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: KL interbank rates largely steady in quiet trading.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, May 14 (Reuters) - Malaysian interbank rates were largely steady in quiet trading on Thursday with interest stirred only by the central bank's morning tender to inject funds, dealers said. 

 Activity was thin as Bank Negara Malaysia had indicated by recent interventions that it wanted the one-month rate at around 10.80 percent to 11.0 percent, and three-month at around 11.00 percent, they said. 

 "Negara gave the signal that they will give funds to anybody offering 10.80 and below for the one-month. They also got their objective to control 11 percent for the three-month," said a dealer at a Malaysian commercial bank. 

 The central bank earlier accepted bids at a weighted average rate of 10.89 percent for its one-month offer of 500 million ringgit. 

 The bids accepted were in the high/low range of 10.90 percent and 10.85 percent, respectively. 

 It said bids for 400 million ringgit of three-month money were accepted at an average 11.01 percent. Bids accepted were in the high/low range of 11.01 percent and 11.00 percent. 

 Dealers said there was little activity to talk about other than the fund injections by the central bank. 

 There was a one-month lender at 10.80 percent and three-month was traded at 11.0 percent, they said. 

 Banks now tailor their daily activities around the injections as they set the tone and direction for the markets, they said. 

 "It doesn't take much brains to do our job now," said a senior dealer at a local bank. 

 Players were also reluctant to take long-term positions due to uncertainties on the direction of interest rates. 

 Some dealers said the volatile Indonesian situation could increase pressure on the ringgit and other regional currencies, thus forcing the central bank to keep local rates high. ((Reme Ahmad, +60 3 201-4813 fax +60 3 232-6752, kuala.lumpur.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Malaysia Ringgit/Risks Rise -2: Political Differences
text:
'Going forward, we expect the ringgit to strengthen as a result of better regional sentiment,' Goldman Sachs said in its quarterly economic report released earlier this month. But the U.S. investment bank does share some of Supple's concerns about the banking sector. 

 'The crucial local issue is the financial-sector restructuring. Both Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim are dedicated to protecting depositors. This focus will limit the scope for capital flight,' the report says. But Malaysia's two top officials don't gel so well on the question of protecting Bumiputra, mostly ethnic Malay, shareholders. 

 'The two differ on the treatment of bank shareholders, with the prime minister more willing to bail out prominent Bumiputra businessmen. A continuation of this policy... will likely depress capital inflows and delay our expected appreciation in the ringgit,' Goldman Sachs says. 

 In the past few weeks, that seems to be the case. The ringgit has been firmly tethered to a MYR3.60 to MYR3.80 range, despite some signs that the economy and banking system are in danger. That's largely because of short-term anxiety that the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, is ready to intervene to protect the currency. 

 But with foreign reserves at $20.59 billion (equivalent to around three-and-a-half months of imports), analysts say the central bank won't be aggressively selling down their supply of dollars. 

 Moreover, foreign currency dealers say they'd be fighting a losing battle as sentiment in the market turns more bearish. In February, the Industrial Production Index fell 2.2% year-on-year, forcing a number of economists to seriously consider the possibility of a full recession in 1998. 

 SocGen-Crosby Securities is looking at a possible 1% contraction this year, and Paribas Asia Equity has put out a 2.6% shrinkage estimate. The government, however, is targeting 2%-3% economic growth this year.

title: Malaysia Ringgit Stablizes At MYR3.79 After Central Bk Move
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--The Malaysian ringgit is stabilizing midday in Asian trading thanks to dollar-selling from the central bank to stop the U.S. currency rising above MYR3.80. 

 Dealers said there was modest intervention from Bank Negara Malaysia selling through agent banks in the morning session after the currency fell to MYR3.82 against the dollar. The fall was triggered by Standard & Poor's move Friday to downgrade Malaysia's long-term foreign currency rating to single-A-minus from single-A. 

 S&P based the downgrade on the first stagnation in the Malaysian economy for a decade. This has deepened asset quality problems, and the rating agency expects non-performing loans to result. 

 However, after this downgrade, S&P said the ratings outlook for Malaysia is stable. 

 At 0414 GMT (12:14 a.m. EDT), the dollar is at MYR3.7900, still higher than MYR3.7675 late Friday, but off its intraday peaks. The U.S. currency reached a high of MYR3.8200 earlier in the day. 

 However, concerns about the Malaysian government's apparent willingness to provide funds for troubled companies continues to unsettle the market. Analysts have said recent comments to this effect from Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad given the impression that the government believes that it can ride out the continuing turmoil without restructuring the way the economy is run.

title: Malaysia shares, ringgit down at midday, off lows.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, April 17 (Reuters) - Malaysian stocks and the currency were battered early on Friday on growing concerns over the economy, but staged a partial recovery later in the day. 

 The Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's benchmark Composite Index ended the morning session 5.24 points, or 0.83 percent lower at 624.10, after falling over two percent earlier. 

 By 0453 GMT the ringgit stood at 3.7800/3.8000 per U.S. dollar, lower than the late Thursday level of 3.7300. It touched 3.8000 in morning trade. 

 "It's mostly been due to short covering action by some of the foreign houses, plus the fact that it's Friday so some of the local funds are propping up the market a bit," said a dealer at a local brokerage. 

 Malaysia has been hit by a slew of confidence-damaging factors this week. 

 On Thursday the Malaysian Institute for Economic Research said the country's business confidence index for the first quarter of 1998 fell by 8.6 points to 41.0, the lowest level in the index's 10-year history, from the previous quarter's 49.6 points. 

 The government reported a 2.2 percent decline in industrial production for February and an increase in inflation of 5.1 percent for March. 

 Investors also avoided Malaysian shares on fears that several more companies could be in trouble. Two listed companies have already been placed in receivership, with another facing a winding-up petition from one of its bankers. 

 Troubled construction group Ekran Bhd  was requoted on Friday morning, and immediately slumped 30 percent to its limit-down trading floor for the morning session. 

 On Thursday the group confirmed that it was pursuing a restructuring that would create a new majority owner at the firm. 

 Malaysia Airlines System Bhd  lost 13 cents to 2.85 ringgit, after losing 20 cents on Thursday. 

 A newspaper report on Thursday said the group was planning a restructuring exercise which would allow its chairman to borrow funds against the company's aircraft and ultimately settle his personal debts. 

 "I don't think anyone with a brain would look at this stock at the moment. Why subject yourself to more pain," said the dealer. 

 "People are saying the index will go further down. One local fund is saying it may even go as low as 500," said another local share dealer. 

 Bank Negara Malaysia intervened in the foreign exchange market on Friday to support the ringgit, currency dealers said. 

 They said the central bank sold dollars at 3.80 ringgit through an agent bank. 

 "The agent is still offering dollars at 3.80 and this is capping the dollar's rise," a dealer with a European bank said. 

 No confirmation was available as Bank Negara does not normally comment on its open market operations. 

 "Ringgit is at risk for a pullback to the 4.00 (a dollar) level if 3.80 is broken," the European bank dealer said. 

 The Malaysian palm oil market rallied in early trading, extending its overnight bullish trend on the back of the weaker ringgit against the U.S. dollar.

title: Malaysia monetary policy to be kept tight - Negara.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, March 25 (Reuters) - Bank Negara said on Wednesday that the risks of inflation remain high following the depreciation of the ringgit, and monetary policy will be kept tight this year to check rising prices. 

 The central bank reiterated in its 1997 annual report that authorities considered the ringgit to be "grossly undervalued" against the U.S. dollar, and that it retains the option of intervening in the foreign exchange market. 

 It said the bank's policy is to intervene to maintain a degree of stability, not to support any specific level of the ringgit. 

 "Although the growth of the Malaysian economy is expected to moderate in 1998, the risks of inflation remain high following the significant depreciation of the ringgit since mid-1997," the report said. 

 "In this environment, monetary policy will remain tight." 

 The central bank said a tight monetary policy was essential to restore macroeconomic stability and promote stability in the domestic financial markets. 

 "The primary focus of monetary poicy in 1998 will, therefore, continue to be directed at containing any rise in inflation, in particular, inflationary expectations that may be generated by the increase in import prices following the ringgit depreciation," it said. 

 Bank Negara said, however, that monetary policy would have to be flexible given uncertainties in the external environment, including the magnitude and duration of the regional financial crisis, the course of U.S. monetary policy and developments in Japan. 

 "It will not be the intention of policy to create an over-adjustment or correction of the economy," it said. 

 The central bank said the slowdown in credit growth will allow for an expansion of monetary aggregates that is more consistent with output growth. 

 But credit growth has "moderated at a much faster pace than expected as a result of an uneven expansion in credit growth among the banking institutions", it said. 

 "These developments, if allowed to persist, can precipitate a credit crunch," it said, adding that tight monetary policy needs to be reinforced with policy adjustments to ensure an efficient functioning of the intermediation process. 

 Bank Negara said the sharper increases in prices emerging in 1998 "are caused entirely by the depreciation in the ringgit exchange rate" as domestic demand has slowed and is expected to remain subdued. 

 The central bank said its exchange rate policy had remained unchanged during the recent turbulence. 

 "No targets are set for the ringgit exchange rate level and market forces will continue to determine the value of the ringgit," it said. 

 "Currently, the ringgit is assessed as being grossly undervalued," it said, adding that the rate has been driven more by changes in market sentiment than economic fundamentals. 

 The ringgit has depreciated about 30 percent against the U.S. dollar since a regional financial crisis erupted last July. On Wedneday afternoon it was quoted around 3.63/3.64 to the dollar. 

 As Malaysia's adjustment measures take effect, "it is envisaged that the exchange rate will adjust to reflect the economic fundamentals of the country". 

 "As in recent years, the option for Bank Negara Malaysia to intervene in the foreign exchange market will continue to remain." ((Kuala Lumpur newsroom, +60 3 201-4813 fax +60 3 232-6752, kuala.lumpur.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Emerging market  forex  - zloty falls as NBP sells.
text:
LONDON, March 24 (Reuters) - The recent rally in emerging market currencies was interrupted on Tuesday by National Bank of Poland (NBP) intervention to cap the zloty and some disappointment at Malaysia's latest economic package. 

 While sentiment toward high-yield local currency markets in general remained robust, the NBP action and the temptation to take profits from recent sharp gains in emerging Asian units may mark a period of consolidation around the globe, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso outperformed on the day in Asia, meantime, while the rouble continued to hold firm in the wake of Monday's dismissal of the Russian cabinet. 

 The zloty's retreat was the focus in European hours after the NBP sold zlotys for dollars on several occasions. 

 The currency retreated to 6.24 percent above its parity against a basket of officially-targeted currencies versus 6.78/54 percent above at the opening on Tuesday. 

 Tuesday's intervention followed the central bank's surprise decision on Monday to fix the currency at 6.51 percent above parity, well below prevailing market levels about 6.70 percent. 

 "There's been confusion over the zloty's direction over the past week, but the lower fixing on Monday and the intervention today means the central bank is saying enough is enough," said Miranda Xafa, currency strategist at Salomon Smith Barney. 

 "Fighting inflation in Poland is clearly an important policy objective but opposition to excessive currency strength shows there is also some worries about the external accounts." 

 The past week has been a roller-coaster for the zloty. 

 The volatility started with a sudden bout of profit taking last Wednesday after investment firm Goldman Sachs recommended it was time to cut long positions. 

 The zloty recovered its losses by Friday, however, and then soared to as high as 7.50 percent after reported comments, later denied, that the central bank was happy with recent strength. 

 "The sheer volatility of the zloty over the past week will probably be enough to take the pure currency speculation out of the market, but the yield story is still attractive unless you think there is going to be a complete collapse," said a trader at a U.S. investment firm. 

 The Russian rouble held firm following President Boris Yeltsin's decision to dismiss Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and his cabinet on Monday. 

 Analysts said the underlying uncertainty of Russian politics had been highlighted again, but it looked as if a reconstituted cabinet would lean toward reformers rather than signal any great change in economic policy. 

 Elsewhere in Europe, the Czech crown was steady about 18.61 per mark, with chart analysts saying there was strong trendline resistance on any uptick above 18.64. 

 In more exotic European markets, the collapse of the Belarussian rouble stole the show. 

 Local dealers said the Belarussian unit plummeted on the interbank market to as low as 64,000-69,000 per dollar against 52,000-54,000 per dollar late last week. 

 In Moscow, the Russian central bank recommended that Russian citizens refrain from trading the Belarussian unit and said it ceased quoting an official rate against the Russian rouble. 

 This was in response to the Belarussian central bank's decision on Monday to stop foreigners trading its currency. 

 The Belarussian rouble was at 45,000-47,000 to the dollar at the beginning of this year. 

 In Asia, the Malaysian ringgit erased much of Monday's gains amid profit-taking and some disappointment that a package of new economic measures announced by Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim fell short of easing restrictions on foreign investment.

title: FOCUS-Bank Negara keeps interest rates steady.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, March 23 (Reuters) - Malaysia's central bank intervened on Monday to borrow funds in the money market for the first time in months to check falling interbank rates, suggesting monetary policy will be kept tight. 

 Money market dealers said Bank Negara Malaysia borrowed overnight, one-month and three-month money at 10.0 percent through an agent bank. 

 The central bank has been a lender since July to help ease market tightness, after its massive intervention in the foreign exchange market to defend the ringgit caused a liquidity squeeze. 

 Bank Negara at the same time was lending at 11.0 percent on Monday, dealers said. 

 No confirmation was available as the central bank does not normally comment on its open market operations. 

 "I think Negara is trying to keep rates steady. They are borrowing quite a bit of money but lending out a small amount," a dealer with a Malaysian bank said. 

 Dealers said the market had turned long, and even some finance companies, which were extremely short earlier, were seen lending last week. 

 "There are now more lenders in the market and Bank Negara will have to borrow to prevent rates from coming off," another dealer with a local bank said. 

 The one-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Rate (KLIBOR) fell to 10.91 percent on Monday from 11.04 percent at the end of February. The benchmark three-month KLIBOR was at 11.0 percent, also from 11.04 percent. 

 Dealers said persistent market talk of a cut in the liquid assets ratio of banks was also keeping pressure on rates. 

 "Rumours are still circulating in the market that the liquid assets ratio will be cut to 15 percent from 17 percent," said a dealer with a merchant bank. 

 But most dealers and analysts said such a move was unlikely, given the improving liquidity in the market and so soon after a cut in banks' statutory reserve requirement (SRR). 

 Bank Negara in February cut the SRR - or funds required to be kept interest-free with the central bank - to 10 percent of total deposits and other liabilities from 13.5 percent, releasing an additional 14 billion ringgit to the banking sector. 

 "I don't think they will cut it. There's no need for such a move," said Sani Hamid, an analyst at Standard & Poor's MMS International. 

 "The problem is not that the market is short but that funds are not being channelled properly across the market," he said. 

 He said foreign banks were basically lenders as recent ringgit buying had saddled them with excess funds. 

 Analysts said monetary policy would be kept tight to contain inflationary pressures and support a recovery in the ringgit. 

 Malaysia's annual inflation rate was 4.4 percent in February, its highest level in five years. 

 Analysts have forecast a consumer price index rise of between five and six percent for Malaysia this year, compared with 2.7 percent in 1997, following the sharp drop in currency values. 

 The ringgit has depreciated by about 30 percent against the U.S. dollar since a regional financial crisis erupted last July. But it has rebounded sharply from a historical low of 4.88 to the dollar in early January, and on Monday was around 3.56. 

 Bank Negara's move on Monday came a day before Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim was scheduled to announce fiscal policy measures and discuss inflation. 

 The finance minister was quoted by Taiwan's Economic Daily News on Monday as saying Malaysia planned measures to boost the ringgit to three to the dollar. ((Kuala Lumpur newsroom, +60 3 201-4813 fax +60 3 232-6752, kuala.lumpur.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS-Asia markets still jittery over Indonesia.
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 23 (Reuters) - Indonesia's revised budget did little to stabilise Asian markets on Friday, and some traded weaker on continued worries about the country's debt crisis. 

 Indonesian Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad raised revenue projections and expenditures in a new budget that appeared to closely track last week's deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 But traders said that in the absence of any big budget surprises, markets remained focused on the sliding rupiah and the nation's inability to pay its corporate debt. 

 "So what?" one Hong Kong trader said of the latest budget announcement. "There isn't a single solvent company in Indonesia with the rupiah so weak." 

 The central bank, Bank Indonesia, stepped in to support the rupiah on Friday morning. Dollar sales at the 14,000 level restored some short-term strength, but traders said the outlook was poor. 

 "This is not intervention designed to more permanently prop up the value of the rupiah...It is entirely centred on the spot, providing dollars to enable onshore Indonesian banks to repay their liabilities," Daniel Lian, head of markets research at ANZ in Singapore told Reuters Financial Television. 

 The rupiah interest rate is not high enough to compensate for uncertainty about the country's banking sector, private debt burden and political unease, he said. 

 "The rupiah rate doesn't offer compensation for investors for the risk premium, so there will not be support for the rupiah," Lian said, adding that he felt capital controls were inevitable. 

 The strongest stock market on Friday was Tokyo, which resumed its recent rally after Thursday's dip and closed up 2.34 percent at 16,789.11. 

 But the rupiah's freefall hurt parts of the region, even though many stock and currency markets managed to claw back some lost ground in late trading. 

 Hong Kong's Hang Seng index closed slightly stronger on Friday, reversing course in mid-afternoon as bargain-hunting surfaced. The index ended 36.47 points higher at 8,920.20 after a week-long battering triggered by the liquidation of brokerages Peregrine and C.A. Pacific Securities. 

 Dealers said the mood in Hong Kong remained grim, with the territory's confidence under siege just a few months after its July 1 return to Chinese sovereignty. 

 The overall tone in Asia was weak, with thin trading ahead of next week's Chinese New Year holiday exaggerating market movements. The rupiah's woes kept currencies soft while stock markets were mixed with sporadic signs of foreign interest. 

 Singapore's dollar was weaker at 1.7610 against 1.7565 on Thursday while its stock market dipped 0.76 percent to end at 1,259.83. 

 The Malaysian ringgit recovered from its low in the morning of 4.61 against the dollar, rising to 4.5280 in late trading. Dealers said ringgit investors took heart in the Indonesian central bank's rupiah intervention. 

 But longer-term concerns over Indonesia's currency pushed Malaysia's Composite Index of stocks down 2.89 percent to close at 558.57. 

 The Thai baht was virtually unchanged at 54.75 but stocks closed marginally higher, up 2.07 points, or 0.49 percent, at 422.87. 

 The Philippine peso recovered some ground to 43.80 after crashing through its third volatility band in early trade. But the unit's weakness in the absence of foreign buying helped to depress stocks by 0.21 percent to 1,704.07 points. 

 The Taiwan dollar quickly fell through the T$34 level, partly because of the weakness of the rupiah, but it recovered to close at T$33.925. The stock market was closed. 

 Jakarta stocks managed to gain ground throughout the day and closed 1.68 percent stronger at 450.98 on arbitrage with American Depositary Receipts, and domestic support, traders said. 

 Holiday cash demand lifted the South Korean won on Friday to 1,745.0 from 1,752.0 on Thursday while stocks made marginal gains to close at 486.86 points.

title: FOCUS-Malaysian ringgit soars, more upside seen.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Jan 14 (Reuters) - The Malaysian ringgit rallied against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday on offshore and interbank dollar selling, with dealers and analysts saying they expect more gains after the currency's recent selloff. 

 The ringgit jumped to 4.3000 to the dollar early on Wednesday against 4.6050 in Kuala Lumpur late on Tuesday. It was trading around 4.3600/4100 a dollar at 0330 GMT. 

 Dealers said U.S., European and Japanese banks were seen unwinding their long dollar positions, triggering stop-loss dollar sales. 

 "The market appears to be squaring out of long dollar positions," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore. "We may be in for a sharp retracement after recent overshooting." 

 The ringgit had fallen about 20 percent last week to a record low of 4.8800 to the dollar, dragged down by a sliding Indonesian rupiah. Intervention by central Bank Negara Malaysia prevented it from going lower. 

 "While a mad rush into Malaysian assets is not expected, a 30 to 40 percent adjustment to the overshooting seen recently is a safe bet," said Sani Hamid, emerging markets analyst at Standard and Poor's MMS International. 

 Analysts said recent visits of U.S. and International Monetary Fund (IMF) officials to Indonesia and Malaysia may have restored calm in the regional financial markets. 

 "There is the possibility that we have seen the bottom in Asian bourses and currencies," Sani said. 

 The Malaysian currency has lost over 40 percent of its value against the dollar since July last year when Bank Negara, after an initial defence, allowed the ringgit to depreciate under the pressure of selling by hedge funds and speculators. 

 The ringgit was also helped by Tuesday's remarks from U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers, analysts said. 

 Summers, who met Malaysian Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim and central bank officials during a brief stopover in Kuala Lumpur, said he was gratified by Malaysia's commitment to take new economic measures if necessary. 

 "A number of steps taken in recent months have been strong ones," he said, adding that Malaysia had "demonstrated a clear commitment to take further steps if those become necessary". 

 In response to weakened economic growth, Malaysia has cut spending, delayed a slew of infrastructure projects and reduced imports. It is also curbing bank lending. 

 Analysts said a report by U.S. investment bank Morgan Stanley Dean Witter suggesting a bottom may be near for Asian markets also discouraged holding of long dollar positions. 

 "If there is a perfect remedy for investors' confidence, it is such positive reports, as these are the people with large funds to put their money where their mouths are," Sani said. 

 With the present situation indicating that the worst may be over, the market could be looking for a consolidative range for dollar/ringgit, dealers and analyst said. 

 "The ringgit should stay above four (to the dollar) for the time being," the European bank dealer said.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Ringgit recoups against dollar.

 Dealers said the dollar's rise was capped later by selling of dollar/ringgit on intervention by Bank Negara.

title: Malaysia Bk Negara/Ringgit -3: Stayed Out Of Mkt In Jan.
text:
During early January when the ringgit strengthened strongly against the dollar, dealers note that Bank Negara was conspicuous by its absence in the market - with no reports of intervention to depress the local currency. 

 Some had expected the central bank to step in given the speed of the ringgit's advance. 

 The dollar fell as far as 2.4680 ringgit on January 13 after overseas funds piled into the Malaysian currency early this year on the back of bullish expectations for the economy. 

 Analysts note there were various statements from government officials at that time, and since, indicating they welcomed a stronger local currency against the dollar. 

 Nevertheless, many dealers and economists were surprised by the bank's apparent move to stand in the way of the ringgit's recent slide - and one said it couldn't possibly have happened. 

 Many economists took Bank Negara's recent annual report, issued March 28, as a signal that the central bank would be even less likely to intervene in the market. 

 'Malaysia does not set targets for its currency,' Bank Negara noted in its report. 

 But, given the speed of the dollar's recent ascent against the ringgit, one dealer said that may have overcome any central bank scruples about intervention. 'Would you want your ringgit to weaken so quickly - in a matter of three days?,' asked one dealer.

title: Malaysia Bk Negara Seen Signaling Support For Strong Ringgit
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (AP-Dow Jones)--Malaysia's central bank apparently intervened in the currency markets Wednesday to stem the ringgit's recent depreciation against the dollar, dealers said, signaling its preference for a strong currency. 

 While Bank Negara didn't openly intervene in the market, most ringgit dealers said they were quite certain the central bank was responsible for selling some $150 million to buy the local currency in early trading. 

 'Players smelled Bank Negara's intervention in the market,' said a senior dealer at a well-placed Malaysian bank, who declined to be identified because of the sensitivity of the subject. 

 The ringgit rose strongly as a result, with the dollar trading late Wednesday at 2.5035 ringgit, down from 2.5075 ringgit late Tuesday and well below a peak early Wednesday at 2.5111 ringgit. 

 One locally-based ringgit dealer, who also declined to be named, said Bank Negara had intervened to sell dollars around 2.5110 ringgit, pushing the dollar down from its intraday peak. 

 Dealers and analysts agreed that the central bank favors a strong ringgit, both to keep the cost of imports down and to stifle inflationary pressures in the fast-growing Malaysian economy. But it doesn't routinely intervene in the market and doesn't comment on rumors of such movements.

title: Malaysia stocks, ringgit not seen setting new trend.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, April 9 (Reuter) - Malaysian stocks are drawing value-seekers even as the ringgit faces overseas selling this week in what will likely be short-lived trends, analysts and fund managers said on Wednesday. 

 After a 6.8 percent tumble since curbs on property and stock lending were announced on March 28, the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index staged a 2.47 percent rebound on Tuesday. 

 At midday on Wednesday, the index was up 0.34 percent to 1,166.23 points. 

 "We see no reason for investors to underweight positions during this consolidation," Jupiter Securities said in its morning research note on Wednesday. "There is still gold in the market." 

 Analysts noted that Malaysian stocks were trading at a price-to-earnings multiple of between 16 to 19 times compared with historical valuations of 20 to 21 times. 

 As for the ringgit, it has been hit by sales of the Malaysian unit against the Singapore dollar. Dealers said there was also talk a U.S. hedge fund was closing its outright three-month long ringgit position this week. 

 "The concern of the market is that the U.S. fund who had been previously buying up the ringgit-Sing cross may be inclined to take profits and appear to be doing so since last week," said Andy Tan, an economist at MMS International. 

 But he said his firm was not changing its forecast for the ringgit of 2.45/dollar at year-end. At 0600 GMT on Wednesday, the ringgit was at 2.5058/68 to a dollar. 

 Dealers said Bank Negara Malaysia, the country's central bank, intervened on Wednesday to stem the currency's fall at 2.5120 a dollar. 

 Referring to the stock market's rise over the past two days, Robert Coombe, executive director of Commerce Asset Fund Managers, said: 

 "I don't think there's any need to get excited. Nothing's changed, but maybe people are starting to realise they overreacted to the Bank Negara news and (interest rate) hike in the U.S." 

 Bank Negara announced at the end of March it was imposing stricter rules for bank loans on property and stock purchase financing. 

 It required banks and finance companies to trim their exposure to the property sector to 20 percent of total outstanding loans from the present 30 percent level. 

 The central bank also imposed new curbs on using shares as collateral to buy other stocks. 

 "This rebound will be short-term," said Ang Kok Heng, general manager at TA Asset Management, referring to the stock market's performance. "I don't think the market has stabilised." 

 But Ang said he still maintained his target for the Composite Index, a blue chip barometer, at 1,300 at the end of 1997.

title: FOCUS- Malaysia intervenes  to stem ringgit's fall.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, April 9 (Reuter) - The Malaysian central bank on Wednesday intervened in the foreign exchange market after the ringgit fell to a three-month low against the U.S. dollar, dealers said. 

 "The central bank was acting through some large Malaysian banks. The intention seems to just slow the ringgit's fall, not stop it," said a dealer with a large Malaysian bank. 

 The central Bank Negara Malaysia came into the market after 0230 GMT to sell an estimated $100-200 million to stop the ringgit's fall beyond 2.5120 per dollar, they said. 

 There was no confirmation from Bank Negara, which does not usually comment on its market intervention operations. 

 Some dealers even said it may not have been central bank intervention at all. "It could have just been corporate selling," said a dealer with a foreign bank in Malaysia. 

 But, most dealers, including those from banks who act as agents for Bank Negara, said the central bank was in the market and its selling lasted until the ringgit came down to 2.5100, with the bulk of transactions done around 2.5110. 

 Bank Negara's action triggered an all-round halt to ringgit selling and helped the Malaysian unit recover to around 2.5055/65 by 0400 GMT, the dealers said. 

 Support from the central bank also brought in Malaysian exporters, who had wanted a strong U.S. unit when selling their dollars, dealers said. 

 "Speculators who had been buying dollar/ringgit this morning also started squaring up as soon as they heard selling from Kuala Lumpur side," said a dealer with another Malaysian bank. 

 "This exaggerated the volumes (after the intervention)," he said. 

 However, the strength of the dollar against the majors would not allow a major correction in dollar/ringgit, which has risen nearly 200 points in the past two days, dealers said. 

 In the morning, dollar/ringgit broke through 2.51 per dollar, triggering stop-loss selling, and the rinnggit was expected to fall further as result. 

 The Malaysian unit, which had been on the rise since early January thanks to strong economic fundamentals and high interest rates, has fallen sharply this week. 

 A U.S. hedge fund, squaring up a large three-month position in the ringgit, was said to be mainly responsible for the Malaysian currency's latest decline. The position is estimated to be in excess of two billion ringgit. 

 In addition, dealers said the strength of the U.S. dollar against the yen and other major currencies was also weakening regional currencies such as the ringgit. 

 The Malaysian unit has gained up to 2.2 percent this year before settling in a wide range of 2.4750-2.4900 per dollar. It broke out of this range on Monday on selling by the hedge fund. 

 "With the assumed presence of Bank Negara, there should be strong resistance at the 2.51 level," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore. 

 A dealer with a Malaysian bank said the ringgit's fall was not an attack on the currency, but just squaring of positions by the hedge fund and covering of long ringgit holdings against the Singapore dollar. 

 "Once the market is done with covering long positions, there should be a recovery in the ringgit. Long-term sentiment is still in favour of the ringgit," the dealer said.

title: Ringgit hits four-month high on speculative buying. [CORRECTED 7:55 GMT]
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Jan 7 (Reuter) - The Malaysian ringgit hit a four-month high against the U.S. dollar in New York overnight, powered by widespread speculative buying in the first rally of the new year, foreign exchange dealers said on Tuesday. 

 Rumours of Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara, intervening during New York trading hours halted the rise and triggered profit-taking. The ringgit touched a high of 2.4940/50 per dollar against 2.5218 at close of trading on Friday. 

 By noon on Tuesday, the Malaysian unit retreated to 2.4995/05 to the dollar on profit-taking. 

 No confirmation of intervention could be obtained from Bank Negara. 

 "Everybody seems to have jumped on to the dollar/ringgit bandwagon," said a dealer with a Singapore-based European bank. 

 He said what started as ringgit/Singapore dollar operation early on Monday had turned into a bull run for the ringgit. 

 "Singaporeans who had gone long (on the Singapore dollar) to keep the unit stable before the Singapore elections (on January 2) are returning to ringgit," a dealer with a Malaysian bank said. 

 With a renewed perception of stability in Singapore after the ruling People's Action Party was returned to power last week, normal trading activity has resumed, he said. 

 "They are going back to ringgit in particular for its high yield and strong economic fundamentals," the dealer said. 

 The benchmark three-month interbank rate in Kuala Lumpur is more than four percentage points higher than in Singapore. 

 The ringgit has gained over 250 points to around 1.7790/7810 per Singapore dollar in the last two days. 

 By Monday afternoon, many in London started buying the ringgit against the U.S. dollar, mainly for speculative play. This started a widespread move into the ringgit. 

 Dealers said while the market had expected a good year for the ringgit, the bull run had come much earlier than anticipated, which would limit further rises of the currency and induce consolidation. 

 "It is losing momentum for the time being. Not many will buy ringgit at this level," said the head of foreign exchange dealing at a Malaysian bank. 

 "The profit-taking is mainly out of Kuala Lumpur," he said. 

 "Dollar/ringgit should consolidate around the present levels unless the dollar comes off against other major currencies," another dealer said. 

 "After a massive overnight fall, U.S. dollar/ringgit seems consolidative within 2.4980 (corrects) and 2.5020 range for the short-term," research firm I.D.E.A. said in a technical report. 

 It said the rise was in line with its survey of several banks last week, which suggested that the ringgit would be the favourite currency of the region this year. 

 The two main factors that investors find attractive in the ringgit were an improvement in the country's trade balance and a cooling down of its racing economy. 

 Malaysia's 1996 gross domestic product growth is expected to fall to 8.2 percent, following 9.5 percent growth in 1995. The country has reported nine straight years of growth over eight percent, which is expected to be maintained until the year 2000. 

 Malaysia recorded a sharply lower trade deficit of 954.35 million ringgit ($378.7 million) in the first 10 months of 1996 against around 9.96 billion in the corresponding period of 1995. 

 The country's growing current account deficit and inflation had triggered worries about overheating last year and forced it to maintain a high interest rate regime and to slow growth.

title: FOCUS - Ringgit falls below 2.53/dlr on rumours, technicals.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 30 (Reuter) - U.S. funds and speculators combined rumours and technical reasons to pull down the ringgit sharply to below 2.53 per dollar, dealers said on Wednesday. 

 By 1130 GMT, the ringgit had dipped to 2.5305/15 a dollar in London after closing at 2.5250/60 in Kuala Lumpur and against 2.5135/40 at close of trading on Tuesday. 

 It has lost over 275 points from around 2.5025 on Friday. 

 The dealers said some large speculators based in Singapore and London were testing the tolerance levels of Bank Negara Malaysia, the central bank, which usually intervenes to smooth sharp fluctuations in the currency. 

 "They are testing how long Bank Negara will tolerate this sell down and they are using rumours to do that," said a dealer with a U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 "At least $300 to $400 (million) was bought today," the dealer said. 

 Dealers said it was widely rumoured that Bank Negara was comfortable with the decline of the ringgit to between 2.52 and 2.53 per dollar. 

 Bank Negara did not immediately have a comment. 

 Dealers said the market also used an overnight report from London that the U.S. was seeking sanctions against Malaysia's national oil firm Petronas for its involvement in an Iranian oil project to push the ringgit lower. 

 The report was used despite U.S. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary's comment later that the Clinton government would wait until after the November 5 presidential election to decide how it will enforce sanctions against Libya and Iran. 

 "The ringgit continues to be susceptible to rumours in the market as players search for excuses to sell the ringgit," research firm I.D.E.A. said in a comment late on Wednesday. 

 It said there was also talk about Bank Negara buying U.S. dollars at around 2.5180 per dollar level. 

 "Neither (of these reasons) look credible," I.D.E.A. said. 

 It said a firm ringgit would help keep imported inflation low as the central bank maintains a firm monetary policy and reduce value of imports, particularly against the Japanese yen, when the country is trying to cut its negative balance of payments. However, dealers predicted that the ringgit was likely to go down further unless there was profit-taking or a central bank intervention. 

 They said year-end requirement of dollars by Malaysian corporate sector, repatriation of profits by foreign investors, and government's forecast of large monthly trade deficits for the rest of the year in the Economic Report for 1996/97 were expected to pull down the ringgit. 

 "Once the 2.5180 per dollar resistance was broken, the market was more willing to hold dollars than before," said a senior dealer with a Malaysian bank in Kuala Lumpur. 

 He said beyond 2.5180, there was also a lot of unwinding of long ringgit positions against the Singapore dollar. "Even structured (portfolio) positions are being unwound," he said. 

 Another Malaysian foreign exchange dealer said it was possible that Bank Negara was having problems keeping down domestic interbank liquidity, which has several times threatened its tight monetary policy and forced it to intervene. 

 However, the interventions in the open market to mop up liquidity was becoming expensive, so Bank Negara may be allowing some of the short-term offshore funds to flow out, he said.

title: Futures indicate Malaysia interest rates to fall.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 14 (Reuter) - Malaysian interest rates, pushed up by the central bank over the past year to check inflation, are expected to start softening by mid-1997, futures dealers said on Wednesday. 

 They said a declining trend in yields on the interest rate futures market on the Malaysia Monetary Exchange (MME) was setting the direction. 

 "The perception is that interest rates are going to go lower. People have begun buying futures in anticipation of lower interest rates," said K. Sree Kumar, executive director at futures brokerage KAF-Refco Futures Sdn Bhd. 

 "Interest rate futures have begun leading the way for the cash market. And rates look easy on the long end of futures," said the head of money dealing at a local bank. 

 He said the interest rate futures market based on the benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) had aggressively picked up volumes after languishing for the first two months after its launch at the end of May. 

 Dealers said volumes had been averaging between 350 and 400 lots a day with a growing number of participants, mainly individual members and foreign banks. 

 The MME, Malaysia's second futures bourse, was launched on May 28 to trade in interest rates, bonds and currency futures. The first market, the Kuala Lumpur Options and Financial Futures Exchange (KLOFFE), trades in stock index futures. 

 A futures dealer with another bank said growing liquidity in the Malaysian money market and apparent inaction from the central bank was triggering speculation that interest rates would come down in the not so distant future. 

 "Short-term interest rates have fallen by nearly 30 basis points in the last few weeks and Bank Negara has not done anything," the dealer said. 

Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara, regularly intervenes in the local interbank money market to check liquidity or set interest rates as part of its inflation-fighting efforts. 

 Bank Negara has not been in the market the last two months despite large maturities of government paper and overseas fund inflows that have increased liquidity and pushed rates downward. 

 On the MME, the three-month KLIBOR contract for June 1997 indicated a yield of 7.19 percent at the end of Wednesday's morning session against 7.32 percent in the cash market. 

 The December 1996 contract was at a yield of 7.23 percent and March 1996 at 7.19. 

 Other futures dealers said the trend in the futures market was speculative. The rising inflation and growing current account deficit that forced Bank Negara to tighten its monetary policy earlier this year have not eased. 

 "A lot of the current push I would term as speculative because they are based on a belief that rates would come off, but that may not be the case at all," said Radhakrishnan Nair, executive director at Amanah Futures & Options Sdn Bhd. 

 "I don't think the tightening phase is over yet," he said, adding rates may have peaked but may not decline for a while. 

 Sree Kumar of KAF-Refco said that even if rates had peaked, the central bank may not allow a sharp decline. "I think many people in the futures market may be caught on the wrong side."

text:
A ringgit dealer in Singapore said that Tuesday morning, a Japanese trust company was selling dollars to buy ringgit 'very agressively,' strengthening the Malaysian currency. At that point, the dollar was at 2.4880 ringgit - its lowest point of the day. 

 Then several Malaysian banks stepped in to buy dollars at that level, keeping the ringgit from strengthening further. The move fueled unconfirmed rumors that the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, had intervened. 

 Several U.S. investment houses stepped in to sell dollars for ringgit. But a Hong Kong party came into the market and bought two lots of dollars with ringgit - each of $90 million - when the dollar was trading at 2.4900 ringgit. He says that pushed the dollar toward its highest point of the day - 2.4935 ringgit. 

 The dealer said the large-scale buying and selling 'neutralized' moves in the ringgit. 

 A ringgit dealer in Malaysia added that false rumors that the finance minister had resigned pushed the dollar briefly to 2.4940 ringgit from 2.4900 ringgit.

title: Malaysia Ringgit -2: Ringgit's Rise Tempered: Dealer
text:
A ringgit dealer in Hong Kong said that early Monday investors bought Singapore dollars for ringgit after Singapore reported first-quarter growth ahead of market expectations, at 10.7%, up from a revised figure of 8.8% growth in the fourth quarter of 1995. 

 He said that helped to weaken the Malaysian currency against the U.S. dollar. 

 At the same time, he added, the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, secretly intervened in the market late last week to signal it wanted the dollar to trade around 2.4825 ringgit. The intervention couldn't be confirmed. 

 'The speed of the Malaysian ringgit's rise will be tempered for a while,' the dealer said. 

 He expects the dollar to trade between 2.4800 ringgit and 2.5000 ringgit this week. 

 Bank Negara Malaysia borrowed 1-month funds at 6.95% Monday. Noting that the rate was the same level at which the central Bank has been borrowing for some time, dealers said it didn't signal anything but the central bank's desire to mop up some of the liquidity in the market.
