title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Ringgit retreats on profit-taking.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 18 (Reuter) - Ringgit trade again dominated exotic currency dealings on Thursday. 

 The Malaysian unit corrected against the Singapore dollar and the U.S. unit in early Asian trade, sliding back to 2.5000 per U.S. dollar on heavy profit-taking. 

 But dealers are wary of calling for further easing of the ringgit, saying sustained ringgit demand will keep it from falling too sharply. 

 "The 0.5650 is definitely a sell level for the ringgit against the Sing but I would be very wary of shorting the ringgit at these levels right now," said one regional currency dealer in Singapore. "The trend is still for the ringgit-Sing to go up," he added. 

 At about 0430 GMT, the ringgit was trading at 2.4985/95 to the dollar and 0.5628/38 to the Singapore dollar. 

Currency markets awaited clues for central bank action as Bank Negara has been notably restrained in its efforts to cap the Malaysian unit's surge over late last week and this week. 

 They said dollar-buying by agents of Bank Negara was also continuing, albeit in small quantities. 

 "But the indication is that it does not want to stop the ringgit's rise. They want this international show of confidence to continue for a while," a Singapore-based dealer said. 

 "Pressure is building up on Bank Negara Malaysia to step up its market intervention policies in the coming weeks since it faces a series of maturing bills and loans and as foreign funds continue to flood into the country from Japan and from U.S. names unwinding short ringgit positions," said a Singapore currency strategist. 

 Some dealers added, though, that apart from central bank action, ringgit direction may also be affected by the strength of the yen. 

 They said rumours circulating in Japan's money markets that Bank of Japan may tighten monetary policy may boost the yen and add further strength to the Malaysian unit. 

 In Thailand, moves by the Bank of Thailand to curb domestic money supply and the inflow of short-term funds on Wednesday left the baht little affected on Thursday. 

 "The market hasn't reacted a whole lot to the news, it doesn't seem overly concerned," said one strategist for a Singapore bank. "The baht is still trading within a band and the forwards are a bit softer," he added. 

 The baht firmed to 25.305-25.309 to the dollar in early quiet trade from 25.315-25.318 late on Wednesday. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah firmed against the dollar. 

 One Japanese bank dealer in Jakarta said sentiment on the rupiah remained upbeat, possibly on the back of moderately tight liquidity. 

 Dealers said uncertainty on the liquidity front appeared to have caused the rupiah to inch closer to the upside of the central bank's band. 

 Rupiah was at 2,326.00/7.00 at 0500 GMT against an opening at 2,326.50/27.50. 

 Overnight swap was at 0.75/0.85 and tom/next at 2.1/2.2.

title: Malaysia banking liquidity up sharply in January.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, April 17 (Reuter) - Liquidity in the Malaysian banking system expanded in January 1996 with a resource surplus of 4.5 billion ringgit against 417 million the month before, the national Bernama news agency quoted Bank Negara as saying. 

 Bank Negara, the central bank, said in its latest monthly statistical bulletin that the expansion was due to excess liquid assets held by the banking system. 

 Liquid assets rose to 2.8 billion ringgit at the end of January 1996, compared with 1.5 billion at the end of December 1995, it said. 

 Although liquidity expanded, interbank interest rates edged upwards in the second half of January after remaining generally stable in the first half of the month. 

 "Intervention operations by Bank Negara Malaysia to maintain stability in the foreign exchange market as the ringgit came under speculative pressure during the third week was contractionary on liquidity. 

 "As a consequence, interbank rates increased across the board to 7.02-7.20 percent on January 19, 1996, from 5.96-6.88 percent at the end of December 1995," it said. 

 On total loans and advances (excluding housing loans sold to national mortgage corporation, Cagamas Bhd) extended by the banking institutions, Bank Negara said they moderated to increase by 4.9 billion ringgit in January, or a two percent rise year-on-year, against an increase of 7.5 billion, or a 3.1 percent rise, in December 1995. 

 Bernama said Bank Negara attributed the moderation in loan growth mainly to slower increases in loans extended to the broad property and manufacturing sectors and for consumption purposes which rose by 1.3 billion ringgit, 600,000 ringgit and 900,000 ringgit, respectively. 

 In addition, loans extended to individuals for the purchase of stocks and shares and units of unit trust funds registered a net repayment of 500,000 ringgit, it said. 

 "These, however, were partially offset by higher loans channelled to the finance, insurance and business services sector (2.5 billion ringgit). 

 "On an annual basis, growth in total loans and advances remained relatively unchanged at 28.2 percent at the end of January for the fourth consecutive month," the central bank was quoted as saying by Bernama.

title: Malaysia Ringgit Down Vs U.S. Dlr; Thin Volume
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (AP-Dow Jones)--The Malaysian ringgit was weaker than the U.S. dollar, in thin volume trading Friday, traders said. 

 Though the trading remained subdued, traders said there were a lot of bidders for the dollar in the morning especially from Singapore. 

 Around 0830 GMT, the dollar was at 2.5490 ringgit, up from 2.5430 ringgit late Thursday, trading between 2.5430 and 2.5518 ringgit during the day. 

 A dealer with a local bank said that earlier in the trading day there was some selling pressure on the ringgit following a report in the Asian Wall Street Journal on the deepening financial crisis at state-owned steelmaker Perwaja Terengganu Sdn. Bhd. 

 The report said the company is unable to pay its 5.7 billion ringgit debt. 

 But dollar/ringgit trading quickly settled into familiar ranges, and stayed lackluster, throughout the trading day, he said. 

 Dr. Daniel Lian, an economist with Natwest Markets Singapore said the selling was minimal, and that the thin volume exaggerated the movement of the currencies. 

 He said the market is reflecting traders squaring positions ahead of the long holidays, rather than anything else. 

 The market will be closed next week for the dual celebration of Chinese New Year and Muslim Eid Al-Fitr. 

 'Many traders were caught short on the dollar, thus they liquidated their ringgit positions,' said a chief dealer with a local bank. 

 They don't want to be long on the ringgit going into the holidays, he said. 

 Market observers said though there was a spate of figures released this week, like the money supply figures, inflation and production index, it failed to have any significant impact on the dollar/ringgit trading. 

 'As none of the figures was adversely bad, it didn't influence the trading,' he said. 

 In the money market, the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia intervened in the money market by borrowing three months ringgit funds at 7.00%, unchanged from Thursday. 

 At the late morning fixing, the one-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rates (KLIBOR) was at 7.11%, down from 7.12% Thursday. The three-month KLIBOR was also slightly lower at 7.20%, compared with 7.21% Thursday. The six-month KLIBOR was down to 7.27% from 7.28% Thursday.

title: George Soros seen behind ringgit sales - dealers.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 25 (Reuter) - The shadow of billionaire American investor George Soros was glimpsed behind a continued attack on the Malaysian ringgit in favour of the Singapore dollar on Thursday, forex dealers said. 

 The ringgit recovered slightly after Bank Negara Malaysia intervened to sell the U.S. dollar at around 2.5640 in the morning. It was quoted at 2.5605/15 in late afternoon trade. 

 "There's no confirmation. But I do think it's the only fund with big enough pockets to fly so aggressively in the face of the central bank of Malaysia," said a dealer with a U.K. bank. 

 He said the nature and location of the activity mirrored movements last week, when Soros was also believed to be behind an attack on the ringgit before Bank Negara effectively raised interest rates. 

 The Hungarian-born Soros is considered one of the world's most successful hedge fund managers. 

 The U.K. bank dealer estimated Soros' Quantum Group of funds had probably sold about one billion ringgit over the past two days. 

 The Singapore dollar's status as a safe haven and its relative lack of volatility made it an obvious choice for an investor speculating in Asian currencies, he added. 

 Sentiment for the ringgit has turned bearish due to growing anxiety about Malaysia's trade figures. 

 The Singapore dollar benefited from its neighbour's woes for the second straight day on Thursday, firming to around 1.4168/78 to the U.S. dollar in late afternoon trade, despite the greenback's strong tone against the major currencies. 

 Chia Woon Khien, Union Bank of Switzerland's economist for Singapore and Malaysia, said she would not rule out the possibility of Bank Negara raising interest rates again. 

 "It's understandable that the ringgit would weaken given that the U.S. dollar has gained a lot of ground in the last couple of days. But I don't think they (Bank Negara) like the way the market has been speculating," she said. 

 The ringgit made a sharp but short-lived recovery last week after Bank Negara raised three and six-month deposit rates by an average 25 basis points. 

 Dealers said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had not intervened to curb the Singapore dollar's rise on Thursday, but it was expected to step in if the U.S. dollar showed signs of slipping below S$1.4150/60. 

 "There's no really fundamental reason for the MAS to want to allow the Singapore dollar to appreciate in this fashion," Chia said.

title: Malaysia Trade Gap/Amplifier-3: Awaiting Sept Figures
text:
The ringgit came under selling pressure throughout the year as Malaysia's trade gap widened - inspiring repeated central bankinterventions. 

 The last time the central bank sold dollars aggressively was in early November when it intervened at the 2.5460-2.5470 ringgit level. 

Central bank intervention was unsighted so far late Tuesday and Wednesday. 

 The dollar ended 1994 at 2.5578 ringgit, and then fell to under 2.4400 ringgit in June, before rising in the second half of the year. 

 But the government has repeatedly stressed that since Malaysia's imports consist primarily of capital goods such as heavy machinery used in manufacturing, the prolonged period of high imports posted in the interium will eventually contribute to higher exports. 

 Market participants, in the absence of fresh news, have been especially cautious this week in anticipation of the September trade figures. 

 MMS's Tan forecasts a stronger ringgit if the September trade deficit narrows to under 700 million ringgit, and a weaker local currency if the trade gap widens to more than 1.3 billion ringgit. 

 'The market will be relatively neutral if the trade deficit is within the 900 million to 1 billion ringgit region,' said Tan.

text:
The central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, did not intervene or check rates Monday, traders said. 

 There was little reaction to comments by Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim who said over the weekend that the local currency should remain stable and reflect market conditions and forces. 

 He said that there was a limit to what the central bank should do to intervene in the process. In the short term it may satisfy immediate needs but in the long term intervention would disturb it, local newspapers reported from the U.S. 

 In the money market, Bank Negara borrowed one-month ringgit funds at 6.00%, keeping rates unchanged from its previous interventions. 

 Late Monday, the overnight rate was at 5.0% compared with 6.5% Friday. Traders said that the low rate reflected plentiful liquidity in the interbank market. ''Bank Negara borrowed less than what was offered,'' said a money market dealer. 

 The Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rates (KLIBOR) were mostly higher, with the one-month KLIBOR at 6.10%, up from Friday's 6.08%, and the three-month KLIBOR at 6.18%, also up from 6.15% previously.<

title: Bank Negara  intervenes  to slow ringgit fall.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 21 (Reuter) - Malaysia's Bank Negara has been pumping huge funds into the foreign exchange market since August to slow the ringgit's fall against the U.S dollar, dealers said on Thursday. 

 They said the central bank's intervention had cost nearly $1 billion, although they did not think it had made any net trading losses. 

 "At first they tried to prevent the ringgit sliding beyond 2.50 per dollar level and then, after the dollar broke through the 100-yen barrier, they have been trying to slow its fall," a dealer with a large local bank said. 

 "Even today, the central bank is in the market, but only checking the rates." 

 The daily Star newspaper said on Thursday that Bank Negara had last week spent more than $400 million to support the ringgit. The central bank has not responded to the newspaper report. 

 The Malaysian currency has been sliding against the dollar since the U.S currency began its rally against the yen and other major currencies a few weeks ago. The ringgit has declined by 3.48 percent since June 30 to about 2.5300 to a dollar. 

 Bank Negara confirmed its market intervention operations at a briefing for local media on Tuesday saying it was "aimed at smoothing out extreme fluctuations" in the exchange rate. 

 Local dealers said the central bank could not have made any losses as its trading in other currencies would have offset any notional losses on dollar/ringgit trading. 

 Dealers said the central bank had become extremely sensitive about foreign exchange trading costs since it incurred huge losses in 1992 and 1993.

title: Malaysian ringgit uptrend intact despite slip.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 1 (Reuter) - The Malaysian ringgit, under pressure against the dollar, should climb back from recent falls as the country's buoyant economy continues to lure offshore funds, analysts and foreign exchange dealers said. 

 The ringgit was trading at 2.4533/43 to the dollar on Tuesday against 2.4480 a week ago. The Malaysian currency hit a nine-year high of 2.4380 in early June. 

 "We're still looking at the ringgit hitting 2.40 and probably breaching it by the end of the year," said a dealer with a foreign bank in Malaysia. 

 "With the economy doing very well, the uptrend for ringgit is still intact." 

 Malaysia's economy is heading for its eighth straight year of eight percent growth or better. 

 The only stumbling block towards a much stronger ringgit will be Bank Negara, Malaysia's central bank, dealers said. 

 "If not for Negara intervention, the ringgit should be trading at 2.40-2.42 against the dollar now," the foreign bank dealer said. 

 Bank Negara was detected in the market in late June to support the dollar and the ringgit's rise was capped at 2.44. 

 Analysts said that while the general perception is that the central bank favours a stronger ringgit to curb inflation, it may not allow it to rise too fast and risk hurting exports. 

 "I don't think Bank Negara will allow the ringgit to appreciate too quickly as exporters will suffer. They will let it rise gradually so as to give exporters time to adjust," said an analyst at a local brokerage. 

 In 1994, Malaysia exported 21 percent of its products to the U.S., its leading export market. The exports, mainly electrical and electronic goods, were worth some 32.52 billion ringgit, Bank Negara estimated. 

 Dealers said the local currency was also holding firm due to buying against the Singapore dollar as traders capitalised on interest rate differentials between the two countries. 

 Bank Negara was widely seen as not letting interest rates fall much in an effort to ease inflationary pressures created by buoyant economic growth. 

 The Malaysian Institute of Economic Research, the country's official think tank, said recently the inflation fight is not over as pressures remain strong. The government, which began an anti-inflation drive in June aimed at curbing consumer spending, is trying to cap inflation at 4.0 percent in 1995. 

 Malaysia's inflation rate was 3.7 percent in 1994. 

 "There's no reason for rates to go up because U.S. interest rates are falling, and no reason for them to go down either given our target for inflation," said Mustafa Mohamad Nor, chief economist at Arab-Malaysian Securities. 

 "Unless U.S. rates are pushed higher again, I think our benchmark three-month rate will be capped at six percent this year," he said. 

 The three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate is averaging around 5.88 percent.

title: Malaysia 's Bank Negara won't  intervene  on ringgit.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, June 17 (Reuter) - The Malaysian central bank will not intervene to slow the ringgit's surge unless the country was flooded with "hot money", the national Bernama news agency quoted deputy finance minister Wong See Wah as saying. 

 He was also quoted as saying he hoped the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) would grow by 9.9 percent in the second quarter, as it did in the first quarter. 

 Wong said although the ringgit was strengthening against the dollar, the situation was different from last year when a heavy inflow of speculative money forced the central bank, Bank Negara, to intervene. 

 "It has always been the central bank's policy to let the ringgit dictate its own movement against major currencies, especially the U.S. dollar, by floating it in the open market," he was quoted as telling reporters at an accounting conference. 

 "Unless the hot money situation re-emerges, which is not very beneficial to our country, we will continue to let the ringgit move on its own strength," Wong was quoted as saying. 

 The ringgit has surged in recent weeks, fuelled by dollar weakness against the major currencies, Malaysia's robust economy and high Malaysian interest rates. 

 The ringgit ended Friday trading at 2.4433/43, up about five percent against 2.5575/85 at the end of last year, and close to nine-year intraday trading high of around 2.4370/80. 

 Bank Negara in early 1994 introduced tough capital control measures to choke off ringgit speculation and the flood of hot money. 

 These controls, most of which have been lifted, include a ban on sale of short-term money market instruments and long-term papers to foreigners and a negative interest rate chargeon foreign-held ringgit accounts. 

 On the GDP, Wong was quoted as saying: "We hope the figure will be consistent with that of the first quarter." 

 "Hopefully, we will be able to maintain the same figure, as a sudden drop or a sudden growth of the economy within this year is not good for the country," Wong said. 

 The 9.9 percent growth in the first quarter compares against 9.0 percent in the fourth quarter of last year and 8.8 percent in the first quarter of that year.

title: Ringgit rise vs dlr may run out of steam - analysts.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, April 17 (Reuter) - The ringgit, trading around nine-year highs against the dollar, could run out of steam at around 2.45 ringgit as Malaysia's central bank is wary of losing the country's export competitiveness, analysts said. 

 Although global dollar weakness will support further strengthening of the ringgit in the near term, there is increasing expectation that Bank Negara's tolerance level may be breached soon, they said. 

 The ringgit has risen by some 3.3 percent against the dollar this year and by 2.4 percent in the last two weeks alone. 

 "Negara is reluctant to see the ringgit appreciate too rapidly as it hurts exporters," said Paul Schymyck, regional economist at Smith Barney Shearson HG Asia. 

 In 1994, Malaysia exported 21 percent of its products to the U.S., its number one export market. The exports, mainly electrical and electronic goods, were worth some 32.52 billion ringgit ($13.19 billion), Bank Negara estimated. 

 The ringgit rose to a nine-year high of 2.4580 ringgit to the dollar in early Kuala Lumpur trade on Monday, the first time the 2.4600 level has been broken since January 1986. 

 It retreated later on profit taking, to end at 2.4650/60 ringgit, hardly changed from 2.4645/55 ringgit on Friday. 

 Analysts said Bank Negara's intervention will be swift if it feels the ringgit's spiral has been overdone, as the central bank has repeatedly warned against a rapid rise in the currency. 

 Bank Negara governor Ahmad Mohamad Don said recently "If (the ringgit) appreciates too much in a very short period of time, we have to come in to stabilise the market." 

 He said at the presentation of the central bank's 1994 annual report on March 29 that Bank Negara could tolerate a higher currency if it reflects Malaysia's economic fundamentals. 

 Bank Negara has intervened in the past when the ringgit threatened to jump by between 300-500 points in a day, said a dealer at a local bank. 

 Analysts said Bank Negara had tolerated the currency's jump in recent weeks to try reduce the impact of the mighty yen on the economy. 

 The ringgit has fallen by 12.7 percent against the yen this year, affecting the ringgit's rate in Malaysia's basket of trade currencies. "On a trade-weighted basis, there's not been much change for the ringgit," said Marco Wong, director at Yamaichi Capital Management. 

 On Monday, 100 yen was worth 3.0049/65 ringgit. The ringgit was also at 1.7804/26 marks. 

 The ringgit is expected to end the year at around 2.45-2.50 to the dollar, suported by expectations of higher interest rates in Malaysia, analysts say.

title: Ringgit jump vs dollar has Negara's nod - analysts.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, April 14 (Reuter) - The ringgit's sharp spiral against the dollar has the quiet blessing of Malaysia's Bank Negara as it tries to reduce the impact of the mighty yen on the economy, economists and dealers said on Friday. 

 The ringgit is set to test nine-year highs versus the dollar soon, but Bank Negara, Malaysia's central bank, has not intervened to stop or even try to slow the surge recently, they said. 

 "Our impression is that Bank Negara is not concerned about the rate of the dollar-ringgit," said Andy Tan, economist at MMS International, a Standard & Poor's company. 

 "When the ringgit appreciates against the dollar, the ringgit will depreciate more slowly against the yen," he added. 

 With a huge inflow of capital goods from Japan, Bank Negara is using the dollar-ringgit weakness to hedge against the rise of the yen-ringgit, economists said. 

 Japan, Malaysia's biggest trading partner, accounted for 26.7 percent its total imports of 156 billion ringgit ($63 billion) in 1994. 

 Malaysia's trade deficit with Japan grew to around 23 billion ringgit ($9 billion) last year, against 17 billion ($7 billion) in the previous year. 

 Analysts said the country's deficit, forecast at 13.8 billion ringgit ($5.5 billion) in the current year, could balloon further if the yen's rise against the ringgit is not checked. 

 The ringgit has risen by 3.3 percent against the dollar this year, but has fallen by some 12.7 percent versus the yen. 

 At mid-mmorning on Friday, the ringgit was at 2.4670/80 ringgit-to-the-dollar against 2.5490/00 on Jan 3. 

 The ringgit was also at 2.9169/07 per 100 yen, against 2.5442/64 at the beginning of the year. 

 Economists said the central bank's inaction may also be due to the fact that it wants the Malaysian currency to appreciate before hiking interest rates later to cool an overheating economy. 

 "It will be the perfect textbook situation where the central bank first lets the currency rise and then raise interest rates," said one economist. "There won't be a flow of speculative funds and Negara will be perceived as a competent central bank," he added. 

 Bank Negara imposed a series of capital controls beginning in January of 1994 after a sudden gush of hot money poured into the banking system. The bank said it feared the flood of funds was threatening its control over the ringgit. 

 The controls have largely been lifted. 

 Malaysia's key three-month interbank rate has risen sharply this year after two years of decline. It was at 6.08 percent on Friday against 5.44 percent at the beginning of the year.

 At mid-morning on Friday, the ringgit was at 2.4670/80 ringgit to the dollar against 2.5490/00 on January 3. 

 The ringgit was also at 2.9169/07 per 100 yen, against 2.5442/64 at the beginning of the year. 

 Economists said the central bank's inaction may also be due to the fact that it wants the Malaysian currency to appreciate before hiking interest rates later to cool an overheating economy. 

 "It will be the perfect textbook situation where the central bank first lets the currency rise and then raises interest rates," said one economist. "There won't be a flow of speculative funds and Negara will be perceived as a competent central bank," he added. 

 Bank Negara imposed a series of capital controls beginning in January of 1994 after a sudden gush of hot money poured into the banking system. The bank said it feared the flood of funds was threatening its control over the ringgit. 

 The controls have largely been lifted.

 Dealers said the central bank could easily bring the ringgit down if it wants to as the local market is short of dollars.

title: Malaysia  central bank  boosts ringgit ahead of data.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, March 28 (Reuter) - Malaysia's Bank Negara has intervened strongly in the foreign exchange market, driving up the ringgit against the U.S. dollar ahead of the central bank's annual report which is expected to show a large current account deficit, money dealers said. 

Foreign exchange dealers said the central bank, which will release its 1994 report on Wednesday, sold the dollar heavily last Friday to ward off ringgit selling from offshore banks and came in aggressively again on Monday. 

 Bank Negara was estimated to have sold about $800 million over the two days, helping the ringgit to gain 120 points against the dollar. The ringgit strengthened further on Tuesday morning to 2.5360 to the dollar although the central bank stayed away from the market. 

 Bank Negara seems to be capping dollar gains against the ringgit but the actual reason behind the intervention is open for speculation, financial analysts said. 

 The central bank may be protectively pushing up the ringgit on fears the market will over-react after the release of the current account data, they said. 

 If the ringgit is to weaken after the report, it would probably fall back to its earlier level of around 2.55 ringgit to the dollar due to the central bank action. 

 "Negara is sending a strong signal for people not to mess around with the ringgit even if the deficit is wider. They're trying to show who's the boss," said an economist at a foreign brokerage. 

 Dealers also said the pressure on the ringgit could also be due to the repatriation of profits by Japanese investors before they close their books for the March year-end. 

 "Negara could be trying to pump in liquidity (by releasing dollars) in the forex market to balance outward remittances which are quite huge," said a currency manager at a local bank. 

 "Also, a lot of payments for importation of goods are being carried out now," he said. 

 Financial markets in Malaysia have been speculating that Bank Negara will report a widening of the current account deficit to between 15 and 17 billion ringgit for 1994, higher than 6.3 billion in 1993 and the official forecast of 12 billion. Offshore investors, apparently concerned about the deficit, have been dumping ringgit lately, dealers said. 

 Some foreign fund managers have drawn parallels to Mexico, which sharply devalued its currency in the midst of its balance of payments crisis. 

 Malaysian officials have expressed annoyance with that comparison, saying its foreign reserves are strong at 79 billion ringgit and its foreign debt manageable at around 50 billion ringgit. 

 Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim had said Malaysia's deficit was widening due to larger imports of capital equipment as a result of surging foreign investment.

title: Malaysia Finance Minister Hints At Lowered Growth Rates
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Malaysia's Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim Sunday signalled that the government may have to revise down its 1998 economic growth forecast in light of the severe depreciation of the ringgit last week. 

 The U.S. dollar gained 17% against the Malaysian currency to around MYR4.60 late Friday. Since the Asian currency crisis began in July, the ringgit has lost 45% of its value. 

 In a significant admission of the economic problems afflicting Malaysia, Anwar revised down economic growth targets for 1998 to 4.0% through to 5.0%, sharply lower than the 8.0%-plus growth rates which the country has enjoyed over the last decade. The International Monetary Fund, however, has forecast economic growth of 2.5% for Malaysia in 1998. 

 Talking to reporters about the growth rates, Anwar said, "We will have to review the situation in the next few weeks. If the ringgit recovers slightly I don't think we need to review growth estimates for this year." 

Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara, has been steadily intervening to support the ringgit in the past week. 

 "Intervention is necessary to reflect the economic fundamentals," Anwar said. "We haven't been very aggressive, but we haven't allowed it to slide." 

 Bank Negara first stepped into the market Wednesday when the ringgit was threatening to break through the MYR5.00 per dollar barrier. Anwar declined to say how much the central bank spent. "We have been very prudent, cautious, and mindful of the fact that foreign reserves have to be substantial." As of Dec. 31, Malaysia's foreign reserves totaled $21.71 billion.

title: Malaysia  central bank  finds ringgit defence tricky.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Jan 11 (Reuters) - Defending the Malaysian ringgit is proving tricky for the country's central bank as it walks a fine line between supporting the currency and strangling the economy, analysts said. 

 The central bank is using the twin tools of direct currency intervention and interest rates to defend the ringgit, but Asia's economic gloom has made that job harder than usual. 

 Last week the ringgit slid 13 percent, forcing Bank Negara Malaysia to nudge up interbank rates and repeatedly intervene to buy ringgit and sell dollars, traders aid. 

 But in protecting the currency, the central bank must tread between not depleting the country's reserves and not squeezing the economy with higher interest rates, the analysts said. 

 "At this point of time, they can't afford to hike interest rates too much because equities and the property market are already weak," said Jimmy Koh, regional economist at financial market consultant I.D.E.A. 

 "And you can sell dollar/ringgit, but how much can you sell?" he added. 

 He said the central bank would probably opt to keep rates firm to encourage savings while not choking off the economy. 

 On Monday, Bank Negara tried, but failed, to prevent the ringgit from falling below 4.0 a dollar. 

 It then spent the rest of last week successfully defending the ringgit from falling to 5.0 as Asian currencies came under fire. 

 "It's not a question of a wise move or not to intervene, but a question of integrity. Bank Negara can't let the currency weaken as far as people like," said a spot currency dealer at a European bank in Singapore. 

 The ringgit ended Kuala Lumpur trading on Friday at 4.5700 a dollar, down 13.4 percent from 3.96 only a week ago. 

 The ringgit has lost more than 40 percent of its value against the dollar since early July when the Asian economic crisis first erupted. 

 Analysts said stoutly defending the ringgit as a matter of policy would ultimately fail and the central bank knew this. 

 "If they are providing liquidity to the market it's okay. But if you're changing your policy then it's wasting money. They need all the money they can get," said Desmond Supple, head of currency research at BZW. 

 Analysts said Bank Negara may have spent around $1 billion in its intervention last week. 

 Last Thursday, the central bank said its international reserves stood at $21.71 billion as at December 31 last year, before the January intervention. 

 Some currency dealers speculated that to prevent the reserves from depleting, part of the intervention funds could have come from state oil company Petroliam Nasional Bhd (Petronas). 

 Petronas, the country's most profitable company, earns its oil revenue in dollars and was rumoured to have converted these to ringgit in large amounts in the recent past to stop drastic slides in the Malaysian currency. 

 No confirmation from Petronas could be obtained on the speculation. 

 On another battlefront, the central bank has been nudging up interbank rates to make the ringgit more attractive to hold, analysts said. 

 Concerns over higher inflation as the price of imported goods jump with the declining ringgit were also a reason for allowing rates to creep higher. 

 "The perception is that we may see strong inflation, so Bank Negara may be willing to let rates rise," said a futures dealer at a merchant bank. 

 Futures contracts on the benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) slid to record lows last week as players expect firmer rates in coming months. 

 The futures contracts move in opposite direction to expectations of interest rate movements. 

 The key March KLIBOR futures contract ended Friday trading at 88.70 for an implied yield of 11.3 percent, against 89.50 or an implied yield of 10.5 percent only a week ago. 

 A third method of defending the currency is through capital controls, but Malaysian leaders have emphasised they will adhere to a flexible exchange rate policy.

title: Asian exotics frail but aided by  intervention  hope.
text:
TOKYO, Jan 9 (Reuters) - Asian exotic currencies stayed mostly fragile on Friday morning after recent free-falls, but hopes that central banks in the Asia-Pacific may act jointly against slides of currencies in the region supported them against the dollar. 

 Indonesia's rupiah, which had smashed below 10,000 to the dollar on Thursday, surged to a high of 7,900 following selling of dollars by some state banks, dealers said. 

 They said the rupiah was quoted at 7,750/8,500 at 0320 GMT, compared with Friday's opening rate of 10,500/11,500. 

 There were spreading wild rumours of riots and increased troop presence in early trade, which made trading nervous. 

 A U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said: "These are all baseless rumours. The only true one was that there was a rush on basic commodities. I think Singapore players have built up extensive long dollar positions." 

 Thursday's plunge came after the IMF urged the Indonesian government to comply with austerity terms of the International Monetary Fund's $40 billion bailout package. 

 Meanwhile, Malaysia's Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad reiterated on Friday that his country does not need financial aid from the IMF, saying Malaysia's fundamentals remained sound although its growth was expected to be at a more moderate level than in the past. 

 The ringgit slipped against the dollar in early trading despite continued intervention by central Bank of Negara Malaysia. The central bank sold dollars at around 4.7000 ringgit on Friday morning. Bank Negara had also intervened to defend the ringgit on Wednesday and Thursday. 

 A trader at an Asian currency desk at a major Japanese bank in Tokyo said: "Trading of Asian currencies, particularly Indonesian rupiah, remained quite nervous. 

 "But growing hopes that nations across the region may team up to work against slides of currencies checked falls of these currencies," she added. 

 Overnight dollar/yen bids were sidelined after unconfirmed rumors of quiet dollar sales by the Federal Reserve against Southeast Asian currencies or the yen. 

 Market sources in Europe and New York reported that the Fed had checked rates on the Malaysian ringgit and the Indonesian rupiah. 

 Asked about wider cooperation in Asian nations, Larry Duke, vice president at Citibank, told Reuters Financial Television: "Sure, it's always possible. But I think it's going to be a big challenge." He added that there is a need for a change in the underlying fundamentals and aggressive policy response in the region. 

 Richard Samuelson, head of research at SBC Warburg Dillon Reed, told RFTV that the market still sees major risks in South Korea, including the possibility of more bank failures and weakness of the won, and there is generally an aversion to investing there. 

 The U.S. unit weakened slightly against the mark after Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer said the dollar's rise was greater than expected given present economic fundamentals. 

 The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) was rumoured to have sold U.S. dollars against the Aussie dollar. 

 A RBA spokesman declined to comment on the rumours. 

 The Japanese bank dealer said: "Concerted action from central banks in Asia, including the MAS (Monetary Authoritie of Singapore) and RBA, could be needed to prevent currencies in the region from sliding." 

 U.S. Treasuries edged down by midday in Tokyo as Asian operators sold holdings to raise dollars, traders said. Sales stood out in the five-year sector, putting downward pressure on overall prices, they said. 

 Tokyo stocks lost nearly two percent by midday as buying of blue-chip shares weakened amid worries that the Japanese government might not take new economy-boosting measures any time soon, brokers said. 

 The dollar was down versus yen but off lows in Tokyo at midday. Its topside was capped by views that Japan may take extra economic stimulus steps in return for U.S. help in defending yen and Asian currencies. 

 Yen-based gold futures on the Tokyo Commodity Exchange were lower by midday, with benchmark December down 16 yen per gram at 1,190 yen per gram. Prices fell in reaction to overnight losses in gold bullion which were triggered by a sharp slide in silver prices, traders said.

title: Malaysia 's Mahathir -2: Anwar Says  Intervention  Appropriate
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Malaysia's Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad Thursday dismissed talk the country may impose foreign exchange controls, and said the ringgit's dramatic decline this week was the result of market forces. 

 Speaking to reporters after attending an official function, the unusually reticent premier said that any trading restrictions on the currency would further worsen sentiment. 

 At 0344 GMT (10:44 p.m. EST), the dollar had climbed to MYR4.6000, up from MYR4.5130 late Wednesday. Bank Negara intervened to defend the ringgit after it plunged to MYR4.8800 Wednesday afternoon, a historic low. 

 'Now there is no proposal for foreign exchange controls,' Mahathir said. 'The introduction of foreign exchange controls will lead to loss of confidence. We cannot now speak about foreign exchange controls.' 

 He put the blame for the ringgit's fall firmly on market forces, instead of blaming currency speculators and vested foreign interests as he has often done in the past. 

 'We must accept (this depreciation) as the result of market forces. We don't have any control of the market,' Mahathir said. 'Now the market disciplines the goverment, and governments in East Asian countries are being disciplined.'

 High interest rates often encourage investors to shift their money from the stock market to fixed-income instruments, like bonds or fixed deposits. High interest rates also put a damper on most companies' earnings, making their shares less attractive to investors. 

 The slower economic growth forecast for Malaysia in the coming year will also discourage investors from putting their money in stocks, analysts said.

title: Malaysia Unveils Reform Plan In Effort To Avoid IMF Rescue
text:
KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- Battling speculation in the financial markets that Malaysia would be the next country after South Korea to go to the International Monetary Fund for a bailout, Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim Friday unveiled what many economists say is the next best thing. 

 "It's an IMF program without the IMF," said Simon Mahadevan Flint, an economist at Independent Economic Analysis Ltd. "They're delivering an IMF formula to restore confidence in the management of the economy." 

 The prescription delivered by Anwar, also Malaysia's finance minister, is wide-ranging. Abandoning what analysts said was the government's tendency to stick to rigid forecasts, Anwar set gross domestic product growth targets at 4% to 5% for 1998, a sharp revision from the 7% previously anticipated by government officials. 

 He said government spending will be cut by 18%, and there will be no bailout for financial institutions facing liquidity problems. The government also won't bail out corporations, although companies with temporary cash-flow problems will be helped under the new plan, Anwar said. 

 The package helped revive the Malaysian ringgit, which had sunk to record lows against the dollar in volatile trading earlier Friday. The dollar surged as high as 3.8400 ringgit at one point, amid fears Kuala Lumpur would shortly be knocking at the IMF's door. 

 The dollar fell back to 3.7350 ringgit late Friday in Asia after Anwar's announcement and after some mild intervention from Bank Negara, Malaysia's central bank. Share prices also bot a boost from the statement, with the benchmark Composite Index rallying 5.5% to close 31.51 points higher at 607.40, buoyed by what dealers said was a more realistic analysis of Malaysia's economic fundamentals. 

 But whether Anwar's plan will survive the scrutiny of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and actually be implemented is still in doubt, some analysts said. Anwar and Mahathir already seem to be contradicting each other on at least one point in the plan - the decision to delay the 10 billion ringgit Landbridge project developing infrastructure links between northern Malaysia and southern Thailand. Thursday, Mahathir was reported as saying the plan would be going ahead. But Friday, Anwar said it would be delayed, and only an oil pipeline between the two countries would be constructed on schedule. 

 Mahathir is viewed as being keen to keep as many major infrastructure projects going as possible to meet his goal of Malaysia becoming an industrialized nation by the year 2020. Some observers are concerned he will veto Anwar's plan through the National Economic Action Council (NEAC), which was formed last week to tackle Malaysia's worsening economic problems. 

 Anwar tried to downplay those suggestions. He said the cabinet was fully committed to the just-announced economic plan, and that the NEAC wouldn't be able to override it. However, he couldn't confirm who would be included on the NEAC, and he didn't rule out the possibility that influential business people - who would be less keen to see major projects cancelled - could sit on the panel. 

 The immediate reaction to Anwar's program was overwhelmingly upbeat. "If this package can come about, then Malaysia can put its house in order. If they can trim domestic demand, they can close the current account deficit," said Daniel Lian, an economist at ANZ Investment Bank. 

 Closing balance-of-payment gaps is the key point in IMF programs, he said. Lian estimates that Malaysia's current account deficit stood at around 8.7% in the early part of the year but that it could fall to 5%-6% by the end of 1997, as the impact of the economic slowdown brought on by Southeast Asia's five-month-old currency crisis takes hold. Anwar said a current account deficit of 3% is achievable next year. 

 Despite favorable implications for Malaysia's external accounts, the economic slowdown could bring problems of its own. Lian said the deceleration could surpass Anwar's estimates and hurt the banking sector, which already is bearing the signs of liquidity problems as nonperforming loan rates rise. Although the government says nonperforming loans stand at 5.9% of total lending in the banking sector, many economists say the real figure may be higher than 10%. 

 As banks sell off collateral securing these loans, "a collapse in property prices could come next year," Lian said. "There could be a lot of pain in store." 

 It could be worse if the government and the central bank make a concerted effort to halt the ringgit's slide in the currency markets. "The only way they can relieve the slide is to hike short-term interest rates," Lian said, adding that this is something the IMF would recommend. 

 Anwar revealed Friday that the IMF had suggested that Malaysia increase its interest rates. But the Malaysian authorities are loath to increase rates, as it would discourage investment in the stock market and also squeeze highly leveraged corporations. A stock market that already has lost over 50% of its value since February concerns analysts, who point to commercial banks' practice of accepting stock as collateral. Anwar didn't say whether the Malaysian government would heed the IMF's advice.

title: Key dates in Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 21 (Reuters) - South Korea said on Friday it was talking to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) about emergency loans. 

 This was the latest development in a string of financial crises across Asia. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits a 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils an austerity plan and complete revamp of its finance sector as part of IMF-suggested policies for a rescue package. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits an historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 19 - The South Korean won hits an all time low of 901 to the dollar. The currency has been sliding gradually during the year. On January 1 it stood at 842. 

 August 20 - The IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Oct 2 - Won slips to 913.50 on news Ssangbang Wool faces a debt default. Corporate defaults have been one of the reasons for the won's fall. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 28 - The won's fall accelerates. It ends at 953 despite central bank intervention. 

 Oct 30 - The won -- which has a 2.25 percent daily trading band -- hits its lowest permitted level of 984.70. 

 Oct 31 - The IMF package for Indonesia is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - The won will "never, never, never" breach the psychologically important 1000 barrier a Korean central bank official says. 

 Nov 2 - Indonesia announces the liquidation of 16 unhealthy banks under the IMF economic reform programme. 

 Nov 4 - Thailand's government collapses as Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh resigns. The baht rises to 38.75 from 40.95 on the unpopular premier's departure. 

 Nov 7 - The markets are now openly speculating Seoul will have to go to the IMF to help defend the won. The won ends at 979.90 and traders are targetting the 1000 barrier. 

 In Thailand, opposition Democrat leader Chuan Leekpai says he will form the new government. 

 Nov 9 - Chuan is appointed new Thai premier. 

 Nov 10 - The won closes at 999.00 to the dollar. 

 Nov 17 - South Korea cracks. The central bank announces it will no longer defend the 986 level to the dollar. The won immediately falls its daily limit down to 1008.60. 

 Nov 18 - The Korean central bank suggests to the finance ministry that Korea should seek an IMF bailout loan. The won is at its 1012.80 daily limit low. 

 Nov 19 - Korean finance minister Kang Kyong-shik resigns to take responsibility for the financial turmoil. South Korea also widens its daily band limit on the won to 10 percent. 

 Nov 21 - Finance ministry official announces that Seoul is discussing details of a bailout package with the IMF.

text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The Thai baht greeted Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's promise to resign with gusto on Tuesday, bringing cheer to most Southeast Asian currencies. 

 The baht made a strong start after Chavalit's surprise announcement late on Monday, sparking predictions that the rally was overdone and would soon fizzle out. 

 But official assurances that political changes would not hurt implementation of IMF-backed economic reforms and news of government spending cuts kept the baht well bid through the day. It ended at its day high of 38.60/80 to the dollar onshore, more than five percent above late Monday levels of 40.90/41.00. The offshore rate was at 38.40/50 at 1040 GMT against 39.85/40.35 previously. 

 "It seems the market is quite receptive to Chavalit's resignation," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 He said spirits were further lifted by announcements that the government would lop another 18 billion baht from 1997/98 spending, on top of a previous 100 billion baht cut. 

 Thai stocks also rallied with the composite SET index adding 6.9 percent to end at 478.33. But currency traders remained conservative about the baht's potential for more gains. 

 "I just can't see dollar/baht continuing to come off. I can't see the baht strengthening much further than 37.50/38.00," one said. 

 And while Chavalit's decision to resign removed some of the market's immediate gloom, Thailand still faced a long, arduous road in rehabilitating its economy, analysts said. 

 "A change of leadership obviously means something has to be done and decisions which have to be taken are not going to be popular," said Kim Teo, managing director of Nicholas-Applegate Capital Management Asia. 

 Teo said Southeast Asian markets were in for more pain in the next six to 12 months as Thailand and Indonesia moved to restructure their economies in line with IMF requirements. 

 "The reaction we are seeing in the markets is more a technical bounce from an oversold position," he said. "Currencies will remain weakish but certainly not at the near panic collapses we've seen," he added. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah continued to rise on appreciation of the government's efforts to reform the economy in response to a massive IMF-led international aid package. 

 Dealers said the scramble caused by tighter liquidity after three central banks intervened on Monday to buy the rupiah lifted forward rates in early trade. 

 The value of concerted dollar sales for rupiah in Singapore on Monday by the Bank of Japan (BOJ), the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Bank Indonesia was estimated at $300 to $500 million, senior Japanese traders said. 

 Singapore dealers said Bank Indonesia had intervened again on Tuesday to sell dollars. 

 "They sold quite a few times even around the low of 3,210. I don't think it was really big amounts but they tried to cap (the dollar) above 3,270," the U.S. bank dealer said. 

 The rupiah was at 3,260/70 to the dollar against its New York close at 3,205, sharply up from its Monday Asian close at 3,300/10. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.5555/75 to the U.S. dollar, off its highs of 1.5450 after active U.S. dollar buying by local banks below the 1.5500 level. 

 Dealers said there were rumours the dollar purchases were on behalf of the MAS, which was believed to be buying back dollars after Monday's intervention to support the rupiah. 

Malaysia's ringgit was at 3.2675/775 to the dollar against 3.2600/700 late on Monday. 

 Dealers said selling was expected after the ringgit's recent bounce, but they saw a further test of the 3.20 per dollar resistance. 

 The Philippine peso ended higher at 34.84 to the dollar from a previous 35.14 close. The central bank offered dollars at 34.85/90 pesos but found no takers. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the policy-making Monetary Board would discuss by how much to lower the overnight lending rate at a regular meeting on Wednesday. The rate is at 16.125 percent. 

 Even the Taiwan dollar and South Korean won perked up on Tuesday. The Taiwan dollar ended sharply up at T$30.730 against Monday's 10-year low of T$31.245. 

 Dealers said investors took profit on U.S. dollar gains after the central bank said on Monday the Taiwan dollar had lost too much value. 

 On Tuesday, the central bank said the Taiwan dollar's recent depreciation made Taiwan remained "extremely competitive" against South Korea and Singapore in global export markets. 

 The South Korean won ended at 961.00 against Monday's 969.90 close after the central bank poured an estimated $300 million into the market to support it. 

 Only the Hong Kong dollar slipped as traders unwound long positions on a belief that the premium of Hong Kong dollar interest rates over U.S. rates would wane. 

 Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said last week that domestic interest rates were likely to ease in the short term.

title: Ringgit firms vs dollar on corporate demand.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 7 (Reuter) - The ringgit recovered sharply against the dollar on Tuesday on corporate demand and stop-loss selling of the dollar, dealers said. 

 They said dollar sales were triggered by rumours that central Bank Negara had intervened to support the ringgit and fears that Malaysia might implement a two-tier market, similar to Thailand's system, after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's repeated calls for curbs on currency trading. 

 There was confusion in foreign exchange markets early on Tuesday when the format on a Reuters currency quotation page was mistakenly changed. 

 The changes gave the impression that a two-tier market had been created in the ringgit, Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso. 

 This mistake was subsequently corrected to reflect global consolidated contributions. 

 "There was a brief panic that a two-tier market may have been implemented. Then came rumours in Singapore of Bank Negara intervention which further hit the dollar," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank. "A lot of stop losses were triggered." 

 Some dealers estimated up to $250-300 million may have been sold. 

 At 1000 GMT, the ringgit was at 3.2775/875 to the dollar against its opening around 3.3400. It earlier hit a high of 3.7400 a dollar. 

 Dealers said buying of the ringgit against the Singapore dollar and thin market condition also helped the Malaysian currency post one of its biggest intra-day gains against the U.S. dollar this year. 

 Malaysian dealers said they had not detected the central bank's presence. 

 "There was a large corporate order to buy ringgit which was executed by a Bank Negara agent, and I think this prompted talk that the central bank had actually intervened," a local bank dealer said. 

 Bank Negara does not normally comment on its open market operations. 

 Dealers said further corporate selling and liquidation by players caught long could immediately cap the dollar/ringgit at 3.30.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals firm on  central bank  fea.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 7 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies regained their footing on Tuesday as traders turned cautious about buying the dollar too aggressively amid growing talk of central bank intervention in very thin markets. 

 Bank Indonesia, which stepped in to sell dollars when the rupiah slumped to an all-time low of 3,850 per dollar on Monday, was believed to have intervened again on Tuesday. 

 Dealers said the central bank had sold dollars in small amounts, pushing the rupiah to a high of 3,475 against its opening 3,600/50. 

 But persistent dollar demand from underhedged domestic companies and offshore funds jumping on the bandwagon pushed the rupiah back down to 3,640/50 by 0455 GMT. 

 The rupiah's overnight gains after State Secretary Murdiono said the government would take steps to stabilise the rupiah, while remaining committed to free foreign exchange flows, also helped sentiment. 

 The Philippine central bank also stepped in to prop up the peso as it fell prey to pent-up dollar demand from foreign banks, diving to a record low of 35.981 per dollar. 

 Manila traders said the central bank's dollar sales from the 35.85 peso level helped turn the tide, pushing the peso back up to 34.65/75 by 0455 GMT. 

 The reimposition of a volatility band added to the market mayhem as the peso twice breached its limits before the central bank intervention, leading to trade suspensions. 

 The Bankers Association of the Philippines, which operates the electronic forex dealing system, decided late on Monday to reintroduce the band due to the peso's recent volatility. 

 It calls for a 30-minute recess if the peso moves outside a two percent limit. Upon resumption of trading, the band is narrowed to one percent and trading can be suspended two more times before being stopped for the rest of the day. 

 Elsewhere, the Malaysian ringgit recovered sharply amid rumours in Singapore that the central Bank Negara Malaysia was intervening to support the unit. 

 But Malaysian dealers said they had not detected the central bank's presence and most attributed the ringgit's rise to commercial demand and buying of the unit against the Singapore dollar. 

 "U.S. names were said to be buying about $200-$300 million in ringgit/Sing," said one Singapore dealer. 

 Dealers said the market was also plagued by fears Malaysia might implement a two-tier market, similar to Thailand's system, after Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's repeated calls for further curbs on currency trading. 

 There was confusion on foreign exchange markets when the format on a Reuters currency quotation page was mistakenly changed early on Tuesday. The changes gave the impression a two-tier market had been created in the ringgit, rupiah and peso. 

 This mistake was subsequently corrected to reflect global consolidated contributions. 

 The Singapore dollar recovered from its lows around 1.5470 to the U.S. dollar in line with the ringgit's move, but its gains were capped by buying of the ringgit/Sing cross. 

 Dealers said the market was awaiting discussion in parliament, later in the day, about the impact of the Southeast Asian currency crisis on Singapore's economy and whether steps were being taken to address it. 

 The Thai baht showed a firm bias on growing optimism about the government's finance sector reform package, due to be announced on October 15. 

 "It is a very narrow bid and offer, I think people are looking into the future for October 15 and some people think the news will come out positively," a local bank dealer in Bangkok said. Onshore baht was at 36.60/65 to the dollar while the offshore rate was at 35.65/75.

title: Malaysia  Ringgit/Early -2:  Intervention  Rumors Abound
text:
Dealers said the market was awash with rumors that the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, had intervened to buy the ringgit, but none felt confident enough to say they felt sure that was the case. 

 A Hong Kong-based dealer said there were growing suspicions that the monetary authorities of Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia were working together to support their currencies. 

 If that were the case, he said, the central banks were probably trying to keep their currencies from falling much further or, at least, trying to slow the fall. He doubted they were trying to bring about a reversal. 

 A Singapore-based analyst was skeptical about the rumors of a concerted effort on the part of the three countries to check the drop in their currencies, noting that his sources close to the central bank denied the talk. He said it was probably just a coincidence that the regional currencies were strengthening around the same time. 

 A Singapore-based dealer also said that, though the market was rife with speculation of central bank intervention, he had no confirmation. 

 Nevertheless, the Hong Kong-based dealer said the rumors would keep investors jittery and, therefore, trading would continue to be volatile. He said the dollar would probably trade between 3.1800 ringgit and 3.3200 ringgit during Asian trading. 

 So far the dollar has traded in a wide range, between 3.2450 ringgit and 3.3680 ringgit this morning.

title: S.E. Asian  currencies  slide,  central bank  lifts won.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 26 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies slipped again on Tuesday and dealers said they could be ready for a new round of falls with the market still worried and regional bourses dropping sharply. 

 In Indonesia, improving liquidity depressed the rupiah, propped up in recent sessions by the central bank's sharp rates rise last week. 

 Dealers said swap rates fell across the board as interest rates dropped, with overnight rupiah falling to 20 percent from 100 percent in the morning. 

 "There are rumours ranging from interest rate cuts to central bank offerings of short-term securities (SBPUs). But none of them are true," a European bank dealer said. 

 "What we have today is sufficient liquidity supply. I think it's resulting from maturing central bank papers which are not rolled over," the dealer said. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,770/75 at 0945 GMT against an opening of 2,690/2,710. 

 A Japanese bank dealer in Jakarta said offshore players started the round of swap selling, probably in anticipation of interest rates easing. 

 The South Korean won made an about-turn and ended firmer on stop-loss dollar sales sparked by the central bank's repeated intervention. 

 The won ended at 900.50 to the dollar, up both from Monday's 904.60 and from a historic low of 909.50 on Tuesday morning. 

 The Bank of Korea's dollar sales, estimated by dealers at about $500 million, initially pushed the won up to an intraday high of 899.80. 

 Dealers attributed the won's morning fall to talk that this month's trade deficit would be bigger than expected. They said the won was likely to remain firmer for the time being due to fears of more central bank intervention. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit fell against the U.S. dollar on talk that U.S. funds were accumulating long dollar/ringgit positions in the forward market. 

 "We've been hearing that U.S. funds have been buying dollar/ringgit heavily in the forward market, especially in the six-months and one-year," the U.S. bank dealer said. 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.7820/70 to the dollar after briefly falling through 2.79 against 2.7700/50 late on Monday. 

 The ringgit fell to new lows against the Singapore dollar on follow-through sales after the cross breached stop-loss limits overnight. Ringgit/Sing was at 0.5359/76 at 0945 GMT. 

 "There were still some long positions on the cross so once we broke 0.5450 and 0.5400, there was more selling. But fundamentally, I don't see any reasons why we should be selling it," the U.S. bank dealer said. 

 The Singapore dollar briefly fell through 1.5000 to the U.S. dollar in line with the ringgit's drop. 

 It was quoted at 1.4935/55, little changed from its noon levels, after firming to 1.4895 earlier on sales of an estimated $50 million by a Tokyo party, dealers said. 

 The Thai baht was subdued as domestic demand for the dollar subsided, but dealers said sentiment remained weak on lingering concerns about Thailand's economic and political outlook. 

 The Philippine peso weakened as foreign funds pulled out of the badly bruised stock market. The peso ended at 30.02 to the dollar against Monday's 29.895 close while the key stock market index finished at a new 21-month low of 2,300.82. 

 The Philippine central bank raised its rediscount rate for September to 13.188 percent from 12.572 last month. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended unchanged as the central bank maintained its defence of the T$28.727 level in the face of heavy demand for the U.S. dollar.

title: FOCUS - Ringgit hits weakest level since flotation.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 15 (Reuter) - The Malaysian ringgit took a fresh beating on Friday, hitting its lowest level against the U.S. dollar since the currency was officially floated in 1973, dealers said. 

 Fresh speculative selling out of Singapore pushed the currency to a record low of 2.8250 to a dollar, dealers said. It had recovered to 2.8000/50 by 0635 GMT. 

 Dealers said the weakness in the Indonesian rupiah has spilled over to the ringgit. 

 The rupiah dropped to a record low of 2,890 to the dollar on Friday after the central Bank of Indonesia allowed it float the day before. 

 Dealers said thin market liquidity had made it easier to push the dollar/ringgit across the key psychological level of 2.8000. 

 "Most of the selling came out of Singapore. Volume is thin which makes it easy to move the market," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore. 

 "For now, it is likely that some players who were already long on the dollar may want to take some profits which may see the dollar/ringgit back to 2.8000 over the short term," said another Singapore dealer. 

 Talk of intervention by the central Bank Negara Malaysia at around 2.7910 earlier in the day could not be confirmed. 

 Dealers said the worst may not be over as regional currencies remained under pressure. 

 "So long as the regional crisis is not over, weakness will remain," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank. "European players are likely to react when they enter later." 

 The ringgit, like the Thai baht, the Philippine peso and the rupiah, has been hit by speculative attacks over the past month. It has lost nearly 13 percent of its value. 

 Technically, the ringgit is seen heading for 2.8385 with support for the dollar seen at 2.7950, dealers said.

title: Malaysia  Ringgit/Midday -4: Talk Of Negara  Intervention
text:
A currency analyst in Singapore felt confident Bank Negara Malaysia had intervened around 2.8100 ringgit to try to stop the dollar's advance, but she had no details. Others said they had no proof of the intervention. 

 She didn't believe the central bank could keep the dollar from gaining further on the ringgit, however, noting that those pushing the dollar higher 'have more money to spare than the central bank has.' The central bank has spent quite a bit of its reserves defending the ringgit in recent months. 

 The analyst thought the dollar could reach 2.8300 ringgit in Asian trading, and then when investors in London and New York start trading, she said 'you will see more pressure.' 

 Overnight, she sees the dollar moving up toward 3.0000 ringgit. Whether it will make it all the way there so soon, however, was unclear, she said, explaining, 'I think Bank Negara Malaysia is very worried and would try to be around.' 

 An emerging markets analyst in Singapore said he was worried about how investors in the stock market would react. The market is closed for the midday break. 

 The analyst felt certain that authorities would cut the statutory reserve requirement of banking institutions, which is now 13.5%. The move would put more money in the market, which should bring down interest rates, and therefore free up still more money for investors to buy stocks with. 

 That would at least boost investor confidence with regard to the stock market. And if foreigners move back into the stock market, they will need ringgit, which could therefore bring support to the currency.

title: Malaysia economic growth forecast lowered.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 12 (Reuter) - Economists have lowered their forecast for Malaysia's economic growth this year and in 1998 due to slower-than-expected export growth and high interest rates, a Reuters poll showed on Tuesday. 

 In the poll, 12 research houses in Malaysia and Singapore forecast an average 7.9 percent gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1997 against the 8.0 percent they projected at the end of last year. 

 The government has forecast a growth of 7.8-8.2 percent after reporting rise of 8.2 percent in 1996. 

 The economists forecast the 1998 GDP growth at an average 7.4 percent. 

 The houses polled were Crosby Research, J.M. Sassoon & Co, Jupiter Securities, Kleinwort Benson, Merrill Lynch, MMS International, Natwest Markets, OSK Research, Phileo Allied Securities, TA Securities, UBS Securities and Vickers Ballas. 

 Their forecasts for the current year ranged between 7.5 and 8.2 percent and for 1998 between 5.4 and 8.0 percent. 

 Economists said they had also mostly revised downward their growth projections after taking into account the recent currency turmoil. 

 The Malaysian ringgit has fallen more than 11 percent against the dollar to a 42-month low of 2.7930 on Tuesday over the past month due to heavy selling by offshore funds. 

 The ringgit was around 2.7700 to a dollar at 0700 GMT. 

 "Most people are knocking down their numbers after recent developments," said Kevin Chew, economist at Caspian Securities. "The ringgit is weakening and the period of high interest rates is longer than what we have anticipated. This will curb domestic demand." 

 Heavy intervention by the central Bank Negara Malaysia in June to defend the ringgit mopped up large funds from the banking system, pushing interbank rates sharply higher. 

 Slower exports and foreign investment had also prompted economists to lower their forecast. 

 Malaysian exports in the first six months of this year rose by only 1.9 percent, to 98.4 billion ringgit against the same period of 1996. 

 The slower export growth in part contributed to Malaysia's unexpectedly large trade deficit of 2.8 billion ringgit for June. 

 Malaysia's approvals of foreign investment slumped to 5.41 billion ringgit in the first half of this year, against 17.06 billion ringgit for the whole of 1996, government figures showed.

title: FOCUS-Malaysian markets tripped up by falling ring.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 11 (Reuter) - A storm rocking Malaysia's financial markets turned ferocious on Monday, hammering the already beleaguered currency to a 42-month low and the key stocks index to a 21-month nadir low. 

 The ringgit lost another two percent to 2.74 per dollar, taking its month-long fall to nearly 10 percent, and the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index ended 3.24 percent lower at 902.14, just above the key 900-point psychological barrier. 

 But commodity prices -- palm oil and tin -- rallied on hopes that a weak ringgit would boost export earnings. Malaysia's benchmark palm oil October futures contract closed 20 ringgit higher at 1,220 ringgit ($446.07) a tonne and tin rose to a 5-1/2-month high of 14.70 ringgit per kg. 

 Analysts and dealers said foreign funds again led the dramatic downward slide in the stock and currency markets. 

 Malaysian authorities stayed on the sidelines following remarks by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad on Friday that Malaysia was satisfied with the ringgit's level and would not let speculators profit by trying to prop up the currency. 

 "I thought we had seen the worst, but today is quite bad on all fronts," said Sani Hamid, economist with MMS International in Singapore. 

 "I think it was the PM's comments (on Friday) that triggered the selling of the ringgit. He added to the bearishness." 

 The currency plunged nearly two percent on Friday and has remained under pressure since. 

 Analysts said Mahathir's remarks were taken to mean that the central Bank Negara Malaysia would not intervene to stop the local unit from being sold. 

 "This was the last thing that the ringgit needed, given (that) regional currency woes (were) still pretty much unresolved, thus opening the way to more ringgit downside," research house I.D.E.A. said in a Monday morning commentary. 

 Sani of MMS said the stocks index and ringgit were getting dangerously close to their lowest levels this decade. 

 The ringgit's lowest level since 1990 is 2.80 per dollar reached in July 1991 and for the Composite Index it is 836 points in January 1995, he said. 

 "All hell's breaking loose," said a dealing manager at a local brokerage. "It seems like foreigners want to get out of the ringgit." 

 "Almost everybody agrees that 880 is the next support level (for the index). There is only limited support around 900. 

 "There is a lot of foreign selling, but the rest is forced selling, including some selling by banks and even the local funds on their clients shares held as collateral," said the dealing manager. 

 Hugh Young, managing director of Aberdeen Asset Management in Singapore, said the selling was mainly due to exchange rate uncertainty, "elements of a bubble economy", and borrowing for the construction of large infrastructure projects. 

 Lack of a clear policy during the current currency crisis was another reason for the continuing attack on Malaysian financial markets, analysts said. 

 "I think hedge funds (selling the currency) are encouraged by the fact that Malaysia does not have a well thought-out policy on the ringgit," said Danial Lian, regional economist with NatWest Markets in Singapore. 

 He cited contradictory statements by Mahathir and half-hearted policy moves by the government. 

 Dealers said they were surprised by Mahathir's remarks on Friday, following his recent stinging verbal attacks on speculators and the introduction of capital control measures. 

 Bank Negara last week introduced its first capital control measure in three years, ordering local banks to limit non-trade-related currency swaps to $2.0 million with each overseas customer, in an attempt to reduce foreigners access to the ringgit.

title: BANK NEGARA MALAYSIA SELLS DOLLAR/RINGGIT -DEALERS.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Aug 8 (Reuter) - Malaysia's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market to sell the dollar in late afternoon trade to defend the ringgit following strong bids for the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 The said Bank Negara sold the dollar/ringgit through an agent bank at 2.6500/10 at 0900 GMT. 

 "The selling was quite aggressive and I think they are still in the market offering dollar/ringgit," said a European bank dealer in Singapore. 

 No confirmation was available from Bank Negara, which does not normally comment on its open market operations. 

 Dealers said they were quite surprised over the central bank intervention as the dollar was not rising too fast. 

 "Probably Negara does not want the dollar to go above the recent high of 2.6530," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank. 

 At 0930 GMT, the ringgit was at 2.6498/10 to a dollar, after hitting a high of 2.6520. 

 The ringgit remained under pressure after falling sharply overnight on rumours, later denied, that central bank governor Ahmad Mohamed Don had resigned. 

 Bank Negara's support of the ringgit followed Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's remark on Thursday that he was concerned with the sharp fall in the ringgit. 

 Dealers said dollar bids from offshore players as well as local corporates were evident throughout the day. This was met by some dollar sales by exporters around the 2.6500 level, they said. 

 Dealers said given the current weak fundamentals in Malaysia and bullish dollar sentiment, the ringgit could be heading for 2.70 against the dollar in the near term.

title: Malaysia Ringgit Slightly Higher; Seen Weak Enough
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (AP-Dow Jones)--The Malaysian ringgit was up slightly against the U.S. dollar in late trading Wednesday as investors in London picked up the currency on what one trader there suspected was the feeling that, for now at least, 'ringgit weakness has gone far enough.' 

 In Malaysia, a dealer said she suspected investors feared Bank Negara Malaysia, which hasn't been seen intervening to defend the currency for some time, would step in if the dollar rose to 2.6450 ringgit. And that was keeping some from trying to push the dollar higher. 

 But she noted that investors were aware the dollar's general strength against the major currencies should spill over and make it more valuable against the ringgit. 'There's no reason to sell dollars,' the dealer noted. 

 She said there were rumors that bank heads were to meet with Bank Negara Malaysia on Thursday. 'People are worried they might come out with more restrictions,' she said. 

 An economist said there were other rumors that the central bank would be meeting with Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim, who is also deputy prime minister, to assess the impact of the curbs imposed Monday in ringgit swap trading. 

 Dealers agreed that these rumors were keeping many wary of taking positions. 

 Around 0820 GMT (4:20 a.m. EDT), the dollar was at 2.6325 ringgit, down slightly from 2.6335 ringgit late Tuesday and down still further from 2.6405 ringgit early Wednesday. 

 The dollar has traded between 2.6305 ringgit and 2.6430 ringgit during the day.
