title: Malaysia/Swap Curbs/Amplifier -2: Mahathir Hinted At Move
text:
The ringgit has been battered around since mid-May by a speculative attack on regional currencies, as well as genuine outflows of investors on fears of economic troubles of the same sort rattling Thailand. 

 Although the central bank first fought back by using intervention to try to keep the ringgit from sliding below 2.5250 ringgit/dollar, it was draining its reserves, which fell about 12% in the first two weeks of July. The defense of 2.5250 ringgit was abandoned July 14. 

 U.S. investment bank Merrill Lynch estimated at the time that Malaysia only has enough reserves for three days of intervention, assuming that in defending its currency the central bank wouldn't be willing to allow its foreign reserves to fall below a minimum level of three months-worth of import cover. 

 Economists and currency analysts didn't think the fall in the ringgit was damaging enough to require Malaysia to adopt restrictions on ringgit trading and many doubted authorities would move to institute them on fears that it would taint the country's sought-after image as a free financial center. 

 But they also noted that with Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's tough talk against currency speculators in recent days, he risked damaging his own credibility if he didn't follow through. 

 'Judging by the rhetoric, you would have assumed something would be done,' said Daragh Maher, economist at ING Barings. 

 Indeed, the rhetoric gave many swap market players the chance to adjust positions in the weeks ahead of Monday's move by Bank Negara, traders said. They were thus better prepared than in May, when Thailand's imposition of capital curbs caught many currency traders by surprise. 

 A senior economist at a foreign brokerage house, who declined to be named, said his sources told him the central bank fought against imposing controls but Mahathir, who had come home last month from a two-month vacation abroad to find the ringgit about 5% weaker, 'made a lot of noise with them to come up with something.'

title: Malaysia PM Attacks On Speculators Reflect Limited Options
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (AP-Dow Jones)--Since Malaysia's Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad returned from a two-month vacation last week to find the Malaysian currency about 5% weaker, he has fought back the only way economists believe he can - by trying to 'talk up' the ringgit. 

 Mahathir has discounted the notion that speculators and investors have been moving out of regional currencies because of genuine fears about regional economic problems and instead has insisted it has been a politically-motivated response to the decision by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to admit Burma to the grouping. 

 He has pledged to take action against such 'rogue speculators' and 'anarchists,' singling out prominent U.S. hedge fund operator George Soros in particular. 

 But with the central bank's reserves down 12% in the first two weeks of July, such 'verbal intervention' may the only option for Malaysian leaders, economists say. Bank Negara Malaysia, the central bank, simply can't afford to intervene anymore to prop up the ringgit. 

 'These vague threats are a way of introducing uncertainty into the minds of speculators,' says an economist, who declined to be named because of the sensitivity of criticizing government policy in Malaysia. 

 'They are still trying to talk (the ringgit) up.' 

 Over the past few days, Mahathir's cries against speculators has grown increasingly shrill. 

 'We have worked 20 to 40 years to develop our countries to this level and along comes the man with a few billion U.S. dollars and, within a period of two weeks, he has undone almost the work we have done,' Mahathir charged. 'As a result, the poor people in these countries will suffer and these are the people that have to be protected from George Soros, who has so much money and power but (is) totally thoughtless.'

'There was the usual rhetoric about speculators,' the official said. 'But the point was made a world full of mobile capital is a difficult and dangerous world for central banks that intervene.' 

 The Bank of Japan officials argued against intervention to defend the currency in all cases - arguing that its experience of intervening in the markets showed that the best policy is to let the currency find a bottom and only then give it a boost when it's already headed higher. 

 An official in the Bank of Japan's international department confirmed that is the BOJ attitude - based on its past experience, it's better to let the currency find a bottom or a ceiling rather than try to pinpoint a certain level via intervention, he said. 

 Despite heavy intervention to stem speculative pressures, Thailand, the Philippines and Malaysia have all been forced this month to abandon efforts to support their currencies

 If created, the EMEAP fund would likely be of greatest immediate interest to Thailand and the Philippines, both struggling with the aftermath of the decisions to float their currencies. Thailand announced this week it will seek help from the IMF to right its economy after the plunge of the baht. The Philippines has already stepped up its borrowings from the IMF to rebuild reserves that were depleted in defending the peso. 

 But such an EMEAP fund would likely come with strings attached, according to the central bank official. 

 Japan in particular insisted at the meeting that any EMEAP money wouldn't be used to fight currency speculators. It would only be used to further IMF-inspired economic adjustments - though that was loosely defined at the meeting, according to the official. 

 The money, which would likely go into reserve accounts at the central bank, could be used to fund a budget deficit or provide funds for the banking sector. 

 Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita led the Japanese delegation. After the meeting, BOJ executive director Takashi Anzai told reporters that EMEAP had only agreed to 'study' the issue of extra funding for countries in difficulty.

title: Malaysian PM lashes out at  currency  speculators.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, July 24 (Reuter) - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad on Thursday launched a bitter attack on "rogue speculators" whom he accused of undermining Southeast Asian economies by destabilising their currencies. 

 Opening the 30th foreign ministerial meetings of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), Mahathir said: "We see a well-planned effort to undermine the economies of all the ASEAN countries by destabilising their currencies. 

 "Our economic fundamentals are good, yet anyone with a few billion dollars can destroy all the progress that we have made," he said. 

 Malaysia and neighbouring countries have seen attacks on their currencies in the past month, forcing devaluations in Thailand and the Philippines and expensive intervention efforts in Malaysia. 

 On Thursday, regional currencies dropped to new lows as speculators and corporates continued to pile into the dollar, triggering stop-loss orders. No signs of central bank intervention were yet detected on Thursday. 

 The Thai baht dropped to a low of 32.63/dollar onshore, the Singapore dollar fell below the psychological level of 1.4700 on stop-loss sales while the Malaysian ringgit breached the 2.65 barrier in early trade on spillover weakness from Thailand and Singapore. 

 The Indonesian rupiah slipped back through the 2,600 support level on Thursday. 

 Mahathir, known for his sharp-tongued criticisms of the West, said the countries of the region were told they must open up their markets and that trade and commerce must be totally free. 

 "Free for whom? For rogue speculators. For anarchists wanting to destroy weak countries in their crusade for open societies, to force us to submit to the dictatorship of international manipulators," Mahathir told the ASEAN gathering. 

 "We want to embrace borderlessness but we still need to protect ourselves from self serving rogues and international brigandage," he said. 

 Mahathir did not mention any speculators by name in his speech. 

 Malaysia is the current chairman of ASEAN, which was expanded on Wednesday to nine members with the inclusion of Laos and Burma. Its other members are Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Indonesia, Brunei and Singapore.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals weak in late trade.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 23 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies remained on slippery ground in late Wednesday trade after coming under renewed pressure as the Thai baht slid to new lows, forex dealers said. 

 Poor market liquidity and wide spreads added to market volatility as players turned increasingly nervous ahead of an Asian central bankers meeting in Shanghai on Friday. 

 Expectations the meeting might result in some form of coordinated intervention to counter the speculative onslaught on the region's currencies kept the dollar well bid, dealers said. 

 "The big issue for the market at the moment is this meeting in Shanghai as there is the possibility of concerted intervention or a statement that they are willing to join hands to support currencies," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in Singapore. 

 In Thailand, the central bank intervened to stem the baht's slide as the currency was pulled down by heavy commercial demand for dollars in the domestic market. 

 "We noticed the central bank intervened to stop the baht's fall at around the 32.50/32.60 to the dollar level," a senior dealer at a local bank in Bangkok said. 

 The baht hit a record low earlier with some dealers reporting transactions at as low as 32.60 to the dollar. At 1050 GMT, it was quoted at 32.250/32.550 onshore and 31.500/31.550 offshore. 

 Dealers attributed the sharp plunge in the onshore market maqinly to sales by importers seeking dollars to pay their bills and by corporations needing the dollar to repay foreign loans. 

 They said the central bank did not need to sell large amounts of dollars to curb the baht's fall because the pressure on the currency was mainly from local players trading in small amounts. 

 A senior Thai central bank official attributed the baht's weak tone to poor first-half earnings reported by local banks and finance companies. 

 The Singapore dollar succumbed to fresh selling after comments by Finance Minister Richard Hu which players treated as yet another signal to buy the U.S. dollar. 

 Hu told parliament Singapore dollar's exchange rate was determined by market forces and its recent appreciation against its neighbours, especially the baht and Indonesian rupiah, did not pose a significant threat to its competitiveness. 

 "Our exchange rate policy should not be guided by short-term expediency considerations. We always focus on managing the exchange rate of the Singapore dollar on a trade-weighted basis with a medium-term perspective," Hu said. 

 The Singapore dollar fell to a low of around 1.4690 to the U.S. dollar after the comments, compared with 1.4645 earlier. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was hit by fresh waves of selling by offshore U.S. banks despite talk that Bank Negara Malaysia had intervened to sell dollars around 2.6350/70 ringgit. 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.6355/85 to the dollar against a morning low of 2.6230. 

 "We are not sure if there is any intervention at all. The said banks could be taking their own positions," a dealer at a Malaysian bank in Kuala Lumpur said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah remained weak after being dragged down by the slump in the baht. Spot rupiah was at 2,587/97 against an opening of 2,570/80. 

 "We saw some central bank intervention at the 2,580 level which helped boost the rupiah to 2,540 level in late morning, but uncertainty in Thailand kept the dollar tone biddish," a U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said. 

 "If the rupiah could break the 2,500 resistance level, then there is potential for a strong comeback. But if it falls below the 2,600 level, speculators would launch an attack to test the band again," a local bank dealer said. 

 The Philippine peso fell on commercial demand for dollars, closing at 28.50 to the dollar against 28.15 previously. 

 Manila traders said there was no sign of central bank intervention and the peso remained under pressure despite new rulings aimed at encouraging dollar sales and curbing speculation.

title: Troubled regional Asian  currencies  recover poise.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 22 (Reuter) - Strife torn Southeast Asian currencies recovered some of their poise on Tuesday as operators decided it was time to bank some profits on the U.S. dollar's recent sharp rise. 

 Despite calmer and more stable conditions, dealers and economists were still jittery and said the risk to the downside still loomed large for most of the region's currencies. 

 The market is awaiting the Asian central bankers meeting in Shanghai later this week which could well come up with major league verbal intervention by the authorities in an attempt to stop the rot. 

 "This wave of contagion hitting the regional currencies will be a relatively long running affair. The danger is that this is a temporary calm we're seeing," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at BZW Asia. 

 Supple said the central bankers meeting could yield strong verbal support for the region's currencies but added that he did not expect it to result in actual coordinated intervention. 

 "There's a broad-based reassessment of risk-reward valuations in the region. Given that genuine funds are leaving as well as speculators, that significantly increases the cost to the real economy of any intervention," he said. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit received a boost from Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's displeasure with the recent speculative assault on the currency. 

 News reports quoted Mahathir, due to return to Malaysia on Tuesday after a two-month absence, as saying there may have been a political agenda behind the recent moves in regional currency markets. 

 "That's a very strong statement from him. So those funds which were very long (dollars) from below the 2.60 level started to take profit," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.6200 to the dollar at 0445 GMT against 2.6270 at its Kuala Lumpur close on Monday. 

 The Singapore dollar firmed above the 1.46 level against its U.S. counterpart as players turned less bearish after the release of better-than-expected trade data on Monday. 

 Dealers said wariness of possible central bank resistance was also preventing operators from pushing the Singapore dollar down towards 1.47 to the U.S. dollar. 

 He said local corporates had sold about $100 million from the 1.4635 level, but the U.S. dollar was likely to meet fresh buying interest around 1.4550. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah hovered around the 2,600 to the dollar level after an aggressive speculative attack on Monday. 

 "It's a fight to break the 2,600 resistance level for the rupiah. Singapore players are defending the resistance. We are waiting to see who has more bullets," a U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said. 

 The rupiah became the latest victim of a speculative attack, plunging about 150 points to a historic 2,665 low against the dollar before staging a marginal recovery on central bank intervention. 

 Indonesian Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said on Tuesday the attack on the rupiah was not related to fundamentals and the government had no plans to change its monetary policy. 

 The Thai baht lost ground in domestic markets, where players returned from a long weekend fretting about the impending release of data on financial institutions' non-performing loans. The baht was quoted at 30.880/30.980 to the dollar in the local market versus 30.42/30.47 baht late Friday.

 Singapore's non-oil domestic exports rose a nominal 8.8 percent year-on-year in June against forecasts of a 6.3 percent nominal rise after May's 1.0 percent fall. 

 Comments by government officials predicting a turnaround in global electronics demand in the coming months also supported sentiment, dealers said. 

 Electronic exports account for about 70 percent of Singapore's non-oil domestic exports.

title: FOCUS-Bank Negara reserves fall after  intervention .
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, July 22 (Reuter) - Bank Negara Malaysia's foreign exchange reserves fell by 12.5 percent in the fortnight to July 15, confirming market estimates of the size of central bank's recent interventions to defend the ringgit. 

Malaysia's central bank announced on Tuesday that its foreign exchange, gold and other reserves fell to 61.9 billion ringgit as at July 15, 1997, compared to 70.71 billion ringgit a fortnight earlier. 

 Bank Negara is estimated to have spent over $2.0 billion in defending the ringgit in the last few weeks against speculators who have been selling down all currencies in Southeast Asia. 

 "This just proves what the market has been believing. In U.S. dollar terms two to three billion is what they (Bank Negara) have spent in the last few weeks, from mid-May to second week of July," said Daniel Lian, regional economist with NatWest Markets in Singapore. 

 The pressure on the ringgit increased over the last two weeks after Thailand allowed the baht to float and the Philippines widened the peso's trading band, both effectively devaluing their currencies. 

 On July 8, Bank Negara struck heavily against speculators, selling between $1 billion to $2 billion to prop up the ringgit. 

 After an initial defence, Bank Negara since last week has allowed the ringgit to fall against the dollar. The Malaysian unit fell to a 38-month low of 2.6450 to a dollar on Friday, or over 5.5 percent lower than the 2.5050 level two weeks ago. 

 At 0900 GMT on Tuesday, the ringgit was at 2.6225/45 to a dollar. 

 Economists said the fall in reserves will not have any impact on the economy as Malaysia's reserves were more than adequate to provide it a comfortable import cover. 

 "It is not a shocking number. It will not have very much impact on the economy," said Lian. 

 "Normally a decline in reserves means a decline in money supply. That can be offset by more generous injections of liquidity into the system," he said. 

 With the decline of nearly nine billion ringgit ($3.46 billion) in its foreign exchange reserves, "it (the intervention) could not have gone on for too long," said Eddie Lee, chief economist at Vickers Ballas in Singapore. 

Foreign exchange reserves as at July 15, 1996 amounted to 66.68 billion ringgit, showing a fall of 4.78 billion ringgit on a year-on-year basis. 

 Total assets stood at 96.82 billion ringgit on July 15 against 100.99 billion ringgit on June 30, but were slightly higher than 95.72 billion ringgit a year ago. 

Currency in circulation stood at 22.07 billion ringgit, compared to 21.95 billion ringgit in June. 

 "It actually does not mean the country is any poorer, if the ringgit recovers, they (Bank Negara) could recoup the losses," said Lian. 

 Economists said they applauded Bank Negara's policy of not defending the ringgit further. 

 "In the past week Bank Negara has let the ringgit float more freely. Already they have chosen the wiser path," said Lee at Vickers Ballas.

title: KL overnight steady at 8.7 pct, Negara seen lending.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, July 22 (Reuter) - The overnight interbank rate was steady at 8.7 percent on Tuesday with the central Bank Negara seen injecting fresh funds into the market, dealers said. 

 "Bank Negara is lending funds at 8.7 percent and this is capping the overnight at that level," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank. 

 Agent banks of Bank Negara were seen lending one-month funds in the morning, pulling interbank rates lower. 

 Earlier, one-month money was at 8.5 percent against 9.0/9.3 percent on Monday. 

 The three-month rate was at 8.0/8.3 percent against 8.0/9.0 percent. 

 Dealers said there was room for more downside. 

 "Rates should come off further but the fall is expected to be gradual," said another dealer. 

 He expects the one-month to stablise around 8.0 percent. 

 Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim said last week that Malaysia did not favour a high interest rate regime. 

 Dealers said direction of interbank rates would continue to be determined by the central bank's operations. 

 "It's a matter of how quickly Bank Negara wants rates to fall and to what level," one said. 

 Bank Negara was said to have injected funds over the past week to help ease market tightness. 

 Recent heavy buying of the ringgit by the central bank to defend the currency from speculative attack had caused a liquidity squeeze. 

 Bank Negara said on Tuesday its foreign exchange reserves fell to 61.9 billion ringgit as at July 15 against 70.71 billion a fortnight earlier, which confirmed market estimates of the size of its interventions. 

 Interest rate futures on the Malaysia Monetary Exchange were steady after recent gains. 

 At 0800 GMT, the three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) September contract was unchanged at 92.43, or an implied yield of 7.57 percent. 

 The December contract was also unchanged at 92.64, or 7.36 percent.

text:
Because the reserves were released in ringgit, they may mask an even steeper drop in foreign reserves in dollar terms because of the plunge in the ringgit's value between June 30 and July 15. One economist said the central bank may have spent as much as U.S.$4 billion defending the ringgit. 

 'This is astronomical,' TA's Loh added. 

 'Now you know why they couldn't afford to defend the ringgit any more,' said Sani Hamid, emerging markets analyst at MMS International. 'Ten billion ringgit is a lot to throw down the drain.' 

 Daragh Maher, economist at ING Barings, said the loss highlights the cost of intervening and reveals what little it achieves. 

 And TA's Loh said it will make intervening more difficult in the future. 

 U.S. investment bank Merrill Lynch said in a report Tuesday that Malaysia only has enough reserves for three days of intervention, assuming that in defending its currency the central bank wouldn't be willing to allow its foreign reserves to fall below a minimum level of three months-worth of import cover. 

 Economists suspected the revelation could lead to further pressure on the central bank, which has already been widely criticized for the confusing way in which it announced loan curbs to the property market in April - in an attempt to head off a financial crisis like the one that has rattled Thailand. 

 That announcement of property curbs sparked a sell-off in the stock market that was exacerbated by the subsequent attack on the ringgit. Malaysia's attempts to defend the currency and then its sudden desertion of its defenses fueled further selling of stocks, mostly because of confusion about central bank policies. 

 'I think there's going to be some repercussions,' one economist said. He and others said Bank Negara should have realized it was fighting a losing battle, noting that the speculators were taking on the entire region. 

 'Once Thailand caved in and the peso floated, it was hard to see how Malaysia could stem the tide on its own,' TA's Loh said.

title: Singapore Dollar Higher Late On Liquidity Squeeze
text:
SINGAPORE (AP-Dow Jones)--The Singapore dollar is higher against the U.S. dollar in late trading Monday afternoon compared with its level two hours ago. The Singapore currency is also higher than its level in early morning trading on a liquidity squeeze in the swaps market which has forced short term interest rates up to their highest levels in a year. 

 At 0915 GMT (5:15 p.m. EDT) the U.S. dollar is quoted at S$1.4615, a touch lower than its level in early afternoon trading and below S$1.4638 early Monday. 

 The U.S. dollar initially fell during morning trading as domestic market participants running substantial long U.S. dollar positions found sourcing Singapore dollar liquidity - to allow them further to short the currency - increasingly difficult. 

 'Everyone was on the same side of the market. With everyone short of Sing' dollars, financing the positions was becoming impossible,' said the chief regional currency trader at a major Asian bank in Singapore. 

 Under the squeeze, overnight rates on Singapore dollar deposits reached 7%-7.5%, from 3.625%-3.75% Friday. 

 The liquidity squeeze had the effect of capping the dollar's rise against Singapore's currency, which has seen the U.S. dollar appreciate by nearly 2.5% over the previous month. 

 'With interest rates this high, we are likely to see the dollar/Sing' rate capped at S$1.4680 for this week,' predicted a trader at a leading U.S. commercial bank in Singapore. 

 The Singapore dollar was also boosted in early afternoon trading by the release of better-than-expected trade figures. Singapore's non-oil domestic exports rose 8.8% in June from a year ago, besting economists' average forecast of a 7.0% improvement. 

 The effect was relatively short-lived, however, as the Singapore currency weakened when, as reported, the Singapore Trade Development Board said the government continues to monitor the Singapore dollar's real exchange rate, not its nominal rate against the U.S. dollar alone.

title: FOCUS - Ringgit stays weak after touching 33-mth low.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, July 15 (Reuter) - Malaysia's ringgit remained soft on Tuesday after hitting its weakest level in 33 months against the dollar, despite Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's supportive comments about the economy and currency, dealers and analysts said. 

 They said that although the ringgit recovered as funds took profits on the dollar, it remained vulnerable. 

 The ringgit touched 2.5700 per dollar overnight in New York, its weakest level since October 1994. But by 0600 GMT, the ringgit was trading around 2.5550/60 after closing at 2.5310/30 on Monday in Kuala Lumpur. 

 The Malaysian unit lost almost two percent against the dollar on Monday as speculators found a fresh target after attacking the Thai baht and Philippine peso. 

 Anwar said on Tuesday the ringgit was a victim of speculation and that it was not overvalued. 

 "My firm view is that under the prevailing economic and financial conditions, the ringgit is not overvalued," he told an Islamic capital market conference. 

 Anwar added that the Malaysian economy remained fundamentally sound due to policies long in place for balanced development and growth. 

 "Therefore, we are confident that once the speculative activity subsides, the trend for the ringgit will reverse to reflect the underlying favourable fundamentals," he said. 

 Anwar also stressed that while Malaysia was committed to ensure the ringgit would not fall prey to speculative activity, its policy of allowing market forces to determine the exchange rate remained unchanged. 

 "Given the speculative pressure on the ringgit, this is not surprising," said P.K. Basu, regional economist at UBS in Singapore. 

 "It's good not to be predictable. A flexible regime will make speculators think twice before hitting the ringgit," he said. 

 Dealers said the statement by Anwar reinforced their belief that the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, has swung its intervention strategy toward soothing intraday volatility, rather than vigorously defending a particular level. 

 Bank Negara sold dollars overnight through agents in New York at around 2.5700, dealers said. The central bank's presence was not detected this morning. 

 Dealers said the dollar/ringgit rate could reach 2.60 before it stablised, adding they expected trading to remain volatile in the short term. 

 "Speculators have won this battle, but not the war. Ultimately they will have to take profit. Then who will buy from them," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank. 

 Anwar said Malaysia did not favour a high interest rate regime in the long term. 

 "I don't think we are for (a) continued rise in interest rates, or a strong interest rate regime," he said, adding that the recent rise in interest rates was prompted by the recent speculative selling of the ringgit. 

 Analysts said that the rumoured injection of one-month funds by Bank Negara on Monday suggested that the central bank may be easing its defence of the ringgit in order to ensure that economic growth was not affected. 

 Bank Negara was believed to be lending funds to ease market liquidity and guide interest rates lower, market players said. 

 The benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) was fixed at 11.3 percent at 0300 GMT on Tuesday, down from 14.9 percent on Monday. 

 Interbank rates recently jumped to unusually high levels due to a sudden tightening of liquidity after massive intervention by the central bank in the foreign exchange market to defend the ringgit. 

 Although the actual size of the intervention was not known, dealers were estimating between $1 billion and $2 billion was drained from the system.

title: Southeast Asian  currencies  under siege.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 14 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies were hit by waves of selling on Monday as uncertainty following the Philippine peso's effective devaluation last week spread like wildfire through the region. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit fell to a 16-month low of 2.5500 to the dollar in early trade amid Bank Negara Malaysia's failure to intervene aggressively, dealers said. 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.5375/95 to the dollar at 0400 GMT against 2.5042/52 at its Kuala Lumpur close on Friday. 

 "It's crazy," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 "Because of the story of the Philippine peso, which they devalued last week, the market is expecting the ringgit and rupiah to follow suit," she added. 

 Another European bank dealer in Singapore said Bank Negara was heard to have sold dollars around the 2.5500 ringgit level. "But I think Negara was in just to slow down the fall rather than stop the flow," he said. 

 Dealers said the market was still long of dollars, leaving room for the ringgit to head lower. 

 They said Bank Negara may be allowing market forces to dictate the spot's value rather than defending the ringgit aggressively in the face of heavy selling interest. 

 Dealers estimate the Malaysian central bank spent over $1 billion to support the ringgit last week. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah rebounded from its early lows as offshore players began unloading dollars. 

 Dealers said offshore players seemed to be trying to cash out from the market after they drove the rupiah to a low of 2,469.0 on Monday morning. 

 "I think some feel that the rupiah is low enough for a buy back, reversing the market trend," a local bank dealer in Jakarta said.

 "Bank Indonesia (BI)'s band widening last week is not helping to strengthen the rupiah. With BI having the lowest reserves, the rupiah will be the next currency to attack," a Singapore-based dealer said. 

 The central bank widened its intervention band to 12 percent from eight percent last Friday, in what was seen as a move to pre-empt possible turbulence in the rupiah after speculative attacks on the peso and baht. 

 In the Philippines, the peso fell to a low of 29.75 to the dollar in thin trade as banks remained wary after the central bank's move on Friday to allow the peso-dollar rate to trade within a wider band. 

 Volume was a light nine million dollars after two-and-a-half hours of trading on Monday. 

 The central Bank of Thailand (BOT) intervened to stem the baht's fall in domestic markets, selling dollars at the 30.75-30.80 baht level, dealers said. 

 "The central bank intervened through a small local bank by selling the dollar at around 30.75-30.80," a European bank dealer in Bangkok said.

 Commercial dollar demand and lingering jitters from the peso slide pushed the baht to new lows. The currency was quoted at 30.500/30.800 to the dollar in the domestic market at 0400 GMT, after the intervention, against 30.00/30.60 late on Friday. 

 "The amount of intervention was insignificant. But it capped the baht at around 30.80," the dealer said.

title: Malaysia's Bank Negara Allows Ringgit To Slide: Amplifier
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (AP-Dow Jones)--Malaysia's central bank shocked the currency market Monday when it gave up the vigorous defence of the ringgit it had maintained over the past two months to cap the dollar at 2.5250 ringgit. 

 After the ringgit fell through that level early in Monday's session, without triggering intervention by Bank Negara Malaysia, the currency plunged on a wave of sell orders. 

 Speculators swiftly drove the dollar up to 2.5500 ringgit - the weakest level the rinngit has traded in about 18 months, according to economists. It was only then that the central bank stepped back in, capping the dollar with relatively modest sell orders of around $100 million, dealers said. 

 Dealers and some economists viewed the move as a tacit acceptance of a de facto ringgit devaluation. At its weakest point, the currency was down 1.8% from the 2.5047 ringgit/dollar level late Friday. The ringgit recovered some of its losses subsequently to trade around 2.5300 late Monday in Asia. 

 Others suspected Bank Negara was trying to lure in the speculators who have been putting downward pressure on the ringgit since mid-May, amid attacks on other regional currencies such as the Thai baht and Philippine peso. 

 They believe the central bank is simply biding its time before launching a crushing counter-attack that will force the dollar down towards 2.5000 ringgit. 

 'I think they're trying to squeeze the speculators,' says Neil Saker, head of regional economic research at SocGen-Crosby. 'Bank Negara are quite skilled. They'll certainly win this battle.' 

 He says the central bank wants to win the battle quickly, so it can get interest rates back down to more appropriate levels. On Monday, the daily weighted average 3-month interbank rate was at 16.40%, up from 13.40% Friday and at almost double Thursday's level of 8.60%.

title: Speculators seen targetting Malaysian ringgit next.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, July 11 (Reuter) - The Malaysian ringgit is likely to be the next target of currency speculators after they successfully forced two central banks in the region to devalue their currencies, analysts said on Friday. 

 But they said Malaysia's central bank would put up a tough fight. 

 Bank Negara has itself warned would be aggressive in its efforts to stamp out speculation in the ringgit. It is backed by economic fundamentals widely regarded as stronger than most other countries in the region. 

 Analysts said the failure of the Thai and Philippine central banks to defend their currencies could lead to greater pressures on the Malaysian currency. 

 The Philippine central bank said on Friday it would allow the peso to trade in a wider range against the U.S. dollar, with immediate effect. 

 Dealers saw the move as the second de facto devaluation of an Asian currency in less than two weeks. The move came nine days after Thailand's decision to stage a managed float float of the baht. 

 The Philippine move sent Southeast Asian currencies into a tailspin on Friday. At 0600 GMT, the ringgit was quoted at 2.5020/30 to a dollar after opening around 2.4930. 

 "The bet is on that the ringgit will be the next currency to fall prey to speculators," said Sani Hamid, market analyst at research house MMS International in Singapore. 

 "But Bank Negara will do all it can to defend the ringgit. They can also impose capital controls as a last resort," he added. 

 Bank Negara governor Ahmad Mohamed Don on Wednesday warned of tough steps, including increasing interest rates, to curb speculation in the ringgit. 

 On Tuesday, Bank Negara intervened aggressively in the foreign exchange market, spending an estimated $1.0 billion to help the ringgit. 

 Ahmad said the intervention was warranted in the interest of long-term stability, adding that the central bank had sufficient reserves to fund such interventions. 

 Analysts said speculators are betting that Bank Negara will not be able to sustain its dollar/ringgit interventions as reserves are drawn down. But some believe Malaysia has sufficient reserves to defend its currency. 

 Bank Negara's reserves at the end of June stood at 70.71 billion ringgit ($28.3 billion). 

 "That provides substantially more ammunition than is available to the Philippine central bank which had about $11.5 billion at the beginning of the pressure, and was down to about $10 billion yesterday," said P.K. Basu, director of regional economics at UBS Securities. 

 "I don't see the ringgit succumbing to the pressures emanating from the currency market," he said. 

 Analysts said speculators are also betting that Bank Negara would not revert to capital controls as this would prove a major setback to Kuala Lumpur's goal of becoming an internationally recognised capital market. 

 In 1994, faced with a strong flow of hot money into the country, Bank Negara imposed negative interest rates on foreign deposits, banned swaps and stopped foreigners from buying Malaysian government paper. 

 Analysts said a ringgit devaluation was also unlikely. 

 "I don't see the real justification for it," said Nathan Balakrishnan, general manager at SBB Unit Trust Management. "Some are trying to short the ringgit because they think sentiment might affect the ringgit, but not fundamentally. Fundamentally I think we are better than Thailand and the Philippines," he said. 

 Unlike Thailand and Philippines, Malaysia's current account deficit is funded by long-term inflows. 

 In addition, Malaysia is the only economy in the region which has been able to maintain a strong economic growth, having posted growth of more than eight percent a year in the past nine years. 

 Unlike the baht and peso, the ringgit has been a free-floating currency since 1971. 

 "I would emphasise that Malaysia has always had a flexible currency regime ... over the past one year, the ringgit has fluctuated about 2.5 percent above and below the dollar. In the past 10 years, it has moved 10 percent either side," said Basu.

title: FOCUS-Bank Negara strikes at ringgit speculators.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, July 8 (Reuter) - Malaysia's central bank on Tuesday intervened aggressively in the foreign exchange market to flush out ringgit speculators after defending the currency for nearly two weeks, dealers and analysts said. 

 They said Bank Negara's action sent the dollar down about 200 points against the ringgit within an hour. 

 Dealers said Bank Negara began hitting the market just after 0800 GMT in lots of $50 million each time. "They did not face much resistance until dollar/ringgit came down to 2.5100," said a dealer with a Singapore-based U.S. bank. 

 At 2.5100, there was some resistance and dollar/ringgit climbed back to 2.5145 before the central bank struck again around 0930 GMT, dealers said. 

 "It was amazing, it was as if everyone (speculators) had laid down arms after all the efforts (to pull down the ringgit)," said the U.S. bank dealer. 

 He said the volumes were not large throughout the afternoon and if Bank Negara stayed in the market in London and New York, where liquidity was low, it could effectively drive out speculative short ringgit positions from the market. 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.5060/70 to a dollar at 1130 GMT. 

 Dealers said they were not surprised over the central bank's action as dollar/ringgit was trading very close to 2.5250, the level at which Bank Negara had aggressively defended the ringgit, for most of the day. 

 Before the intervention, offshore players out of London were seen testing the authorities after acquiring ringgit through swaps to run their long dollar/ringgit positions, they said. 

 "It was a question of who would act or give way first. The battle may have just begun but Bank Negara has demonstrated it's not going to hold back its punches," said research house MMS International in its market commentary. 

 Some dealers said the central bank could have sold more than $2 billion since last week to defend the ringgit. 

 Last Wednesday, Bank Negara intervened in the foreign exchange market using its own name for the first time in many years, against its usual practice of using a broker or a bank. 

 The central bank could not be reached for comment. It does not usually comment on its open market operations. 

 "The message is: speculators, don't mess around with central banks," said Jimmy Koh, economist with research firm I.D.E.A. in Singapore. 

 "This move to wipe out speculators has been on the authorities' agenda," he said. 

 Dealers and analysts said it was likely the central bank, after squeezing speculators in the spot market, will come with another squeeze in the forward market. 

 "This will force these players who have borrowed ringgit at exorbitant levels to liquidate their positions. This effectively will flush out speculators with dollar/ringgit outright positions from the market," Koh said. 

 The authorities had expressed their concern over local banks' active involvement in the forward market. 

 Dealers said a fresh attack on the Malaysian currency had looked imminent as speculators were building up long ringgit positions on the swaps. 

 Such a position would allow speculators to sell ringgit without worrying about being squeezed by the central bank.

title: Bank Negara  intervenes  to protect ringgit.
text:

 It was the first time in many years that Bank Negara used its own name while intervening in the foreign exchange market. It usually uses a broker or some of Malaysia's biggest banks for its market operations, dealers said. 

 "Negara came out himself to sell the dollar instead of normal exercise of proxy," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore. 

 The intervention followed a sharp weakening in the baht after Thailand announced a managed float for the baht from Wednesday, allowing market forces to set the value of the currency. 

 Bank Negara bought ringgit at 2.5250 to the dollar, dealers said. The currency had weakened to that level on Wednesday and had tested it several times in the past week. Market players said the 2.5280-2.5300 level was viewed as a stronger barrier.

 The actual size of the intervention was not known but dealers believed the amount of dollars sold by Bank Negara was small. 

 No confirmation was available from the central bank, which does not usually comment on its intervention operations.

 He said the spillover effect of the baht float on regional currencies would be brief.

 Economists said after the ringgit came under speculative attack in May, Bank Negara and other regional central banks would not hesitate to show their presence in the market on any sign of an attack on their currencies. 

 In May, speculators unloaded the ringgit because of Thailand's financial crisis. Bank Negara intervened aggressively to stem the ringgit's losses, but dollar sales were done through agent banks. 

 The intervention saw the central bank's foreign reserves fall by 1.4 billion ringgit ($555 million) to 69.7 billion ringgit at end-May compared with a fortnight earlier.

title: Ringgit seen rising to 2.47 by year-end.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, July 1 (Reuter) - The Malaysian ringgit remained under pressure from selling by offshore players as well as concern over the Thai baht, but its weakness was seen as temporary, economists said on Tuesday. 

 Strong economic fundamentals and high interest rates in Malaysia would pull the ringgit out of the slump, they said, expecting the currency to hit 2.47-2.48 per dollar by the end of the year. 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.5240/50 a dollar at midday on Tuesday. 

 Economists said the ringgit has still not overcome the spillover effect of the baht crisis. The Thai currency came under severe attack by speculators in May which prompted intervention by the region's central banks. 

 "It's still pretty uncertain in Thailand. Baht sentiment is still pretty negative," said Sim Moh Siong, economist with Citibank in Singapore. "But the comparison between Thailand and Malaysia may not be justified." 

 Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said last month that the impact of the baht crisis would be temporary. The ringgit should not fall much "because the context of the Thai baht is different and the economic fundamentals are different," he said. 

 "Until we see stability in the baht, there will be a cloud over the regional currencies," said Desmond Supple, head of currency research at BZW in Singapore. 

 Bank Negara Malaysia intervened last Friday to support the ringgit at 2.5250. Foreign exchange dealers said there was talk that the central bank had placed more orders to sell the dollar at that level. 

 Economists said that by intervening, the central bank had reaffirmed its preference for a strong ringgit. 

 The ringgit was unlikely to weaken above 2.5300, they said. 

 The currency hit a 17-month high of 2.4680 on January 13, this year after ending 1996 at 2.5305. 

 Economists said the ringgit was currently undervalued and did not reflect the country's economic fundamentals. 

 "The economy is still among the strongest in the region and barring any fallout from the baht, the ringgit should trade below the 2.50 level," Supple said. 

 "We are looking at 2.47 by year-end," he said. 

 The Malaysian Institute of Economic Research, a government-backed think-tank, on Monday maintained its projection of Malaysia's real gross domestic product (GDP) growth at 8.2 percent in 1997 and 8.5 percent in 1998. GDP growth in 1996 was 8.2 percent. 

 Economists said the interest rate differential would also favour the ringgit. 

 Though local interbank rates have fallen from their highs in May, they were still much higher than those in neighbouring Singapore. 

 The benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur interbank offered rate stood at 7.50 percent on Tuesday, about four percentage points higher than in Singapore. 

 Some money market dealers said rates were being kept high by Bank Negara to ward off speculators because it would be expensive to maintain short ringgit positions. 

 "Interest rates in Malaysia have limited scope to come down because of the strong economy. And this should favour the ringgit," said Sim of Citibank. He expects the ringgit to trade at 2.48 a dollar by the end of the year.

title: Other Asians exposed if Thais forced to devalue.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 20 (Reuter) - If the political and economic turmoil in Thailand does leads to a devalution of the baht it would have regionwide repercussions, with Malaysia the first in the speculators' firing line, currency analysts said on Friday. 

 Many analysts said they thought Thailand would not devalue and that such a move would only come if it is forced to politically following the resignation of its finance and commerce ministers this week. 

 So far the government and central bank have held their firm currency line. But what if a devaluation does come? 

 The Malaysian authorites are aware the ringgit is at risk again and last week top Bank Negara officials met local and locally-incorported foreign banks over foreign exchange activities. 

 Analysts believe the central bank was whipping up support should the ringgit come under full-scale attack. News reports said the central bank had warned local banks not to lend money offshore for currency speculators. 

 "If baht jitters continue there could well be some more slippage of the ringgit, but after last week's meetings it's doubtful anyone will take a real pop at it," said one Singapore based analyst. "Bank Negara usually means business and things could get dangerous if you were short at the wrong time." 

 The Philippine peso is another possible target for selling and has indeed been hurt by the baht crisis, but like Bank Negara, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has already moved to stave off further pressure. 

 On Thursday the central bank raised its overnight borrowing rate to 15 percent from 12.75 percent after the peso slid as the baht came under pressure following the departure of Thai finance minister Amnuay Viravan. 

 Last month, it raised rates to a two-year high of 20 percent when the baht's weakness pressured the peso. 

 The Indonesian rupiah also stands out as a speculative target and has already suffered amid fears by offshore investors that Thailand's problems could spill over into Indonesia. 

 Analysts said Malaysia would be the first target because as well as some similar economic background factors, it also has a liberal enough exchange rate regime to allow speculators the liquidity they need to sell short. 

 "They do have some comparable economic figures," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "Speculators have been looking at Malaysia for some time now and the risk is obviously there if Thailand goes." 

 It was the ringgit which suffered most during the speculative attack on the baht in mid-May, prompting the central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, to intervene aggressively. 

 But the spirit of regional cooperation seems to be alive and well and analysts said speculators will remain wary of aggressive selling, particularly those which were stung by the Bank of Thailand's aggressive moves during the baht crisis. 

 Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu said on Thursday that Singapore would continue to help Thailand defend the baht against speculators. 

 "It's all very well looking at these currencies and seeing which is the most vulnerable, but after what Richard Hu said yesterday you have to be careful before taking a big position," said one forex trader at a leading European bank. 

 "You would certainly see the likes of the ringgit take a hit if we get a Thai devaluation, but you could get hit by intervention from every side...they've acted in concert before they could well do it again."

title: Malaysia /Bank Negara -2: Shows Less  Intervention  -Economist

Daragh Maher, an economist at ING Baring Securities (Singapore) Pte. Ltd., said the increase in Bank Negara's gold, foreign exchange and other reserves seemed to show that the central bank hadn't intervened very much in the currency market recently. 

 'While the increase in foreign reserves is only marginal, it does indicate that Bank Negara has not had to intervene so aggressively in the Forex market to support the ringgit,' said Maher. 

 As reported earlier, Maher said the previous half-month's decline in the central bank's gold, foreign exchange and other reserves had partly been caused by Bank Negara's efforts to support the ringgit in the latter part of May. 

 Bank Negara Malaysia announced June 10, its gold, foreign exchange and other reserves added up 69.71 billion ringgit as of May 31, down from 71.13 billion ringgit on May 15, 1997. 

 Bank Negara used its reserves to buy ringgit, and also pushed up interest rates, to protect the Malaysian currency as it had weakened in a spillover effect from speculators who were also attacking the Thai baht in mid-May. 

 The attack weakened the ringgit beyond the point where, on May 14, the U.S. dollar was fetching 2.5245 ringgit which dealers said forced the central bank to intervene. 

 The central bank's efforts paid off and the ringgit regained some of its strength against the dollar, so that it was trading at for 2.4865 ringgit two days later on May 16. 

 Since then, and despite continued economic problems in Thailand, many dealers say that while Bank Negara has continued to monitor the currency closely, it hasn't intervened in any major way, if at all, as the fear of speculators seems to be abating and the ringgit hasn't weakened dramatically.

title: Malaysia Ringgit/Late -2: Strong Dollar Environment Seen
text:
A Hong Kong-based dealer said Tuesday trading, although more subdued than Monday's dealings, was still influenced by the 'strong dollar environment,' caused by the weekend French elections. 

 The Hong Kong dealer noted that the dollar had in general gained against the majors since the weekend, with many foreign funds buying dollars on increased jitters surrounding Europe's planned 1999 currency union. 

 Dealers noted that, as the ringgit is closely linked to the majors, when the U.S. currency gains, or depreciates, against the majors, it usually follows the same trend against the ringgit. 

 A locally-based dealer said this recent strong demand for the dollar had also kept many local players out of the market Tuesday, because they were 'confused about the market direction.' 

 Dealers said unless there is some domestic news to influence the market, they again expect Wednesday dealings to be dominated by the 'dollar play,' with the U.S. currency trading in a narrow range of between 2.5150 ringgit and 2.5200 ringgit. 

 Some dealers said they thought the dollar could break above 2.5200 ringgit, but they were unsure whether it would stay much above this level, owing to many player's belief that Malaysia's central bank could intervene to check the market at this level, by selling dollars and buying ringgit. 

 Bank Negara didn't openly intervene in the money market Tuesday. 

 In the money market, at the late morning fixing, the one-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rates (Klibor) were at 8.02%, up from 7.89% Monday. The three-month Klibor were at 7.96%, up from 7.85% Monday, while the six-month Klibor were at 7.89%, also up from 7.81% Monday. 

 The overnight rate, which indicates short-term liquidity conditions, closed at 8.5%, unchanged from Monday.

title: KL overnight steady after fall in interbank rates.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, May 27 (Reuter) - The overnight interbank rate was steady at 8.8/9.0 percent due to improved liquidity and a fall in interbank rates in the morning session, dealers said. 

 The overnight indicated that interbank rates were returning to normalcy after two weeks of turbulence in the foreign exchange markets. 

 The fall in rates started on Monday after heavy lending by big local banks in the one-month segment, said to be on behalf of the central bank. 

 No confirmation was available from Bank Negara Malaysia as it does not comment on its market intervention operations. 

 The intervention helped bring down the overnight rate to around nine percent on Monday from 18/20 before the weekend. 

 This brought down other interbank rates on Tuesday morning. 

 The dealers said movement of swaps to the left and continued lending by big banks aided in the easing of interbank rates. 

 One-week money was at 8.0/9.0 percent against 10/11 percent previously and two-week was at 8.0/9.0 percent against 9.0/11.0 percent. 

 One-month was at 7.5/8.0 percent against 8.5/9.0, while three-month and six-month were steady at 7.5/8.0 percent. 

 The overnight rate on Monday fell to 8.0/8.5 percent from 18/20 percent on Friday. 

 "It helped that swaps have also been moving left (or easing) in the last few days," said a dealer with another Malaysian bank. 

 One-month swaps were quoting at 35/40 points on Tuesday, which translated into an implied yield of 7.3/4 percent, dealers said. A few days ago one-month had touched a high of 500, which implied a yield of 20 percent. 

 "The swaps are back to normal and so are the interbank rates," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore. 

 He said the markets had calmed down after the interest rate rises caused by an aggressive central bank intervention to prevent the ringgit's fall two weeks ago. The central bank was said to have sold around $1 billion. 

 The intervention drained liquidity from the system, causing the market to be short, and interbank rates to rise to unusually high levels, dealers said. 

 Interest rate futures on the Malaysia Monetary Exchange were mixed as the selling triggered by interest rate falls were countered by covering of positions, futures dealers said. 

 At the close, the three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) contract for June 1997 was unchanged at 92.49, or an implied yield of 7.51 percent. 

 September 1997 contract was down one point at 92.60, or 7.40 percent and December was down two at 92.60, or 7.40 percent.

title: S.E. Asia Central Bks/Baht -2: Tighter Monetary Policy
text:
The Bank of Thailand was joined by the other members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in supporting the Thai central bank in its defence of the currency, Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said early Friday. The Monetary Authority of Singapore described the intervention as 'effective'. 

 But the sources said the coup de grace of the banks' operations was the squeeze in short term interest rates engineered Thursday and Friday in Thailand, Malaysia and the Philippines. 

 'I'm less impressed with the intervention and more impressed with the rise in Thailand's interest rates,' said the senior foreign exchange trader at a U.S. investment bank, speaking on condition of anonymity. '(The Bank of Thailand) dried up liquidity to punish the speculators,' he said. 

 Overt measures by the Bank of Thailand - urging domestic banks not to lend baht to offshore counterparties at rates less then 1,000% - ensured that many speculators who wanted to liquidate short positions in the Thai currency could do so only at an unacceptable cost. 

 Bank Negara has also pushed up short-term interest rates to defend the ringgit, though it was quick to deny suggestions Friday that it was penalizing offshore players in the ringgit swaps market. Bank Indonesia issued a similar denial Friday. 

 And the Philippine central bank jacked up its overnight interest rates in stages to 20% by Friday from 12% Wednesday, steadying the Philippine peso by the end of the day. 

 Regional currency dealing rooms were frantic Friday as liquidity in the forward and swap markets evaporated. 

 'The (local) banks were quoting such ridiculous spreads... basically Thailand and Malaysia were barricading their capital accounts (from offshore players),' said Chia Wooh Khien, treasury economist at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken (South East Asia) Ltd. in Singapore. 

 The sources agreed the effect of sharply higher short-term interest rates in Malaysia and Thailand had much the same effect Friday as a temporary imposition of exchange controls. 'This hasn't been a natural market,' said StanChart's Van der Wath.

title: Malaysia Ringgit/Late -2: Confusion Surrounds Klibor
text:
Most dealers said the main reason for the strong appreciation in the
ringgit Friday, had been the continued high Kuala Lumpur Interbank
Offered Rates (Klibor).



Many overseas and local dealers believe the central bank raised the
three main Klibor on Thursday, to support its rumored intervention
earlier in the week, by drawing players to the local currency and so
keeping it from weakening further.


 The ringgit had depreciated significantly Wednesday in what dealers said was a 'spillover effect' from the problems surrounding the Thai baht. 

 And many dealers widely believe Malaysia's central bank intervened Wednesday at around the 2.5248-ringgit-level, to stop the dollar appreciating above this level. 

 Friday's money market was filled with confusion surrounding the Klibor. At the late morning fixing, the one-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rates (Klibor) were quoted as dropping slightly to 7.57%, down from 7.59% Thursday. The three-month Klibor were quoted at 7.53%, from 7.60% Thursday, while the six-month Klibor were at 7.53%, also down from 7.60% Thursday. 

 But despite this apparent fall in the Klibor, many dealers said most banks were charging higher rates than those in the fixing. 

 A dealer at a local bank said many banks had been too busy trading early Friday and hadn't had time to input their rates into the fixing average. He added that the one-month Klibor at his bank was 9.0%, the three-month Klibor was 8.5%, while the six-month Klibor were also at 8.5%. 

 Bank Negara didn't openly intervene in the money market Friday.

title: Malaysia Ringgit/Early -2: Klibor Slightly Lower
text:
The Hong Kong-based dealer said he thought the central bank's action in raising the Klibor Thursday was a 'signal to speculators that they shouldn't attack the ringgit' like they have the Thai baht. 

 Dealers said they widely believed Malaysia's central bank had intervened Wednesday at the 2.5248-ringgit level, to stop the dollar strengthening above this level. 

 And a Singapore-based dealer said he thought the increase in the Klibor Thursday to levels not seen since February 1993 was to help further strengthen the ringgit. 

 In the money market Friday, at a later fixing than usual, all three Klibor were slightly lower. The one-month Klibor were at 7.57%, lower slighlty from 7.59% Thursday. The three-month Klibor were at 7.53%, also down from 7.60% Thursday, while the six-month Klibor also came down to 7.53%, from Thursday's 7.60%. 

 At around 0109 GMT (9:09 p.m. EDT) Friday, the local currency reached a high of 2.4730 ringgit. This means that from its level of 2.5245 ringgit late Wednesday to Friday's high, the ringgit has strengthened by 2.0% over the past two days. 

 A locally-based dealer said he didn't think the ringgit would strengthen much in later trading Friday, after the dramatic movements of the past few days. And he thought the dollar would trade between 2.4910 ringgit and 2.4950 ringgit for the rest of Friday dealings.

title: Malaysia/Stock Mkt -2: Investors Leaving Southeast Asia
text:
As Thailand's economy has slowed, so has demand for property, leading to defaults on property loans that have crippled some banks. Analysts say foreign investors who missed the warning signs in Thailand don't want to make the same mistake in Malaysia. 

 'The central bank's move focused people's attention on potential problem areas,' said Simon Woods, senior investment adviser at Caspian Securities (Hong Kong) Ltd. 'That has sparked negative vibes toward Malaysia.' 

 So, after Thai share prices plunged Wednesday, following an attack on the baht that sent shudders through other Southeast Asian currency markets, analysts said four major foreign funds decided to sell off large holdings in Malaysia's market Thursday morning. 

 'They're just getting rid of them. They're just doing it at whatever price they can,' said Jonathan Duckett, a member of the institutional sales team at Mohaiyani Research Sdn. Bhd. 'They just want to get out of Southeast Asia.' 

 Although economists and analysts insist the possibility of a financial crisis in Malaysia on the order of Thailand's is still unlikely for now, they believe investors don't want to take any chances. 

 'It makes people nervous,' said an analyst at a foreign brokerage house, who declined to be identified. 'You don't trust your instincts.' 

 Added Alex Tan, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell: 'Foreign investors are becoming risk-averse to the market. Now people are starting to run first, before they assess any measures.' 

 Rumors that Thailand would devalue its currency have also shaken investors in the Malaysian market who fear such a move would spook foreign investors out of the region even faster. 

 The Malaysian currency weakened Wednesday, as participants in the currency market moved into safer currencies, such as the U.S. and Singapore dollars. But dealers said Bank Negara Malaysia then intervened Wednesday to keep the ringgit from weakening beyond 2.5248 ringgit per U.S. dollar.

title: Malaysia Ringgit Higher Vs U.S. Dollar In Late Trading
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (AP-Dow Jones)--The Malaysian ringgit was higher against the U.S. dollar in late trading Thursday, boosted by various factors, including a sharp rise in interbank rates. 

 Dealers and economists said Bank Negara had pushed up the rates to levels not seen since February 1993, to draw players to the local currency and keep it from weakening further. 

 The ringgit weakened significantly Wednesday in what dealers said was a 'spillover effect' from the problems surrounding the Thai baht. 

 Dealers said they widely believed Malaysia's central bank had intervened Wednesday at around the 2.5248-ringgit level, to stop the dollar strengthening above this level. 

 And many said that Malaysia's central bank had raised all three main Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rates Thursday, to support Wednesday's rumored intervention and make the local currency more attractive for investors. 

 Around 0750 GMT (03:50 a.m. EDT), the dollar was at 2.5065 ringgit, down from 2.5245 ringgit late Wednesday and 2.5177 ringgit early Thursday. 

 In the money market, at the late morning fixing, the one-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rates were at 7.59%, up sharply from 7.30% Wednesday. The three-month Klibor jumped to 7.60% from 7.36%, while the six-month Klibor also increased to 7.60% from 7.40% Wednesday. 

 The dollar traded in a wide range between 2.5025 ringgit and 2.5215 ringgit during the day.

title: Malaysia Ringgit Higher Early; Dlr-Majors Dominating
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (AP-Dow Jones)--The Malaysian ringgit was higher against the U.S. dollar in early trading Thursday, mainly on the back of the U.S. currency's falls against the yen. 

 Around 0350 GMT (11:50 p.m. EDT), the dollar was at 2.5177 ringgit, down from 2.5245 ringgit late Wednesday and 2.5225 ringgit early Wednesday. 

 A locally-based dealer said the dollar had weakened against the yen, largely because figures from the U.S. Wednesday showed that inflation wasn't rising. This made players feel interest rates won't be raised when the Federal Open Market Committee meets on May 20. If it appeared interest rates would rise, investors would tend to buy dollars to capitalize on the higher yield. 

 Dealers note that as the ringgit is closely linked to the majors, when the U.S. dollar appreciates or depreciates against the majors, it usually follows the same pattern against the ringgit. 

 A locally-based dealer said trading so far had been 'dollar/yen dominated,' noting that it had helped the ringgit recover from Wednesday's weakening. 

 Locally-based dealers, as well as those in Singapore and Hong Kong, widely believed that Malaysia's central bank intervened Wednesday at around the 2.5248-ringgit level, by selling dollars and buying the local currency, to stop the dollar from strengthening above the 2.5250-ringgit level. 

 A dealer based in Hong Kong said the ringgit had weakened Wednesday, after a 'crisis situation' hit the Thai baht, on rumors of a possible devaluation. The weakening of the baht had a spillover effect as investors pulled out of regional currencies. 

 Most dealers said they didn't think the problems surrounding the Thai baht would have too much of an effect on the ringgit Thursday because the dollar is down so much against the yen and, therefore, trading in those currencies is dominating the Asian scene. 

 The locally-based dealer said he thought the dollar could weaken further to around the 2.5150-ringgit level in later Thursday trading. The dollar has traded between 2.5165 ringgit and 2.5215 ringgit so far this morning.

title: Ringgit recovers but market remains jittery.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, May 15 (Reuter) - The ringgit recovered in early Asian trading on profit-taking of dollar/ringgit positions after heavy selling of the Malaysian unit on Wednesday, dealers said. 

 "The market looks a bit squarish at the moment, maybe people don't know what to do," said a European bank dealer in Kuala Lumpur. "Dollar/ringgit came down quite fast this morning but I expect some buying on dips." 

 Dealers said demand for the dollar from offshore centres would continue to weigh on the ringgit. 

 But worries about further intervention by Bank Negara Malaysia was limiting activity, they said. 

 Dealers said the central bank intervened strongly at 2.5250 late on Wednesday to stem the dollar's rise. A dealer with a European bank in Singapore said as high as $700 million could have been sold. 

 The Malaysian unit came under heavy selling from foreign funds on Wednesday as weakness in the Thai baht, due to rising concerns about the slowing Thai economy and rumours of political turmoil within that country's cabinet, spilled over to regional currencies including the ringgit. 

 Dealers said softer dollar/majors also helped the ringgit's recovery. 

 At 0200 GMT, ringgit was at 2.5155/65 a dollar against 2.5240/50 at close of Kuala Lumpur on Wednesday. It had fallen to as low as 2.5260, its lowest level since January 3.

title: Malaysia Ringgit/Late -2: 'Spillover Effect': Dealer
text:
Dealers said there had been a 'spillover effect' Wednesday, with
players buying dollars following market rumors of a possible
devaluation of the Thai baht.



A Singapore-based dealer said although the rumored devaluation didn't
directly involve the ringgit, players had reacted by selling ringgit,
and other currencies, such as the Indonesian rupiah, and buying U.S.
dollars.


 Dealers said players had bought the U.S. currency, and to a lesser extent the Singapore dollar, because they are regarded as 'safe haven' currencies. 

 A dealer from a local bank, said the fact investors continued Wednesday to desert Malaysia's stock market also meant there was little buying interest in the ringgit. 

 'Everyone is running away from our market,' said the dealer. The Composite Index of 100 blue-chip stocks closed Wednesday, down 12.06 points, at 1072.49 points. 

 Ringgit dealers were divided as to whether Malaysia's central bank may have intervened to stop the local currency weakening further late Wednesday. 

 Some dealers said they thought Bank Negara may have intervened by selling some dollars at around the 2.5248 ringgit level, to stop the local currency falling below the 2.5250 ringgit 'psychological level.' 

 But a locally-based dealer said he didn't think the central bank came in, because the 'issue Wednesday was Thailand not Malaysia.' 

 The dealer from the local bank said that while Bank Negara may have 'tested the level around 2.5248,' he didn't think it involved much dollar selling, because there had been so much dollar buying throughout Wednesday trading. 

 Bank Negara didn't openly intervene Wednesday, and doesn't comment on rumors of such intervention. 

 Dealers said the dollar could start Thursday trading, at the 2.5230 ringgit level if some players sell dollars in later overseas trading to capitalize on its gains. 

 In the money market, at the late morning fixing, the one-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rates (Klibor) were at 7.30%, unchanged from Tuesday. The three-month Klibor were at also unchanged at 7.36%, while the six-month Klibor remained the same as Tuesday's figure of 7.40% 

 The overnight rate, which indicates short-term liquidity conditions, closed at 7.6%, up from 6.0% Tuesday.

title: Malaysia  Ringgit/Early -2:Rumors Of Bank Negara  Intervention
text:
The dollar has traded between 2.5092 ringgit and 2.5121 ringgit so far this morning. But overnight the dollar was trading at the 2.5137-ringgit level. 

 It had come off that level, dealers said, because someone - believed to be Bank Negara Malaysia - was selling just enough dollars and buying ringgit. That selling was keeping the dollar from moving much beyond its current trading level. 

 'Somebody is selling up there,' the Singapore-based dealer said. 'Rumors are it's Negara, but we haven't really seen its name.' 

 A second ringgit dealer, this one in Kuala Lumpur, said he was confident the central bank had intervened to buy ringgit with dollars at the 2.5120-ringgit and 2.5125-ringgit levels. That would strengthen the Malaysian currency and push the dollar lower. 

 'We can be fairly sure it's Negara,' the dealer said. 'They were there.' 

 The central bank doesn't comment on such rumors. 

 If the rumors are true, this would confirm suspicions last week that the central bank preferred a strong ringgit. Dealers said then that Bank Negara had intervened to stop the ringgit's recent depreciation against the dollar, buying dollars between 2.5110 ringgit and 2.5120 ringgit. 

 In the money market Wednesday, Bank Negara didn't officially intervene. At the late-morning fixing, the one-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rates were at 7.39%, up from 7.31% Tuesday. The three-month Klibor were at 7.40%, up from 7.37%. The six-month Klibor were at 7.42%, up from 7.39%.
